SYNTH-0002♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donna Lewis♔♔♔♔♔♔Dear Deputy Secretary and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology,⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF IRREVERSIBILITY AND DEMOCRATIC AUTHORIZATION⏎⏎My client Ruthie is eighty-three years old, lives alone past Greenbrier, Arkansas, on a fixed income, and has congestive heart failure. I have been her home health aide for going on four years now. The discharge instructions from her cardiologist after her second near-hospitalization were written at what I would estimate was a fourteenth-grade reading level, and I say that as someone with thirty years in this work who had to read them twice myself. So I want to be clear that I am not writing as someone who believes AI has nothing to offer. I certainly agree with the compelling arguments made in Eric Topol's 2019 Nature Medicine article about how algorithms and doctors can work together to provide better tool-level assistance. What I dispute is the framing of this RFI itself. The HHS Office of the National Coordinator's 2024 request, published in the Federal Register, describes regulatory uncertainty as something that "impedes AI innovation" — and that framing tells me everything about the posture behind this process. It is an acceleration agenda, not a stewardship agenda. Those are different things, and the difference matters more than HHS appears to have considered. Once AI systems are woven into clinical infrastructure at scale, the institutional knowledge required to function without them atrophies. Emre Coiera and colleagues noted in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2018 that post-deployment evaluation of AI in clinical settings is structurally underfunded, which means that harms accumulate without triggering removal. Ziad Obermeyer's 2019 Science paper regarding algorithmic prejudice within an incredibly common care management program provides the clearest example I know of this: documented harm, published in one of the most-read scientific journals in the world, did not result in rapid system removal. That is what irreversibility looks like in practice. And Leemore Dafny and Thomas Lee's work in the New England Journal of Medicine on healthcare consolidation offers an instructive parallel — path dependencies created by market embedding become practically irreversible even when the original rationale weakens.⏎⏎ON PROPRIETARY OPACITY AND THE LIMITS OF DEMOCRATIC CORRECTION⏎⏎The second problem is that the systems HHS proposes to accelerate into clinical infrastructure are, by design, resistant to the transparency that democratic oversight requires. Frank Pasquale's argument in The Black Box Society, and the related analysis by Andrew Selbst and Solon Barocas in the Fordham Law Review in 2018, establish that proprietary algorithmic systems are not incidentally opaque — they are structurally designed to resist the kind of auditing that public accountability demands. A society has the legitimate right to decide that medicine should remain stubbornly human even at some cost to efficiency. HHS does not have a democratic mandate to preempt that judgment by treating government oversight like a roadblock to be cleared. SYNTH-0004♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Rebecca Allen♔National Organization for Rare Disorders♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL ORGANIZATION FOR RARE DISORDERS⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by Rebecca Allen, Executive Director⏎Docket Reference: HHS AI-Clinical Care RFI, 2024⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD) submits these comments with specific reference to the structural equity gap embedded in HHS's current accelerationist posture toward clinical AI adoption. Our member community — patients navigating rare disease diagnoses, many of whom reside in rural states including Vermont, Montana, and rural Appalachia where specialist access is severely constrained — has direct, documented experience with both the promise and the distributional harm of algorithmic clinical tools. Our 2024 Policy Summit, drawing clinicians, researchers, and patients representing 38 states, produced consistent feedback that fragmented reimbursement pathways and the absence of validated equity standards are the two most consequential barriers to responsible AI deployment. NORD does not oppose AI acceleration in principle. What NORD opposes — and what these comments address directly — is the HHS posture of accelerating deployment without first making reimbursement eligibility contingent upon required bias assessments prior to rollout, post-deployment fairness surveillance, and disaggregated performance reporting. The RFI contains no such requirements. Leaving these out represents an intentional regulatory decision, bringing predictable distributional consequences that our member community is not in a position to absorb.⏎⏎REGULATORY AND REIMBURSEMENT FRAMEWORKS: THE STRUCTURAL GAP⏎⏎The peer-reviewed record on algorithmic harm in clinical settings is no longer a matter of theoretical concern. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453) showed how a broad-scale population management tool consistently undervalued the clinical requirements of Black individuals by utilizing medical spending to estimate medical necessity — an estimation method embedding long-standing discriminatory access patterns directly into the model's predictions. Sjoding et al. (N Engl J Med, 2020;383(25):2477-2478) documented how blood oxygen sensors — tools already embedded in clinical practice at massive scale — produced systematically elevated numbers for individuals possessing deeper complexions, masking hypoxemia and delaying intervention. Wong et al. (JAMA Intern Med, 2021;181(8):1065-1070) demonstrated how a commercial infection forecasting system validated at one academic medical center performed substantially worse when externally validated across community hospitals — precisely the setting where patients with fewer resources and fewer care options are concentrated. Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatol, 2018;154(11):1247-1248) identified significant underrepresentation of darker skin tones in dermatology AI training datasets, producing tools that perform well for the populations already best served by dermatology and poorly for those already most underserved. Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (Nat Med, 2021;27(12):2176-2182) extended this finding to chest radiograph interpretation, showing that AI algorithms demonstrated systematic underdiagnosis bias in under-served patient populations across multiple disease categories.⏎⏎NORD submits that this pattern — algorithmic performance degradation at the precise intersection of deployment context and patient vulnerability — is not incidental. It is structural. As Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Intern Med, 2018;178(11):1544-1547) documented, the digitized patient histories upon which most clinical AI programs learn reflects not the underlying distribution of disease burden in the population but the distribution of healthcare access, coding practices, and institutional resources — variables that are themselves products of historical inequity. When machine learning programs built upon this information are deployed at community hospitals, remote clinical outposts, and clinics serving uninsured populations, performance degradation is not a bug. It is the predictable output of a validation methodology that never tested for it. Vyas et al. (N Engl J Med, 2020;383(9):874-882) made the analogous argument about race correction in clinical algorithms: embedding race as a variable in tools like the eGFR calculator encodes historical measurement bias into future clinical decisions. Furthermore, the perceived infallibility of computer-generated output — what the literature terms automation bias — makes these embedded disparities far more difficult to notice and fix than equivalent errors made by individual clinicians.⏎⏎The HHS RFI does not address any of this. The ONC's 2023 Draft Transparency and Accountability for Health AI framework gestures toward disaggregated reporting but contains no enforcement mechanism and no reimbursement linkage. The GAO's 2022 report (GAO-22-104629) explicitly pointed to the lack of uniform fairness validation mandates as a gap in federal AI oversight. The RFI's silence on compulsory fairness evaluations prior to rollout, on disaggregated performance reporting under 45 CFR Part 170, and on post-deployment adverse-outcome surveillance tied to CMS conditions of participation is not a drafting oversight. Institutional decision-makers — CMOs, CIOs, revenue cycle administrators — operate within incentive structures that reward speed-to-deployment and cost reduction. Without equity auditing requirements embedded in regulatory and payment frameworks, those decision-makers face no structural pressure to prioritize equity validation before going live. Char et al. (N Engl J Med, 2018;378(11):981-983) identified this institutional dynamic explicitly, noting that the organizations deploying machine learning tools in healthcare are not the organizations bearing the costs when these applications malfunction in underserved settings.⏎⏎NORD therefore calls on HHS to condition any reimbursement eligibility for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools on demonstrated, independently verified equity performance across ethnic background, socioeconomic level, location, and disability status — not as a future aspiration but as a pre-deployment requirement. Wiens et al. (Nat Med, 2019;25(9):1337-1340) outlined a responsible machine learning roadmap for healthcare that included prospective bias assessment as a non-negotiable step; HHS has the regulatory authority to make that step mandatory rather than aspirational. Pierson et al. (Nat Med, 2021;27(1):136-140) showed that algorithmic approaches can actually reduce unexplained pain disparities when designed with equity as a primary objective — which means the technical capacity exists. What is missing is the regulatory requirement to use it.⏎⏎See Appendix A (submitted separately): NORD 2024 Policy Summit Summary and Member Survey Data on AI Diagnostic Delay.⏎⏎www.rarediseases.org/hhs-ai-comments-2024⏎policy@rarediseases.org⏎⏎NORD Comments | HHS AI-Clinical Care RFI | Page 2♔♔2026-02-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔urgent♔Vermont♔executive director♔30♔A 2024 National Multiple Sclerosis Society survey of 2,800 people living with MS found that 67% reported delays of six months or longer in receiving a confirmed diagnosis, with neurologist shortages cited as the primary barrier in rural and underserved communities. SYNTH-0005♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Moore♔♔♔♔♔♔Thomas Moore⏎⏎Casper, Wyoming 82601⏎⏎⏎⏎June 12, 2025⏎⏎⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎⏎THE PROBLEM WITH ACCELERATING INTO A BROKEN SYSTEM⏎⏎⏎⏎My brother Dale spent eleven days in a Casper hospital in March 2023 following a cardiac event. In that time, I watched three separate nursing staff manually transcribe the same medication list into three different computer systems that did not communicate with each other. The process was not merely inefficient. It was dangerous. One transcription dropped his beta-blocker entirely. I caught it myself, standing at the bedside, reading over a nurse's shoulder, because I had learned by that point in four years of caregiving that the chart in front of a clinician and the clinical reality of the patient in the bed are not always the same document. The ONC's own Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024-2030 acknowledges that interoperability gaps of precisely this kind remain widespread across American health systems, with significant portions of care settings still unable to share structured data reliably. We have not solved the scotch-tape problem. HHS is now proposing to wallpaper over it with machine learning.⏎⏎⏎⏎I want to be precise about what I am objecting to, because this is not a general complaint about technology in medicine. I am objecting to the specific framing of this RFI, which treats AI adoption as a productivity and efficiency problem to be accelerated. That framing is a philosophical category error, and I do not think it can be corrected at the margins. The questions HHS is asking — how to reduce regulatory friction, how to expand reimbursement pathways, how to speed deployment — are the wrong questions when the prior questions about safety, equity, and preserved human responsibility have not been answered. What follows are my comments on two aspects of this RFI that concern me most directly.⏎⏎⏎⏎ON THE THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP AS A CLINICAL INSTRUMENT⏎⏎⏎⏎The relationship between a clinician and a frightened patient is not a soft amenity that can be stripped away in the interest of throughput. It is a clinical instrument with measurable outcomes. An extensive 2014 PLOS ONE study by Kelley and her research team proved that the interpersonal connection between doctors and those they treat produces measurable improvements in physical recovery for many different illnesses, completely separate from the mechanical precision of the treatments provided. Epstein and Street, writing in the Annals of Family Medicine in 2011, made the case that prioritizing the individual's personal experience is not simply a values preference but a mechanism through which diagnoses are actually made — through the disclosure of information that patients only share with clinicians they trust, through the interpretation of ambiguity that requires reading what is not being said.⏎⏎⏎⏎Consider what that means in practice:⏎⏎⏎⏎o A patient who cannot describe where it hurts, but whose face tells the nurse something the patient will not say out loud.⏎⏎⏎⏎o A family member standing in the doorway whose expression communicates a trajectory of decline that no vital sign has yet captured.⏎⏎⏎⏎o A clinician who knows, before the chart does, that something has changed — because she has seen this patient three times this week and the baseline is in her head, not in the electronic record.⏎⏎⏎⏎These are not rare exceptions. They form the everyday fabric of medical practice. AI intermediation does not merely fail to replicate these functions. It actively damages the conditions that make them possible, by redirecting the clinician's attention toward a screen and away from the person, by substituting pattern-matched output for the interpretive attention that the encounter demands. This happens regardless of whether the AI's output is technically accurate. The damage is relational and perceptual, not informational, and an RFI framed around accuracy metrics and productivity gains will never capture it.⏎⏎⏎⏎ON DESKILLING AND THE SLOW-MOTION HARM HHS IS NOT MEASURING⏎⏎⏎⏎The acceleration framing in this RFI concerns me for a second reason that I think is underappreciated in the policy literature, though it is not absent from the clinical literature. Skinner and Weiss, writing in the Journal of Medical Ethics in 2021, drew on lessons from aviation and radiology to argue that when skilled practitioners become overseers of automated systems rather than primary reasoners, they lose the independent cognitive capacity that made them skilled in the first place. The aviation parallel is imperfect but the direction is right: pilots who rely on autopilot in routine conditions perform worse when autopilot fails. Radiologists who defer to AI-assisted reads show measurable increases in what a 2012 JAMIA research paper by Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt called automation bias — meaning people blindly trust computer generated answers, despite those answers being incorrect.⏎⏎⏎⏎Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on judgment under uncertainty, published in Science in 1974, established that human cognition is not degraded by cognitive offloading in a vacuum. The degradation is contextual and cumulative. A clinician who spends five years deferring to an algorithmic recommendation system for differential diagnosis is not the same clinician she was at the start of those five years. She has been practicing oversight, not reasoning. The skills are not the same. And when the software makes an error — when it encounters a patient whose presentation does not match the training distribution, when the alert fires on the wrong patient, when the recommendation is confidently wrong — the clinician who has been deskilled is precisely the clinician you need most.⏎⏎⏎⏎Eric Topol, in his frequently cited 2019 paper in Nature Medicine, argued that AI and human intelligence would converge in ways that free clinicians for deeper relational work. I find this argument genuinely interesting, and I do not think Topol is careless. But I think the convergence he describes assumes a deployment environment with functional infrastructure, thoughtful governance, and deliberate attention to the conditions under which human skills are preserved. The deployment environment HHS is proposing to accelerate into is not that environment. It is an environment where, as I watched firsthand in a Casper hospital, the same medication list gets transcribed three times by hand because the systems do not talk to each other. Accelerating AI adoption into that environment does not free clinicians for deeper relational work. It adds another layer of complexity onto a system already held together by the individual vigilance of exhausted nurses.⏎⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD DO INSTEAD⏎⏎⏎⏎My direct request is this: reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and rewrite the inquiry around a precautionary standard. Before any reimbursement pathway is expanded or regulatory friction reduced to speed AI deployment in clinical settings, HHS should require demonstrated answers to the following:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. What is the evidence of safety in the specific deployment context, not in controlled trial conditions, but in the actual care environment where the tool will be used, with the actual patient population it will encounter?⏎⏎⏎⏎2. What mechanisms preserve the clinician's independent reasoning capacity, such that deskilling does not occur as a function of routine use?⏎⏎⏎⏎3. What evidence exists that the human connection during treatment avoids being harmed by the AI's presence in the encounter, and how is that evidence collected?⏎⏎⏎⏎4. What equity analysis has been conducted on the training data and on the likely differential performance of the system across race, language, financial coverage, and zip code?⏎⏎⏎⏎5. Who bears legal and ethical responsibility when the system is wrong, and is that responsibility structure enforceable in the actual institutional context?⏎⏎⏎⏎These are not novel questions. They are the questions any responsible deployment framework would begin with. The fact that this RFI does not begin with them is itself a signal about the philosophical orientation of the exercise.⏎⏎⏎⏎I am one caregiver from Wyoming. I do not have a medical degree. What I have is four years of standing at bedsides and learning, slowly and sometimes at significant cost, that the gap between what the documentation says and what is actually happening to a patient is a gap that human beings close through relationship, attention, and independent reasoning. Those capacities are not infinitely renewable. They are built through practice and eroded through disuse. Any government rulebook accepting their erosion as a fair trade for efficiency gains has misunderstood what medicine is for, and I think HHS should hear that from someone who learned it the hard way before deciding how fast to move.⏎⏎⏎⏎Sincerely,⏎⏎⏎⏎Thomas Moore⏎⏎Casper, Wyoming♔♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔angry♔Wyoming♔caregiver♔59♔My brother Dale spent eleven days in a Casper hospital following a cardiac event, and in that time I watched three separate nursing staff manually transcribe the same medication list into three different computer systems because none of them communicated with each other — a process so absurd and error-prone that one transcription actually dropped his beta-blocker entirely until I caught it myself. SYNTH-0006♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Robert Lewis♔♔♔♔♔♔My cardiologist at NYU Langone mentioned it almost in passing during a routine follow-up recently. The imaging software flagging my stress test results for review had changed twice in eighteen months, and each time her team had to re-learn documentation workflows and recalibrate their clinical instincts around what the algorithm was and wasn't catching. She said it without complaint, the way you say something that has simply become a feature of the job: the technology moves faster than any framework governing how she's supposed to trust it. I run a twelve-person payroll services firm. I know exactly what it costs, in time, money, and quiet compounding error, when your tools outpace your protocols.⏎⏎⏎⏎That conversation is why I'm filing this comment. I want to talk about something specific, not about AI adoption generally, but about the gap between average performance and tail-risk performance in clinical AI systems, because that gap is where the liability accumulates, and right now there is no systematic requirement that vendors or deploying institutions account for it before a tool goes into clinical use.⏎⏎⏎⏎AVERAGE PERFORMANCE IS THE WRONG STANDARD⏎⏎⏎⏎The reimbursement and deployment incentive structures HHS is considering appear to be oriented around whether a tool works, meaning whether it performs acceptably in aggregate across a validation dataset. That framing is understandable but operationally insufficient. In any risk-sensitive business, the question isn't whether a process works on average. The question is where it fails, how badly, and for whom. A payroll system that processes 98% of checks correctly but systematically misclassifies a specific category of employee is not a 98% accurate system. It's a system with a structural defect that will generate concentrated harm and, eventually, legal exposure.⏎⏎⏎⏎The clinical AI literature has documented exactly this pattern across multiple domains. Research led by Obermeyer in 2019 showed that a popular corporate tool designed to manage community wellness consistently downplayed how sick Black patients actually were, not because it was poorly designed in aggregate, but because the proxy variable it used (prior healthcare costs) reflected differential access to care rather than differential health need (Science, 366(6464), 447-453). This prejudice didn't show up at all in the top-line performance metrics. In 2020, Sjoding's team discovered that pulse oximeters, which are not AI but are a computational tool embedded in clinical workflow in ways that anticipate AI integration, overestimated arterial oxygen saturation in Black patients at rates that went largely undetected in standard accuracy reporting (New England Journal of Medicine, 383(25), 2477-2478). Daneshjou and colleagues showed in 2022 that dermatology AI models performed significantly worse on images of darker skin tones, and that this disparity persisted across a diverse, curated clinical image set specifically assembled to test it (Science Advances, 8(31), eabq6147).⏎⏎⏎⏎What these findings share is not that the tools were bad. They performed within acceptable ranges by conventional metrics. The problem is that conventional metrics average across subgroups rather than disaggregating by them, which means the harm concentrates in populations that are already clinically underserved and the signal never surfaces in the aggregate reporting that regulators and payers rely on.⏎⏎⏎⏎THE VALIDATION GEOGRAPHY PROBLEM⏎⏎⏎⏎There is a related issue that I want to flag specifically because I haven't seen it addressed in the framing of this RFI. Kaushal, Altman, and Langlotz shared a 2020 analysis in JAMA showing that the regional makeup of patient groups utilized to build foundational deep learning algorithms for medical imaging was heavily concentrated in a small number of university research hospitals, most of them in the Northeast and on the West Coast, and that this concentration has downstream effects on how those models generalize to patient populations in other regions (JAMA, 324(12), 1212-1213). A tool validated at NYU Langone or UCSF may perform meaningfully differently at a rural hospital in upstate New York or at a government-funded community clinic in Mississippi. The performance gap isn't random noise. This is an expected result of building models on non-representative data, and it will show up as worse outcomes in the populations and geographies least likely to generate the kind of adverse event reporting that triggers regulatory attention.⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department of Health and Human Services has a clear opening here to require that validation datasets for any AI tool seeking reimbursement eligibility or deployment endorsement include demographic and geographic disaggregation sufficient to detect subgroup-level performance variance. That's a concrete, implementable standard. It does not require resolving deep philosophical questions about algorithmic fairness. It requires the same kind of stratified reporting that clinical trial regulations have required for years in other contexts.⏎⏎⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM AND WHY IT COMPOUNDS THE ABOVE⏎⏎⏎⏎There is an additional, cascading risk that I want to name, because it interacts with the validation problem in ways that make the tail risk worse than it would be otherwise. Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt released a comprehensive 2012 study documenting the frequency and conditions of automation bias, defined as the inclination of people making decisions to lean too heavily on computer-generated suggestions even when those recommendations are incorrect (Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 121-127). Their research concluded that this over-reliance on machines does not primarily stem from individual carelessness or inexperience. It's a function of workflow design, cognitive load, and the degree to which the human operator has independent access to the information needed to override the system. When clinical AI tools are deployed in high-volume, time-pressured environments, the conditions for automation bias are essentially guaranteed.⏎⏎⏎⏎The real-world implication is that when a model underperforms for a specific subgroup, the clinician is less likely to catch it, not more, because the presence of an algorithmic recommendation shifts the cognitive burden in ways that reduce independent verification. Wong's research team proved this point in 2021. They independently tested a popular, privately-owned algorithmic tool for identifying sepsis, discovering that its real-world accuracy fell far short of the manufacturer's own claims, with major discrepancies in how well it worked for different demographics (JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065-1070). The model was in clinical use at multiple institutions before that external validation was published. That's the sequence that concerns me: deployment first, independent validation later, with the gap between them absorbed by patients.⏎⏎⏎⏎I want to be honest that I'm not entirely sure what the right regulatory mechanism is here. Mandatory pre-deployment external validation is one option but it has real costs and could slow beneficial adoption in ways that also cause harm. What I'm more confident about is that the current incentive structure, where vendors self-report performance metrics and institutions adopt based on those reports without systematic independent verification, is not adequate to the risk. Without required fairness checks, disparate harm will accumulate as an undetected liability, and by the time it surfaces in outcomes data, the tool will be embedded in workflows in ways that make it very hard to remove.⏎⏎⏎⏎REGARDING RACE CORRECTION AND LEGACY ALGORITHMIC ASSUMPTIONS⏎⏎⏎⏎Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones published a 2020 analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine examining the use of race as a correction factor in clinical algorithms, and the findings are relevant here even though they predate the current AI adoption push (NEJM, 383(9), 874-882). The concern they raised is that many clinical decision support tools embed race as a biological variable in ways that are not empirically justified and that can systematically alter treatment recommendations in ways that disadvantage Black and other minority patients. As clinical AI tools are built on top of existing EHR data and existing clinical decision support logic, they risk inheriting these embedded assumptions, laundering them through a more sophisticated modeling layer that makes them more difficult to spot and dispute.⏎⏎⏎⏎HHS should require that any clinical AI tool seeking reimbursement eligibility include explicit documentation of whether race, ethnicity, or other demographic proxies are used as input variables, how they are used, and what the empirical justification is for that use. This is a disclosure requirement, not a prohibition. It allows clinicians, institutions, and regulators to make informed decisions about deployment rather than discovering the embedded assumptions after the fact.⏎⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎⏎⏎To be direct about what I'm asking for:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. Demonstrated equity outcomes for specific demographic brackets, not just aggregate performance metrics, should be a prerequisite for any clinical AI tool to be eligible for reimbursement or deployment endorsement under HHS programs. These specific categories must cover at least racial background, ethnic origin, gender, generational cohort, and geographic region, with sample sizes sufficient to generate reliable estimates.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. Validation datasets should be required to include documentation of their geographic and demographic composition, and tools trained primarily on information sourced from university research hospitals in high-resource regions should be required to demonstrate performance in lower-resource settings before being deployed there.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. Post-deployment monitoring requirements should include mandatory subgroup-level performance reporting at defined intervals, with a mechanism for that data to be accessible to regulators and, in aggregate, to the public. Right now, once a tool is deployed, the performance data largely disappears into institutional quality improvement processes that are not systematically reviewed.⏎⏎⏎⏎4. Any tool that uses race, ethnicity, or demographic proxies as input variables should be required to disclose that use explicitly in documentation provided to deploying institutions and, where feasible, to patients.⏎⏎⏎⏎None of these requirements prohibit innovation or slow beneficial adoption in ways that couldn't be addressed through reasonable implementation timelines. They are the kind of operational accountability standards that any serious vendor should be able to meet if their tools actually perform as claimed.⏎⏎⏎⏎My cardiologist's observation has stayed with me because she wasn't complaining, she was just describing the situation accurately: the framework for trusting these tools hasn't kept pace with the tools themselves. The imaging software changed twice in eighteen months at one of the better-resourced hospital systems in the country, and the governance around what that change meant for clinical judgment hadn't changed at all. That's not a technology problem. That's an accountability structure problem, and it's precisely the sort of issue that accumulates quietly until it doesn't.⏎⏎⏎⏎There is one final thought that remains stuck in my mind, and I'll admit this is somewhat tangential to the main point: I received a $3,200 bill after an ER visit that was supposed to be in-network, and while I understand that's not what this RFI is specifically about, it does shape how I think about what "accelerating adoption" means in practice. The reimbursement and billing infrastructure that surrounds clinical care is already opaque in ways that cause real harm to patients and small employers trying to manage health costs. Layering AI into that infrastructure without first requiring that it be auditable and accountable to the populations it serves is, from where I sit, the wrong sequence.♔♔2026-02-27T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-27T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔New York♔small business owner♔57♔My cardiologist at NYU Langone mentioned, almost in passing during a routine follow-up, that the imaging software flagging my stress test results for review had changed twice in eighteen months — each time requiring her team to re-learn documentation workflows and recalibrate their own clinical instincts around what the algorithm was and wasn't catching. SYNTH-0007♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Edward Williams♔Georgetown University Medical Center♔♔♔♔♔Georgetown University Medical Center⏎Department of Bioethics and Health Law⏎4000 Reservoir Road, N.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20057⏎⏎October 14, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care (Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001)⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center respectfully submits the following comment in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. This submission focuses on the RFI's treatment of governance frameworks and liability infrastructure, as those questions bear most directly on the institutional and legal concerns this submission is designed to raise. The Department has invited broad input; having reviewed the docket materials, this comment will not attempt breadth. It will attempt precision on what we regard as the most consequential structural defect in the RFI's underlying policy posture.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE CHIME FINDING AS A WARNING, NOT AN INVITATION⏎⏎The 2024 CHIME Health IT Leadership Survey — drawing on responses from 610 health IT executives and presented at CHIME's Fall Forum before being submitted to HHS as part of ongoing federal affairs engagement — found that 68% of respondents identified regulatory ambiguity around AI liability and clinical validation requirements as the primary barrier to deploying AI-assisted decision support tools at scale. Only 23% reported that their organizations had established formal governance frameworks for AI oversight. The Department appears to read these numbers as a call to action: clear the ambiguity, reduce the friction, and deployment will follow. Georgetown Medical Center reads them differently. When two-thirds of health system leadership identify liability ambiguity as the barrier and fewer than one in four institutions have even attempted internal governance structures, the correct inference is not that the regulatory environment is too slow. The correct inference is that the field does not yet know where the ultimate liability falls in the event of an adverse outcome, and that the field knows it does not know.⏎⏎This is not a bureaucratic gap that certification mechanisms can paper over. This constitutes an architectural defect which the RFI's accelerationist framing treats as peripheral when it is, in fact, foundational. The CHIME survey also documented that fragmented federal guidance — spanning CMS reimbursement policy, FDA software-as-a-medical-device classifications, and ONC interoperability standards — extends procurement cycles by an average of 14 months. The Department seems to want to compress that timeline. Before doing so, it should ask whether the 14-month delay reflects bureaucratic dysfunction or whether some portion of it reflects institutions doing the hard, slow work of figuring out whether they can actually be accountable for what they are about to deploy.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE LIABILITY VACUUM AND ITS DOCTRINAL DIMENSIONS⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center⏎⏎The doctrinal problem is not hypothetical. When an AI system intermediates a clinical decision — a risk stratification algorithm flags a patient as low-acuity, a sepsis prediction model fails to trigger an alert, a diagnostic support tool returns a probability score that the clinician misinterprets — existing legal frameworks distribute responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that allow each party to credibly deflect to the others. Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified this problem with precision in their 2019 JAMA analysis, noting that the reasonable physician standard, which anchors medical malpractice doctrine, was designed for a world in which physicians make unaided judgments and cannot coherently assign liability when the judgment is co-produced by an opaque algorithmic system. The learned intermediary doctrine, which might nominally assign responsibility to the clinician who uses the tool, presupposes that the clinician has sufficient information about the tool's limitations to exercise genuine informed discretion — a presupposition that routinely proves false in practice, a reality highlighted by Sendak et al. within their 2020 FAT* proceedings paper concerning deep learning and automated care selections (Sendak et al., 2020, p. ). Clinicians frequently do not know what the model is optimizing for, what training data shaped its outputs, or under what patient populations it has been validated.⏎⏎The FDA's software-as-a-medical-device classification framework adds another layer of ambiguity. The agency's enforcement discretion policies and the iterative refinements to its Digital Health Center of Excellence guidance have produced a landscape in which many AI clinical decision support tools occupy a regulatory gray zone — not clearly a device subject to premarket review, not clearly excluded, and therefore not clearly subject to any manufacturer-side accountability obligation. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen's 2020 Academic Press chapter covering the statutory and moral hurdles present in AI-driven healthcare documented this gray zone in detail and concluded that existing regulatory categories are structurally inadequate to the task. The ONC's Draft Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024–2030 acknowledges interoperability and transparency goals but does not resolve the underlying question of who bears non-delegable responsibility for an AI-assisted clinical decision that produces patient harm.⏎⏎The result is what this comment will call organized irresponsibility: a system in which accountability is not merely diffuse but is architecturally designed to remain diffuse because no single actor — not the developer, not the hospital, not the clinician — has accepted or been assigned final, non-delegable responsibility for the decision. Cohen's team flagged a version of this concern as early as 2014 in their Health Affairs analysis covering sophisticated forecasting algorithms applied to healthcare, arguing that the legal and ethical frameworks governing clinical responsibility remained vastly outstripped by the distributional logic of algorithmic tools. That was ten years ago. The gap has widened, not closed.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center Comments < > HHS AI RFI 2024 < > Page 3⏎⏎Obermeyer and Emanuel's 2016 New England Journal of Medicine analysis covering automated pattern recognition applications for clinical medicine noted that these systems can perform with impressive aggregate accuracy while failing systematically on subpopulations — a finding that Char, Shah, and Magnus extended in their 2018 NEJM piece on ethical challenges in machine learning implementation, where they argued that deployment without robust bias auditing and accountability structures amounts to a transfer of clinical risk to patients who have not consented to serve as validation populations. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert's 2020 JAMA review of malpractice liability and healthcare quality demonstrated that liability structures, when properly designed, function as accountability mechanisms that incentivize safety investment. The current AI deployment environment, by contrast, provides liability-avoidance incentives: vendors structure contracts to limit indemnification, hospitals invoke clinical judgment defenses, and clinicians point to institutional protocol. The patient, meanwhile, has no named human being who is legally and institutionally answerable for their care.⏎⏎Pasquale, in his 2020 Harvard University Press volume on the new laws of robotics, argued that the appropriate regulatory response to this structure is not acceleration but a prior commitment to what he calls human oversight as a non-negotiable precondition for deployment. Doshi-Velez and co-authors, in their 2017 Berkman Klein Center working paper on AI accountability under law, similarly concluded that explainability requirements alone are insufficient — what is needed is a clear assignment of legal responsibility to an identifiable actor before deployment occurs, not as a post-hoc litigation question. Topol's 2019 Nature Medicine analysis of high-performance medicine, which is often cited by AI proponents as evidence that clinical AI is ready for broad adoption, is more cautious on this point than its boosters acknowledge: Topol explicitly conditions his optimism on the existence of robust validation and oversight structures that, as the CHIME survey data confirm, most institutions have not built.⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHAT THE RFI GETS WRONG AND WHAT HHS MUST DO INSTEAD⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center's core concern with this RFI is its sequencing. The Department proposes to accelerate adoption and simultaneously develop governance frameworks, treating the two as parallel tracks. They are not parallel tracks. The governance framework is the precondition, not the companion. Once clinical workflows embed AI dependency — once ordering patterns, staffing ratios, and documentation practices become anchored to the premise of an algorithm performing a monitoring or diagnostic function — the underlying power dynamics of accountability assignment change fundamentally. Institutions that have invested in deployment will resist liability frameworks that would require them to re-engineer those workflows. This is not speculation; it is how every prior health IT adoption cycle has proceeded.⏎⏎The Department's proposal to develop accreditation and certification mechanisms for AI tools, while not without merit, will not resolve this problem. Certification attests to performance characteristics at a point in time; it does not assign ongoing accountability for clinical decisions made using a certified tool. This specific differentiation holds immense consequence. What HHS must establish, prior to any acceleration of deployment at scale, is a binding cross-agency framework — developed jointly with FDA, CMS, and ONC — that assigns non-delegable legal responsibility to a specific institutional actor for every AI-assisted clinical decision that materially affects patient management. The framework need not resolve every downstream question about contribution and indemnification among vendors, hospitals, and clinicians. But it must identify a responsible party who cannot, by contract or by custom, transfer that responsibility to another actor when harm occurs.⏎⏎Georgetown University Medical Center recognizes that this demand is difficult to satisfy quickly and that it may slow some deployments that would otherwise produce clinical benefit. That tradeoff is real. But the moral dimension of accountability — a patient's right to know that a specific, named, answerable human institution is responsible for the care they receive — is not a legal technicality that can be deferred pending the development of case law. It is a foundational ethical commitment that the Department is currently proposing to subordinate to deployment velocity, and the institutional record of that choice will be difficult to correct once the workflows are in place.⏎⏎The Department should also be aware that the certification pathway it envisions will face significant implementation challenges if the underlying liability architecture remains unresolved. Institutions that participated in CHIME's 2024 survey consistently reported that procurement delays were driven not by uncertainty about tool performance but by uncertainty about what their legal exposure would be if the tool contributed to an adverse event. No accreditation seal addresses that question.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Edward Williams, J.D., Ph.D.⏎Associate Professor, Department of Bioethics and Health Law⏎Georgetown University Medical Center⏎edward.williams@gumc.georgetown.edu♔♔2026-01-25T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-25T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔academic_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Arizona♔associate professor♔40♔A 2024 CHIME survey of 610 health IT executives found that 68% identified regulatory ambiguity around AI liability and clinical validation requirements as the primary barrier to deploying AI-assisted decision support tools at scale, with only 23% reporting that their organizations had established formal governance frameworks for AI oversight. SYNTH-0008♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Emily Nelson♔Emory University Rollins School of Public Health♔♔♔♔♔Emory University Rollins School of Public Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Page 1⏎---⏎COMMENT OF EMILY NELSON, ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR⏎EMORY UNIVERSITY ROLLINS SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH⏎Submitted in Response to: HHS Health Sector Artificial Intelligence Request for Information —⏎Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: [HHS-2024-AI-RFI]⏎Submitted: Via regulations.gov⏎---⏎PRELIMINARY REMARKS: THE FRAMING PROBLEM⏎The RFI's organizing premise deserves careful scrutiny before any specific questions are addressed. HHS frames this solicitation around the problem of accelerating AI adoption, treating the speed of clinical integration itself as the policy challenge requiring remedy. The structural barriers named in the RFI — regulatory uncertainty, reimbursement ambiguity, implementation lag — are real, and the institutional data that informs this comment bears that out directly. A 2024 internal assessment conducted across the University of Kansas Health System's 130-plus care sites found that 68% of attending physicians and advanced practice providers reported significant uncertainty about liability boundaries when acting on AI-generated recommendations, and that 43% of those providers indicated this uncertainty directly influenced their willingness to incorporate these technologies into everyday practice. The same system's Center for Clinical and Translational Science documented, through a multi-site review spanning oncology, cardiology, and emergency medicine departments, that reimbursement ambiguity contributed to a median 14-month delay between tool validation and full clinical deployment. These are not trivial barriers and this comment does not dismiss them.⏎What this comment argues, however, is that HHS has organized its entire analytical framework around the wrong set of questions. The barriers to AI adoption that the RFI foregrounds are procurement-side and administrative in character — they concern how quickly health systems can get tools approved and paid for. Almost entirely absent from the RFI's framing is any serious attention to the workforce on whom these tools are deployed: who is consulted before procurement decisions are made, what happens to the professional autonomy of clinicians who must interact with these systems daily, how labor conditions change when AI-enabled monitoring and productivity metrics are embedded in clinical environments, and whether the empirical support backing workforce benefit claims is anywhere near adequate to support the acceleration HHS appears to be encouraging. This comment addresses those questions directly and argues that responsible acceleration is only achievable if HHS treats frontline workforce governance as an absolute prerequisite instead of an afterthought.⏎WORKFORCE EXCLUSION FROM AI PROCUREMENT AND GOVERNANCE⏎Historical data detailing how AI tools enter clinical settings is not reassuring on the question of worker participation. Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020), writing in the Academy of Management Annals, documented extensively that algorithmic management systems in professional workplaces are consistently introduced through administrative and procurement channels that systematically exclude the workers whose daily practice they will govern. Their analysis, drawing on cases across industries including healthcare, found that this exclusion is not incidental but structural: the incentive alignment between institutional administrators and technology vendors diverges sharply from the interests of frontline workers in ways that procurement processes rarely surface. In healthcare specifically, this dynamic is compounded by the professional authority relationships between hospital administration and clinical staff — physicians and nurses who raise concerns about AI tools during procurement cycles are frequently positioned as obstacles to institutional modernization rather than as expert stakeholders whose input is operationally necessary.⏎The American Nurses Association addressed this problem directly in its 2023 position statement on AI and nursing practice, calling explicitly for mandatory consultation with frontline nursing staff before any AI system affecting clinical workflow or staffing decisions is procured or deployed. The ANA's position is grounded not in technophobia but in the recognition that nurses — who constitute the largest segment of the clinical workforce and bear the most direct daily contact with AI-enabled monitoring and decision support systems — are almost never at the table when procurement decisions are made. Dillahunt-Aspillaga and colleagues (2022), writing in Health Affairs Scholar, found that algorithmic management and AI-enabled productivity surveillance in healthcare settings is associated with measurable erosion of clinical discretion, with frontline staff reporting reduced capacity to exercise contextual professional judgment when AI-generated metrics are embedded in performance evaluation frameworks. This is not an abstract concern about autonomy in the philosophical sense; it is a documented operational problem with consequences for care quality and staff retention.⏎Emory University Rollins School of Public Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Page 2⏎HHS should require, as a condition of establishing compensation mechanisms covering AI-assisted clinical tools, that health systems document a meaningful frontline worker consultation process prior to deployment. "Meaningful" should be defined in federal guidance to include at minimum: structured input from clinical staff at the unit level where the tool will be used, documentation of concerns raised and how they were addressed, and ongoing review mechanisms that give clinical staff formal standing to flag workflow or autonomy problems post-deployment. This is not a novel governance model — participatory design frameworks with roughly this structure have been implemented in Scandinavian healthcare systems for decades — but it is conspicuously absent from the U.S. regulatory environment, and HHS has both the authority and the opportunity to establish it here.⏎THE BURNOUT PROBLEM AND THE EVIDENCE GAP⏎This comment wants to be precise about something that the RFI conflates: there is a difference between AI tools that genuinely reduce the conditions driving clinician burnout and AI tools that are marketed as burnout-reduction solutions while actually serving administrative cost-cutting objectives. HHS should not accept these as equivalent categories, and current federal policy provides no mechanism for distinguishing between them.⏎Shanafelt and colleagues (2022), writing in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, documented that burnout rates among U.S. physicians increased substantially between 2011 and 2020 even as electronic health record adoption accelerated — a finding that complicates any simple narrative about digital tools improving clinician wellbeing. Moy and colleagues (2021), in a scoping review published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, found that EHR documentation burden is one of the most consistently identified drivers of clinician burnout, with physicians spending between one and two hours on documentation for every sixty minutes of face-to-face clinical contact. Wachter and Goldsmith (2018), in the Harvard Business Review, made the case that the documentation burden embedded in EHR systems was itself a product of administrative and billing requirements layered onto clinical tools, not an inevitable feature of digitization. Gawande (2018), in a well-documented New Yorker piece that drew on his own clinical experience, described the cognitive and emotional cost of documentation systems that were designed for billing compliance rather than clinical utility, and that had progressively colonized the space of physician-patient interaction.⏎Ash and colleagues (2023), reviewing mitigation strategies for alert fatigue in clinical decision support systems in Applied Clinical Informatics, found that poorly designed AI-enabled alerts increase rather than decrease cognitive burden on clinicians, and that health systems frequently deploy alert systems without the workflow analysis necessary to distinguish clinically actionable signals from noise. Bates and colleagues (2021), in an exhaustive literature synthesis featured in npj Digital Medicine, found that while AI tools have genuine potential to reduce documentation burden, evidence of actual workforce benefit in deployed systems — as opposed to controlled pilots — remains thin and methodologically inconsistent. The gap between vendor claims about AI's burnout-reduction potential and the peer-reviewed evidence base for deployed systems is substantial. HHS should not allow that gap to be papered over by accelerationist policy postures.⏎The specific concern this comment raises is that tools marketed explicitly as burnout or efficiency solutions are structurally incentivized to generate metrics that satisfy administrative purchasers rather than clinical users. A tool that reduces the time a physician spends on a given task may, in practice, increase the number of tasks that physician is expected to complete in a shift — a dynamic that Topol (2019), writing in Nature Medicine, identified as a predictable hazard of AI deployment in productivity-intensive environments. Rajpurkar, Chen, Banerjee, and Topol (2022), also in Nature Medicine, noted that AI's demonstrated clinical utility in tasks like radiology image analysis and pathology screening does not automatically translate to workforce benefit if the institutional response to efficiency gains is to increase throughput expectations rather than to reinvest capacity in quality of care.⏎AI-ENABLED SURVEILLANCE AND THE DESKILLING RISK⏎Separate from the burnout question, and deserving its own analytical frame, is the problem of AI-enabled workforce surveillance and the deskilling of roles that require contextual human judgment. My analysis specifically targets three distinct categories of clinical work where this risk is most acute: managing treatment transitions, guiding individuals through the healthcare system, and prior authorization review. These are roles that have historically been performed by experienced clinicians and social workers whose value lies precisely in their capacity to exercise discretionary judgment in complex, individualized situations. AI tools are increasingly being deployed in these domains not to support worker judgment but to replace or standardize it, with productivity monitoring systems that flag deviations from algorithmic recommendations as inefficiencies requiring correction.⏎Kellogg and colleagues (2020) describe this dynamic as "contested terrain" — a workplace in which algorithmic control systems and professional workers are in ongoing negotiation over the scope of discretionary authority, and in which the institutional power of administrators and vendors typically advantages the algorithmic system. Dillahunt-Aspillaga and colleagues (2022) found specifically in healthcare contexts that AI-enabled monitoring of case management activities was associated with⏎Emory University Rollins School of Public Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Page 3⏎reduced worker-reported autonomy and increased turnover intent among transition managers and care guides — precisely the workforce segments where attrition is already a documented problem. The connection to patient outcomes is not speculative: understaffed and demoralized case management teams produce measurable gaps in care continuity, and any national directives designed to hasten the deployment of AI systems without attending to these workforce dynamics is accepting a foreseeable harm.⏎Obermeyer and colleagues (2019), in their landmark Science paper investigating demographic discrimination within a proprietary population risk-scoring model, demonstrated that AI tools embedded in clinical workflows can encode and perpetuate systemic inequities in ways that are invisible to the clinicians using them. This finding has a workforce dimension that is rarely discussed: when clinicians are required to act on AI-generated recommendations in managed-care contexts, and when those recommendations carry implicit institutional authority, the practical space for clinical workers to exercise the kind of contextual, relationship-based judgment that would catch algorithmic error is systematically reduced. This danger is far from theoretical. It is a documented mechanism of harm.⏎POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎This comment does not argue against AI adoption in clinical settings. The potential for well-governed AI to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce unnecessary documentation burden, and support evidence-based practice is real, and the literature cited above acknowledges it. What this comment argues is that HHS cannot responsibly accelerate adoption unless the agency prioritizes creating governance conditions that make adoption safe for the workforce and, by extension, for patients. The following recommendations are offered as conditions for responsible acceleration, not as objections to the RFI's core purpose:⏎1. Obligatory engagement with clinical staff as a condition of federal reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical tools. HHS should define minimum standards for pre-deployment consultation that include structured input from clinical staff at the bedside or clinical interface, documentation of how concerns were addressed, and post-deployment review mechanisms with formal worker standing.⏎2. Independent, longitudinal workforce impact assessment as a condition of reimbursement approval. Vendor-supplied evidence of burnout reduction or efficiency benefit should not be treated as adequate proof. HHS should require independent assessment of staffing ratios, caseload changes, worker-reported autonomy, and turnover rates at defined intervals following deployment, with reimbursement conditioned on evidence of sustained workforce benefit rather than one-time pilot results.⏎3. Federal standards prohibiting AI-enabled productivity surveillance that bypasses professional governance structures or collective bargaining agreements. Where clinical workers are covered by collective bargaining, the introduction of AI-enabled monitoring systems that affect workload, scheduling, or performance evaluation should require negotiation. Where workers are not covered by collective bargaining, professional governance structures — medical staff committees, nursing practice councils — should be given formal standing in AI deployment decisions.⏎4. HHS should commission, through the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality or a comparable body, an extensive methodological evaluation covering the peer-reviewed evidence base for workforce benefit claims made by AI vendors marketing to health systems, focusing intensely on the disparity separating highly supervised pilot evidence and outcomes in routine deployment. Bates and colleagues (2021) and Ash and colleagues (2023) both identify this gap as a significant problem; federal policy should not proceed as though it does not exist.⏎One additional concern warrants mention, even if it falls slightly outside the comment's primary frame. The RFI's emphasis on reimbursement pathways as an accelerant for AI adoption raises a question about the sequencing of incentives. If reimbursement is established before workforce governance standards are in place, health systems will have strong financial incentives to deploy tools rapidly and limited regulatory pressure to consult or protect the clinical workers affected. The University of Kansas Health System data cited at the outset of this comment — particularly the finding that faculty governance processes consistently identified reimbursement ambiguity as the primary structural barrier to AI adoption — suggests that once reimbursement pathways are clarified, deployment will accelerate quickly. HHS should ensure that the workforce governance standards described above are established concurrently with, and not subsequent to, any new reimbursement frameworks, because the window for getting the governance conditions right is likely narrower than the current policy timeline assumes.⏎Correspondence regarding this comment may be directed to:⏎emily.nelson@sph.emory.edu⏎Department of Health Policy and Management⏎Emory University Rollins School of Public Health⏎1518 Clifton Road NE, Atlanta, GA 30322⏎---♔♔2026-01-18T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-18T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔academic_organization♔high♔hopeful♔Maryland♔associate professor♔31♔A 2024 internal assessment of AI-enabled clinical decision support tools deployed across The University of Kansas Health System's 130+ care sites identified that 68% of attending physicians and advanced practice providers reported significant uncertainty regarding liability boundaries when acting on AI-generated recommendations, with 43% indicating this uncertainty directly influenced their willingness to integrate such tools into routine workflows.
