SYNTH-0010♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas Perez♔American Academy of Neurology♔♔♔♔♔American Academy of Neurology — Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0001⏎Contact: Thomas Perez, Community Engagement and Policy Division, American Academy of Neurology⏎tperez@aan.com⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket HHS-OD-2024-0001 | Page 1⏎⏎Our network's data does not support the framing of this RFI, and we think it is worth saying that plainly before proceeding to anything else. During the third quarter of 2024, a policy landscape survey distributed to our 847 member clearinghouses and exchange organizations found that 64% reported receiving AI-processed claims or clinical data submissions containing systematic errors traceable to model hallucination or training-data gaps. Those errors, in aggregate, delayed reimbursement for an estimated 2.3 million patient encounters. We are not describing edge cases or isolated failures. We are describing a pattern that our affiliated entities encounter routinely, and that pattern was already well-established before this RFI was published. By inquiring about ways to hasten artificial intelligence implementation in medical settings, the Department is pursuing an entirely misguided line of questioning—or at minimum, approaching the issue backwards. The fallout from this reversed prioritization will most severely impact the very individuals least equipped to endure such disruptions.⏎⏎We want to address specifically the RFI's treatment of administrative functions — including organizing clinical pathways, guiding individuals through complex systems, reviewing coverage prerequisites, and advising on benefits — because the framing in this solicitation reflects a misunderstanding of what that work actually is. The RFI characterizes these functions as processing overhead, as friction to be reduced, as a domain where AI efficiency gains will free clinical staff for higher-order tasks. That characterization is wrong, and it is wrong in ways that matter enormously for the constituencies we represent within the state of Florida and throughout the wider United States. Administrative healthcare work is not clerical processing. It is skilled, contextual, human advocacy, and the difference between those two things is not semantic. A care coordinator who manages Medicaid-enrolled patients in Broward County does not simply route forms through a workflow. She knows which managed care plan supervisors will approve a referral if you call them directly rather than submitting through the portal. She understands how a specific household's lack of legal residency status turns a supposed assistance program into a liability—a reality absent from any standardized electronic intake form, yet obvious to her through three years of continuous relationship building. She knows, in Michael Polanyi's framing from The Tacit Dimension (1966), more than she can tell, and that surplus of knowing is not a gap in documentation practices — it is the substance of the work itself.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket HHS-OD-2024-0001 | Page 2⏎⏎Polanyi's argument that tacit knowledge — the embodied, relational, contextually specific knowledge that practitioners develop through sustained practice — defies complete verbalization and consequently resists total digital encoding is not merely a philosophical point. It has direct, operational consequences for what AI systems can and cannot do in administrative healthcare contexts. The knowledge that experienced administrative workers carry about local exceptions, bureaucratic pressure points, community resource gaps, and individual patient circumstances is built over years of institutional experience and human relationship. It is not in the training data. It cannot be scraped from claims histories or clinical notes or payer portals. When AI systems are deployed to automate the functions that depend on this knowledge, they do not replicate the knowledge at scale — they eliminate the function that the knowledge was performing, while creating the appearance of having preserved it. The errors that result are, as established by Garg, Haynes, and their co-authors during their 2005 JAMA evaluation of computerized clinical decision support systems, systematic and underdetected: they do not announce themselves as errors, they persist across cases, and they accumulate invisibly until a patient or family or advocate notices that something has gone wrong (Garg, A.X., et al., "Effects of Computerized Clinical Decision Support Systems on Practitioner Performance and Patient Outcomes," JAMA, 293(10), 2005).⏎⏎What bothers us most, and what we want HHS to sit with before moving forward, is that the tacit knowledge held by experienced administrative workers will not simply be unavailable to AI systems — it will be permanently destroyed when those workers are displaced. This is not a recoverable situation. The care coordinator in Broward County who retires or is laid off because her function has been automated does not leave behind a knowledge base that can later be retrieved. The institutional memory she carried walks out the door with her, and the patients she served are left with a system that does not know what she knew and does not know that it does not know it. We have seen this dynamic play out in other sectors, and the health sector is not different in the ways that would make it more resilient to this loss. The American Health Information Management Association's 2023 workforce readiness survey documented that administrative health information staff are already operating under severe capacity constraints, with vacancy rates in some regions exceeding 20%, and that the entities most likely to implement these automated administrative tools concurrently lack the necessary oversight frameworks capable of detecting when those systems are producing errors (AHIMA, AI Governance in Health Information Management: Workforce Readiness and Risk Assessment Survey, 2023).⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket HHS-OD-2024-0001 | Page 3⏎⏎The efficiency argument advanced in this RFI also needs to be confronted directly, because it rests on a premise that our affiliated institutions' experience does not support. The premise is that administrative functions are currently well-staffed, that human administrative workers are the bottleneck, and that AI can absorb their workload while freeing human capacity for clinical engagement. None of that is accurate. Himmelstein and colleagues documented in a 2020 New England Journal of Medicine analysis that administrative costs in the U.S. health system consume approximately 34.2% of total health expenditures — more than twice the share in Canada — and that the bulk of that spending reflects not excessive staffing but the complexity of a multi-payer system that requires extensive human labor to navigate (Himmelstein, D.U., et al., "Health Care Administrative Costs in the United States and Canada, 2017," NEJM, 382(15), 2020). Casalino and co-investigators demonstrated through a 2009 Health Affairs publication that physician practices spend, on average, 3.4 hours per physician per week interacting with health plans on prior authorization and related administrative tasks — time that is not reducible by automating the plan-facing portions of the workflow unless the automation performs correctly, which our data suggests it frequently does not (Casalino, L.P., et al., Health Affairs, 28(4), 2009). A 2016 time-motion evaluation published in the Annals of Internal Medicine by Sinsky and co-authors revealed that physicians devoted roughly double the minutes to bureaucratic and software duties compared to their face-to-face clinical encounters — and that automation tools, rather than reducing this burden, frequently generated additional documentation and correction labor (Sinsky, C.A., et al., "Allocation of Physician Work Hours in Outpatient Settings," Annals of Internal Medicine, 165(11), 2016). Donelan's research team arrived at comparable findings within their 2019 Mayo Clinic Proceedings investigation into software-linked provider exhaustion, determining that automation tools introduced to reduce administrative burden had, in many settings, increased it by generating alerts, flags, and correction queues that required human resolution (Donelan, K., et al., "Physician Burnout in the Digital Medical Chart Era," Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 94(7), 2019).⏎⏎The picture that emerges from this body of evidence is consistent and it is not the picture the RFI presents. Administrative functions are already critically understaffed. AI errors generate corrective labor — appeals, resubmissions, patient callbacks, escalations — that falls on the same depleted workforce. The efficiency gains that AI vendors promise are not realized when the error rate is high enough to require human review of a significant fraction of AI-processed transactions, which is precisely the situation our Q3 2024 survey documented. And the administrative friction that the RFI characterizes as waste sometimes serves a protective function: checkpoints where human judgment can intercept mistakes before they harm patients. Prior authorization processes are genuinely burdensome and genuinely in need of reform — the National Academy for State Health Policy documented in its 2024 analysis of Medicaid managed care how delayed clearance protocols directly correlate with quantifiable negative medical consequences for enrollees and that reform is urgently needed (NASHP, Prior Authorization Reform and Administrative Burden in Medicaid Managed Care: State Implementation Challenges, 2024). But the solution to an administratively burdensome system is not to automate the burden away; it is to redesign the system with human judgment preserved at the points where judgment matters, and to ensure that any automation operates with demonstrated accuracy, full transparency, and binding accountability.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket HHS-OD-2024-0001 | Page 4⏎⏎HEALTH EQUITY CANNOT BE AN AFTERTHOUGHT IN THIS ANALYSIS⏎⏎The populations most harmed by administrative AI errors are low-income patients, patients with limited English proficiency, patients navigating Medicaid and CHIP, and patients in rural or underserved communities. These exact demographic groups represent the individuals for whom human administrative advocacy proves most critical, most relationship-dependent, and least replaceable by automated systems. The watershed 2019 Science paper by Obermeyer and co-authors examining demographic prejudice within an extensively utilized medical triage model revealed a devastating flaw. The automated tool consistently downplayed the medical urgency of Black individuals compared against Caucasian individuals experiencing identical levels of medical complexity. Consequently, Black individuals faced significantly lower referral rates into intensive disease management programs — an outcome that was invisible to the health systems deploying the software because the outputs appeared, on their face, to be functioning correctly (Obermeyer, Z., et al., "Dissecting Racial Prejudice in a Predictive Tool Utilized to Direct Population Health," Science, 366(6464), 2019). The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in its 2023 report Automating Inequity that AI systems deployed in health insurance administrative processes have produced systematically worse outcomes for patients of color, for patients with disabilities, and for patients in non-English-speaking households — not stemming from malicious intent but rather functioning as an anticipated outcome of utilizing historical datasets that heavily reflect the structural inequities already embedded in the health system (National Partnership for Women & Families, Automating Inequity: AI in Health Insurance and Administrative Processes, 2023). Virginia Eubanks made the same structural argument in Automating Inequality (2018): that automated systems deployed in contexts of resource scarcity and social vulnerability do not neutrally process information — they amplify the biases of the systems they are built to replicate, and they do so in ways that are harder to contest because the decision appears to come from a machine rather than a person (Eubanks, V., Automating Inequality, St. Martin's Press, 2018).⏎⏎Our governing board adopted a formal resolution in response to these findings. It is not a suggestion. It is an institutional demand, and we are submitting it here as such. The resolution calls on HHS and ONC to establish binding preconditions for any AI deployment in clinical administrative workflows, including the following:⏎⏎1. Demonstrated pre-deployment safety validation, with error rates stratified by patient population, payer type, and administrative function, with binding accuracy thresholds below which deployment is prohibited.⏎⏎2. Mandatory fairness evaluations executed by external, unaffiliated reviewers, examining performance disparities across race, ethnicity, language preference, insurance type, and geographic designation, with results made publicly available in machine-readable format prior to deployment authorization.⏎⏎3. Binding vendor transparency documentation describing the AI models embedded in administrative transaction pipelines, including training data provenance, known performance limitations, version history, and update protocols — documentation that fewer than 12 percent of our affiliated clearinghouses and exchanges had received from vendors as of our Q3 2024 survey, and whose absence creates significant liability exposure under existing HIPAA and X12 transaction standards.⏎⏎4. Preserved human accountability at every decision point with material consequences for patient access, coverage, or care — meaning that no AI system may issue a denial, a delay, a routing decision, or a benefits determination without a named, qualified human being who has reviewed the decision and is accountable for it.⏎⏎5. Mandatory workforce impact assessments prior to any AI deployment that would reduce the number of human administrative staff, with requirements to demonstrate that the affected workforce has been retrained, redeployed, or transitioned with adequate support — not simply eliminated.⏎⏎AAN Comments | HHS Health Sector AI RFI | Docket HHS-OD-2024-0001 | Page 5⏎⏎The ONC's own 2023 annual update to Congress on health information blocking and interoperability barriers documented persistent structural failures in the information exchange infrastructure on which AI administrative systems would depend — failures that include incomplete data, inconsistent coding practices, and systematic gaps in data availability for Medicaid and safety-net populations (ONC, Report on Health Information Blocking and Interoperability Barriers: Annual Update to Congress, 2023). Machine learning models educated upon or operating within this infrastructure inevitably absorb its gaps and distortions. Deploying those systems at scale, in advance of the structural repairs the ONC report identifies as necessary, is not acceleration — it is the construction of a faster mechanism for producing the same errors that already exist, with the additional problem that the errors are now attributed to a system rather than a person and are therefore harder to contest and correct.⏎⏎We want to be precise about what we are asking HHS to do, because there is a version of our argument that could be read as simply opposing AI in healthcare, and that is not our position. Our position is that the sequencing matters, the preconditions matter, and the populations bearing the risk of a botched implementation matter deeply. The RFI's accelerationist framing — its orientation toward removing barriers to adoption, streamlining regulatory pathways, and expanding reimbursement for AI-enabled services — treats speed as the primary value and treats the harms our affiliated groups have documented as acceptable costs of progress. We reject that framing. The 2.3 million patient encounters affected by AI-driven administrative errors in our survey data represent real people who did not receive timely care, real families who navigated bureaucratic mazes without the human advocates who might have helped them, and real communities in Florida and elsewhere where trust in the health system is already fragile and where one bad administrative experience can mean a patient stops seeking care altogether.⏎⏎What we are asking HHS to do is to treat the preconditions we have identified — safety validation, equity auditing, transparency documentation, human accountability, workforce protection — not as regulatory obstacles to be minimized but as the floor below which no AI deployment in administrative healthcare functions should be permitted. We are asking HHS and ONC to resist the pressure from vendors and from efficiency-focused policymakers to treat administrative AI as a category that can be deployed on the basis of promised benefits rather than demonstrated ones. And we are asking HHS to recognize that the administrative workers whose labor this RFI implicitly proposes to automate are not overhead — they are, for millions of patients in underserved communities, the most important people in the health system, and the knowledge they carry cannot be recovered once it is lost.⏎⏎The Q3 2024 data our network generated will be made available to HHS staff upon request. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss the methodology and findings in more detail, and to work with ONC on the development of the binding disclosure and auditability standards our board resolution calls for. SYNTH-0012♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Michael Young♔American Association of Nurse Practitioners♔♔♔♔♔American Association of Nurse Practitioners⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎Submitted by: Michael Young, Senior Policy Analyst⏎Date: [Submission Date]⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT GAP IS REAL, BUT IT IS NOT THE CORE PROBLEM⏎⏎The American Association of Nurse Practitioners (AANP) recognizes the operational pressures that have driven HHS to frame this RFI around acceleration. Survey data from practice administrators — including the 2024 RBMA member survey of 412 radiology practices, in which 58% of deployers reported no reimbursement mechanism to recover AI software licensing and integration costs — document a genuine structural misalignment between clinical deployment and payment recognition. AANP members who work in primary care, rural health, and community-based settings feel this misalignment acutely. The absence of Category III CPT code coverage for the large majority of FDA-cleared AI diagnostic applications is a real problem. We do not dispute that. What we are submitting today, however, is a concern that the Department's framing of reimbursement facilitation and regulatory streamlining as the primary levers for AI adoption has displaced a prior question that should be non-negotiable: whether the tools being accelerated are safe and equitable for all patient populations, not merely for the well-characterized, well-insured patient populations whose data shaped the models being deployed.⏎⏎The AANP represents more than 385,000 nurse practitioners working in all clinical environments across the United States, with concentrated membership in primary care, government-supported community clinics, rural health clinics, and safety-net environments. These are precisely the settings where AI performance degradation is most reliably documented, and precisely the settings where the individuals most severely impacted by algorithmic error have the fewest structural resources to detect or correct that error. The Department's RFI solicits input on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions to accelerate adoption. AANP's response focuses specifically on the reimbursement recognition questions and the research-and-development framework questions, because it is in those two domains that the lack of required equity requirements is most consequential and most remediable.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED FAILURE MODE: PERFORMANCE DEGRADATION ACROSS PATIENT SUBGROUPS⏎⏎The scientific research concerning computational prejudice in clinical AI is not speculative. It is a body of replicated findings that HHS's RFI fails to sufficiently address. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019) demonstrated in Science that an extensively utilized proprietary software model applied to identify patients for intensive medical management systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients, routing them to lower-priority care tiers at equivalent levels of documented illness severity. The mechanism was not intentional discrimination — it was structural data inheritance. The algorithm used historical healthcare costs as a proxy for health need, and because systemic barriers had historically suppressed healthcare utilization among Black individuals compared to Caucasian individuals possessing comparable disease burden, the model encoded that suppressed utilization as a signal of lower need. This is not a correctable edge case. It is an expected outcome of building machine learning systems on data generated by a healthcare system that was itself inequitable. Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk (2018) described this dynamic in JAMA Internal Medicine with specific attention to how missingness patterns in electronic health records — records with more gaps, fewer documented encounters, less complete medication histories — systematically disadvantage patients from lower-income and minority backgrounds during model training, because the model learns to treat documentation density as a proxy for health status.⏎⏎The pulse oximetry literature deserves particular attention in this submission because it involves a device, not a software algorithm, but the failure mode is directly analogous to what HHS is now proposing to accelerate. Sjoding, Dickson, Iwashyna, Gay, and Valley (2020) published findings in the New England Journal of Medicine demonstrating that pulse oximeters produced occult hypoxemia — clinically meaningful oxygen desaturation that the device failed to detect — at significantly higher rates in Black individuals compared to Caucasian patients. The device had been validated on predominantly lighter-skinned populations, and its optical measurement technology functioned less effectively on deeper cutaneous pigmentation. That measurement error, when combined with clinical decision support systems trained on pulse oximetry readings, would propagate the bias downstream into any AI-assisted triage or deterioration prediction tool that incorporated pulse oximetry as an input feature. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) documented a parallel problem in the New England Journal of Medicine regarding race correction in clinical algorithms — the embedding of race as a biological variable in tools like kidney function calculators that then systematically steered patients of certain racial backgrounds toward less aggressive treatment thresholds. These are not isolated failures. They are illustrations of how bias accumulates across the data pipeline.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎In imaging AI, Seyyed-Kalantari, Zhang, McDermott, Chen, and Ghassemi (2021) published findings in Nature Medicine demonstrating that AI algorithms applied to thoracic x-rays routinely underdiagnosed pathology in underserved patient populations — specifically patients who were female, Black, Hispanic, Medicaid-insured, or who had limited English proficiency. The underdiagnosis rates were not marginal. The disparity in model performance between the highest-performing and lowest-performing demographic subgroups was large enough that deploying these tools in community health settings without subgroup-stratified validation would predictably result in missed diagnoses at higher rates for the individuals with the lowest probability of accessing the diagnostic redundancy — specialist follow-up, second-opinion access, repeat imaging — that might catch what the AI missed. Adamson and Smith (2018) reported in JAMA Dermatology that dermatology AI classification software built primarily using pictures of lighter-skinned patients exhibited notably inferior accuracy regarding skin conditions presenting in darker-skinned patients, including conditions where delayed diagnosis carries significant clinical consequence.⏎⏎The research covering systemic infection forecasting is particularly instructive for AANP's purposes because sepsis prediction algorithms have been among the most aggressively marketed and deployed AI tools in hospital settings, including in the rural and community hospitals where many AANP members practice. Wong, Otles, Donnelly, Krumm, and Singh (2021) published an independent verification analysis within JAMA Internal Medicine of the Epic Sepsis Model, a proprietary algorithm implemented throughout numerous hospital systems. The external validation found that the model's performance in the study hospital proved significantly inferior compared to what was reported in the original development and internal validation literature — the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.63 in external validation, compared to figures in the 0.76 to 0.83 range reported by the developer. More concerning, the algorithm generated a high volume of false-positive alerts that contributed to alert fatigue, and its sensitivity for detecting true sepsis cases was low enough that it missed a massive share of patients who went on to require ICU-level care. This is the external validation collapse problem: a model that performs adequately on the university teaching hospital population from which it was developed degrades significantly when deployed in a different patient population. The patients in community and rural hospitals — older, with more comorbidities, lower incomes, higher rates of incomplete prior medical records — are systematically outside the distribution of the academic training data.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM IN CLINICAL PRACTICE⏎⏎Wiens, Saria, Sendak, Ghassemi, Liu, Doshi-Velez, and Goldenberg (2019) outlined in Nature Medicine what they called a "blueprint for ethical predictive learning for health care," and among the most practically important observations in that paper is the documentation of automation bias as a distinct harm pathway. System-deference—the inclination of practitioners to yield to computer-generated recommendations and suppress independent clinical judgment — is not a character flaw in individual clinicians. It is a documented behavioral response to the definitive presentation of AI-generated outputs, particularly when those outputs are presented with confidence scores or risk percentages that convey a false precision. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018) raised directly analogous concerns in the New England Journal of Medicine, arguing that the moral complications surrounding integrating predictive analytics into health care are not primarily about the algorithms themselves but about the clinical and organizational contexts into which they are inserted, and specifically about whether those contexts create structural pressures for deference to algorithmic output.⏎⏎AANP's concern is not theoretical. Nurse practitioners in primary care and community health settings frequently work in under-resourced environments where the cognitive and time demands of clinical practice are high, where digital medical charting platforms are already generating alert fatigue, and where the addition of AI-generated recommendations will arrive with an implicit institutional endorsement — "this tool is reimbursable, this tool has been cleared, this tool has been integrated into your workflow." In that context, the automation bias risk is heightened, not diminished. And the individuals with the highest probability to be harmed by an erroneous AI recommendation that goes unchallenged are patients whose presentations are atypical, whose records are incomplete, whose demographic profiles fall outside the distribution of the training data. Those are the same patients — rural, low-income, limited English proficiency, racial and ethnic minorities — who are already at elevated risk from the underlying performance degradation documented in the literature above.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎THE REGULATORY GAP IN HHS'S CURRENT PROPOSAL⏎⏎The FDA's 2021 AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan outlined a framework for thinking about the total product lifecycle of AI-based clinical tools, including the concept of predetermined change control plans and the recognition that adaptive algorithms require ongoing post-release efficacy tracking. That framework serves as a logical initial point. But it does not mandate subgroup-stratified performance reporting as a condition of clearance, and it does not require that performance data be broken down by racial background, cultural origin, language, insurance status, or geographic care setting before a tool can be deployed in clinical practice. The HTI-1 Final Rule (45 CFR Parts 170 and 171), published by ONC in 2023, introduced model visibility standards governing clinical decision support tools certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program, including requirements that developers disclose the information leveraged to build and test their algorithms. This is a meaningful step. AANP commends ONC for it. But revealing the characteristics of the foundational datasets is not the same as demonstrated performance equity, and the HTI-1 requirements do not mandate that developers demonstrate equivalent efficacy among distinct demographic cohorts as a condition of certification or reimbursement recognition.⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy and the Duke-Margolis Center for Health Policy documented this gap in their 2023 policy brief regarding computational prejudice within health care, identifying the lack of required pre-implementation fairness evaluations as the single most consequential missing element in both federal and state AI governance frameworks. Their analysis of existing regulatory levers found that HHS has clear statutory authority under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, and the ADA to condition reimbursement recognition of health IT tools on demonstrated non-discrimination across patient subgroups — authority that has not been exercised in any systematic way with respect to clinical AI.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The AANP urges HHS to condition any reimbursement recognition of clinical AI tools — whether through new CPT codes, new HCPCS Level II codes, or new value-based payment pathways — on the following requirements, which should be treated as preconditions rather than post-hoc reporting obligations:⏎⏎1. Stratified pre-deployment performance reporting. Any AI tool seeking reimbursement recognition through CMS must submit performance data stratified by, at minimum: race and ethnicity (using OMB categories disaggregated to the extent the training data permits), primary language, insurance status (Medicaid, Medicare, commercial, uninsured), and geographic care setting (academic medical center, community hospital, rural health clinic, government-supported community clinic). Performance must be reported using clinically meaningful metrics — sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value — not aggregate AUROC statistics, which can mask substantial subgroup-level performance disparities.⏎⏎2. Independent third-party equity audit as a condition of clearance and reimbursement. Developers should not be permitted to self-certify equity performance. An independent audit requirement, modeled on the financial audit requirements under SEC regulations for public companies, should require that a qualified third-party auditor with demonstrated expertise in algorithmic fairness and health equity review the training data, the validation methodology, and the subgroup performance results before any reimbursement pathway is opened.⏎⏎3. Mandatory post-deployment surveillance with subgroup stratification. Analogous to FDA's Total Product Life Cycle framework for medical devices, HHS should require that clinical AI tools under active reimbursement recognition submit annual post-deployment performance reports stratified by the same subgroup categories required at pre-deployment. These reports should be submitted to a publicly accessible registry — not merely to CMS or FDA as confidential commercial information — so that health systems, patient advocates, and independent researchers can review real-world performance data.⏎⏎o   A note on the registry requirement: AANP is aware that some AI developers will argue that mandatory public disclosure of performance data constitutes a disclosure of proprietary information. This argument should be rejected. The performance of a tool on a patient population is not proprietary. The architecture of the algorithm may be; the training data sources may be; the performance outcomes belong to the patients and the public health system.⏎⏎4. Equity impact assessment as a precondition for regulatory facilitation. HHS should establish, by rulemaking, a process analogous to the environmental impact assessment process under NEPA, requiring that any proposed regulatory facilitation of a clinical AI tool — including expedited clearance pathways, safe harbors, or reimbursement coding — be accompanied by a documented equity impact assessment that models the expected differential effects of deployment across patient subgroups, identifies settings where performance degradation is predicted, and proposes mitigation measures.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 7⏎⏎COMMUNITY AND RURAL HEALTH SETTINGS REQUIRE SPECIFIC ATTENTION⏎⏎AANP's membership includes a substantial concentration of nurse practitioners practicing in rural health clinics and government-supported community clinics. These settings are consistently underrepresented in the training data for commercial clinical AI tools, which are disproportionately developed and validated at major university-affiliated teaching hospitals within urban markets. The external validation collapse documented by Wong et al. (2021) for the Epic Sepsis Model is not an anomaly. It is the expected result when a tool trained on data from a high-volume, well-resourced academic center is deployed in a facility with different patient demographics, different documentation practices, different staffing ratios, and different baseline disease prevalence. Wiens et al. (2019) specifically identified this distribution shift problem as one of the most practically important failure modes in deployed clinical AI, and they recommended that external validation in the intended deployment setting be treated as a mandatory step before clinical deployment, not an optional post-market activity.⏎⏎HHS's RFI does not address this problem with any specificity. The acceleration agenda, as written, would extend reimbursement recognition to tools validated at academic centers and then deployed across the full spectrum of care settings — including the rural and safety-net settings where AANP members practice — without any requirement that performance be demonstrated in those settings before deployment. This is the structural equity threat that AANP is most concerned about. It is not about malicious intent on the part of AI developers. It is about the physics of how machine learning systems generalize: they generalize well to populations that resemble their training data, and they degrade on populations that do not. Rural and underserved communities are, by definition, underrepresented in academic-center training datasets. Deploying tools in those communities without setting-specific validation is not acceleration — it is an experiment conducted on the patients with the fewest resources to identify or report the harm.⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 8⏎⏎A SPECIFIC CONCERN ABOUT REIMBURSEMENT STRUCTURE AND INCENTIVE DESIGN⏎⏎AANP also wishes to flag a concern about the incentive structure that would be created by the reimbursement recognition pathways under discussion. If CMS creates new CPT or add-on payment mechanisms that compensate clinicians or health systems for the use of AI-assisted diagnosis or clinical decision support — and if those mechanisms do not include explicit performance accountability requirements — the reimbursement structure will create a financial incentive to deploy AI tools without regard to whether those tools perform equitably in the actual patient population being served. Health systems operating in rural and safety-net settings are often operating under significant financial pressure. A reimbursement mechanism that rewards the use of an AI tool, without conditioning that reward on demonstrated performance, will function as a subsidy for potentially harmful deployment. AANP does not oppose reimbursement recognition for clinical AI in principle. The 58% of radiology practices reporting no cost-recovery mechanism for FDA-cleared AI tools is a real problem that HHS should address. But cost-recovery mechanisms and equity accountability are not in tension — they can be designed together, and the failure to design them together represents an intentional regulatory decision carrying predictable consequences.⏎⏎There is also a question, which AANP does not believe HHS has adequately addressed in the RFI, about who bears liability when an AI-assisted clinical decision factors into adverse medical outcomes in a demographic subgroup where the tool was not specifically validated. Existing oversight structures are ambiguous on this point. FDA clearance creates a presumption of safety and effectiveness that may complicate malpractice claims even when a tool performs demonstrably worse for a particular demographic group. CMS reimbursement recognition would likely amplify that presumption. Clarifying liability allocation — and ensuring that developers bear some share of liability for documented subgroup performance failures — is a necessary component of a responsible AI governance framework, and it is conspicuously absent from the current RFI.⏎⏎The AANP respectfully urges HHS to issue a supplemental RFI or proposed rulemaking that specifically addresses required pre-implementation fairness evaluations, subgroup-stratified performance reporting, and post-deployment surveillance requirements as preconditions for any reimbursement recognition or regulatory facilitation of clinical AI. The acceleration agenda, as currently framed, would extend the benefits of AI adoption primarily to well-resourced health systems serving well-characterized patient populations, while distributing the risks of algorithmic error disproportionately to the rural, low-income, and minority populations that AANP's members serve every day. The Department has the statutory authority, the regulatory infrastructure, and the scientific evidence base to design a different path. AANP strongly recommends it do so before the first new CPT code for AI-assisted clinical decision support is⏎⏎AANP Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 9⏎⏎aanp-hhs-ai-rfi-comments-2024@aanp.org⏎www.aanp.org/policy♔♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-23T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔10♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔Indiana♔senior policy analyst♔34♔A 2024 RBMA member survey encompassing responses from 412 radiology practice administrators found that 67% had deployed at least one FDA-cleared AI algorithm in clinical workflow, yet 58% of those practices reported that existing reimbursement structures provided no mechanism to recover the costs of AI software licensing, integration, or ongoing quality assurance. SYNTH-0013♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Steven Robinson♔♔♔♔♔♔Docket: HHS-2025-0020⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information, Federal Register Vol. 90, No. 47 (March 2025)⏎Submitted by: Steven Robinson, Milwaukee, Wisconsin⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎Page 1 of 4⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎My coworker Marcus collapsed on a warehouse loading dock in February of this year. Three of us kept him alive using an AED that talked us through every step out loud. The paramedics who arrived told us the real-time guidance made a measurable difference. I stood in the waiting room at Froedtert that night thinking: if technology can do that on a concrete floor in the dark, what could it do inside a clinic, where there is actual equipment and actual training? Marcus is back at work. I want more of that. I want AI in healthcare to actually work.⏎⏎That is exactly why I am troubled by what I read in this RFI.⏎⏎THE MARKET STRUCTURE PROBLEM⏎⏎HHS is asking how it can accelerate AI adoption. My concern is that before asking how fast, the Department should ask who benefits. The AI health sector is not competitive in any meaningful sense. A 2023 Health Affairs article by Gee et al. found that a small number of large vendors control the platforms through which most clinical AI will ultimately be deployed, and that this concentration gives those vendors structural advantages that have nothing to do with whether their products perform well. Writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022, Dafny and Lee highlighted a similar dynamic: health IT markets systematically fail to reward quality because switching costs are so high that buyers cannot credibly threaten to leave. That is not a normal market. That is a market where acceleration primarily rewards incumbents.⏎⏎I recognize I am a warehouse worker, not a health economist. But I have watched this pattern before. I watched it in the trucking logistics software my company uses, where we are locked into a platform that everyone on the floor agrees is worse than alternatives, but changing would cost more than the bad software does. The mechanism is the same: once a vendor's product is embedded in clinical workflows, billing systems, and regulatory reporting requirements, removing it becomes nearly impossible regardless of performance. Being trapped by a single vendor is a very real, everyday nightmare for the people stuck using the software. It happens constantly in the real world, and the RFI's proposals for reimbursement modernization and public-private partnerships will make it worse before they make it better.⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎Page 2 of 4⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎REIMBURSEMENT AND THE SUBSIDY QUESTION⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about how reimbursement structures can be updated to support AI adoption. I need to challenge this straightforwardly since the whole premise seems backwards to me. The question is not whether CMS should pay for AI tools. The question is what conditions should attach to that payment.⏎⏎Here is what worries me about the current direction:⏎⏎1. Reimbursement signals function as market-shaping subsidies. If CMS creates billing codes for AI-assisted diagnosis or AI-assisted documentation, it is effectively guaranteeing revenue to whatever vendors hold those product approvals at the moment the codes go live. A 2024 GAO report on AI in healthcare (GAO-24-106752) found that existing accountability mechanisms for AI tools in clinical settings are inconsistent and that there is no standard framework for ongoing performance monitoring post-deployment. Creating reimbursement pathways before fixing that accountability gap means paying for tools before we know they work.⏎⏎2. Large vendors can navigate new billing codes; small innovators often cannot. This is not speculation. We can look straight at the history of HITECH's EHR incentive programs for proof. Schulte and Fry documented in their 2019 Kaiser Health News / Fortune investigation how those incentives accelerated adoption of EHR systems that were poorly designed and actively harmful to clinical workflow, partly because the vendors who could meet certification requirements quickly were the ones with the lobbying infrastructure to shape those requirements. The same dynamic will repeat if HHS moves fast on AI reimbursement without structural safeguards.⏎⏎3. Interoperability conditions need to come before, not after, reimbursement expansion. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer wrote in the Milbank Quarterly in 2017 that information blocking by health IT vendors was widespread and that voluntary compliance was insufficient to address it. The tools for addressing this have gotten somewhat better since then, but the incentive to block data sharing has not changed. If AI reimbursement creates new data flows that are proprietary to specific vendors, we will have funded a new generation of silos.⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎Page 3 of 4⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎THE CRADA AND PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP CONCERN⏎⏎The RFI mentions Cooperative Research and Development Agreements and expanded public-private partnerships as mechanisms for accelerating AI development. I want to flag something that I think deserves more scrutiny than this RFI gives it.⏎⏎Whenever a private corporation signs a CRADA with a government department, that business gets handed the keys to government data, government expertise, and sometimes government intellectual property. What the public gets in return is supposed to be a product that benefits the public. In health AI, that exchange involves patient data, which was generated by patients, collected by providers, and is now being offered as input material for commercial AI training. A 2023 Journal of Health Economics paper by Obermeyer's team detailed what they termed "algorithmic rents" -- the way AI vendors extract value from health systems and patient populations without proportionate accountability or return. That paper specifically looked at cases where vendors used data from safety-net hospitals serving low-income patients to train tools that were then licensed back to those same hospitals at prices those hospitals struggled to afford.⏎⏎I am not saying CRADAs are inherently bad. I am saying the terms matter enormously and the RFI does not engage with the question of terms at all. It asks how to accelerate partnerships, not what conditions should govern them. That omission bothers me. Who retains rights to models trained on Medicare claims data? What happens to a CRADA product if the vendor is acquired? Can a hospital system that contributed patient data to a training dataset later switch to a competitor's tool, or does the data contribution create a practical lock-in? These are not obscure questions. They are the questions that determine whether the public's investment in this infrastructure comes back to the public.⏎⏎WHAT I AM ASKING FOR⏎⏎I am not asking HHS to slow down AI adoption in healthcare. I genuinely believe this technology, done right, could do for patients what that AED did for Marcus. What I am asking is that HHS write rules that serve patients rather than the vendors who are selling to them.⏎⏎Specifically, and in response to the reimbursement and partnership questions raised in the RFI:⏎⏎o Any new reimbursement pathway for clinical AI tools must force vendors to continuously track and report how well their software actually works in the real world after it gets approved as a condition of continued coverage, with publicly accessible performance data disaggregated by patient population. The GAO-24-106752 findings make clear that current accountability structures are not adequate for this.⏎⏎o Public-private partnerships and CRADAs involving patient data should include explicit data portability conditions, so that a health system that contributes data to a training process retains the right to move to a different vendor without forfeiting the value of that contribution.⏎⏎o HHS should mandate that every piece of AI software getting paid through federal healthcare dollars publish its training data sources and validation methodology in a form that independent researchers can audit. The information blocking literature going back to Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer shows that voluntary transparency commitments from health IT vendors do not hold under commercial pressure.⏎⏎o Small and safety-net providers should have explicit preference or set-aside access in any AI adoption support program, because the market dynamics described in Gee et al. and Dafny and Lee mean those providers will be last in line if HHS does not actively intervene.⏎⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎Page 4 of 4⏎- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -⏎⏎I want to be honest about one more thing. I have read through this RFI several times now, and I keep noticing that the framing throughout is about removing friction for adoption. The word "accelerate" appears repeatedly. What I do not see is comparable attention to what happens when AI tools perform badly in clinical settings, or to who bears the cost when they do. That asymmetry in framing is itself a signal. If a government notice focuses harder on how fast these systems can be rolled out instead of the damage caused by rolling them out recklessly, that tells you exactly who had the loudest voice in the room during the drafting process.⏎⏎The people in exam rooms are not the same people who will negotiate the CRADA terms or navigate the new billing codes. Most of them will never read this Federal Register notice. They are trusting that someone is thinking about this on their behalf. I hope HHS is actually doing that, and not just creating conditions for the next generation of health IT problems to replicate the last one. Schulte and Fry's reporting on EHR failures documented real patient harm from technology that was deployed too fast under incentive structures that rewarded adoption over performance. That was not an accident of bad timing. SYNTH-0015♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Carol Lopez♔University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences♔♔♔♔♔University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences⏎ Comments Submitted to the HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎ Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎ Docket No. HHS-OD-2024-0001⏎ ⏎ THE DEMOCRATIC QUESTION HHS HAS NOT ASKED⏎ ⏎ The University of Chicago Center for Health and the Social Sciences submits these comments in response to the above-referenced Request for Information. Our submission focuses precisely on the RFI's framing premises and their implications for democratic governance of health system infrastructure, rather than the operational adoption questions the RFI primarily poses. We focus on two of the RFI's thematic areas: regulatory and oversight frameworks, and research and development priorities. We do not address reimbursement mechanisms in detail, not because that area is unimportant, but because the prior questions are more fundamental and have received inadequate attention.⏎ ⏎ The Center's perspective is grounded in empirical familiarity with the operational realities the RFI describes. The 2024 CHIME survey of 380 health system CIOs and CMIOs found that 67% identified interoperability gaps between AI-enabled clinical decision support tools and existing EHR infrastructure as the primary barrier to scaled deployment, and 54% pointed to the lack of uniform model validation protocols as a critical obstacle to institutional governance approval (CHIME, 2024). We cite these figures not to celebrate the adoption trajectory they document, but to establish that the Center is not speaking from a position of ignorance about deployment realities. We understand why health systems want faster adoption pathways, and we understand the genuine operational pressures driving that demand. That understanding is precisely why the following argument is offered with some urgency.⏎ ⏎ THE RFI'S ACCELERATIONIST FRAMING AS A TELL⏎ ⏎ The RFI's stated objective is to identify actions HHS can take to "reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" in clinical settings (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 2024, 89 FR [XX]). That phrase is worth dwelling on. It does not ask whether uncertainty should be reduced; it presupposes that uncertainty is the problem and innovation is the goal. This is not a neutral framing. It is an accelerationist posture dressed in the language of regulatory modernization, and it forecloses in advance the deliberative question that democratic self-governance requires be asked first: whether this domain, at this moment, with these tools, under these oversight conditions, should be accelerated at all.⏎ ⏎ The framing is not a minor rhetorical choice. When an agency defines the policy question as "how fast" rather than "whether and under what conditions," it has already made a substantive determination — one that has not been authorized by any democratic deliberation at the scale the determination requires. Sheila Jasanoff has argued that the legitimacy of technology governance depends not only on the outcomes it produces but on whether the processes by which those outcomes are reached are recognizable as exercises of collective self-determination (Jasanoff, 2016). The RFI's framing fails that test. It asks the public to comment on the mechanics of acceleration without first asking whether speeding up adoption represents the correct posture for this moment, rather than presupposing acceleration as the objective.⏎ ⏎ IRREVERSIBILITY AND THE ATROPHY OF INSTITUTIONAL CAPACITY⏎ ⏎ The Center's most serious concern is one that does not appear anywhere in the RFI: the structural irreversibility of AI integration in clinical care. Eric Topol's influential 2019 synthesis in Nature Medicine argued for a model of "collaborative intelligence" in which AI tools augment rather than displace physician judgment (Topol, 2019). That framing has provided much of the intellectual scaffolding for optimistic adoption arguments. The Center respects that work, but believes it significantly underestimates the degree to which workflow reorganization, once completed, becomes self-reinforcing in ways that foreclose the collaborative model Topol envisions.⏎ ⏎ Coiera's analysis of AI implementation dynamics is more precise on this point. He identifies what he terms the final integration hurdle: the gap between technical performance and clinical integration is bridged not by the AI system alone but by the wholesale reorganization of surrounding workflows, staffing patterns, documentation practices, and institutional memory (Coiera, 2019, e16323). Once that reorganization has occurred — once residents are trained in workflows that presuppose the AI tool, once the human expertise that preceded the tool has retired or been defunded, once the baseline comparators against which the tool's performance could be evaluated have been discontinued — the practical ability to reverse course is gone. This is not a theoretical risk. The institutional lock-in dynamics documented in healthcare markets more broadly (Dafny & Lee, 2016) apply with particular force to AI systems, because AI systems do not merely provide services that could in principle be contracted elsewhere; they reorganize the human and institutional substrate that any alternative would require.⏎ ⏎ The specific mechanisms of irreversibility deserve enumeration, because the RFI's framing treats reversibility as a default condition:⏎ ⏎ 1. Atrophy of clinical expertise: When AI tools are integrated into diagnostic workflows, the human skills those workflows previously required are exercised less frequently, trained less rigorously, and eventually lost as an institutional resource. This is not hypothetical — it is the documented pattern of automation-induced skill degradation across complex domains.⏎ ⏎ 2. Staffing model reorganization: Health systems adopting AI tools at scale typically restructure staffing ratios and role definitions in ways that presuppose the tool's continued availability. Reversing those structural decisions after the fact is not merely technically possible; it requires rehiring, retraining, and renegotiating labor agreements under conditions where the relevant expertise may no longer exist in the labor market at the required scale.⏎ ⏎ 3. Contractual and architectural dependencies: Proprietary AI systems embed themselves in EHR architecture, data pipelines, and vendor contracts in ways that create switching costs that are not merely financial. The CHIME survey's finding that 67% of health system CIOs identify interoperability gaps as the primary adoption barrier is, read from the other direction, a finding that existing AI integrations have already created lock-in conditions that make alternatives difficult (CHIME, 2024).⏎ ⏎ 4. Loss of baseline comparators: Once AI-assisted care becomes the standard, the pre-AI baseline against which performance claims are evaluated disappears. Health systems lose the ability to evaluate whether the AI tool is actually producing better outcomes or merely different ones.⏎ ⏎ The RFI does not acknowledge any of these mechanisms. Its silence on irreversibility is not a technical oversight; it reflects the accelerationist framing that treats adoption as a one-directional ratchet whose forward motion requires only lubrication.⏎ ⏎ University of Chicago CHSS | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎ ⏎ THE STRUCTURAL IMPOSSIBILITY OF DEMOCRATIC OVERSIGHT UNDER CURRENT LAW⏎ ⏎ A separate but related problem concerns oversight. The RFI gestures toward the importance of "responsible AI deployment" and references transparency as a value, but it does not confront the structural conditions under which oversight of proprietary clinical AI is currently conducted. The argument here is not that individual AI systems are opaque — though many are — but that the combination of trade secret protections under federal and state law, the proprietary architecture of commercial AI systems, and the absence of standardized audit frameworks makes democratic oversight categorically impossible under current legal and regulatory conditions, not merely difficult or incomplete.⏎ ⏎ Pasquale's analysis of black-box governance frameworks established the theoretical architecture of this problem a decade ago (Pasquale, 2015), but the clinical AI context has sharpened it considerably. Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 study in Science documented how an extensively implemented proprietary predictive tool, which was tasked with directing health care resource allocation for large populations systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients — not because of explicit discriminatory intent, but because the algorithm used health care costs as a proxy for health needs, and health care costs are themselves a product of historical access inequities (Obermeyer et al., 2019). The study was possible only because the researchers obtained access to the underlying algorithm under conditions that are not routinely available to regulators, health systems, or the public. Under normal conditions of proprietary protection, the bias would have been invisible.⏎ ⏎ Selbst and Barocas have argued that even well-designed explainability requirements cannot fully resolve this problem under proprietary constraints, because the interpretive frameworks needed to evaluate an explanation are themselves dependent on access to training data, model architecture, and validation methodology that trade secret law routinely withholds (Selbst & Barocas, 2018, pp. 1085-1139). The RFI's invocation of transparency as a value does not engage with this structural argument. It treats opacity as a problem of degree — something that better disclosure requirements might ameliorate — rather than as a structural condition produced by the intersection of intellectual property law, proprietary architecture, and the complete lack of compulsory uniform audit protocols. Democratic self-governance requires the ability to examine, evaluate, and if necessary reject the systems that govern consequential decisions. Under current law, that ability does not exist for the clinical AI systems HHS is proposing to accelerate.⏎ ⏎ The 54% of health system CIOs who flagged the lack of uniform model validation protocols as a critical obstacle to institutional governance approval (CHIME, 2024) are describing, from a purely operational perspective, the same structural gap. They cannot govern these tools internally because the frameworks needed for governance do not exist. What the RFI treats as an obstacle to adoption is, from a democratic accountability perspective, an appropriate institutional signal that the governance preconditions for adoption have not been met.⏎ ⏎ THE DEMOCRATIC PREROGATIVE ARGUMENT⏎ ⏎ The deepest objection to the RFI's framing is one that cannot be resolved by better validation frameworks or improved interoperability standards. It is the objection that a democratic society retains the sovereign prerogative to determine that certain domains of human life belong to a category where human judgment is preserved as a matter of democratic value rather than technical necessity — where the question is not whether AI could perform a function adequately but whether we, collectively, want it to.⏎ ⏎ Robert Dahl's foundational treatment of democratic theory establishes that the legitimate scope of collective self-determination includes not only governance procedures but the substantive determination of which domains of social life will be organized by which principles (Dahl, 1989). Medicine is a domain in which the relationship between the practitioner and the patient carries moral weight that is not reducible to its informational content. Asking if that relationship ought to be restructured around AI-assisted decision-making poses a profound moral inquiry, rather than a mere engineering puzzle that HHS can resolve by reducing regulatory friction. It is a question of democratic value that requires the kind of broad deliberative engagement that the RFI explicitly does not invite.⏎ ⏎ Virginia Eubanks's comparative work on automated decision systems in criminal justice and social services provides a useful frame here (Eubanks, 2018). Her argument is not that automation always produces worse outcomes on measurable metrics — in some cases it does not — but that automated systems in high-stakes domains systematically displace the human judgment and local accountability that democratic self-governance requires, and that this displacement is itself a democratic harm independent of outcome metrics. The same argument applies to clinical AI. A society may legitimately conclude that medicine, like criminal justice and education, is a domain where the preservation of human judgment is a democratic priority that efficiency arguments cannot override. HHS has no mandate to foreclose that determination through an acceleration agenda, and the RFI's framing does exactly that.⏎ ⏎ The precedent for precautionary governance frameworks in medicine exists. Mello and colleagues' 2013 analysis of clinical trial data sharing in the New England Journal of Medicine argued for governance frameworks that prioritized democratic accountability and reversibility over speed of access, precisely because the domains at stake were ones where errors could not be easily corrected and where public trust in the integrity of the process was itself a social good (Mello et al., 2013). The same logic applies here with greater force, because AI integration in clinical care is considerably less reversible than the data sharing arrangements Mello and colleagues were analyzing.⏎ ⏎ University of Chicago CHSS | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎ ⏎ WHAT THE RFRFI SHOULD HAVE ASKED⏎ ⏎ The Center does not oppose AI development in health care. The research conducted at this institution includes work on AI-assisted epidemiological surveillance, predictive modeling for population health intervention targeting, and natural language processing applications in clinical documentation. We are not arguing that these applications are without value, or that regulatory frameworks should be designed to prevent their development. The argument is narrower and, we believe, more important: asking if and under what democratic conditions AI systems ought to be integrated into medical care determinations represents a prior inquiry that the RFI has not raised, and that the Department cannot answer unilaterally.⏎ ⏎ The specific policy recommendation of this comment is that HHS should reissue this RFI with a neutral framing that explicitly invites comment on whether speeding up adoption represents the correct posture for this moment, rather than presupposing acceleration as the objective and soliciting comment only on its mechanics. A reissued RFI should at minimum ask whether the governance preconditions for responsible AI adoption — including standardized audit frameworks, mandatory model disclosure to regulatory bodies, interoperability requirements that preserve institutional exit options, and affirmative protections for the human expertise that AI tools are proposed to supplement — have been met. It should also explicitly invite comment on whether certain clinical decision domains should be designated as areas where human judgment is preserved as a matter of democratic value, independent of AI performance metrics.⏎ ⏎ The Department's authority to issue this RFI does not include the authority to determine, on behalf of the democratic polity, that medicine is a domain where efficiency optimization takes precedence over the values of human accountability, local knowledge, and reversibility. That determination belongs to a deliberative process that this RFI, as currently framed, does not initiate. The Center strongly urges HHS to reframe the inquiry accordingly before the adoption trajectory documents in the CHIME survey data becomes the kind of structural fait accompli that forecloses the deliberative options democratic self-governance requires.⏎ ⏎ One practical note: the Center is aware that the comment period for this RFI closes before several significant institutional governance decisions — including at least three prominent university-affiliated research hospitals across the Midwest that have publicly announced AI integration timelines for fiscal year 2025 — will have been made. The timing itself illustrates the irreversibility dynamic the comment describes. By the time deliberation has produced clearer democratic guidance, the operational decisions will already have been made and the institutional reorganization will already be underway.
