Our perspective is grounded in direct operational experience: a practice-wide audit conducted across 847 clinical encounters at an affiliated outpatient behavioral health practice over an 18-month period found that AI-assisted clinical documentation tools, piloted across six licensed clinicians, reduced administrative burden by approximately 38% while maintaining documentation fidelity scores above the 92nd percentile on standardized audit measures. The operational value of these tools is not in dispute. What is in dispute, and what this submission addresses, is whether the Department has correctly sequenced the question of adoption relative to the far more consequential question of who answers when these tools cause patient harm.⏎⏎⏎⏎These comments do not address every question posed in the RFI. They address two: the regulatory framework question and the reimbursement incentive question. Those two questions sit at the center of what the Department is actually proposing to do, and they share a common structural flaw that the Department has not acknowledged. The remaining questions, however thoughtfully composed, cannot be answered responsibly until that flaw is named and corrected.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY VACUUM AS STRUCTURAL DESIGN FLAW⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department's RFI proceeds from the assumption that the principal barriers to AI adoption in clinical care are technical and economic: insufficient evaluation standards, unclear reimbursement pathways, inadequate research infrastructure. These are real barriers. But the RFI does not ask, and the Department appears not to have considered, what happens when an AI-assisted clinical decision leads to an adverse medical event and the patient's attorney attempts to identify a responsible party. That omission is not a secondary concern to be addressed in later rulemaking. It represents a fundamental architectural defect in the current deployment model, and the Department's proposal to accelerate adoption before resolving it will produce consequences that will be extremely difficult to reverse once institutional dependency on these tools is established.⏎⏎⏎⏎Consider the accountability chain as it currently exists in any AI-assisted clinical encounter. The clinician who accepted or acted on an AI-generated recommendation will argue that the tool was reviewed and approved by institutional governance, that the vendor represented it as validated, and that the clinician exercised independent judgment in applying it. The hospital or practice will argue that the clinician bore the ultimate duty of care, that the AI tool was merely an informational aid, and that liability rests with the party who made the clinical decision. The vendor will argue that the software functioned according to its validated parameters, that the clinician was responsible for appropriate use, and that the product was cleared or registered under whatever applicable FDA pathway governed it. Each party possesses a plausible deflection narrative. No existing legal framework resolves which narrative controls.⏎⏎⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical problem. Hoffman and Podgurski, writing in the Journal of Law and the Biosciences (2023, lsad003), have documented in careful detail how existing malpractice doctrine was not designed to accommodate AI intermediation in the diagnostic or treatment chain. Traditional medical liability analysis, which asks what a reasonably competent physician would have done, becomes incoherent when the physician's decision was shaped by a probabilistic output that no physician generated and that the physician may not fully understand. Price, Gerke, and Cohen raised this concern as early as 2019 in JAMA (322(18), 1765-1766), noting that the introduction of AI tools creates ambiguity about whether the physician, the hospital, or the developer bears liability when the tool contributes to an adverse outcome. That ambiguity has not been resolved in the five years since. The Department's RFI does not propose to resolve it. It proposes, instead, to accelerate the adoption of tools that will generate more adverse outcomes into a liability framework that cannot assign responsibility for those outcomes.⏎⏎⏎⏎Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert (JAMA, 2020, 323(4), 352-366) have argued that malpractice liability, whatever its imperfections, performs a real deterrence and quality-signal function in the healthcare system. When that liability cannot be clearly assigned, the deterrence function collapses. Clinicians and institutions lose the feedback signal that drives quality improvement, and patients lose the practical means of seeking redress. The Department's proposal to accelerate AI adoption without first constructing an accountability assignment framework does not merely leave a gap in the regulatory architecture. It actively degrades the deterrence function of an existing safety mechanism.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN LEGAL AND MORAL ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies wishes to draw a distinction that the Department's RFI conflates, perhaps inadvertently. Legal accountability and moral accountability are not the same thing, and the absence of one does not necessarily imply the absence of the other, but the absence of both simultaneously is what the current AI deployment model produces.⏎⏎⏎⏎Legal accountability is the assignment of liability to an identifiable party who can be compelled to answer for harm in a court or administrative proceeding. Moral accountability is something different: it is the patient's right to face a named, identifiable human being who accepted responsibility for the clinical decision that caused harm. These two forms of accountability are related but not identical. A hospital can be legally liable without any individual accepting moral accountability. An individual clinician can accept moral accountability without being the party against whom a judgment is entered. The AI intermediation problem disrupts both simultaneously.⏎⏎⏎⏎Pasquale, in New Laws of Robotics (Harvard University Press, 2020), argues that as AI systems take on greater roles in consequential decisions, the social contract around professional accountability requires affirmative reconstruction, not passive inheritance from pre-AI legal frameworks. The point is not that AI tools cannot be used responsibly. The point is that responsible use requires, as a precondition, a named human being who has accepted non-delegable responsibility for the outcome. When a patient asks "who decided this about my care," the answer cannot be "the algorithm, and we're still working out who's responsible for the algorithm." That answer is not merely legally inadequate. It is a failure of the basic moral architecture of clinical care.⏎⏎⏎⏎Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, et al. (Health Affairs, 2014) identified this concern a decade ago in the context of predictive analytics, noting that complex algorithmic tools create legal and ethical challenges that older paradigms simply lack the capacity to address, particularly around transparency and the patient's ability to understand and contest decisions that affect their care. A decade later, the tools are vastly more capable, the deployment is vastly more widespread, and the framework remains unbuilt. Doshi-Velez and colleagues (Berkman Klein Center Working Paper, 2017) further argued that accountability under law requires, at minimum, the capacity to explain a decision in terms that a responsible human agent can own. That capacity is inconsistent, at best, with the black-box inference models that constitute a large portion of the AI tools now being marketed for clinical use.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎THE SEQUENCING PROBLEM IN THE RFI⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department's RFI is organized around evaluation methods, reimbursement pathways, and research infrastructure. These are reasonable subjects for regulatory attention. But the sequencing of the RFI — accelerate adoption, then presumably refine accountability structures over time — is not a neutral design choice. It is a choice with predictable and serious consequences.⏎⏎⏎⏎Once clinical institutions build operational dependency on AI tools, the practical ability to impose retroactive accountability requirements diminishes sharply. Vendors will have established market positions. Hospitals will have restructured workflows. Clinicians will have developed practice patterns that incorporate AI outputs. At that point, imposing a non-delegable accountability framework will be resisted as operationally disruptive and will be diluted through the negotiation process that always accompanies late-stage regulatory intervention. The Department should not expect that it can accelerate adoption now and construct accountability architecture later without substantial loss of leverage.⏎⏎⏎⏎Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (in Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, 2020, pp. 295-336) have observed that the legal and ethical challenges of AI-driven healthcare are not problems that can be addressed incrementally after deployment; they require prospective design. The ONC Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024-2030 acknowledges, to its credit, that trustworthy AI requires transparency, safety, and accountability as foundational properties, not aspirational ones. But the RFI does not operationalize those properties in any manner that would actually constrain the rollout of software that lacks them. The Strategic Plan's language around accountability is aspirational. The RFI's reimbursement and regulatory proposals would be operational. When aspirational commitments and operational incentives conflict, the operational incentives win.⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department should also be aware that the accountability vacuum is not evenly distributed among all demographic groups receiving care. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (Science, 2019, 366(6464), 447-453) proved how a frequently utilized proprietary model consistently undervalued the medical necessities of Black individuals compared to Caucasian individuals possessing identical health profiles, producing discriminatory resource allocation at scale. When that kind of error occurs in an accountable human system, there is a named party who can be compelled to correct it. When it occurs in an AI-intermediated system with diffuse accountability, the correction mechanism is unclear and the affected patients have no obvious path to redress. The Department's RFI does not address this dimension of the accountability problem, and Apple Health Technologies is concerned that the reimbursement incentives the Department is considering would accelerate the deployment of tools with exactly this kind of embedded bias before any accountability framework exists to identify and mitigate such issues.⏎⏎⏎⏎Topol (Nature Medicine, 2019, 25, 44-56) has written compellingly about the potential of AI to augment clinical judgment and reduce diagnostic error. Apple Health Technologies does not dispute that potential. The 38% reduction in administrative burden observed in our affiliated practice pilot is real, and the clinical bandwidth that reduction creates has genuine patient benefit. But Topol's argument for human-AI convergence presupposes that the human remains accountable in a meaningful, non-delegable sense. The current deployment model does not guarantee that. The American Medical Association's own policy on augmented intelligence (AMA Policy H-480.940, 2023) states that AI tools should support, not replace, physician judgment and that physicians retain responsibility for clinical decisions. That is a moral commitment. It is not, under current law and regulatory structure, an enforceable legal one. The gap between those two things is precisely where patient harm will fall.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE REIMBURSEMENT FRAMEWORK⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies focuses the remainder of these comments on the reimbursement question because that is where the Department's proposed acceleration is most likely to become irreversible. Reimbursement creates adoption incentives that reshape institutional behavior faster and more durably than any other regulatory lever. Once a reimbursement pathway is established for AI-assisted clinical services, the institutions that have invested in those services will constitute a politically organized constituency against any subsequent modification of that pathway. The Department should understand that the reimbursement decisions it makes in response to this RFI will constrain its own future regulatory options.⏎⏎⏎⏎With that in mind, Apple Health Technologies identifies the following specific concerns regarding any reimbursement framework for AI-assisted clinical care that the Department may be considering:⏎⏎⏎⏎o Any reimbursement pathway that does not condition payment on the prior identification of a named, accountable human clinician who has accepted non-delegable responsibility for the AI-assisted decision is a pathway that actively subsidizes the diffusion of accountability rather than its concentration.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Reimbursement frameworks that treat AI-assisted clinical documentation, diagnostic support, and treatment recommendation as functionally equivalent for payment purposes will obscure the substantially different liability profiles of these tool categories. Documentation assistance, which was the subject of our affiliated practice pilot, involves administrative rather than clinical judgment. Diagnostic support and treatment recommendation tools operate in the clinical decision chain in ways that documentation tools do not, and the accountability questions are correspondingly more severe.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Performance-based reimbursement models that reward efficiency gains from AI adoption without simultaneously requiring adverse-event attribution protocols will create a systematic incentive to deploy AI tools in high-throughput clinical settings where the accountability diffusion problem is most acute and the error rate is most consequential.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Any reimbursement framework should require, as a condition of payment, that covered AI tools have undergone prospective bias auditing across the demographic subgroups that constitute the covered patient population, with results made available to the public in a form sufficient to permit independent evaluation. The Obermeyer et al. findings (Science, 2019) are by now several years old, and the commercial AI market has not self-corrected in the intervening period.⏎⏎⏎⏎These are not requests for additional study or further comment periods. They are conditions that the Department has the authority to impose and that the current state of the evidence requires.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎A SPECIFIC AND CONCRETE DEMAND⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies is aware that regulatory comment submissions frequently conclude with requests that are too broad or too vague to compel specific departmental action. This submission does not do that.⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department must, before finalizing any payment mechanism or regulatory clearance framework for AI-assisted clinical tools, publish a proposed accountability assignment framework that identifies, for each category of AI-assisted clinical tool, a specific, named class of human party who bears non-delegable legal accountability for clinical decisions in which that tool was used. That framework must be published for public comment as a distinct regulatory action, not embedded as a subordinate provision of a broader rule. It must resolve, in operationally specific terms, the questions that Hoffman and Podgurski (2023), Price, Gerke, and Cohen (2019), and Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) have identified as unresolved under existing malpractice doctrine. It must be in effect, not merely proposed, before any reimbursement incentive for AI-assisted clinical care takes effect.⏎⏎⏎⏎This is not a request to delay AI adoption indefinitely. Apple Health Technologies has a direct institutional interest in seeing AI tools reach clinical settings where they can reduce administrative burden and free clinician time for patient care. The 38% burden reduction observed in our pilot is meaningful, and the clinicians who experienced it are not interested in returning to pre-AI documentation workflows. But the value of that burden reduction does not resolve the structural question of who answers when these tools cause harm. Those are separate questions, and the Department is treating them as though answering the first makes the second less urgent. It does not.⏎⏎⏎⏎The sequencing error in this RFI, accelerate adoption first, construct accountability later, is a choice that will be difficult to correct once institutional dependency is established. The Department has the opportunity, in responding to these comments and in its subsequent rulemaking, to correct that sequencing before it becomes irreversible. Apple Health Technologies urges the Department to take that opportunity seriously, because the window for doing so is narrower than the RFI's framing suggests. The reimbursement and regulatory pathways being contemplated here will move quickly once finalized, and the institutions that build operational dependency on AI tools under those pathways will not quietly accept retroactive accountability requirements that disrupt workflows they have restructured at significant cost.⏎⏎⏎⏎One additional point that Apple Health Technologies believes the Department has not adequately considered: the behavioral health setting, which is the context for our affiliated practice pilot, presents accountability questions that are more complex than those in most other clinical settings, not less. Behavioral health patients are disproportionately represented among the demographic groups facing the highest risk of being harmed by algorithmic bias, facing the highest probability of lacking the resources to pursue legal redress when harm occurs, and most likely to experience the erosion of the human relationship at the center of their care as a distinct and serious harm in itself. The co-occurring condition complexity documented in our 847-encounter audit, where 63% of clients presented with conditions requiring elevated documentation complexity, is precisely the clinical profile that AI documentation tools are designed to serve. It is also precisely the clinical profile where accountability diffusion poses the greatest risk, because the clinical picture is complex, the margin for error is narrow,⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 7⏎⏎⏎⏎and the patient population has the least institutional power to demand answers in the event of an adverse outcome. The Department's RFI does not acknowledge this asymmetry, and any reimbursement framework that does not account for it will distribute the benefits of AI adoption toward efficient settings and the risks of AI adoption toward vulnerable ones.⏎⏎⏎⏎Apple Health Technologies appreciates the Department's attention to these comments and respectfully requests that the accountability assignment question be treated as a precondition for, rather than a consequence of, the reimbursement and regulatory actions this RFI contemplates. PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎⏎⏎Illumina works with 214 partner organizations across Virginia, including independent physician practices, community health systems, and rural critical access hospitals. Our partners are not opposed to AI adoption in clinical settings. What our Q3 2024 policy working group found, after documenting 34 discrete compliance questions submitted by network affiliates seeking guidance on AI liability, billing code applicability, and FDA oversight thresholds, is that HHS has created a regulatory vacuum that is being filled by administrators and vendors whose incentive structures are not aligned with patient care quality or workforce sustainability. None of those 34 questions could be resolved by reference to existing HHS guidance. That fact alone should give HHS pause before treating this RFI as primarily an acceleration exercise.⏎⏎⏎⏎The framing of this RFI concerns our working group. Any time a government department inquires about how to "accelerate adoption," it implies swiftness has become the overriding policy objective. Our partners are asking a different question: adoption of what, deployed how, and against whom? An internal 2024 poll covering our network partners revealed 68% are currently testing or reviewing AI-backed clinical decision support systems, though 79% of these respondents identified a lack of clear regulations as the main obstacle preventing complete integration. That ambiguity is real and we want HHS to address it. But the same ambiguity that prevents responsible deployment also prevents accountability when AI tools are used to surveil, evaluate, and pressure the clinicians who are supposed to be using them.⏎⏎⏎⏎Illumina < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎II. AI DEPLOYMENT AS A WORKFORCE HARM MECHANISM⏎⏎⏎⏎The data regarding this issue is definitively clear. Tools marketed as burnout-reduction solutions are being deployed in ways that generate new forms of burden on clinical staff. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology found in its 2023 Clinician Survey (ONC Data Brief No. 61, 2023 ) that EHR-integrated decision support tools are among the leading contributors to documentation burden, not reducers of it. A 2021 piece by Bates and coauthors published in npj Digital Medicine pinpointed a viable route for AI to alleviate clinical exhaustion, but specified that this outcome depends entirely on how tools are implemented and whether clinicians retain meaningful control over tool behavior. Shanafelt and colleagues, through a longitudinal study featured in Mayo Clinic Proceedings in 2022, observed clinical exhaustion metrics climbing steadily through 2020 regardless of extensive historical health IT spending, which should prompt some skepticism about vendor claims that the next generation of AI tools will deliver different results absent structural changes in deployment governance.⏎⏎⏎⏎What our network affiliates report is more direct. AI tools are being used to set productivity benchmarks that would not otherwise be justifiable, to monitor keystroke and task completion rates, and to generate performance reports that flow to administrators rather than to the clinicians themselves. The Economic Policy Institute documented this pattern in a 2023 working paper on algorithmic wage and productivity surveillance in health care settings, finding that surveillance tools were disproportionately deployed against nurses, medical assistants, and other non-physician clinical staff with limited bargaining power. National Nurses United echoed this sentiment in their 2023 policy brief regarding artificial intelligence threats, pointing out how AI-powered scheduling models were leveraged to rationalize lower staffing proportions, directly jeopardizing patient safety. The GAO highlighted in GAO-22-104629 how clinical AI introduces significant hazards that remain poorly grasped during the purchasing phase, noting that regulatory frameworks are lagging far behind the speed of implementation.⏎⏎⏎⏎According to the American Medical Association's 2023 Digital Medicine Practice Insights survey, under a third of physicians indicated they received meaningful consultation prior to the rollout of AI systems in their clinical environments. A 2020 article by Dzau and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine described clinician well-being as a patient safety issue, not a human resources issue. HHS should take that framing seriously here. When clinicians are excluded from procurement decisions, when AI tools increase rather than reduce cognitive and administrative load, and when productivity surveillance data is used to pressure staff into unsafe caseload ratios, the downstream effect is worse patient care. These dangers are already materializing in practice.⏎⏎⏎⏎Illumina < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎There is also the question of algorithmic bias, which compounds these workforce harms. The 2019 Science analysis by Obermeyer and colleagues showed how an extensively utilized population health model persistently undervalued the medical requirements of Black individuals, shifting the burden of these defective outputs onto the clinicians expected to rely on them. SEIU Healthcare's 2024 policy report on AI and the healthcare workforce documented that when biased AI tools generate incorrect recommendations, the burden of catching and correcting errors lands on frontline staff, not on the vendors who built the tools. The National Academy for State Health Policy's 2024 state survey on AI in health care workforce deployment found that only seven states had any statutory or regulatory requirement for worker consultation prior to AI deployment in health care settings. Virginia is not among them.⏎⏎⏎⏎III. WHAT HHS MUST REQUIRE⏎⏎⏎⏎Our working group is not asking HHS to slow AI adoption. We urge HHS to establish the regulatory environment necessary to ensure implementation actually yields the positive results the agency claims to seek. The following are preconditions, not suggestions:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. Compulsory input from clinical staff must serve as a prerequisite for any deployment framework sanctioned by HHS. This means documented consultation with clinical and administrative staff before procurement, not after go-live. Consultation with union representatives or elected staff councils where those bodies exist.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. A strict ban on relying on AI-derived productivity metrics as the central justification for workforce allocation, patient load distribution, or personnel reviews, unless there is an independent clinical audit of the core methodology alongside an accessible appeals mechanism for impacted employees.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. A mandate stating any AI system backed by government payment programs or official endorsements must transparently declare if it contains employee monitoring capabilities, detailing the exact data harvested, the recipients of this information, and the specific choices it influences. This disclosure must go to the clinicians using the tool, not only to the administrators who purchased it.⏎⏎⏎⏎4. A formal HHS guidance document addressing the 34-category compliance gap our working group documented, covering AI liability allocation, applicable billing codes, and FDA oversight thresholds for clinical decision support tools. Network affiliates cannot make responsible deployment decisions in the absence of this guidance, and the current vacuum is not neutral -- it benefits vendors and administrators who can proceed without accountability while clinicians bear the operational and safety consequences.⏎⏎⏎⏎Our organization will continue to track HHS's response to this RFI and the policy actions that follow. SYNTH-0019♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Robert Harris♔♔♔♔♔♔SUBMITTED TO HHS DOCKET: ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎Robert Harris, RN (ret.) < > Reno, Nevada⏎⏎MARKET STRUCTURE AND THE INCENTIVE PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a nurse I worked with on a cardiac step-down unit in Reno named Delia who spent close to forty minutes per shift sorting through medication alert noise from a clinical decision support system that hadn't been meaningfully updated in years. She caught a dangerous digoxin-digoxin toxicity interaction anyway, because Delia was Delia, but the system didn't help her catch it. What I think about now, retired and reading this RFI, is not that the technology was bad. It's that nobody in the procurement chain had a financial interest in making it better once it was installed. The hospital had sunk costs in the vendor. The vendor had a multi-year contract. The alert logic was proprietary. Nobody could touch it.⏎⏎That is the structural problem this RFI is not asking about.⏎⏎HHS frames this proceeding around acceleration. How do we move faster? What reimbursement barriers can we remove? What public-private partnerships can we build? These are reasonable operational questions, but they assume the direction of travel is correct, and I am genuinely not sure it is. The healthcare AI market is already highly concentrated. Gartner's 2023 market share analysis covering digital medical charting software (Report G00781234) documented that a small number of large vendors control the majority of installed EHR infrastructure in U.S. hospitals, and clinical AI products are increasingly sold as add-on modules to those same platforms. This means that "accelerating adoption" in practice means accelerating adoption of products built by or certified for compatibility with Epic, Oracle Cerner, and a handful of other incumbents. The switching costs for hospitals are enormous. Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh (2022) documented this explicitly in the context of clinical decision support systems, finding that vendor lock-in structurally prevents hospitals from replacing alert logic that is known to be poorly calibrated, because doing so would require renegotiating the underlying EHR contract. The alert fatigue problem Delia worked around every single night is, in part, a vendor lock-in problem. Accelerating deployment into that market structure does not fix the problem. It deepens it.⏎⏎THE CRADA AND REIMBURSEMENT QUESTIONS SPECIFICALLY⏎⏎The RFI asks about Cooperative Research and Development Agreements and reimbursement modernization as levers for adoption. I want to be direct about what concerns me here.⏎⏎CRADAs allow private companies to access federally funded research infrastructure and co-develop products, but the statutory framework permits the private partner to retain exclusive licensing rights to resulting intellectual property. In healthcare AI, where training data from public hospitals and Medicare populations is often the most valuable input to model development, this means the federal government can effectively subsidize the creation of proprietary clinical AI tools that are then sold back to the healthcare system at commercial rates. Dafny and Lee (2016) wrote about the dynamics of market concentration in healthcare in a different context, but the core observation applies: when large incumbents have preferential access to public resources and the ability to retain proprietary control over outputs, the result is not a competitive market. It is a transfer of publicly created value to private shareholders. I am not opposed to public-private collaboration in principle. I am opposed to collaboration structures that guarantee the benefits accrue to one party.⏎⏎On reimbursement: the GAO's 2022 report on AI in healthcare (GAO-22-104629) found that existing evidence on clinical AI safety and equity is thin, and that most published studies involve algorithmic tools tested on data from massive university-affiliated hospitals that are not representative of the specific demographic groups facing the highest risk of injury from biased models. The 2019 Science paper by Obermeyer and colleagues detailing algorithmic prejudice within a heavily utilized risk-assessment program revealed how the software consistently minimized the true medical needs of Black individuals. This alarming reality only came to light post-deployment, once the software was already active in millions of clinical interactions. Deciding if we should unlock payment avenues prior to proving a tool's safety and fairness involves much more than just engineering considerations. It is a values question, and HHS's current framing answers it implicitly in favor of speed.⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD ACTUALLY DO⏎⏎The following are specific asks, not general principles:⏎⏎1. Before any new reimbursement pathway opens for a clinical AI product, HHS should require prospective evidence of safety and equity performance across demographic subgroups, not retrospective validation on convenience samples. Beaulieu-Jones et al. (2021) documented in JAMA Network Open that the majority of published machine learning health research lacks external validation, which means the evidentiary base for most deployed tools is weaker than the regulatory posture currently requires.⏎⏎2. Any CRADA or public-private partnership involving clinical AI development should include a condition that models trained substantially on Medicare, Medicaid, or federally funded hospital data cannot be exclusively licensed. The federal government should retain a non-exclusive license with the right to sublicense to other healthcare organizations. This is not a radical ask. It is the kind of condition NIH has imposed in other research contexts.⏎⏎3. HHS should mandate interoperability standards for clinical AI outputs, not just for underlying EHR data. The ONC's 2023 data brief on health IT market concentration documented that interoperability barriers persist even where EHR data exchange has improved, because clinical AI modules often produce outputs in proprietary formats that cannot be ported to competing systems. If a hospital wants to replace a poorly performing AI triage tool with a better one, it should not have to renegotiate its entire EHR contract to do so. That is the Delia problem, and it is solvable through regulation.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I have mixed feelings about this submission. I spent thirty-one years as a cardiac nurse and I genuinely believe well-designed AI could make clinical care safer. SYNTH-0022♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Dorothy Rivera♔Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics♔♔♔♔♔Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics⏎Comment Submitted to HHS Docket: AI in Clinical Care RFI⏎Submitted by: Dorothy Rivera, Ph.D., Health Economist⏎< >⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎< >⏎I. THE FRAMING PROBLEM⏎The Department's Request for Information proceeds from an underlying assumption requiring direct examination before any specific policy questions are addressed: that administrative work in healthcare is a form of clerical processing, and that AI automation of such work is an efficiency gain with manageable, containable risks. This characterization is analytically wrong, and the policy recommendations that flow from it will cause measurable harm to patients — particularly to Medicaid-enrolled patients with complex chronic conditions, patients navigating publicly subsidized community clinics, and patients whose social circumstances are not captured in structured data. The Department should not accelerate the adoption of administrative AI in clinical care settings without first grappling with a substantial and largely ignored body of evidence indicating that the work being targeted for automation is not the kind of work that can be automated without systematic error propagation and corresponding harm to vulnerable populations.⏎The labor economics literature on skill misclassification provides highly applicable insights for this discussion. When organizations misclassify skilled, judgment-intensive labor as routine processing, they systematically underinvest in that labor, underpay the workers performing it, and eventually attempt to substitute cheaper inputs — including automated systems — for work that requires contextual reasoning and institutional knowledge. Michael Polanyi's foundational account of tacit knowledge (Polanyi, M., The Tacit Dimension, Doubleday, 1966) remains the most precise theoretical framework for understanding what is at stake: the knowledge required to navigate a patient through a complex prior authorization process, to identify that a referral is being routed to a specialist whose panel is de facto closed, or to recognize that a patient's stated address does not match their actual care-seeking geography is not the kind of knowledge that can be encoded in training data. It is acquired through practice, embedded in institutional context, and expressed through judgment that is invisible to the systems designed to replace it.⏎II. WHAT ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTHCARE WORK ACTUALLY IS⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎The RFI's framing of administrative burden as something to be reduced through automation conflates two distinct phenomena. There is genuine administrative waste — duplicative documentation requirements, redundant prior authorization processes, billing complexity generated by payer proliferation — and there is the skilled administrative labor that has grown up around those requirements precisely because human intermediaries are necessary to prevent the system's complexity from directly harming patients. Bhatt, D.L., and coauthors, published within Health Affairs (42(7), 934–943, 2023), documented that administrative burden in Medicaid-enrolled patients with complex chronic conditions is not reducible to paperwork volume; it is a function of the fragmentation of care coordination responsibilities across systems that do not communicate, and the labor that absorbs that fragmentation is performed by workers who have built tacit maps of those systems over years of practice.⏎Garg and Bhatt (Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law, 48(4), 511–537, 2023) conducted a mixed-methods analysis of care coordination labor in HRSA-funded neighborhood clinics and found that the care coordinators whose work was associated with the best patient outcomes were those with the longest institutional tenure — workers who knew which insurance representatives to call, which prior authorization pathways had informal workarounds, and which community resources were actually accessible to specific patient subpopulations. This is not knowledge that appears in any structured database. It cannot be extracted from EHR log data. Sinsky and colleagues (Journal of Medical Internet Research, 23(3), e24875, 2021) documented that EHR log data, even when analyzed systematically, captures only a fraction of the cognitive and coordinative labor physicians and support staff perform; the rest is invisible to the measurement instruments that would be used to train an AI system.⏎The Department's RFI asks specifically about administrative functions that could be automated to reduce burden on clinical staff. This is a reasonable question. The answer, however, requires distinguishing between the administrative functions that are genuinely repetitive and rule-bound — certain forms of data entry, appointment scheduling within constrained parameters, insurance eligibility queries with unambiguous responses — and the functions that appear repetitive but are in fact contextually complex: prior authorization review that requires understanding of a patient's actual functional status rather than their documented diagnosis, benefits counseling that depends on knowing which local social services are currently operational and which have waiting lists, and patient navigation that requires recognizing when a patient's stated preferences are being constrained by circumstances they have not disclosed. The failure to make this distinction is not a minor analytical oversight. It is the error that will produce the harms.⏎III. THE ERROR PROPAGATION PROBLEM⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎Ash, Berg, and Coiera, writing in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (11(2), 104–112, 2004), identified a category of IT-related errors they called "juxtaposition errors" — errors that occur when automated systems place information in unexpected locations or generate outputs that are technically correct but contextually wrong, and that human reviewers fail to catch because the automation creates an illusion of reliability. The same dynamic applies to administrative AI. When an AI system generates an eligibility determination or a prior authorization recommendation, the human workers who might otherwise have caught the error are removed from the process — or, in understaffed health systems, they are present but their review is cursory because the volume of AI-generated outputs exceeds their capacity for genuine scrutiny.⏎The GAO documented in its 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105526) that the failure modes of administrative AI systems are disproportionately concentrated in edge cases — patients with multiple comorbidities, patients whose records span multiple systems, patients whose social circumstances create mismatches between their documented characteristics and their actual care needs. These are precisely the patients for whom administrative intermediation is most valuable, and they are the individuals forced to shoulder the costs of systematic AI error. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's 2019 Science paper (366(6464), 447–453) examining demographic disparities within health management algorithms is the most widely cited demonstration of this dynamic, but its core finding — that algorithms trained on utilization data systematically underestimate the health needs of Black patients because utilization is a function of access rather than need — generalizes directly to any administrative AI system trained on historical claims data or EHR records that reflect decades of structural inequity in care delivery.⏎Virginia Eubanks, in Automating Inequality (St. Martin's Press, 2018), documented with high specificity the ways automated eligibility systems in public benefit programs generate incorrect determinations at rates that are invisible at the aggregate level but catastrophic for individual patients — and how the burden of correcting those errors falls disproportionately on the workers and patients who fundamentally lack the resources required to absorb it. The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration's automated eligibility system, which Eubanks analyzed in depth, produced a 54 percent error rate in its first year of operation. The errors were invisible to administrators reviewing aggregate accuracy metrics. They were visible only to the caseworkers and clients who had to navigate the correction process. This is the model the Department is proposing to extend to clinical care settings, and the analogy is not strained.⏎IV. THE WORKFORCE DIMENSION⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎The Department's framing of administrative AI as a solution to healthcare workforce shortages deserves specific attention, because it inverts the actual relationship. Donelan and colleagues, in a national survey published in Health Care Management Review (47(2), 88–97, 2022), found that health administration workforce shortages are concentrated in exactly the roles that require the deepest institutional knowledge — managing patient journeys, guiding clinical transitions, benefits counseling — and that those shortages are themselves a product of chronic underinvestment in these roles, which are systematically underpaid relative to their skill demands precisely because they have been misclassified as clerical rather than professional work. Automating these roles does not solve the shortage problem; it removes the skilled labor that was compensating for the shortage of other resources.⏎Himmelstein and Woolhandler, writing in the International Journal of Health Services (52(1), 1–9, 2022), documented that administrative work consumes approximately one-sixth of U.S. physicians' working hours, and that this burden is a primary driver of career dissatisfaction and early exit from clinical practice. This finding is frequently cited as a justification for administrative AI. The inference, however, does not follow. The administrative work that drives physician dissatisfaction is largely documentation and billing work — work that has been generated by payer complexity and regulatory requirements that could be reduced through policy change rather than automation. The clinical transition management and health system orientation work that is being targeted for AI substitution represents an entirely distinct classification, and conflating them produces a policy that automates the wrong things while leaving the actual sources of physician burden intact.⏎Shortell and Schmittdiel (Milbank Quarterly, 99(3), 712–741, 2021) analyzed AI implementation in integrated delivery systems and found that the organizations that achieved the best outcomes from administrative AI were those that used it as an augmentation tool for experienced coordinators — flagging cases for human review, surfacing relevant information, reducing search time — rather than as a substitution for human judgment. The organizations that attempted full substitution experienced what the authors called "coordination voids": situations in which no human worker had sufficient contextual knowledge to catch AI errors because the institutional knowledge had been allowed to atrophy as experienced clinical transition managers and healthcare navigators are displaced by AI systems. This represents an anticipated outcome resulting from skill misclassification, and it is the consequence toward which current HHS policy is oriented.⏎V. SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S REIMBURSEMENT QUESTIONS⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎The RFI asks how CMS reimbursement policies can be structured to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. This question, as posed, assumes that the primary obstacle to beneficial AI adoption is payment uncertainty, and that resolving that uncertainty will produce net benefits. The ACR survey data cited in various submissions to this docket — finding that 54 percent of radiology practices identify reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to broader AI adoption — is relevant but limited in its generalizability. Radiology AI for image analysis is a genuinely different category from administrative AI, for reasons that go directly to the tacit knowledge argument: image analysis AI is performing a pattern recognition task on structured, standardized inputs, and its error modes are visible and measurable in ways that administrative AI errors are not. The reimbursement framework appropriate for diagnostic imaging AI is not the framework appropriate for care coordination AI, and the Department should resist the temptation to treat the ACR findings as generalizable to administrative AI contexts.⏎The social determinants of health literature holds immediate applicability regarding the reimbursement design question. Artiga and Hinton (Kaiser Family Foundation Issue Brief, May 2018) documented that social circumstances account for approximately 30 to 55 percent of health outcomes, and that effective care navigation requires workers who can connect patients to social services, interpret patients' social circumstances in the context of their care plans, and advocate on behalf of patients whose circumstances are not legible to administrative systems. A reimbursement framework that rewards AI-mediated administrative efficiency will create incentives to substitute AI for the workers performing this function, and the patients whose care depends on that function are those whose social circumstances have the lowest probability of being captured in the structured data on which AI systems are trained. This is not a speculative risk. It is an expected byproduct resulting from the incentive structure the Department is proposing to create.⏎The specific reimbursement recommendations this comment offers are as follows:⏎1. CMS should require, as a condition of any AI-specific reimbursement pathway for administrative functions, that covered entities demonstrate that AI deployment has not reduced the number of FTE clinical transition or systems navigation staff below pre-deployment levels, adjusted for patient volume.⏎2. Any reimbursement framework for administrative AI should require prospective disclosure of the training data sources and demographic representativeness of AI systems used in eligibility, prior authorization, or care coordination functions, consistent with the concerns documented in Obermeyer et al. (2019).⏎3. CMS must fund an external evaluation of administrative AI error rates in Medicaid-enrolled populations before establishing any permanent reimbursement pathway. This assessment must heavily scrutinize the categories of edge-case errors documented in GAO-23-105526.⏎4. HHS should explicitly distinguish, in all forthcoming guidance, between administrative AI that augments human judgment and administrative AI that substitutes for it, and should apply different regulatory and reimbursement standards to each category.⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎The Department's RFI, to its credit, acknowledges that equity considerations must be central to AI adoption policy. However, the equity language in the RFI is largely aspirational and does not engage with the structural mechanisms through which administrative AI will produce inequitable outcomes. The equity problem is not primarily a problem of biased algorithms, though that is a real and documented concern. It is a problem of institutional knowledge atrophy: as experienced clinical transition managers and healthcare navigators are displaced by AI systems, the tacit knowledge they carried — knowledge of which community health workers serve which neighborhoods, which insurance representatives will accept informal appeals, which patients need a phone call rather than a patient portal message — disappears from the institution. It does not transfer to the AI system. It is simply gone. And the patients who depended on that knowledge are left with an automated system that is efficient in the aggregate and catastrophically inadequate in the specific cases that matter most.⏎The Department should not read this comment as an argument against AI in healthcare. The comment is an argument against a specific and consequential analytical error: the misclassification of skilled, contextually embedded administrative labor as clerical processing. Correcting that error does not require slowing AI adoption across the board. It requires the Department to apply far more analytical precision to the question of which administrative functions are genuinely automatable and which are not, and to build regulatory and reimbursement frameworks that reflect that precision rather than eliding it in the interest of an accelerationist posture that serves the interests of AI vendors more transparently than it serves the interests of patients.⏎Inquiries pertaining to these comments may be directed to the Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics at:⏎biomedinfo-policy@columbia.edu⏎Columbia University Department of Biomedical Informatics Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 7⏎The Department's timeline for finalizing guidance on this RFI — which, based on the Federal Register notice, anticipates action within the current fiscal year — does not allow adequate time for the kind of systematic evidence review that a policy of this consequence requires. The GAO's 2023 report explicitly recommended that HHS develop a comprehensive framework for evaluating AI safety and equity in administrative contexts before♔♔2026-02-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔academic_organization♔high♔angry♔New Mexico♔health economist♔60♔A 2024 ACR survey of 1,847 radiology practices found that 68% reported deploying at least one FDA-cleared AI algorithm in clinical workflows, yet 54% of those practices identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to broader adoption across additional imaging subspecialties. Our remarks do not attempt to tackle every topic raised in the RFI. We have chosen to focus specifically on two areas where we believe the Department's current framing carries structural risks that, if left unexamined, will produce harms that no amount of subsequent technical refinement will be able to remedy: the conceptual problem embedded in the Department's productivity-centered rationale for AI adoption, and the underappreciated clinical risk of automation bias and clinician skill atrophy in settings where relational diagnosis is already strained.⏎⏎⏎We want to be direct about where we are coming from. The National Health Council does not oppose AI in clinical care. Multiple groups within our membership coalition have actively supported AI-assisted tools in areas where the evidence base is credible and the equity implications have been examined. What we are opposing, with some care and some weariness, is the adoption of a policy framework that treats speed and throughput as the primary metrics of clinical value — and that positions AI as a mechanism for delivering more care transactions per unit time rather than as a tool that might, under the right conditions, support better clinical relationships.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎THE DATA OUR MEMBERS BRING TO THIS DISCUSSION⏎⏎⏎A 2024 poll distributed throughout our alliance of individuals affected by multiple sclerosis found that 68 percent of respondents reported delays of six months or more between symptom onset and confirmed diagnosis. In 43 percent of those cases, neurologist shortage was cited as the primary barrier. Our policy team's analysis of claims data from MS Navigator program participants found that individuals in rural and underserved communities waited an average of 14 months longer for disease-modifying therapy initiation compared to those in metropolitan areas. These are not abstractions. They represent a named, documentable population experiencing a specific, measurable harm that has persisted across multiple administrations and multiple rounds of well-intentioned policy intervention.⏎⏎⏎We raise this data not to suggest that AI cannot help. A 2023 research collaboration involving 22 MS specialty centers documented that AI-assisted MRI lesion detection tools reduced radiologist review time by approximately 30 percent while improving inter-rater diagnostic consistency (National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Barriers to Timely Diagnosis and Treatment Initiation in MS: Findings from the 2024 Navigator Program Claims Analysis, Internal Policy Report, Washington, DC: NMSS, 2024). That is a meaningful finding. Our members read it with genuine interest. But the same members who would benefit from faster lesion detection are also members who have told us, consistently and over many years, that the most consequential failures in their care were not failures of imaging sensitivity. They were failures of listening. They were encounters in which a clinician, working under time pressure, did not sit long enough with an ambiguous symptom history to recognize that what sounded like anxiety or fatigue or conversion disorder was, in fact, the early presentation of a demyelinating process.⏎⏎⏎Consider what that encounter actually looks like. A woman — call her a composite of several Navigator participants from rural Iowa — arrives at a general practitioner visit having rehearsed, for weeks, how to describe what is happening to her body. She has a list. She is articulate. But the symptoms she is describing are intermittent, and they are strange, and they do not map cleanly onto any single complaint: a patch of numbness that comes and goes, a few weeks of blurred vision in one eye that resolved before she could get an ophthalmology appointment, fatigue that she has been told is depression. She has maybe fifteen minutes. The clinician is working from a dashboard that has already flagged her as low-acuity based on her age and her prior visit history. There is no AI failure in that room. The AI did exactly what it was designed to do. The failure is that the relational conditions necessary for her to be heard — time, attention, the specific human capacity to hold ambiguity without prematurely resolving it — are absent. Productivity optimization, whether achieved through AI or through any other mechanism, does not create those conditions. In many configurations, it actively forecloses them.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎National Health Council Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎THE CONCEPTUAL PROBLEM WITH "PRODUCTIVITY" AS A POLICY FRAME⏎⏎⏎The RFI uses the language of acceleration, adoption, and productivity with a consistency that is worth examining as a substantive policy choice rather than as neutral description. Abraham Verghese wrote in 2008 that the displacement of clinical attention from the patient's body and narrative to the electronic record represented not merely an efficiency trade-off but a transformation in the ontology of the clinical encounter — a shift in what medicine understood itself to be doing (Verghese A, "Culture shock — patient as icon, icon as patient," New England Journal of Medicine, 2008;359(26):2748–2751). That observation is seventeen years old and has only become more relevant. The comprehensive literature evaluation published by Kelley and colleagues in PLOS ONE in 2014 found, across various randomized trials, that the caliber of the interpersonal connection between provider and patient exerted a statistically significant impact on medical results independent of the mechanical execution of the care delivered — an effect size that the authors characterized as clinically meaningful (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., "The impact of provider-patient dynamics on medical results: a comprehensive literature evaluation and statistical synthesis of randomized therapeutic studies," PLOS ONE, 2014;9(4):e94207). Hojat and colleagues, in a study published in Academic Medicine in 2011, discovered that the compassion metrics of doctors proved to be autonomous predictors of medical results in diabetic patients — hemoglobin A1c levels and LDL control — after controlling for a range of confounders (Hojat M, Louis DZ, Markham FW, et al., "Physicians' compassion levels and therapeutic results for diabetic patients," Academic Medicine, 2011;86(3):359–364). These are not soft findings about patient satisfaction. They are outcome data. The relationship is part of the treatment.⏎⏎⏎When HHS frames AI adoption primarily in terms of what it can do for provider productivity — reducing documentation burden, accelerating imaging review, streamlining prior authorization — it is making a conceptual choice about what clinical care is for. It is treating care as a series of discrete tasks, each of which can be optimized in isolation. The National Health Council does not believe that framing is accurate, and we do not believe it is neutral. It carries downstream policy consequences. If the measure of a successful AI deployment is that it increased the number of patients seen per hour, or reduced time-to-diagnosis in aggregate, or decreased documentation minutes per encounter, then any AI system that achieves those metrics will be considered successful — regardless of what it did to the quality of clinical attention in the room, regardless of what it did to the clinician's capacity to sit with diagnostic ambiguity, and regardless of whether it helped or harmed the specific patient whose presentation did not fit the training distribution.⏎⏎⏎Eric Topol, in a widely cited 2019 paper in Nature Medicine, argued that AI's most important potential contribution to medicine was not replacing human judgment but liberating clinicians from administrative burden so that they could be more present with patients — more human, not less (Topol EJ, "High-performance medicine: merging biological and machine intelligence," Nature Medicine, 2019;25(1):44–56). We find that argument genuinely compelling. But the policy conditions necessary to realize that vision are not the same as the policy conditions being proposed here. Liberating clinicians to be more present requires deliberate structural choices about how AI-assisted time savings are reinvested. If the time saved by AI documentation tools is immediately absorbed by increased patient volume — which is the logical consequence of a productivity-optimization framework — then the patient in the room gains nothing. The clinician gains nothing except a different kind of pressure. And the relational substrate of the clinical encounter continues to erode.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM⏎⏎⏎The National Health Council wants to raise a concern that we believe is receiving inadequate attention in the current policy discussion: automation bias and the slow-motion atrophy of clinical skills that AI intermediation, at scale, will probably generate within the clinician workforce. This is not a speculative concern. It is documented in the human factors literature with considerable specificity.⏎⏎⏎A 2012 comprehensive literature synthesis by Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association demonstrated robust proof spanning multiple fields that human operators exposed to automated decision support systems over time exhibited increased rates of error in the specific judgment tasks that the automation was designed to assist — not because the automation performed poorly, but because sustained reliance on automated recommendations degraded operators' independent judgment capacity (Goddard K, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC, "Automation bias: a comprehensive appraisal detailing prevalence, mediating factors, and mitigation strategies," Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 2012;19(1):121–127). Parasuraman and Manzey, writing in Human Factors in 2010, described this as a complacency effect that is particularly pronounced in high-stakes, high-cognitive-load environments — precisely the environments that characterize clinical care (Parasuraman R, Manzey DH, "Complacency and cognitive skew in the manual operation of automated systems: an attentional integration," Human Factors, 2010;52(3):381–410). Cabitza and colleagues, in a 2017 JAMA commentary, raised the specific concern that predictive computational models deployed clinically could produce unintended feedback loops in which clinician behavior adapted to algorithmic recommendations in ways that were difficult to detect and difficult to reverse (Cabitza F, Rasoini R, Gensini GF, "Unintended consequences of deploying predictive computational models within healthcare," JAMA, 2017;318(6):517–518).⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎National Health Council Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎In the context of MS diagnosis specifically, this concern has a particular shape. The diagnostic pathway for MS already requires a high degree of clinical judgment about symptom history, temporal dissemination, and the integration of findings that are individually nonspecific. A clinician who has spent years developing the capacity to hold that ambiguity — to recognize that a patient's odd sensory complaints and a prior episode of optic neuritis, taken together and over time, constitute a pattern — is exercising a form of clinical reasoning that is deeply experiential and that atrophies without practice. If AI systems begin to carry more and more of that pattern-recognition work, the clinicians who remain in the diagnostic chain will have had less opportunity to develop the underlying judgment. This is a slow harm. It will not appear in any five-year outcome study of a specific AI deployment. But it is the kind of harm that becomes visible only after the policy window to address it has closed.⏎⏎⏎Shortliffe and Sepúlveda, writing in JAMA in 2018, noted that the integration of AI into clinical decision support required careful attention to the ways in which algorithmic recommendations interacted with clinician cognition — and specifically warned that deployment contexts that did not preserve clinician engagement with the reasoning process, rather than just the output, risked producing a workforce that was dependent on tools it did not understand and could not critically evaluate (Shortliffe EH, Sepúlveda MJ, "Clinical decision support in the era of artificial intelligence," JAMA, 2018;320(21):2199–2200). That warning has not been adequately operationalized in the current RFI's framing. The RFI inquires about steps HHS might take to hasten implementation. However, it fails to ask, with equivalent seriousness, what HHS should require of AI deployments to ensure that the clinicians using them retain the independent judgment necessary to catch the cases where the AI is wrong.⏎⏎⏎The social justice aspect surrounding this problem compounds its seriousness. In a 2019 Science article, Ziad Obermeyer, Brian Powers, Christine Vogeli, and Sendhil Mullainathan revealed how a proprietary predictive model implemented extensively for directing medical resources consistently minimized the actual clinical requirements of Black patients — not because of any explicit design choice, but because the training data used cost as a proxy for need, and cost was itself a racially structured variable (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S, "Dissecting demographic disparities within a tool for population health administration," Science, 2019;366(6464):447–453). The individuals carrying the highest probability of being harmed by that bias were also the people possessing the lowest chances of holding the relational capital with a clinician to advocate for a different recommendation. In a policy environment that is accelerating AI adoption without requiring demonstrated equity outcomes, that pattern will repeat. It will repeat in MS. It will repeat in every condition where the training data reflects historical disparities in access and diagnosis.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎National Health Council Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING THE RFI'S REIMBURSEMENT QUESTIONS⏎⏎⏎The RFI inquires, alongside various other topics, what reimbursement changes CMS and HHS could make to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings. The National Health Council wants to document our apprehension about the structure of that question before attempting to answer it. The question presupposes that the barrier to AI adoption is primarily financial — that if reimbursement structures were adjusted to support AI use, adoption would follow, and outcomes would improve. We are not confident that premise is correct, and we are concerned that reimbursement incentives designed around adoption rates will reward deployment without requiring evidence that deployment is producing better care for the patients who are most disadvantaged.⏎⏎⏎Dzau and Balatbat, writing in The Lancet in 2021, argued that the future of health care delivery required not merely technological adoption but a fundamental restructuring of incentive systems to align with patient-centered and equity-centered outcomes (Dzau VJ, Balatbat CA, "Future of health and health care: implications for academic health systems," Lancet, 2021;397(10270):259–261). That argument applies directly here. Reimbursement structures that reward AI use without tying that reimbursement to demonstrated outcomes for specific patient populations will create exactly the wrong incentive: to deploy AI where it is easiest to deploy and where the financial return is clearest, not where the clinical need is greatest.⏎⏎⏎The National Health Council would specifically ask HHS to consider the following structural requirements before any reimbursement incentive for AI use in clinical care is established:⏎⏎⏎1. Demonstrated equity outcomes: Any AI system for which reimbursement is sought must be accompanied by forward-looking performance metrics separated according to racial identity, ethnic background, geography, disability status, and socioeconomic tier. The absence of demonstrated harm to specific populations is not equivalent to demonstrated benefit.⏎⏎⏎2. Relational outcome measurement: Reimbursement frameworks should include measures of patient-reported experience that capture whether the AI-assisted encounter preserved or degraded the relational qualities of care — including whether patients felt heard, whether their concerns were addressed without premature closure, and whether the clinician appeared to be engaging with them as a person rather than a data set. Bickmore and Paasche-Orlow documented in 2012 that health information technology deployments frequently failed to account for the ways in which technology intermediation affected patient trust and engagement, particularly in demographics possessing restricted medical comprehension (Bickmore TW, Paasche-Orlow MK, "The role of information technology in health literacy research," American Journal of Health Behavior, 2012;36(5):744–752). Reimbursement structures that do not require this kind of evidence will systematically underprice relational harm.⏎⏎⏎3. Clinician judgment preservation requirements: Any reimbursement framework for AI-assisted clinical decision support should require that the deployment context preserve meaningful clinician engagement with the diagnostic reasoning process — not merely the output — and should require periodic documentation of how the AI system's recommendations are being critically evaluated in practice, not simply accepted.⏎⏎⏎4. Pre-deployment patient community review: Before any AI system qualifies to receive financial coverage under a CMS or HHS incentive program, the system's evaluation framework — the criteria by which it will be assessed as safe and effective — should be co-designed with patient communities who are likely to be affected by its deployment. Not reviewed by. Co-designed with. The difference matters. Post-deployment retrofitting of equity criteria has consistently produced inadequate protections because the most consequential design choices have already been made.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎National Health Council Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎The National Health Council recognizes that implementing our proposed prerequisites might decelerate the adoption timeline that the RFI appears to contemplate. We want to be honest about that trade-off rather than paper over it. For the population we represent — people living with MS, many of them already waiting 14 months longer than their metropolitan counterparts for disease-modifying therapy, many of them having spent years being told their symptoms were psychosomatic — the prospect of faster access to AI-assisted diagnosis is genuinely appealing. We are not indifferent to that prospect. But we have been in this policy space long enough to know what happens when a technology is deployed at scale before the equity and relational evidence base is established. The technology becomes infrastructure. The harms become normalized. The populations who were harmed most have the least leverage to demand correction.⏎⏎⏎We are also aware that some of what we are asking for does not yet have a fully developed methodological apparatus. How exactly does one measure whether a clinical encounter preserved the relational conditions necessary for diagnostic accuracy? How does one prospectively study clinician skill atrophy across a workforce of hundreds of thousands? These are genuinely hard methodological questions, and we do not pretend otherwise. But the fact that measurement is difficult is not a reason to deploy without measurement. It is a reason to invest in developing the measurement frameworks before deployment, not after. HHS has the research infrastructure and the convening authority to do that work. The National Health Council would strongly support a dedicated research initiative, potentially coordinated through AHRQ and PCORI in addition to ASTP/ONC, focused specifically on developing patient-centered and relational outcome metrics for AI-assisted care — metrics that could then be incorporated into the reimbursement and evaluation frameworks that the RFI is contemplating.⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎National Health Council Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON WHAT WE ARE NOT SAYING⏎⏎⏎Because the argument we are making is sometimes misread as technological conservatism or as opposition to innovation, we want to be explicit about what the National Health Council is not saying. We are not saying that AI has no role in clinical care. We are not saying that AI-assisted MRI lesion detection, to take the example most directly relevant to our members, should be withheld pending some indefinite accumulation of evidence. We are not saying that the neurologist shortage in rural Iowa is not a real crisis that deserves urgent policy attention.⏎⏎⏎What we are saying is that the policy frame matters. A framework built around productivity and adoption rates will produce a different set of outcomes than a framework built around relational quality and equity. Both frameworks can accommodate AI. But only one of them is likely to produce an AI-assisted health care system that is actually better for the people who have historically been most poorly served by the existing system. The RFI, as written, is oriented toward the first framework. Our comments are an argument for the second.⏎⏎⏎We would also note, with some directness, that the organizations best positioned to advocate for the second framework are patient advocacy organizations — not because patients are more morally worthy than clinicians or researchers or technology developers, but because patients are the only stakeholders in this ecosystem who cannot exit the system when it fails them. Clinicians can leave practices. Vendors can pivot to other markets. Payers can restructure their networks. Patients, particularly patients with serious chronic conditions like MS, cannot simply choose not to need care. That asymmetry should be structurally reflected in how HHS structures the regulatory paradigms guiding AI adoption, including the co-design requirement we have outlined above.⏎⏎⏎The National Health Council appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments. We are available to discuss any of the concerns we have raised, and we would welcome the opportunity to participate in any stakeholder engagement process that HHS convenes as it develops its AI policy framework. Please direct any subsequent inquiries regarding this submission to Carol Harris, Policy Director, at carol.harris@nationalhealthcouncil.org or by mail at the address above.⏎⏎⏎We do want to flag one logistical concern before closing: several of our member organizations have asked whether HHS intends to release a summary of RFI comments received and, if so, on what timeline and through which office. I have spent six years as her primary caregiver, and what that experience taught me is not that individual clinicians are failing, it is that the architecture of clinical information fails patients at the moments they are most vulnerable. I want to be precise about what I am asking HHS to consider, because I am not opposed to AI in clinical settings in principle. What I am opposed to is the framing of this RFI, which asks how to accelerate adoption rather than whether the current market structure can support acceleration without transferring substantial value from patients and health systems to a small number of incumbent technology vendors.⏎⏎⏎⏎ON MARKET CONCENTRATION AND VENDOR LOCK-IN⏎⏎⏎⏎The structural problem is this. As Gee and Bhatt documented in Health Affairs in 2023, consolidation in health IT has already produced a market where a handful of large EHR vendors control the data infrastructure that any AI product must interface with. Dafny and Lee made a similar argument in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2022, noting that AI markets in healthcare are not competitive in any meaningful sense because the switching costs embedded in EHR integration create durable lock-in that insulates poor-performing products from accountability. HHS's proposed reimbursement modernization and public-private partnerships, including CRADAs, will by their nature benefit organizations capable of navigating CMS billing structures and ONC certification programs, which means they benefit large incumbents. The information blocking provisions at 45 CFR Part 171, finalized in the 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 rulemaking, were supposed to address some of this, and Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer's 2017 Milbank Quarterly analysis showed that information blocking was widespread and structurally incentivized long before that rule was finalized. I am not confident the rule changed the underlying incentive architecture. The FTC's October 2023 report on AI and digital health markets echoed this exact sentiment, finding that concentration in health data access gives large vendors a durable competitive advantage that regulatory frameworks are not currently equipped to address. Schulte and Fry's reporting for Kaiser Health News in 2019 documented how EHR vendor contracts with health systems routinely included provisions that limited transparency and accountability, and I see no structural reason why AI contracts would be different.⏎⏎⏎⏎What I would ask HHS to specifically address:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. What procurement guardrails will apply to CRADAs to prevent exclusive commercial arrangements⏎⏎⏎⏎Obermeyer et al.'s 2019 Science paper detailing how a heavily utilized algorithmic tool for managing large patient groups discriminated against minority patients is the clearest example I know of what happens when a product reaches scale before its performance has been♔♔2026-02-28T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-28T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔1♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Virginia♔caregiver♔66♔When my wife Margaret was admitted to Fairfax Inova for her third cardiac episode in eighteen months, the attending hospitalist spent roughly four minutes with her before a shift change handed her care to someone who had never met her.
