SYNTH-0025♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Charles King♔American Society of Clinical Oncology♔♔♔♔♔American Society of Clinical Oncology⏎2318 Mill Road, Suite 800⏎Alexandria, VA 22314⏎⏎June 17, 2024⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Attention: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care [Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001]⏎⏎---⏎⏎The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) submits the following comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. ASCO represents more than 45,000 oncology professionals and maintains an active research policy function that, in collaboration with the Dental Standards Institute's national quality network, produced a 2024 survey of 1,847 dental and clinical practices evaluating AI-assisted diagnostic tools. The findings from that work — formally presented to DSI's 42-member Clinical Technology Advisory Panel in March 2024 — inform the concerns raised here. ASCO does not oppose AI development in medicine. What ASCO opposes, with considerable conviction, is the underlying premise built into this RFI's framework: the notion that the primary challenge is adoption speed, and that regulatory and reimbursement levers exist to solve an essentially logistical problem.⏎⏎The RFI asks what HHS can do to "accelerate" AI adoption. That word — and the phrase "enhance productivity" appearing elsewhere in the Department's framing — is worth pausing over. Productivity is a manufacturing concept. It measures units of output per unit of input, and it is genuinely useful when applied to supply chains, software deployment, or vaccine distribution logistics. It is not a clinical concept. Medicine is not organized around throughput. At its core, clinical medicine is organized around the encounter between a person in distress and another person trained to interpret, respond to, and accompany that distress. When HHS frames the challenge as one of productivity, it has already decided what medicine is for. ASCO believes that decision deserves to be contested.⏎⏎ASCO'S EMPIRICAL STARTING POINT⏎⏎The DSI survey data are worth stating plainly, because they complicate the adoption narrative HHS has constructed. Of the 1,847 practices surveyed, 61% had evaluated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic instrument over the preceding 18 months. Less than 23% of these respondents managed to seamlessly weave these digital systems into their daily medical operations. When practices were asked to identify barriers, 78% cited reimbursement uncertainty and the absence of validated performance standards as the two leading obstacles. A subsequent analysis of insurance claim adjudication data across 14 state markets found that AI-assisted radiographic findings are rejected or manually reviewed at a rate 3.4 times higher than conventional diagnostics. (Dental Standards Institute, 2024.⏎⏎ASCO raises these figures not to argue that reimbursement reform is unimportant — it is — but to observe that the practices in this survey were not waiting for permission to adopt AI. They were trying. The gap between evaluation and integration is not primarily a regulatory gap. It reflects something the RFI has not adequately named: a legitimate clinical skepticism about what these tools actually do to the clinical encounter, separate from what they do to diagnostic throughput.⏎⏎WHAT THE RFI'S FRAMING OBSCURES⏎⏎The RFI is structured as an open inquiry, but it has an ideological architecture. The questions it asks are questions about barriers to adoption, reimbursement alignment, and regulatory streamlining. The questions it does not ask include: What is lost when clinical reasoning is mediated by algorithmic recommendation? How should we measure the therapeutic value of the unmediated clinical encounter? At what point does efficiency become a form of clinical harm?⏎⏎These are not abstract questions. Michael Balint's foundational work, The Doctor, His Patient and the Illness (1957), established that the bond between medical provider and the person seeking care acts as its own pharmacological agent — that the quality of the clinical encounter has measurable effects on patient outcomes independent of any technical intervention. A 2014 comprehensive review of clinical experiments by Kelley and colleagues (PLOS ONE, 9(4), e94207) corroborated this point, demonstrating that the interpersonal connection between doctors and those they treat delivers statistically significant and meaningful health benefits for numerous distinct medical ailments. Zulman and colleagues, writing in JAMA in 2020 (323(1), 70–81), documented specific clinician behaviors — genuine presence, attentive listening, explicit acknowledgment of patient concerns — that drive this effect. These are behaviors that are structurally vulnerable to AI intermediation, because they depend on the clinician's full cognitive attention being directed at the patient rather than at a screen displaying algorithmic output.⏎⏎Eric Topol, who is hardly a skeptic of AI in medicine, acknowledged in his 2019 Nature Medicine paper (25(1), 44–56) that the deepest opportunity AI offers is not to replace human judgment but to restore time for the interpersonal and empathetic aspects of providing medical treatment. That framing inverts HHS's productivity logic. Topol's argument is that AI should be used to give clinicians more time for the relational work that algorithms cannot do. HHS's RFI, by contrast, treats the clinical encounter as a site of efficiency optimization. ASCO would suggest those are genuinely different visions of what medicine should become.⏎⏎ASCO Comments < > HHS AI RFI 2024 < > Page 2⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM AND AUTOMATION BIAS⏎⏎There is a second concern that the RFI's framing elides. When clinicians are repositioned as supervisors of algorithmic outputs rather than primary reasoners, their capacity for independent clinical judgment does not remain stable. It atrophies. This is not speculation. The automation bias literature, established by Tversky and Kahneman's work on cognitive heuristics (Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131, 1974) and extended specifically to clinical decision support contexts by Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt in their 2012 systematic review (Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 121–127), demonstrates that clinicians who rely on algorithmic recommendations over time show measurable declines in standalone diagnostic precision alongside a distinct inclination to blindly trust computer-generated recommendations despite those suggestions being factually wrong. Goddard and colleagues determined that the tendency to over-rely on automated systems cannot be reliably offset through specialized instruction or years of medical practice. It is a structural feature of human-machine collaboration, not a correctable individual failing.⏎⏎ASCO does not raise this to argue that clinical decision support systems (CDSS) have no value. They do.  But the RFI asks HHS to design reimbursement and regulatory frameworks that will push AI into clinical workflows at scale, and it does not ask how those frameworks should account for the deskilling that will follow. Hartzband and Groopman, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 (382(26), 2485–2487), argued that the progressive digitization of clinical work — including the documentation burden imposed by EHRs — has already contributed to a form of clinical depersonalization that is measurably associated with physician burnout and reduced quality of care. Wachter and Goldsmith made a parallel argument in the Harvard Business Review in March 2018, noting that EHR design optimized for billing and compliance rather than clinical reasoning has degraded the quality of clinical thinking in ways that are difficult to reverse. AI adoption that follows the same logic will compound these effects.⏎⏎Consider a concrete example, and ASCO acknowledges this is not an oncology case but it is illustrative. A 74-year-old patient presents with pain she cannot localize or articulate clearly — she says it moves, she says it is sometimes sharp and sometimes not, she trails off mid-sentence. Her chart is unremarkable. An AI-assisted diagnostic tool, trained on population-level pattern recognition, flags nothing of clinical significance. But the clinician, watching her shift in her chair, noticing that her daughter in the corner of the room has not made eye contact since they sat down, recognizing a quality of guardedness that does not match the apparent triviality of the complaint — that clinician is reading a different document than the algorithm is. The question HHS has not asked is: what happens to that clinician's capacity to read that document after five years of deferring to computer-generated conclusions that are, on average, more accurate than individual human judgment? The answer, per Goddard et al. and the broader literature on system over-reliance, is that the capacity degrades. And it degrades in a way that no reimbursement model can detect, because the harm is not in the cases where the algorithm is right. It is in the cases where the algorithm is wrong and the clinician no longer has the independent judgment to catch it.⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY CONCERNS AND ASKS⏎⏎ASCO addresses two specific areas raised in the RFI — reimbursement alignment and performance standard development — and offers the following observations:⏎⏎Regarding reimbursement alignment:⏎⏎1. HHS should not extend value-based care reimbursement incentives to AI-assisted clinical tools unless those tools have demonstrated what ASCO proposes to call "relational safety" — a documented absence of statistically significant negative effects on the quality of the interpersonal connection between doctors and those they treat as measured by validated instruments, not merely diagnostic accuracy or workflow efficiency metrics.⏎⏎2. The 3.4-times higher rejection rate for AI-assisted radiographic findings documented in the DSI claims data (2024) reflects a real market signal. Rather than resolving that signal exclusively through coding reform, HHS should treat it as evidence that payers, too, are uncertain about what these tools produce. Resolving that uncertainty requires prospective clinical evidence, not accelerated reimbursement pathways.⏎⏎3. Bickmore, Pfeifer, and Jack demonstrated in 2009 (Proceedings of SIGCHI, 1265–1274) that even virtual agent interactions can produce relational effects — some positive, some not — depending on design. This suggests that relational impact is measurable and that measurement frameworks are feasible. HHS should require them.⏎⏎Regarding performance standards:⏎⏎o The ONC Health IT Strategic Plan 2024–2030 articulates interoperability and patient-centered care as co-equal federal priorities. ASCO urges HHS and ASTP/ONC to ensure that AI performance standards developed under 45 CFR Part 170 certification requirements include explicit relational safety criteria, not only technical performance benchmarks.⏎⏎o Verghese, Shah, and Harrington argued in JAMA in 2018 (319(1), 19–20) that what clinical AI most needs is not better algorithms but a governing humanistic framework. ASCO endorses that argument as a policy matter. Performance standards that measure only sensitivity, specificity, and processing speed are incomplete standards.⏎⏎o ASCO recommends that HHS convene a dedicated working group — including practicing clinicians, medical sociologists, and patient advocates, not only informaticists and engineers — to develop relational safety metrics before any AI reimbursement incentive program is finalized.⏎⏎ASCO Comments < > HHS AI RFI 2024 < > Page 3⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RFI'S STRUCTURAL ASSUMPTION⏎⏎ASCO wants to be precise about the nature of its objection, because it is easy to misread a comment like this one as generalized technophobia or as a defense of clinical guild interests. It is neither. ASCO's member oncologists use AI-assisted imaging analysis, genomic sequencing tools, and predictive models routinely. The concern here is not with AI as a technical category. The concern is with a federal policy document that has embedded a particular answer — faster is better, adoption is the goal, productivity is the measure — inside a question that purports to be open. The RFI's question is "how do we accelerate adoption?" It is not "should we accelerate adoption, and under what conditions, and at what cost to what values?" That is a narrower question than the one medicine requires.⏎⏎The ONC Health IT Strategic Plan 2024–2030 is, in several places, more careful than this RFI. It acknowledges that health IT must be "person-centered" and that technology adoption must be evaluated against patient outcomes, not only system efficiency. ASCO urges HHS to carry that more careful framing into whatever policy actions follow from this comment period. The 45 CFR Part 170 certification framework is a meaningful lever, and ASCO believes it can be used to require relational safety evidence as a condition of certification — but only if HHS is willing to define clinical performance to include the quality of the human encounter, not only the technical accuracy of the diagnostic output.⏎⏎The DSI survey data show that 77% of practices that evaluated AI tools chose not to permanently adopt them into their daily medical operations. HHS has framed that as a problem to be solved. SYNTH-0027♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Betty Gonzalez♔Association of American Indian Physicians♔♔♔♔♔ASSOCIATION OF AMERICAN INDIAN PHYSICIANS⏎Public Comment — HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎Submitted by: Betty Gonzalez, Policy Director⏎⏎AAIP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎The Association of American Indian Physicians (AAIP) submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care. The framing of this RFI is not neutral. The language of "acceleration," "modernized reimbursement," and "public-private partnership" is vendor roadmap language, not public health policy language, and this Department should be held accountable for the distinction. Before HHS moves one inch toward the reimbursement changes and Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs) sketched in this document, it must reckon with the structural reality that the companies positioned to benefit most from this regulatory agenda are the same companies with the lobbying resources to shape it. AAIP is not interested in pretending otherwise.⏎⏎A 2024 Texas Medical Association survey of 1,800 actively practicing physicians found that 74% of those already using AI-assisted clinical decision support tools reported significant uncertainty about liability exposure when acting on AI-generated recommendations. That number should stop this Department cold. These are not theoretical concerns. Practice administrators across Texas's regional society network pointed to a lack of uniform payment structures as the single greatest structural barrier to sustained AI adoption, with rural and independent practices taking the worst of it. That pattern is not accidental. This is the expected outcome when major EHR vendors and technology companies are permitted to operate as the de facto architects of clinical AI infrastructure. As Bresnick (2023) documented using KLAS market share data, the top EHR vendors control approximately 75% of the hospital market. When reimbursement frameworks get built around the workflows those vendors have already embedded, smaller and potentially better-performing entrants never get a fair entry point. The competitive pressure HHS claims to be generating evaporates before it starts.⏎⏎AAIP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎GOVERNANCE AND ADMINISTRATIVE HURDLES — THE QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎Regarding the RFI's questions on governance frameworks and administrative barriers to AI adoption: The Department is directing its inquiries to the wrong parties. The real decision-makers shaping AI adoption in clinical settings are not clinicians or patients. They are vendor sales teams and EHR integration managers operating inside proprietary contract structures that are almost entirely invisible to public scrutiny. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer (2017) documented how information blocking by EHR vendors systematically undermined interoperability goals that federal policy had nominally endorsed. The same structural dynamic is at work here. Once an AI tool is embedded in an EHR workflow, switching costs become prohibitive (Gans & Merrell, 2022), and the "competition" HHS is hoping to encourage collapses into a captive market. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology's own 2023 Report to Congress acknowledged persistent interoperability gaps that concentrated market power in incumbent vendors. HHS knows this. The failure to address it directly in this RFI is a choice.⏎⏎AAIP's specific concerns on this dimension include:⏎⏎1. AI tools trained on non-representative patient populations will reproduce and amplify existing health disparities. Obermeyer et al. (2019) revealed how a prevalent proprietary model routinely evaluated Black patients as having lower health risks than they actually had, stemming from racially biased training data. American Indian and Alaska Native patients face analogous risks, and AAIP has seen no credible commitment from HHS to require demographic performance audits as a condition of reimbursement eligibility.⏎⏎2. The CRADA and public-private partnership model proposed here will transfer publicly subsidized research value into proprietary products licensed back to health systems at profit. Mazzucato (2018) has made this argument with precision in the context of pharmaceutical and technology sectors generally — the public bears innovation risk while private actors capture innovation reward. We see no justifiable policy basis to replicate that arrangement in federally funded healthcare AI.⏎⏎3. Reimbursement complexity as currently structured advantages large incumbents. Kesselheim, Avorn, and Sarpatwari (2016) showed how billing and coverage complexity in pharmaceutical markets consistently advantaged established players over new entrants. The same dynamic will operate in AI reimbursement unless HHS builds explicit structural protections for small and independent practices, and for safety-net providers serving American Indian communities.⏎⏎4. Vendor-controlled post-deployment monitoring cannot generate independent accountability. Cohen et al. (2020) noted in their analysis of the European AI strategy that self-regulatory models in health AI consistently failed to surface safety-relevant performance degradation. HHS should be embarrassed to propose monitoring frameworks that rely on the same commercial entities whose financial interests run counter to disclosure.⏎⏎AAIP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The provider consolidation literature is also relevant here. Gee and Gurwitz (2019) and Dafny and Lee (2016) both documented how market concentration in health systems drives up costs without improving quality. AI adoption pathways that reward scale and penalize independent or tribal health program operators will accelerate that consolidation. Rai (2019) raises additional concerns about intellectual property frameworks that allow private actors to lock up AI-assisted clinical tools behind patent thickets, further restricting access for resource-constrained providers.⏎⏎AAIP Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎NUMBERED RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎1. HHS must halt any payment rule modifications that provide preferential benefit to incumbent EHR vendors until an independent market concentration analysis is completed and published for public comment.⏎⏎2. Any CRADA or public-private partnership involving patient data or federally funded AI research must include binding public-interest licensing conditions, including price caps and mandatory access provisions for tribal health programs and community-based safety-net clinics.⏎⏎3. Demographic performance auditing — broken down across racial, ethnic, and geographic lines — must be a mandatory condition of reimbursement eligibility for any AI clinical decision support tool. This is non-negotiable for AAIP.⏎⏎4. HHS must fund independent post-deployment monitoring infrastructure, operated at arm's length from the vendors whose products are being assessed.⏎⏎5. Reimbursement pathway design must include a small and independent practice impact analysis before finalization, specifically evaluating the burden on rural tribal health programs that lack the administrative capacity to navigate complex billing structures.⏎⏎APPENDIX A: AAIP Survey Data on AI Adoption in Tribal Health Settings (available upon request; not attached to this submission due to file size constraints — contact⏎⏎bgonzalez@aaip.org♔♔2026-01-03T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-03T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔Vermont♔policy director♔37♔A 2024 TMA membership survey of 1,800 actively practicing Texas physicians found that 61% had incorporated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic or clinical decision-support tool into their practice within the prior 18 months, yet 74% of that group reported significant uncertainty about liability exposure when acting on AI-generated recommendations. SYNTH-0028♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Richard Moore♔American Occupational Therapy Association♔♔♔♔♔AMERICAN OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ASSOCIATION⏎Comments in Response to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Richard Moore, Campaign Director⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎⏎AOTA Comments | HHS AI Clinical Care RFI | Page 1⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY DEFICIT IN HHS'S AI ACCELERATION AGENDA⏎⏎The way HHS has constructed this Request for Information represents a deliberate position rather than a neutral inquiry. HHS has structured a document that solicits comment on acceleration, adoption, reimbursement facilitation, and research investment — and has conspicuously declined to propose any binding accountability mechanism for when AI-assisted clinical decisions cause patient harm. The American Occupational Therapy Association represents more than 130,000 occupational therapy practitioners and students nationwide, and our members have watched this pattern before: the Department moves fast on adoption incentives, moves slowly on protection infrastructure, and then expresses surprise when the resulting gap produces litigation, inequity, and eroded clinical trust. We are not expressing surprise. We are documenting a structural design failure.⏎⏎Our members work daily in the exact clinical environments where AI tools are being deployed without any clear answer to the question Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified in 2019 as the threshold liability problem for AI in medicine: when a physician relies on an AI recommendation that turns out to be wrong, which party will ultimately carry the burden of liability (Price, Gerke, & Cohen, 2019, JAMA 322(18), 1765–1766)? That question is not rhetorical. Malpractice doctrine as it currently exists was built around a human decision-maker whose actions are judged by comparing them to established clinical practice norms (Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, & Studdert, 2020, JAMA 323(4), 352–366). AI systems do not fit that model cleanly, and HHS knows this. The FDA's own January 2021 AI/ML SaMD Action Plan acknowledged the governance gap for adaptive algorithms that change behavior post-deployment (FDA, 2021), and yet this RFI does not propose a single enforcement mechanism tied to that acknowledgment.⏎⏎AOTA Comments | HHS AI Clinical Care RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE REIMBURSEMENT AND INTEGRATION PROBLEM OUR MEMBERS ACTUALLY FACE⏎⏎We want to be specific about what AI adoption looks like in occupational therapy practice settings, because the RFI's framing skews heavily toward high-resource environments — hospital systems, large integrated networks, radiology and cardiology departments with dedicated informatics staff. Occupational therapy practitioners in South Dakota and across rural America are being asked to integrate AI-assisted documentation tools, clinical decision support systems, and patient-reported outcome collection platforms into practices that do not have IT departments. A 2024 RBMA member survey across 412 radiology practices found that 58% of those already deploying FDA-cleared AI algorithms report that current payment models do not adequately compensate for the time and infrastructure costs of AI integration, validation, and ongoing monitoring (RBMA, 2024). That finding is from a specialty with far greater capital resources than occupational therapy. The gap in OT settings is worse, not better, and no discrete billing mechanism exists to capture the clinical decision-support value practitioners provide when they adjudicate, override, or supplement AI-generated recommendations.⏎⏎What our members need HHS to understand is that the accountability problem and the reimbursement problem are the same problem. When a clinician uses an AI-generated functional assessment recommendation and that recommendation is wrong — wrong because the training data underrepresented the patient population, as Obermeyer and Emanuel documented as a systemic failure mode in 2016 (Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016, NEJM 375(13), 1216–1219) — the clinician absorbs the liability exposure, receives no additional reimbursement for the time spent validating or overriding the recommendation, and has no regulatory pathway for reporting the failure to any accountable body. Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo identified this structural problem a decade ago: sophisticated forecasting models deployed in health care create legal and ethical exposure that traditional governance structures lack the capacity to handle (Cohen et al., 2014, Health Affairs 33(7), 1139–1147). HHS has had ten years to act on that analysis. This RFI is not evidence of action. It is evidence of continued deferral.⏎⏎AOTA Comments | HHS AI Clinical Care RFI | Page 3⏎⏎SPECIFIC DEMANDS BEFORE ANY ACCELERATION POLICY IS FINALIZED⏎⏎The Government Accountability Office concluded in its February 2022 report that AI in health care presents documented challenges around algorithm transparency, bias, and clinical integration that require coordinated federal oversight (GAO, 2022, GAO-22-104629). The HTI-1 Final Rule at 88 Fed. Reg. 23746 moved toward algorithm transparency requirements in certification, but transparency without accountability is disclosure without consequence. Pasquale has argued, and AOTA agrees, that defending human expertise in clinical settings requires not just transparency mandates but enforceable human-in-the-loop requirements with legal teeth (Pasquale, 2020, Harvard University Press). The European Parliament reached a comparable structural conclusion in 2017 when addressing civil liability frameworks for autonomous systems (Delvaux, 2017). Kesselheim and colleagues further documented that clinical decision support systems require ongoing modification and monitoring to remain clinically safe, and that the litigation risk from inadequate monitoring is not hypothetical (Kesselheim et al., 2011, Health Affairs 30(12), 2310–2317).⏎⏎HHS must not finalize any AI acceleration policy until the Department has established a binding, legally enforceable accountability framework that:⏎⏎1. Identifies a specific, named human decision-maker answerable for every AI-assisted clinical outcome that results in patient harm, with that designation recorded in the patient's medical record at the point of AI use.⏎2. Creates a mandatory adverse-event reporting pathway for AI algorithm failures, separate from existing MedWatch processes and explicitly linked to the ongoing safety monitoring obligations under the FDA's SaMD framework.⏎3. Establishes reimbursement mechanisms that compensate clinicians for the time spent validating, overriding, or documenting AI recommendations — a function that Hoffman and Podgurski identified as structurally undervalued in data-driven clinical environments (Hoffman & Podgurski, 2012, Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics 39(S1), 105–110).⏎4. Requires that any AI tool deployed in clinical settings serving Medicaid or Medicare beneficiaries disclose its training data demographics, validation population characteristics, and known performance disparities by race, age, disability status, and⏎⏎AOTA Comments | HHS AI Clinical Care RFI | Page 3 [cont.]⏎⏎geographic region — before deployment, not after a harm event triggers a retrospective review.⏎⏎The Campaign Director notes for the record that AOTA members in rural South Dakota have reported premium increases on supplemental malpractice coverage of up to 22% in the current plan year, and that insurers have cited AI-related liability uncertainty as a contributing factor in those rate adjustments. HHS should investigate whether AI adoption acceleration, absent accountability frameworks, is already producing measurable cost externalities that fall on individual practitioners rather than on the technology vendors or health systems driving adoption decisions.⏎⏎aota_hhs_ai_rfi_comments_final_submitted.pdf⏎Contact: rmoore@aota.org♔♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔3♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔South Dakota♔campaign director♔45♔A 2024 RBMA member survey conducted across 412 radiology practices—spanning independent groups, hospital-based departments, and teleradiology providers—found that 67% have deployed at least one FDA-cleared AI algorithm in clinical workflows, yet 58% of those practices report that existing reimbursement structures fail to account for the time and infrastructure costs associated with AI integration, validation, and ongoing monitoring. SYNTH-0030♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Martin♔Commure♔♔♔♔♔Commure < > HHS AI RFI Response < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL < > Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎The framing of this Request for Information is wrong, and Commure is not prepared to let that pass without direct comment. HHS has asked how it can accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. That is a procurement and deployment question. The question HHS has not asked, and should have asked before issuing this RFI, is what conditions must exist prior to encouraging faster adoption. Our organization has worked directly with 47 health system clients over the past 24 months. Sixty-eight percent of those clients had initiated at least one AI-assisted clinical decision support pilot. Fewer than 20% had successfully scaled beyond a single department. Our consultants documented an average of 14 months of implementation delay across those engagements, and the cause was not, primarily, insufficient reimbursement pathways or regulatory ambiguity, though both of those problems are real. The cause was that health system leaders, once they looked carefully at the tools they had procured, could not confirm that those tools performed equitably across patient subpopulations. They could not answer that question because the vendors had not required themselves to answer it, and HHS had not required the vendors to answer it either. That is where this comment is directed.⏎⏎⏎⏎Commure < > HHS AI RFI Response < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎The peer-reviewed literature addressing this matter is not ambiguous and has been available to HHS for years. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan published in Science in 2019 an observation showing an extensively utilized vendor predictive tool applied to coordinate patient panels routinely undervalued the illness severity of Black individuals compared to Caucasian individuals presenting identical measured health status, because the program utilized health care cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients had been structurally excluded from care that would have generated equivalent cost (Obermeyer et al., Science, 366(6464), 447-453, 2019). This was far from a theoretical danger. It was observed harm, documented at scale, in a tool that had already been implemented throughout numerous health systems before the analysis was published. Sjoding and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 how finger oxygen sensors, a device so routine it is not typically classified as an AI tool, produced clinically significant overestimates of blood O2 levels in individuals with dark skin pigmentation at a rate that would have gone undetected without targeted subgroup analysis (Sjoding et al., NEJM, 383(25), 2477-2478, 2020). Wong and colleagues published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 an independent evaluation verifying an extensively adopted closed-source infection forecasting system, discovering its accuracy degraded substantially when tested outside the health system where it was developed, with false positive rates high enough to generate documented alert fatigue among nursing staff (Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065-1070, 2021). Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk identified in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 the specific mechanisms by which EHR records leveraged to teach automated modeling programs introduces selection bias, including differential rates of documentation, differential access to care, and differential coding practices across racial and socioeconomic groups (Gianfrancesco et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544-1547, 2018). Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones catalogued in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 the extent to which ancestry adjustments programmed into clinical algorithms encodes historical disparities as clinical fact, perpetuating differential treatment recommendations across generations of patients who never consented to be classified that way (Vyas et al., NEJM, 383(9), 874-882, 2020). Parikh, Teeple, and Navathe argued in JAMA in 2019 that addressing bias in health AI requires prospective audit requirements built into procurement and deployment cycles, not retrospective review after harm has accumulated (Parikh et al., JAMA, 322(24), 2377-2378, 2019). Wiens and colleagues in Nature Medicine in 2019 articulated a responsible deployment roadmap that included continuous post-deployment performance monitoring stratified by demographic subgroup as a minimum standard, not an aspirational goal (Wiens et al., Nature Medicine, 25(9), 1337-1340, 2019). Char, Shah, and Magnus noted in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 that the moral dilemmas inherent in health AI deployment are not addressable through voluntary industry commitments and require structural accountability mechanisms (Char et al., NEJM, 378(11), 981-983, 2018). Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini documented in JAMA in 2017 the unintended clinical consequences that emerge when automated decision support systems are rolled out lacking sufficient human override infrastructure or performance benchmarking against physician comparators (Cabitza et al., JAMA, 318(6), 517-518, 2017). Adamson and Smith identified in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 that dermatology AI software taught largely using pictures of pale-complexioned patients performed materially inferiorly on deeply pigmented complexions, an observation holding clear implications for melanoma detection disparities (Adamson and Smith, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247-1248, 2018). HHS has had access to all of this. The 2023 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability rule at 45 CFR Parts 170 and 171 addressed algorithm transparency to some degree. It did not establish compulsory pre-implementation fairness assessment requirements. It did not require post-implementation discrimination monitoring as a condition of continued certification. The RFI does not propose to change that.⏎⏎⏎⏎Commure < > HHS AI RFI Response < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎Commure's position is that HHS should not establish any payment channel covering AI-based clinical decision support tools until the following conditions are met as a matter of regulatory requirement, not voluntary attestation:⏎⏎⏎⏎o Pre-implementation fairness assessments, performed by external evaluating parties, segmented by racial background, cultural origin, biological sex, chronological age, primary language, and insurance status, with results made publicly available in a standardized machine-readable format as a condition of certification under 45 CFR Part 170.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Post-deployment bias surveillance protocols, requiring health systems to monitor model performance at defined intervals not to exceed six months, with mandatory reporting to ONC when subgroup performance diverges by more than a pre-specified threshold compared to overall baseline statistics.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Vendor disclosure requirements specifying the population makeup characterizing training data, the outcome variables used as proxies for clinical targets, and any known performance degradation in external validation studies, including failed external validations that were not published.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Reimbursement eligibility tied explicitly to compliance with the above, such that CMS and commercial payers cannot reimburse AI clinical decision support services from vendors who have not satisfied audit and surveillance requirements.⏎⏎⏎⏎Our consultants have sat in rooms with health IT directors at client organizations, 83% of whom in a Q2 2024 cross-client survey identified reimbursement uncertainty as the single greatest obstacle to sustainable AI deployment. Commure does not dispute that reimbursement clarity would help. The question is what should be reimbursed. Reimbursing tools that have not been audited for equitable performance is not acceleration. It is the systematic financing of observed harm at scale. The 14-month average implementation delay our consultants documented is frustrating. It is also, in several documented cases, the health system's legal and compliance teams doing exactly what they should be doing: refusing to deploy a tool they cannot vouch for. HHS should be building policy infrastructure that makes it possible to vouch for these tools, not policy infrastructure that makes it cheaper and faster to deploy them without that assurance. The RFI's framing treats the delay as the problem. The RFI's organizing logic is acceleration. Not evaluation. Not precaution. The Department asks how it can "reduce uncertainty that impedes AI innovation" in clinical settings — language that this organization reads not as a neutral policy question but as a declared posture. That posture has consequences, and those consequences are not reversible in the way that most regulatory decisions are. We submit these comments on behalf of a compliance function operating across a network with visibility into the governance conditions of more than 1,500 acute care facilities, and we submit them with the view that HHS has not been authorized to make the foundational choice embedded in this RFI's framing: the choice to treat AI embedding in clinical infrastructure as the correct direction of travel, full stop.⏎⏎The irreversibility concern is not rhetorical. Coiera (2019) characterized the final integration hurdles of clinical AI rollouts using concepts that resonate instantly with risk management teams — once institutional workflows reorganize around algorithmic outputs, the clinical judgment capacity that existed before atrophies. Physicians stop developing certain diagnostic reflexes. Staffing models shift. Documentation practices adapt to feed machine inputs rather than to record human reasoning. Winner (1980) made the broader theoretical point decades earlier: technological systems embed power relations that resist democratic revision not because revision is legally prohibited, but because the institutional preconditions for revision no longer exist once dependency is established. Dafny and Lee (2016) documented analogous dynamics in healthcare market consolidation, where vendor dependency and knowledge concentration produce lock-in that no subsequent regulatory action can meaningfully undo. HHS's acceleration agenda, if executed as framed, is a one-way door. The Department is proposing to walk the health sector through it without having demonstrated that the public, the clinicians, or the patient communities who will live on the other side have had any genuine deliberative role in that decision.⏎⏎Our Q3 2024 member policy survey found that 68% of facilities in our network had deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support tool, while fewer than 30% had a formal governance framework capable of validating algorithm performance across diverse patient populations (PINC AI, 2024). Those two numbers, read together, are not an argument for faster deployment. They are evidence of a governance deficit that acceleration will compound, not resolve.⏎⏎Foundation Medicine | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎THE OPACITY PROBLEM CANNOT BE DISSOLVED BY GUIDANCE DOCUMENTS⏎⏎The RFI inquires, alongside various other topics, about methods HHS can utilize to reduce regulatory uncertainty to support AI procurement. Our membership's compliance officers, in that same Q3 2024 survey, identified algorithm transparency and liability attribution as the top two unresolved barriers — with 54% pointing to the lack of uniform national guidelines as the primary reason AI procurement decisions stall at legal review (PINC AI, 2024). We want to be precise about what that finding means, because it is easy to misread. It does not mean that federal guidance would resolve the problem. It means that without guidance, our legal teams cannot assess whether a given deployment is defensible. With guidance, they might be able to assess defensibility. But guidance cannot make a proprietary black-box system auditable in any democratically meaningful sense.⏎⏎Pasquale (2015) argued in The Black Box Society that proprietary algorithmic systems concentrate interpretive authority in vendors in ways that are structurally incompatible with external accountability, regardless of what disclosure frameworks are layered on top. Selbst and Barocas (2018) made the related point that the surface-level attractiveness of "explainability" as a regulatory fix misunderstands the problem: what regulators receive from vendors who comply with transparency requirements is typically a post-hoc rationalization of outputs, not access to the actual decision logic. Obermeyer et al. (2019) provided empirical evidence of these real-world consequences — an extensively implemented proprietary model directing care management initiatives across hospital networks systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients at scale, and these systemic prejudices remained entirely hidden from the health systems deploying it because the internal weighting logic was proprietary. The HTI-1 Final Rule (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024; 45 C.F.R. Parts 170 and 171) made meaningful progress on predictive decision support transparency requirements, but it left substantial carve-outs for proprietary architecture that vendors have already begun to exploit in contract negotiations with our member facilities.⏎⏎The conditions for democratic oversight of AI in clinical settings do not currently exist, and HHS's proposed acceleration agenda does not create them. What it does is lock in deployment at scale before they can be built.⏎⏎Specifically, our compliance function has identified the following as preconditions that must exist before any acceleration framework can be considered responsible:⏎⏎1. Compulsory reporting of the origin of foundational datasets, including demographic composition, to any contracting health system and to CMS as a condition of Medicare/Medicaid billing eligibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions.⏎⏎2. Independent algorithmic auditing by entities with no financial relationship to the deploying vendor, with audit findings made available to patients upon request — parallel to the transparency obligations Mello et al. (2013) identified as democratic prerequisites in the clinical trial data context.⏎⏎3. Prospective liability allocation standards that do not permit vendors to contract away accountability for foreseeable algorithmic errors, a practice that our legal review teams report is currently standard in enterprise AI procurement agreements.⏎⏎4. Performance benchmarking requirements that account for subgroup variation, not aggregate AUROC metrics, which our network's analysis suggests routinely overstate real-world utility in facilities serving high Medicaid-share populations.⏎⏎None of these prerequisites exist within today's compliance and rulemaking landscape. The RFI does not propose to create them before accelerating deployment. That sequence matters enormously.⏎⏎Foundation Medicine | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC QUESTION HHS HAS NOT ANSWERED⏎⏎There is a question this RFI does not ask, and the omission is not incidental. We must ask if healthcare — like criminal justice, like education — is a domain that democratic communities have a legitimate interest in keeping irreducibly human, even at some cost to efficiency. The Executive Office of the President's Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (OSTP, 2022) acknowledged explicitly that human alternatives must be preserved in automated decision systems affecting consequential life domains. HHS's acceleration framing is in direct tension with that federal acknowledgment. Topol (2019) documented the genuine clinical potential of AI-assisted diagnostics with a rigor that this organization does not dispute — a 12% reduction in 30-day sepsis mortality associated with AI-assisted detection tools in our network's claims data is not a number we dismiss. But Topol himself was careful to frame AI as an augmentation of physician judgment, not a replacement for institutional deliberation about the appropriate scope of machine authority in clinical decisions.⏎⏎The question of scope is a democratic question. This is hardly an engineering puzzle that HHS can answer by convening working groups of vendors, health systems, and clinical informaticists, however expert. The communities who bear the consequences of algorithmic clinical decisions — disproportionately Medicaid-enrolled patients, rural populations, communities of color who have documented reasons to distrust automated systems that have historically miscalibrated against them (Obermeyer et al., 2019) — are not adequately represented in the stakeholder architecture of an RFI process. Winner (1980) was right that artifacts have politics, and the politics of clinical AI are not resolved by technical transparency requirements any more than the politics of urban highway placement were resolved by traffic engineering standards.⏎⏎We are not arguing that AI has no place in clinical care. We are arguing that HHS has framed a question about pace and direction as though it were a question about implementation mechanics, and that this framing forecloses a prior deliberation that has not occurred. The Department does not have the democratic mandate to determine that the health sector should embed AI at scale and at speed. That judgment belongs to a broader deliberative process — one that would include meaningful representation from patient communities, from frontline clinicians who are not employed by health systems with financial stakes in AI procurement, and from the public as such.⏎⏎WHAT WE ARE ASKING HHS TO DO⏎⏎This organization is asking HHS to do two specific things, and we want to be direct about why we are not offering a longer list of policy recommendations.⏎⏎First: Reframe this RFI. The current framing around acceleration and uncertainty reduction for innovation is not a neutral starting point. HHS should reissue the inquiry with demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability as preconditions for deployment scale, not design parameters to be addressed in subsequent rulemaking after deployment has occurred.⏎⏎Second: Acknowledge publicly, in the preamble to any final action taken in response to this RFI, that the decision to embed AI irreversibly in clinical infrastructure is a governance decision of the kind that requires democratic deliberation — and that such deliberation has not yet occurred. This is not a procedural request. It is a substantive one. The acknowledgment matters because it creates the legal and political predicate for the kind of democratic process that should precede irreversible technological lock-in.⏎⏎Our compliance teams will continue to support member facilities in navigating whatever framework HHS ultimately produces. SYNTH-0032♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donna Johnson♔National Alliance on Mental Illness♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL ALLIANCE ON MENTAL ILLNESS⏎Comments to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitted by: Donna Johnson, Policy Director⏎National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI)⏎Date: September 2024⏎⏎— — —⏎⏎NAMI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎I. THE QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎The framing of this Request for Information contains a structural premise requiring immediate pushback prior to answering the specific questions. The RFI asks how HHS can accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. It does not ask whether the current pace of adoption is appropriate, whether the workforce is ready, whether the communities most affected by algorithmic systems have been consulted, or whether some domains of clinical care might legitimately remain organized around human judgment as a matter of democratic preference rather than technical limitation. NAMI submits these comments not to oppose artificial intelligence in mental health care, but to insist that the sequence of decisions matters enormously, and that HHS is currently moving in the wrong order.⏎⏎Data from the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses' 2024 member survey — which surveyed 1,870 perioperative nursing professionals and was presented at the AORN Global Surgical Conference and Expo in Denver in April 2024 — found that 64% of respondents had encountered AI-assisted tools in their facilities within the preceding 18 months, yet fewer than 30% had received any formal competency training specific to those systems. AORN's concurrent analysis of sentinel event disclosures identified workflow integration failures, particularly at handoff points between AI-generated alerts and nursing response protocols, as the most frequently cited contributing factor in AI-adjacent adverse events. These are not teething problems. They are the predictable result of deploying systems at a pace that institutional readiness, democratic deliberation, and regulatory oversight cannot match. The mental health sector, where the stakes of algorithmic error include misdiagnosis, inappropriate medication management, and the erosion of therapeutic relationships that are themselves the treatment, faces these same pressures in an even more acute form.⏎⏎NAMI urges HHS to reread Sheila Jasanoff's foundational analysis in "The Ethics of Invention: Technology and the Human Future" (W.W. Norton, 2016), which argues that democratic societies have a legitimate interest not just in the outputs of technology governance, but in the processes by which transformative technologies are introduced into shared institutions. The RFI's portrayal of government oversight as a barrier to innovation inverts this relationship. Oversight is not a drag on progress. It is the mechanism by which a democratic society retains the authority to course-correct.⏎⏎— — —⏎⏎NAMI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎II. IRREVERSIBILITY AND THE LIMITS OF AGENCY AUTHORITY⏎⏎NAMI's deepest concern with this RFI is one that the document does not acknowledge: the decisions HHS makes now about AI infrastructure in clinical care may not be reversible. This is not a hypothetical concern. W. Brian Arthur's foundational work on path dependency and increasing returns in institutional technology adoption demonstrates that once a technology achieves sufficient market penetration, the costs of switching — in terms of institutional knowledge, workflow restructuring, vendor contracts, and atrophied human skill sets — become prohibitive even when documented harms justify reconsideration (Arthur, "Competing Technologies, Increasing Returns, and Lock-In by Historical Events," The Economic Journal 99(394): 116–131, 1989). Langdon Winner articulated a similar dynamic decades earlier: technological systems embed power relationships that outlast the policy decisions that introduced them (Winner, "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" Daedalus 109(1): 121–136, 1980). HHS is not merely setting reimbursement policy. It is making structural choices that will determine who governs clinical care for a generation.⏎⏎This matters with particular force for mental health care, where algorithmic systems are being deployed in contexts — crisis prediction, treatment recommendation, insurance authorization — that have historically been sites of documented racial and socioeconomic bias. Ruha Benjamin's analysis of algorithmic entrenchment in "Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code" (Polity Press, 2019) demonstrates that the structural opacity of proprietary systems, once embedded in institutional workflows, makes accountability nearly impossible to reconstruct after the fact. Frank Pasquale reaches similar conclusions about the limits of regulatory audit when the underlying systems are proprietary (Pasquale, "The Black Box Society," Harvard University Press, 2015). NAMI is acutely aware that the individuals NAMI serves — people living with serious mental illness, a group encompassing high rates of poverty, significant numbers of people of color, and extreme exposure to coercive systems of care — represent the exact communities at highest risk of bearing the costs of algorithmic errors that nobody can explain or reverse.⏎⏎The question of democratic mandate is therefore not abstract. As Alondra Nelson has written about the governance of science in public institutions, legitimacy requires not just procedural compliance but genuine accountability to the communities most affected by institutional decisions (Nelson, "The Social Life of DNA," Beacon Press, 2016). An RFI published in a federal register, addressed primarily to health systems, technology vendors, and professional associations, does not constitute meaningful consultation with patients living with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or major depression who will be subject to AI-assisted diagnostic and treatment systems. The Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements (5 U.S.C. § 553) exist precisely to create a democratic check on agency action, but that check functions only when the framing of agency questions does not foreclose the possibility of dissent before the comment period opens.⏎⏎— — —⏎⏎NAMI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎III. SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING MENTAL HEALTH APPLICATIONS⏎⏎NAMI addresses here primarily the RFI's questions regarding regulatory frameworks for clinical AI deployment, rather than attempting to address every topic raised throughout the entire document.⏎⏎The following conditions should be treated as preconditions for deployment authorization in mental health contexts, not as aspirational goals to be achieved post-deployment:⏎⏎1. Mandatory transparency and auditability. Any AI system used in mental health diagnosis, treatment planning, or insurance authorization should be required to produce explanations of its outputs that are legible to the clinicians relying on them. Finale Doshi-Velez and colleagues have established the conceptual and technical framework for this requirement (Doshi-Velez et al., "Accountability of AI Under the Law: The Role of Explanation," Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society Research Publication, 2017). Proprietary opacity should not be a defense against accountability.⏎⏎2. Human oversight requirements as a floor, not a ceiling. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 22 and Annex III) establishes mandatory human oversight requirements for high-risk AI systems in health and safety contexts. HHS should adopt equivalent requirements and should resist vendor pressure to characterize them as barriers to adoption. The GAO's 2020 review of AI in health care (GAO-21-7SP) concluded that a lack of robust human accountability structures constitutes a primary governance gap; that gap has not been closed.⏎⏎3. Prospective equity review before deployment authorization. Systems should be required to demonstrate performance equity across demographic subgroups before receiving deployment authorization in federally funded facilities, not after adverse outcomes have been documented. The Institute of Medicine's foundational work on preventable harm established that systemic conditions, not individual failures, produce the most consequential patient safety failures (IOM, "To Err Is Human," National Academies Press, 2000). Algorithmic systems are systemic conditions.⏎⏎4. A formal mechanism for communities to designate certain care domains as human-reserved. This is the ask that may seem most unusual, and NAMI acknowledges that. But the premise is defensible: a democratic society should retain the right to decide that certain relationships — between a person in psychiatric crisis and the clinician responding to them, for example — should remain organized around human judgment and human accountability, not because AI cannot approximate some of those functions, but because the community has decided that the human character of the interaction is itself a value worth preserving. HHS does not currently have a mechanism for receiving or acting on that kind of community preference, and NAMI believes it should.⏎⏎— — —⏎⏎NAMI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎IV. A REQUEST TO REFRAME⏎⏎NAMI respectfully requests that HHS consider issuing a supplemental RFI, or a revised version of this one, that asks a genuinely open question: not how to accelerate AI adoption, but how to ensure that AI deployment in clinical care proceeds at a pace and in a manner that preserves democratic accountability, protects the groups at highest risk of being harmed by algorithmic error, and maintains the conditions necessary for meaningful course-correction if harms emerge. The current document reads as though the destination has been decided and the only open question is the route. That is not a posture that serves the public interest, and it is not consistent with the democratic obligations of a federal agency acting under statutory authority that was not granted with AI infrastructure deployment in mind.⏎⏎NAMI does not oppose the use of AI in mental health care. NAMI is aware that there are genuine potential benefits, and that some of the populations NAMI represents have historically been poorly served by purely human clinical systems as well. But the existence of prior failures in human-delivered care is not a sufficient argument for algorithmic substitution. It is an argument for doing this carefully, with communities at the table, with transparency requirements established prior to implementation instead of retroactively, and with the institutional honesty to acknowledge that some of what is being proposed here is not fully reversible once the path has been taken far enough.⏎⏎NAMI requests the opportunity to participate in any subsequent stakeholder engagement processes HHS convenes in connection with this RFI.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Donna Johnson⏎Policy Director⏎National Alliance on Mental Illness⏎Arlington, Virginia⏎⏎nami.org/policy⏎policy@nami.org♔♔2026-02-25T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-25T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔hopeful♔New Hampshire♔policy director♔65♔A 2024 AORN member survey conducted across 1,870 perioperative nursing professionals found that 64% had encountered AI-assisted surgical planning or intraoperative monitoring tools in their facilities within the preceding 18 months, yet fewer than 30% reported receiving any formal competency training specific to those systems. SYNTH-0033♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Deborah Walker♔♔♔♔♔♔To the Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services:⏎⏎My mother's name is Margaret Walker. She is 79 years old and lives in Scarborough, Maine. In October 2022, she was discharged from Maine Medical Center after her second stroke, and the hospitalist handed my brother and me a printed discharge summary that an algorithmic documentation tool had generated. That summary listed her as "oriented and ambulatory." She could not walk without two-person assist. It listed a blood thinner she had a documented allergy to, an allergy that had been in her chart for eleven years. It got her medication doses wrong in two places. Nobody caught it before it traveled with her to the skilled nursing facility, because the nurses on that floor were each managing eighteen patients and the system had already signed off. I spent four hours on the phone with the SNF's charge nurse correcting it line by line. I am a retired schoolteacher, not a clinician. I only caught it because I had been sitting in that hospital room for six days writing everything down.⏎⏎I am telling you this because HHS is now asking what it can do to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care, and I want you to understand what "accelerating" a technology that already behaves this way will mean for patients who don't have a retired daughter sitting in the room writing things down.⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM⏎⏎The discharge summary my mother received was not produced by a sophisticated diagnostic AI. It was a documentation tool, a relatively simple one. And yet the nurses, the hospitalist, the discharge coordinator, none of them questioned it, because it had the appearance of a completed, authoritative record. This is what researchers call automation bias, which describes how human operators often blindly accept algorithmic outputs without scrutiny, and it is substantially worse when clinicians are overworked, which in American hospitals is nearly always. When a system generates a confident-looking output, the cognitive burden of questioning it falls on whoever is in the room. At Maine Medical Center that night, nobody had the time.⏎⏎Now consider what happens when the outputs are not from a documentation tool but from a clinical decision support system recommending treatment, or a sepsis prediction model, or a discharge risk algorithm. Wong et al. published findings in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 demonstrating that an extensively deployed commercial sepsis forecasting tool, when externally validated across hospitals other than the one where it was developed, performed far more poorly than its creator had promised. The model had been validated in the institution where it was built. It had not been tested in the local medical centers and remote facilities where most Americans actually receive care. When it was deployed in those settings, it generated alerts that were either missed or ignored because clinicians had learned not to trust the volume of false positives. The harm in that scenario cuts both ways: undertriage because of missed alerts, and alert fatigue causing real alerts to be dismissed.⏎⏎This is the environment HHS is proposing to accelerate into. I genuinely do not understand how the Department can frame equity safeguards and pre-deployment performance auditing as potential "barriers to innovation" when the published literature already documents what happens when these safeguards are absent.⏎⏎THE EQUITY PROBLEM IS STRUCTURAL, NOT INCIDENTAL⏎⏎I want to speak very plainly about one specific point. The documented racial disparities in AI performance are not bugs. They are predictable consequences of training using past medical records carrying generations of discriminatory treatment patterns, and then validating in settings that do not represent the demographic groups at the highest risk of being harmed.⏎⏎The evidence on this is not ambiguous. Sjoding et al. published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that pulse oximeters, which are now feeding data into AI monitoring systems throughout hospitals, read blood oxygen levels artificially high for Black patients at a rate roughly three times higher than in white patients. The devices were calibrated on predominantly lighter-skinned populations. When an AI system ingests that oximetry data as though it is accurate, it inherits the error. Patients who are hypoxic are being assessed as stable. This is not a theoretical harm.⏎⏎Obermeyer et al. published in Science in 2019 an analysis of corporate software relied upon by major health systems to identify patients who needed complex care management. The software relied on medical spending as a proxy for health need, which sounds reasonable until you understand that Black patients with the same disease burden as white patients have historically generated lower healthcare costs, because they have traditionally been denied equal medical treatment. The result was that the program consistently downplayed Black patients' health needs, and the health systems using it were therefore routing fewer resources to Black patients who were equally or more sick. The authors estimated that correcting the algorithm would have nearly doubled the percentage of Black patients identified as needing additional care. That algorithm was in use at hundreds of health systems before the research team published their analysis.⏎⏎Adamson and Smith wrote in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 about dermatology artificial intelligence programs built using image datasets drawn overwhelmingly from patients with lighter skin tones. The systems perform poorly on darker skin, which means that a melanoma or a serious dermatological condition in a Black or brown patient is more likely to be misclassified. And Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones published a deeply important analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 examining how race correction is embedded in clinical algorithms across nephrology, cardiology, obstetrics, and other specialties, adjustments that systematically direct Black patients away from interventions they need. When these algorithms are the training data for AI systems, those corrections get baked in and amplified.⏎⏎HHS is asking what it can do to accelerate AI adoption. What it has not asked, at least not with any specificity, is what mandatory safeguards it will require before deployment. That omission is not neutral.⏎⏎WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEEDED⏎⏎Wiens et al. published a framework in Nature Medicine in 2019 titled "Do no harm: guidelines for ethical artificial intelligence in health care." Their argument, which I find entirely persuasive, is that performance metrics averaged across a population are insufficient for clinical deployment decisions, because population-level accuracy can mask severe performance degradation in subgroups. A model that is 92% accurate overall may be 74% accurate in Black patients, 68% accurate in rural patients, and 61% accurate in Medicaid patients. Averaging those numbers produces a reassuring figure that conceals three separate harms.⏎⏎HHS should require, at minimum, the following before any AI clinical decision support program qualifies for federal payment or is certified for use in Medicare and Medicaid settings:⏎⏎1. Stratified performance reporting across racial background, ethnic origin, gender, lifespan stage, insurance status, and rural/urban geography, with specific minimum performance thresholds in each subgroup, not just in aggregate.⏎⏎2. Prospective external validation in settings demographically similar to where deployment is intended. A model validated at Massachusetts General Hospital is not validated for a small remote medical center in Aroostook County, Maine. These are not interchangeable.⏎⏎3. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance, meaning ongoing monitoring of patient outcomes stratified by the same demographic variables used in pre-deployment validation, with a mechanism for reporting and acting on detected disparities. Right now there is nothing. A tool can be performing worse in Black individuals compared to Caucasian individuals in every hospital in the country and there is no system that would tell anyone.⏎⏎4. Public reporting of disparate outcomes. Health systems and vendors should not be permitted to keep performance disparities confidential as proprietary information. Patients and clinicians have a right to be informed if a tool being used on them has demonstrated performance gaps by race or income.⏎⏎I recognize that some of these mandates might delay deployment timelines. I am not persuaded that speed is the right value to optimize for here.⏎⏎ON THE CERTIFICATION QUESTION⏎⏎The RFI asks about certification frameworks and whether existing certification processes are adequate. My experience with my mother's discharge summary suggests that industry-driven self-certification is inadequate, and I want to explain why I think that rather than just asserting it.⏎⏎The tool that generated that discharge summary had presumably passed whatever internal quality checks the vendor required. It was in use at a major academic medical center. It had not been caught doing what it did to my mother's record, or if it had, nobody had been required to report it. There is no mandatory adverse event reporting system for AI clinical tools analogous to what exists for medical devices or pharmaceuticals. A drug that caused the kind of error that tool caused would generate a mandatory report. An AI documentation tool that lists a patient as ambulatory when she cannot walk and prescribes a medication the patient is allergic to generates nothing, unless a family member calls the SNF.⏎⏎The certification framework for AI clinical tools needs to include, at a minimum, a mandatory incident reporting mechanism with defined thresholds for what constitutes a reportable event, and that data needs to be aggregated and publicly available so that patterns of failure can be identified. Industry self-certification with no post-market surveillance is exactly what allowed my mother's discharge summary to be what it was, and it is what will allow racially biased tools to harm patients at scale without anyone ever being required to notice.⏎⏎I want to say something about the framing of this RFI more directly. When HHS asks what "barriers" exist to AI adoption in healthcare, the implicit assumption is that adoption is the goal and that barriers are problems to be removed. I think this framing is backwards. Equity auditing requirements are not barriers to innovation. They are conditions that innovation must meet before it is deployed on patients who cannot opt out. A sepsis algorithm that performs well in white patients and poorly in Black patients is not an innovation. It is a mechanism for delivering worse care to Black patients more efficiently and with greater institutional confidence.⏎⏎The discharge summary my mother received was generated with complete confidence. The system had signed off. The problem was not that the technology was uncertain. The problem was that it was wrong, and nothing in the environment was designed to catch that.⏎⏎I am asking HHS to require demonstrated equity performance across racial background, wealth level, location, and insurance status before any AI clinical software qualifies to receive federal funds. I am asking for mandatory post-deployment monitoring coupled with open disclosure of disparate outcomes. I am asking for a mandatory incident reporting mechanism for AI-related clinical errors, analogous to what exists for other medical technologies.⏎⏎My mother is doing reasonably well now. She uses a walker. She is on the correct medications. But I think about the patients who did not have someone in the room writing things down, and I think about the SNFs in rural Maine that are going to receive AI-generated discharge summaries from systems that were validated at urban academic centers and have never been tested on their patient population, and I find I have very little patience for the argument that requiring these tools to actually work equitably before deploying them at scale is somehow an obstacle to progress.⏎⏎The harm is already documented. Sjoding documented it. Obermeyer documented it. Adamson and Smith documented it. Vyas and colleagues documented it. Wong's team documented it. We must now ask if HHS is going to require the field to address it before accelerating deployment, or whether the Department is going to call the requirement to address it a barrier and move on.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Deborah Walker⏎Scarborough, Maine♔♔2026-01-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔individual♔high♔angry♔Maine♔retired teacher♔48♔When my mother was discharged from Maine Medical Center after her second stroke, the hospitalist handed us a printed summary generated by some algorithmic documentation tool that listed her medications incorrectly and described her as "oriented and ambulatory" — she could not walk unassisted and had been prescribed a blood thinner she'd had a documented allergic reaction to years before.
