Baxter operates across health systems in more than 100 countries and maintains direct commercial and deployment relationships with hospitals ranging from major university research hospitals to critical access facilities serving rural and underserved populations. That breadth of visibility is precisely why we feel compelled to formally raise the issue that the RFI's framing fails to properly tackle: the documented history regarding machine learning prejudice within clinical AI is not speculative or emerging. It is documented, reproducible, and structurally predictable, and an accelerationist policy posture that treats equity auditing as an optional enhancement rather than a mandatory prerequisite before rollout is inconsistent with HHS's own statutory obligations under the ACA's nondiscrimination provisions and the Department's stated health equity commitments. We address here the RFI's questions regarding regulatory actions and research priorities, and we focus specifically on what the record shows about deployment in under-resourced settings, because that is where the gap between the RFI's framing and the available evidence is most consequential.⏎⏎Baxter International Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE PEER-REVIEWED EVIDENCE REGARDING ALGORITHMIC PREJUDICE IN CLINICAL AI⏎⏎The literature on this point is now sufficiently dense that summarizing it risks underselling it. Obermeyer et al. (Science, 2019) demonstrated how an extensively adopted corporate population health tracking tool consistently undervalued the medical acuity of Black individuals when compared with Caucasian individuals demonstrating comparable medical need. This occurred because the system utilized medical expenditure as a proxy for health status, and historical spending patterns encoded existing access disparities. Sjoding et al. (NEJM, 2020) found how blood oxygen monitors, which form the physiological data substrate for a significant portion of AI-assisted monitoring tools, produced occult hypoxemia at nearly three times the rate in Black patients compared to white patients. Wawira Gichoya et al. (Lancet Digital Health, 2022) demonstrated that AI models trained on medical imaging data can infer patient race from images in ways that are not clinically intended and not disclosed, creating a channel through which racial bias can propagate into downstream algorithmic outputs without any explicit race variable in the model. Adamson and Smith (JAMA Dermatology, 2018) documented severe training data underrepresentation for darker skin tones in dermatological AI, which is particularly concerning given that dermatological AI tools are among those being actively promoted for deployment in primary care settings with limited specialist access. Gianfrancesco et al. (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2018) identified multiple pathways through which EHR-derived training data encodes socioeconomic and access-related biases into model outputs. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (NEJM, 2020) documented the specific hazard associated with racial adjustments within clinical algorithms, a practice that has been embedded in tools for kidney function estimation, pulmonary function testing, and vaginal birth prediction, among others. The ONC/ASTP's own 2023 report on health equity and algorithmic bias in certified health IT found that performance disparities across demographic subgroups were a documented pattern in deployed certified tools, and that existing certification criteria did not require disaggregated performance reporting. The GAO reached similar conclusions in its 2023 report on AI in health care (GAO-23-105834), noting the lack of uniform equity evaluation requirements as a material policy gap. The Duke-Margolis Center's 2024 review of published performance disparities across deployment settings documented systematic performance degradation in community hospital and safety-net contexts relative to the primary university hospital validation cohorts in which most tools are initially tested.⏎⏎Baxter International Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎Our own Q3 2024 policy survey of clinical informatics leads across 47 health system partners identified reimbursement uncertainty and the lack of uniform AI performance benchmarks as the primary twin hurdles to adoption, each flagged by more than 65% of respondents. Those findings are consistent with what Wong et al. (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2021) documented in their external validation of an extensively integrated commercial blood infection forecasting tool: when the model was tested outside its original development institution, its discriminative performance dropped substantially, and the pattern of false alerts shifted in ways that would disproportionately burden nursing staff in lower-resource environments. Char, Shah, and Magnus (NEJM, 2018) identified automation bias as a structural risk in clinical AI deployment, specifically the tendency for medical professionals to blindly trust algorithmically generated recommendations in ways that suppress the clinical skepticism most needed when models are operating outside their validation distribution. This issue extends far beyond mere hypothesis. It is a documented behavioral pattern that interacts with distributional shift in ways that are predictable and that will fall hardest on patients in settings where the tools were never properly validated.⏎⏎The concrete policy ask Baxter is making is narrow and we think it is defensible on the existing record alone:⏎⏎1. HHS should condition all payment mechanisms covering clinical AI on mandatory fairness testing prior to launch against disaggregated patient subgroups, including at minimum racial categories, ethnic backgrounds, financial bracket proxies, and rurality.⏎⏎2. HHS should require post-rollout prejudice monitoring to serve as a condition of continued coverage, with reporting intervals no longer than 12 months.⏎⏎3. Validation studies submitted in support of reimbursement or regulatory authorization should be required to include at least one external validation cohort drawn from a community hospital or safety-net setting, not exclusively from the primary university hospital in which the tool was developed.⏎⏎4. ONC's certification criteria should be amended to require disaggregated performance reporting by demographic subgroup as a condition of certification, consistent with the findings of ONC's own 2023 report.⏎⏎None of these conditions would meaningfully impede deployment of tools that actually perform equitably across patient populations. They would, however, create accountability for tools that do not. The RFI asks how HHS can accelerate adoption. SYNTH-0037♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Mark Lopez♔♔♔♔♔♔Mark Lopez < > Public Comment < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎RE: HHS Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Mark Lopez, Portland, Oregon⏎Date: July 2025⏎⏎WHAT PROMPTED THIS COMMENT⏎⏎My orthopedic surgeon at Providence Portland mentioned, almost as an afterthought during a rotator cuff follow-up, that an AI tool had flagged something in my chest X-ray that the radiologist had initially passed over. Early-stage nodule, worth watching. I am seventy-seven and still pulling shifts at a distribution center in Clackamas County, so I am not writing this to say technology doesn't work. That moment was real and I am grateful for it.⏎⏎But this comment is not about that. My mind keeps returning to another issue entirely, one I do not see addressed clearly in the RFI framing: what happens to the people who helped me navigate the system before that scan ever got ordered? The benefits coordinator who told me which imaging facilities were in-network. The care coordinator at my plan who knew that the Providence authorization process runs about six days slower than the published timeline and planned accordingly. These are not clerical workers executing simple lookups. They carry knowledge that does not exist anywhere in a database, and the RFI treats their functions as administrative friction to be optimized away.⏎⏎ADMINISTRATIVE LABOR IS NOT ADMINISTRATIVE OVERHEAD⏎⏎The RFI frames administrative efficiency as a straightforwardly desirable outcome, and I understand the impulse. Sinsky et al. (2022), writing in the Journal of General Internal Medicine, documented how severely understaffed and overburdened administrative roles already are across the health system — the baseline is genuinely bad. But the conclusion HHS seems to draw from that finding is that automation should replace human capacity. The conclusion I draw is different: these roles are already stretched beyond what is safe, and adding AI error-correction load on top of depleted staff is not a solution, it is a compounding failure.⏎⏎What those coordinators do is not well-described by the word "administrative." Hubert and Stuart Dreyfus, in Mind Over Machine (1986), made a distinction that has stayed with me since I read a summary of it years ago: the difference between a novice following rules and an expert who has internalized context to the point where the right response is not computed, it is recognized. Michael Polanyi put the same idea more plainly in The Tacit Dimension (1966): we know more than we can tell. An insurance advisor with four years of experience handling a particular regional plan knows things about how that plan actually operates that are not written down anywhere and cannot be encoded in training data. When you automate that role, you do not transfer the knowledge. You delete it.⏎⏎The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in 2023, in their report on automating inequality in health administration, that AI errors in prior authorization and care coordination do not distribute randomly throughout the demographic pool. They concentrate on patients with complex, non-standard circumstances — exactly the patients who most needed a human being to recognize that their situation did not fit the standard pathway. The GAO reached a related conclusion in its 2022 report on prior authorization in Medicare Advantage (GAO-22-104536): that automated or under-reviewed determination processes were producing adverse outcomes for beneficiaries, and that CMS had not taken adequate steps to address the pattern. A 2019 study published in Science by Ziad Obermeyer's team showed how a popular medical care coordination program consistently downplayed the severity of Black patients' conditions because it used cost as a proxy for need — a proxy that encoded decades of unequal access. The lesson of that paper is not that the algorithm was unusual. It is that this kind of error is structurally predictable whenever a system learns from historical records reflecting existing inequity.⏎⏎Mark Lopez < > Public Comment < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎I am on a basic employer plan. I do not have a patient advocate, I do not have a health system navigator assigned to me, and my plan does not have a concierge line. What I have is the knowledge, accumulated over years, of which humans to call and what to ask them. The regulatory floor for the administrative functions those humans perform is set in part by 45 C.F.R. § 164.530, which requires covered entities to maintain administrative safeguards, and by 42 C.F.R. § 422.568, which governs organization determinations under Medicare Advantage and requires that decisions be made by individuals with appropriate medical expertise. Those provisions exist because Congress and prior administrations recognized that these decisions require human judgment. I am genuinely uncertain whether HHS has considered whether administrative AI deployments that effectively remove that judgment would run into compliance questions under those frameworks, or whether the Department has simply not asked the question yet.⏎⏎The thing that concerns me most is not that AI will make errors. Everything makes errors. What concerns me is that the errors made by human care coordinators are, to some extent, visible and correctable. A coordinator who misread a formulary tier can be called back. A coordinator who recognized that something didn't add up and escalated can tell you what she saw. An AI system that processes a coverage request and returns a denial code does not leave that kind of trace. The friction that HHS wants to eliminate sometimes is the checkpoint. The person who slows the process down because something feels off is doing skilled work, and if we replace that person with a system that processes requests at scale, we have not freed up capacity — we have removed the mechanism that was catching the errors before they became patient outcomes.⏎⏎WHAT I AM ASKING HHS TO DO⏎⏎I want to be direct about what I think this RFI should produce, because I do not have confidence that the framing as written will get there on its own.⏎⏎HHS should not treat the elimination of human administrative judgment as a neutral efficiency gain. Before any administrative AI deployment is approved or incentivized under federal programs, the Department should require demonstrated evidence that the system performs equitably across patient populations separated by skin color, wealth, insurance type, and geographic access — not just on aggregate accuracy metrics. The standard should be prospective, not retrospective; we should not wait for a pattern of harm to emerge in claims data before we require the evidence.⏎⏎HHS should also be clear-eyed about what "freeing up staff capacity" actually means in practice when those staff positions are already underfunded and understaffed. Sinsky et al. (2022) found that the administrative burden on existing staff was already at levels associated with error and burnout before any AI transition. If any time saved through AI deployment is used to justify further reductions in administrative headcount rather than redeployment to higher-complexity functions, the net effect on patients like me will be negative regardless of what the aggregate throughput numbers show.⏎⏎I do not know what the right regulatory mechanism is. That is HHS's job, not mine. But asking if a specific deployment is safe for the patients least able to absorb its errors should come before the issue of⏎⏎Mark Lopez < > Public Comment < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 3♔♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Oregon♔warehouse worker♔77♔My orthopedic surgeon at Providence mentioned, almost offhandedly during a follow-up for my rotator cuff, that an AI flagged an irregularity in my chest X-ray that the radiologist had initially passed over — turned out to be an early-stage nodule worth watching. SYNTH-0038♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Matthew Brown♔American Psychiatric Association♔♔♔♔♔APA COMMENTS ON HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI REQUEST FOR INFORMATION⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎Submitted by: American Psychiatric Association⏎Matthew Brown, Executive Director⏎September 2024⏎⏎APA Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎FRAMING CONCERN: THE RFI'S ACCELERATION PREMISE CARRIES EQUITY CONSEQUENCES THAT REQUIRE DIRECT ACKNOWLEDGMENT⏎⏎The American Psychiatric Association (APA) represents more than 38,500 psychiatric physicians and submits these comments focusing specifically on the fairness implications surrounding AI deployment in clinical care settings. The APA does not oppose the acceleration of AI adoption where evidence supports patient benefit. However, the Department's framing of this RFI as primarily a question of how to accelerate adoption, without first establishing what preconditions must be met prior to speeding up implementation, is inherently an administrative decision carrying documented consequences for patients from underrepresented demographic groups. That framing warrants direct examination before the Department proceeds to implementation guidance.⏎⏎The evidence base here is not speculative. Sjoding et al. (2020) documented how blood oxygen monitors — a foundational clinical measurement technology, not a novel AI application — systematically overestimated oxygen saturation in Black patients, contributing to delayed recognition of hypoxemia (New England Journal of Medicine, 383(25), 2477–2478). Obermeyer et al. (2019) revealed how an extensively utilized proprietary predictive model employed for directing demographic medical outcomes consistently minimized the clinical requirements of African American individuals compared to Caucasian individuals sharing identical disease severity, with the bias embedded in cost as a proxy for need (Science, 366(6464)). Wong et al. (2021) externally validated a privately owned infection forecasting software across multiple hospital systems and found performance degradation that was not disclosed in the original deployment documentation (JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065–1070). Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (2021) found that AI algorithms applied onto thoracic x-rays routinely underdiagnosed pathology in patients from underserved populations, with the underdiagnosis bias correlating with the degree of underrepresentation in training data (Nature Medicine, 27(12), 2176–2182). These are not rare exceptions. They are the documented record of what happens when AI systems are implemented lacking obligatory upfront fairness evaluations.⏎⏎APA Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎THE ABSENCE OF HARMONIZED FEDERAL GUIDANCE IS A DOCUMENTED STRUCTURAL PROBLEM, NOT A THEORETICAL ONE⏎⏎The APA's concern is compounded by the current regulatory fragmentation. A 2024 fifty-state survey conducted by the National Academy for State Health Policy documented that state-level AI oversight frameworks vary substantially in scope, methodology, and enforcement, creating compliance complexity for any health system operating across state lines (NASHP Issue Brief, March 2024). The absence of harmonized federal guidance on AI model validation has been identified consistently as the primary barrier to responsible deployment, not deployment itself. Gianfrancesco et al. (2018) identified the structural mechanisms by which digital medical files introduce bias into machine learning models, specifically through differential data completeness, coding variability, and access patterns that correlate with race, coverage type, and geographic location (JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544–1547). Those mechanisms do not disappear because a tool has received clearance or been incorporated into a reimbursement pathway. They persist unless equity auditing is required as a condition of deployment.⏎⏎The APA notes that Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020) examined demographic adjustments programmed into clinical algorithms across multiple specialties and documented that race-adjusted algorithms can encode historical health disparities as biological constants, with downstream effects on clinical decision-making that disadvantage non-white patients (New England Journal of Medicine, 383(9), 874–882). Psychiatric applications are not immune to this dynamic. Predictive risk models used in behavioral health settings — including tools that estimate suicide risk, readmission probability, or medication response — draw on training datasets that reflect historical patterns of differential access, differential diagnosis, and differential documentation. A model trained on those datasets will reproduce those patterns unless the training and validation process explicitly requires demographic subgroup performance analysis. The RFI, as currently structured, does not establish that requirement, and the Department should address that gap directly.⏎⏎APA Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎WHAT THE REIMBURSEMENT PATHWAY QUESTION ACTUALLY REQUIRES⏎⏎The RFI asks how HHS can use reimbursement mechanisms to accelerate AI adoption. The APA's position is that reimbursement should function as a policy lever for responsible deployment, not merely for speed of deployment. Char, Shah, and Magnus (2018) argued that the ethical implementation of automated algorithms within health care requires institutional structures that can identify and respond to algorithmic failure, and that the absence of such structures at the point of deployment — not the technology itself — is where harm originates (New England Journal of Medicine, 378(11), 981–983). The reimbursement pathway is the most direct mechanism available to HHS for establishing those institutional structures as an absolute requirement instead of an aspiration.⏎⏎Concretely, the APA recommends that HHS condition all funding mechanisms supporting AI-assisted clinical decision support on the following: first, upfront fairness assessments conducted evaluating diverse population segments such as racial background, cultural origin, gender, chronological age, insurance status, and rurality, with results disclosed publicly rather than held as proprietary; second, post-implementation prejudice monitoring alongside mandatory reporting intervals and a defined threshold for suspension pending investigation; and third, performance standards that apply specifically to community hospitals, rural health systems, alongside core care facilities rather than defaulting to validation data drawn exclusively from university research hospitals. Wiens et al. (2019) articulated a responsible machine learning framework for health care that included ongoing monitoring as a non-negotiable component of deployment, not an optional enhancement (Nature Medicine, 25(9), 1337–1340). The APA concurs and urges HHS to operationalize that principle through the reimbursement mechanism rather than leaving it to voluntary practice.⏎⏎APA Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎SECTION 1557 AND THE LEGAL BASIS FOR MANDATORY EQUITY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎The Department's existing civil rights obligations provide an independent legal basis for the equity requirements the APA is recommending. The HHS Office for Civil Rights issued guidance in December 2023 specifically addressing nondiscrimination obligations in health programs and activities that use AI-assisted decision support tools, noting that Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act applies to AI tools used in covered health programs and that discriminatory outcomes produced by those tools are not insulated from civil rights review merely because the discrimination is algorithmic rather than intentional (HHS OCR Bulletin, December 2023). The APA reads that guidance as establishing that the Department already has both the authority and the obligation to require equity auditing as a condition of deployment in covered health programs. The question is not whether HHS has that authority but whether it will exercise it through this rulemaking process rather than waiting for litigation to force the issue.⏎⏎Adamson and Smith (2018) documented that dermatology AI software educated largely via lighter-skinned patient images showed substantially degraded performance on deeper complexions, an observation carrying immediate patient safety implications given dermatology's role in early cancer detection (JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247–1248). Sendak et al. (2020) examined the clinical deployment of deep learning decision support tools and determined that machine reliance — the inclination of physicians to yield to computerized recommendations despite instances where these recommendations conflict with clinical judgment — was a consistent behavioral pattern that varied with institutional culture and training (ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 99–109). The interaction between machine reliance and algorithmically biased tools is not a remote hypothetical: it is the mechanism by which a model's distributional errors become patient-level harms. Upfront fairness evaluations do not fully address machine reliance, but they at minimum ensure that clinicians and institutions are deploying tools whose demographic performance characteristics are known rather than assumed.⏎⏎APA Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎The APA is specifically concerned about psychiatric applications because behavioral health data is among the most historically incomplete and most structurally biased in the EHR ecosystem. Diagnosis rates for conditions including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and PTSD vary systematically by race and socioeconomic status in ways that reflect access patterns and clinician bias rather than true prevalence differences. A predictive model trained on diagnosis codes from a health system with documented racial disparities in diagnosis will encode those disparities as signal. The APA does not believe the Department intends to accelerate the propagation of those disparities at scale, but the RFI's current framing, which does not require equity auditing as a precondition for reimbursement eligibility, would have that effect in practice.⏎⏎The APA requests that HHS revise the RFI's framing to treat equity auditing not as one consideration among many but as a structural precondition for any reimbursement pathway. The Department should publish draft equity audit standards for public comment, specifying minimum subgroup sample sizes, required performance metrics, acceptable performance differentials across demographic groups, and the process by which tools that fail equity audits are suspended or corrected. Those standards should apply with equal force to tools deployed at community hospitals in rural Arkansas as to tools deployed at university research hospitals located in Boston. The absence of that specificity in the current RFI is, frankly, the single most consequential gap in the document as currently structured.⏎⏎The APA also notes, as a practical matter, that the RFI document itself is written at a level of regulatory and technical complexity that makes meaningful public participation difficult for smaller provider organizations and patient advocacy groups. The Department might consider whether a plain-language summary document, published simultaneously with the Federal Register notice, would produce a more representative comment record. The APA raises this not as a formal recommendation but because the comment record for this RFI will presumably inform the equity of the⏎⏎APA Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎subsequent rulemaking, and a comment record that systematically underrepresents the perspectives of community health centers, rural providers, and patient communities will have its own distributional bias baked in from the start.⏎⏎matthew.brown@psych.org⏎1000 Wilson Blvd, Suite 1825, Arlington, VA 22209♔♔2026-01-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔Arkansas♔executive director♔47♔A 2024 policy landscape survey conducted across our 214 member clearinghouses and health information exchanges found that 87% are currently piloting or evaluating AI-driven claims adjudication and clinical data routing tools, yet 73% of those organizations identified the absence of harmonized federal guidance on AI model validation and liability attribution as the single greatest barrier to full deployment. SYNTH-0041♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Christopher Thomas♔♔♔♔♔♔To the Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services:⏎⏎⏎⏎My brother-in-law Gary is a hospitalist in Omaha. Two years back, when my wife had her gallbladder surgery at Alegent, he pulled me aside in the waiting room and described something I haven't stopped thinking about: his team spending significant portions of their shift hunting imaging results across three different software systems that wouldn't communicate with each other. Time that should have gone to patients. I'm a carpenter by trade, not a clinician. But I understand the difference between having the right tool and having a system that actually lets you use it. I understand that when a load-bearing spec is wrong, you don't fix the problem by building faster.⏎⏎⏎⏎That thought stays stuck in my head whenever I look through this RFI. The central issue posed here is how to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. I think that's the wrong question to be asking first.⏎⏎⏎⏎ON THE PROBLEM OF ALGORITHMIC BIAS IN CLINICAL AI⏎⏎⏎⏎It is no longer just a theory that feeding past medical records into machine learning models ends up copying the inequalities we already have. Obermeyer's research group released a paper in Science in 2019 demonstrating how a popular, for-profit software program meant to spot high-risk individuals systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it relied on medical spending as a stand-in for how sick someone was — and decades of unequal access meant Black patients had generated lower costs even when equally sick. The algorithm didn't introduce a new bias. It inherited one that was already there and then gave it the apparent authority of mathematics.⏎⏎⏎⏎That authority is the specific problem I want HHS to take seriously. When a colleague makes a judgment call that seems off, you question it. You ask what they're seeing that you're not. But when a predictive model flags or clears a patient, we have proof that medical professionals will often just trust the computer's judgment, even if their own gut says otherwise. Researchers call this automation bias, and it means that algorithmic errors are less likely to be caught than equivalent human errors. The algorithm's apparent objectivity discourages the second-guessing that catches mistakes.⏎⏎⏎⏎This isn't limited to cost-prediction models. Sjoding's team wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that pulse oximeters — devices already deployed at scale across every medical environment in the nation — read blood oxygen levels artificially high for people with deeper skin tones at rates that create clinically significant errors in identifying hypoxemia. That's a hardware problem, not a software problem, but the principle is identical: a tool validated primarily on one population performs differently on another, and the gap becomes a patient safety problem. Adamson and Smith identified the same pattern in dermatology AI in JAMA Dermatology in 2018, where training datasets skewed heavily toward lighter skin tones produced models that did a much poorer job diagnosing people with deeper complexions — the patients, notably, who already face documented delays in dermatologic diagnosis.⏎⏎⏎⏎The RFI fails to suggest requiring fairness checks before these tools are rolled out. It does not propose stratified performance disclosure. It does not propose post-deployment monitoring paired with open data sharing broken out by race, income, or care setting. Without those requirements, disparate harm will surface only after patients are hurt, and by that point the tool is embedded in workflows, reimbursement structures are built around it, and correcting course is genuinely hard.⏎⏎⏎⏎ON VALIDATION AND REAL-WORLD PERFORMANCE DEGRADATION⏎⏎⏎⏎There is a second problem that I think gets less attention than it deserves, and it matters particularly for Nebraska. Virtually all clinical AI validation studies are conducted at highly funded university research complexes with clean, curated data and dedicated informatics infrastructure. The performance numbers in the published literature reflect those environments. They do not reflect what happens when the same tool is deployed in a 25-bed rural emergency facility out in the Nebraska Sandhills, or in a safety-net clinic in North Omaha working with an EHR that hasn't been updated in four years.⏎⏎⏎⏎Wong's team released an independent real-world test inside JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 examining Epic's sepsis prediction model — one of the most widely implemented proprietary clinical AI tools in the country — at a University of Michigan health system. Even in that setting, a well-resourced academic institution, the model's accuracy fell way below the numbers reported in Epic's own validation work. Sensitivity was lower. The positive predictive value was low enough that for every true sepsis case flagged, there were a significant number of false alarms. The authors were careful and measured in how they framed this, but the implication is clear: if a major academic center can't replicate the developer's numbers, smaller local hospitals and rural clinics almost certainly cannot.⏎⏎⏎⏎HHS's acceleration agenda, as described in this RFI, will push these tools into exactly the settings where they have the poorest chance of working the way the box says they should. The patients in those settings are also the patients who have the fewest alternatives and the smallest safety net to handle the fallout of a bad algorithmic recommendation.⏎⏎⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE BEFORE CREATING REIMBURSEMENT INCENTIVES OR REGULATORY FAST-LANES⏎⏎⏎⏎My specific request is straightforward. Before any reimbursement incentives are structured or regulatory pathways are expedited for clinical AI tools, HHS should require the following:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. Forward-looking fairness reviews done across various population brackets—like ethnic background, age, gender, and financial standing—acting as a hard requirement before getting any government funding or official approval perks. Audits should be conducted by parties independent of the developer.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. Required sharing of success rates broken down by ethnicity, wealth brackets, and facility type, such as local clinics, rural outposts, and taxpayer-funded community clinics. Disclosure should be machine-readable and updated at defined intervals after deployment.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. Post-deployment surveillance requirements with public reporting, structured so that performance degradation in specific subpopulations triggers a defined review process before the tool continues to receive federal reimbursement support.⏎⏎⏎⏎4. Validation studies conducted in settings representative of the intended deployment environment, rather than just inside massive university research hospitals. A tool intended for rural critical access hospitals should be validated in rural critical access hospitals.⏎⏎⏎⏎Vyas's group brought up a similar issue in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 regarding race correction in clinical algorithms more broadly: the use of race as a variable in ways that systematically reduce estimated disease severity for Black patients has been hidden in plain sight across multiple clinical tools for years, and it took deliberate, focused scrutiny to surface it. The lesson is that bias in these systems does not announce itself. It requires active surveillance to find.⏎⏎⏎⏎I genuinely want AI to help clinicians like Gary spend less time fighting broken systems and more time with patients. I'm not opposed to this technology. But in construction, you don't get a building permit based on how well the design performed in a test environment under ideal conditions. You get it based on whether the actual structure, in the actual location, meets the actual load requirements for the people who will be inside it. The inspection is not optional, and the inspector is not the developer.⏎⏎⏎⏎HHS should apply the same logic here. The equity auditing and performance disclosure requirements I've described above are not obstacles to adoption. They are the essential guardrails that make bringing this tech onboard safe enough to speed up.⏎⏎⏎⏎Christopher Thomas⏎⏎Lincoln, Nebraska♔♔2026-01-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔individual♔high♔hopeful♔Nebraska♔construction worker♔45♔My brother-in-law Gary works as a hospitalist in Omaha, and when my wife had her gallbladder surgery at Alegent two years back, he pulled me aside in the waiting room and quietly explained how much time his team burned hunting down imaging results across three separate software systems that barely talked to each other — time that could have gone toward patients. SYNTH-0042♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Anderson♔Patient Advocate Foundation♔♔♔♔♔Patient Advocate Foundation⏎⏎1025 Connecticut Ave NW, Suite 1000⏎⏎Washington, DC 20036⏎⏎⏎⏎Sharon Anderson⏎⏎Director of Government Affairs⏎⏎⏎⏎April 14, 2025⏎⏎⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎⏎200 Independence Avenue, SW⏎⏎Washington, DC 20201⏎⏎⏎⏎Re: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care (HHS-OS-2025-AI-RFI)⏎⏎⏎⏎The Patient Advocate Foundation and its network of 214 member organizations — spanning health systems, digital health companies, university teaching hospitals, and patient advocacy coalitions representing a combined patient population exceeding 40 million covered lives — submits these comments in response to HHS's request for information on accelerating the adoption and use of artificial intelligence in clinical care settings. We do not oppose the Department's stated goal of removing barriers to clinically validated AI tools. What we are compelled to document, at length and with considerable urgency, is that the RFI proceeds from a framing that is dangerously and, we believe, inexcusably incomplete. The document treats "AI in healthcare" as though the term describes a coherent category of benefit to patients, a set of clinical decision-support applications waiting for reimbursement pathways and regulatory clarity to unlock their potential. That framing is not wrong in every respect, but it is wrong in the way that matters most right now: it omits the fact that the most financially significant, most operationally mature, and most widely deployed form of "AI in healthcare" in the United States today is not a diagnostic imaging algorithm or a sepsis early-warning system. It is an automated prior authorization denial engine, and it is already functioning as a financial weapon against patients across Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, and commercial markets. The Department's failure to confront this reality before issuing payment enticements alongside statutory safe harbors for AI deployment will not accelerate the benefits of artificial intelligence in clinical care. It will subsidize and institutionalize a system of algorithmic harm that is, by any honest accounting, already out of control.⏎⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Response | April 2025 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎The evidentiary record on this point is not thin or contested. In October 2024, the U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations released its report, "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Plans Use Algorithms to Restrict Care," documenting with exact specificity the ways large Medicare Advantage organizations deployed AI-driven prior authorization tools calibrated not to clinical appropriateness standards but to cost-containment targets, producing denial rates that bore no statistically defensible relationship to medical necessity determinations made by the patients' own treating physicians. The Office of Inspector General's April 2022 report, OEI-09-18-00260, had already established that Medicare Advantage organizations were denying advance approval petitions which met Medicare coverage criteria at rates that raised serious concerns about beneficiary access to medically necessary care. KFF Health News reported in November 2023 that insurers were denying claims at increasing rates and that AI deployment in that context was making the problem worse, not better. Georgetown University's Health Policy Institute published in January 2024 a detailed analysis by Palanker, Volk, and Lucia documenting the emerging risks of AI-driven prior authorization for patients and providers in commercial and Medicare Advantage markets, including the production of what the authors characterized as effectively final denials — algorithmic determinations that, as a practical matter, patients and providers lack the administrative capacity to appeal, even where appeal rights nominally exist. UnitedHealth Group's nH Predict system and Cigna's PXDX automated review process have both been the subject of investigative reporting and litigation precisely because these tools are generating adverse coverage determinations at a volume and velocity which no human clinical reviewer could replicate, which is, of course, the point. The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94 percent of surveyed doctors stated these administrative holdups led to patients abandoning recommended treatments, and 33 percent reported that a patient experienced severe medical complications as a direct result of a prior authorization delay or denial. These are not anecdotes. This is a documented, systemic pattern of patient harm, and it is being accelerated by AI deployment that the federal government has, to date, done almost nothing to constrain.⏎⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Response | April 2025 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎The RFI's discussion of reimbursement policy as a mechanism to foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders is, in this context, not merely incomplete — it is actively misleading as a policy framework. The most profitable AI application in the health insurance sector requires no additional reimbursement pathway because it generates returns through denial, not through care delivery. Insurers do not need CMS to create a billing code for their AI denial engines. They need the absence of regulatory prohibition. And the absence of regulatory prohibition is precisely what the current environment provides. Academic studies regarding automated prejudice make the civil rights implications surrounding this problem impossible to ignore. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan demonstrated in their 2019 Science paper how an extensively utilized corporate health predictive tool consistently downplayed the health needs of Black individuals compared to Caucasian individuals carrying equivalent disease burden, with the bias arising directly from the algorithm's use of healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a design choice that encoded existing racial disparities in healthcare access directly into the tool's outputs. The Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2023 analysis by Ndugga, Hill, and Artiga documents the persistent racial and socioeconomic disparities in health outcomes and healthcare access that provide the baseline against which any AI system operating in this space will be calibrated. When automated tools optimized for expense reduction objectives operate against a background of structural inequality, they do not merely replicate existing disparities. They automate and accelerate them, and they do so in ways that are opaque to the patients being harmed and, in many cases, to the regulators theoretically responsible for oversight. The NAIC's December 2023 white paper on AI accountability and transparency in insurance acknowledged this problem in general terms but produced no binding requirements. HHS has the authority, and we argue the obligation, to do considerably more than the NAIC.⏎⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Response | April 2025 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎Our network's 2024 survey data, which found that 67 percent of member organizations identified reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to deploying validated clinical AI tools, is real and the concern is legitimate. We are not arguing against reimbursement clarity for AI clinical decision-support systems that have demonstrated clinical validity and equity performance. We are arguing that the Department cannot responsibly address that question without simultaneously addressing the insurance denial context, because any national directive rushing AI adoption in healthcare without mandatory guardrails on the denial side will, in practice, create a two-tier system: reimbursement pathways for AI tools that benefit providers and health systems, and continued regulatory silence on AI tools that benefit insurers at patient expense. The 14-month average procurement delay from FDA clearance to clinical deployment that our Fall 2024 Summit participants documented constitutes a legitimate hurdle. But it is a problem of a different order of magnitude than the one documented by the Senate Subcommittee, and the Department should not allow the former to become the justification for ignoring the latter. The Prior Authorization Process proposed rule published at 88 Fed. Reg. 47,120 in July 2023 established some procedural requirements for Medicare Advantage prior authorization, but it did not address the use of AI in generating adverse determinations, and that gap is not a technicality. It is the central policy question of this moment.⏎⏎⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation | HHS AI RFI Response | April 2025 | Page 5⏎⏎⏎⏎The Patient Advocate Foundation therefore submits the following specific policy demands as a condition of any regulatory or reimbursement action the Department takes pursuant to this RFI:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. Compulsory bias evaluations before launch, performed by external neutral parties with public disclosure of results, for any AI system used in coverage determination, prior authorization, utilization management, or clinical decision-support contexts before deployment in any federally funded program.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. A categorical prohibition on AI-only adverse coverage determinations — no denial of prior authorization, claim, or coverage request may be issued on the basis of an AI or algorithmic recommendation alone, without documented independent clinical review from a credentialed medical professional holding appropriate domain expertise.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. Mandatory human clinical review for all adverse determinations affecting Medicare, Medicaid, and exchange plan enrollees, with a specific requirement that the reviewing clinician be board-certified or otherwise credentialed in a specialty relevant to the clinical question at issue, and that the review not be conducted under production quotas or time-pressure incentives that functionally preclude genuine clinical judgment.⏎⏎⏎⏎4. Public disclosure of denial rate data, disaggregated by AI system, plan, clinical category, and patient demographic characteristics including race, ethnicity, age, alongside impairment classifications, on a quarterly basis and in a machine-readable format accessible to researchers and the public.⏎⏎⏎⏎5. An immediate moratorium on rolling out additional AI-driven prior authorization tools in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care pending the completion of a formal rulemaking process that establishes minimum standards for clinical validity, equity performance, transparency, and appeals rights.⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department should understand that our network will not regard reimbursement pathway clarity for clinical AI tools as progress if it arrives without these protections. The insurer AI denial context and the clinical care AI context are not separate policy problems that can be addressed on separate timelines. They are the same problem viewed from opposite sides of the same transaction, and any rulemaking structure handling them as separable is not a framework — it is an abdication. We note, with some frustration, that the RFI itself does not ask a single question about AI use in coverage determination or prior authorization, which is inherently a deliberate decision, and not a neutral one. The Department should correct that omission in any subsequent rulemaking or guidance.⏎⏎⏎⏎Sharon Anderson⏎⏎Director of Government Affairs⏎⏎Patient Advocate Foundation⏎⏎sanderson@patientadvocate.org⏎⏎(202) 555-0174♔♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-15T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔angry♔North Dakota♔director of government affairs♔43♔A 2024 survey conducted across our network of 214 member organizations—spanning health systems, digital health companies, and academic medical centers—found that 67% identified reimbursement uncertainty as the single greatest barrier to deploying validated AI clinical decision-support tools at scale. SYNTH-0043♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Michael Johnson♔National Consumers League♔♔♔♔♔National Consumers League⏎1701 K Street NW, Suite 1200⏎Washington, D.C. 20006⏎government.affairs@nclnet.org⏎⏎Submitted via Regulations.gov⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎⏎Re: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care; Comments of the National Consumers League⏎⏎The National Consumers League (NCL) submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. NCL is the United States' oldest nonprofit consumer advocacy organization, founded in 1899, and our work on healthcare access, patient rights, and workforce equity gives us a specific vantage point on the questions this RFI raises. We focus our response primarily on the RFI's questions concerning administrative AI deployment and liability frameworks, because we believe the Department's framing of administrative functions as natural candidates for automation reflects a significant misunderstanding of what those functions actually require — and what happens to patients when those functions fail.⏎⏎Healthcare administration, as practiced in care coordination units, patient navigation programs, and benefits counseling offices across the country, is not clerical processing. It is skilled, judgment-intensive work that depends on what researchers in organizational theory would call institutional knowledge: the accumulated, contextually specific understanding of how a particular system actually operates, as distinct from how it is formally designed to operate. A patient navigator working in a federally qualified health center in rural Utah, for example, does not simply match a patient's insurance code to a list of covered services. She knows that a particular Medicaid managed care organization in that region has an undocumented informal process for expediting durable medical equipment approvals if the request is routed through a specific case manager — a workaround that exists because the formal prior authorization pathway has a structural delay that the plan has never corrected. That knowledge is not in any database. It is not captured in structured data fields. It cannot be extracted from historical administrative records and fed into a training dataset, because it was never written down to begin with. When that navigator is displaced by an AI-assisted workflow, that knowledge disappears with her, and the patients who depended on it will simply experience longer delays, or denials, without ever knowing what they lost (Politi & Street, 2023, Patient Education and Counseling, 106(3), 589–596).⏎⏎NCL Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care, and the Department's framing throughout the document treats administrative efficiency gains as an essentially costless benefit — a way to free human workers for higher-value tasks. We want to address this directly, because it reflects an assumption about administrative workforce capacity that is not supported by current operational data. The American Hospital Association's January 2024 survey of health system operations leaders found that administrative functions supporting care coordination and patient access were already operating at or below minimum staffing thresholds in a majority of surveyed organizations (American Hospital Association, 2024, Administrative Burden and Workforce Capacity, AHA Research Series). When AI systems make errors in these environments — and they will make errors — the remediation work does not disappear. It falls on the same understaffed teams. A misrouted referral generated by an AI triage tool requires a human worker to identify the error, contact the receiving provider, correct the routing, and document the correction. In a fully staffed environment, this is manageable. In the environments where administrative AI is most likely to be deployed first, because those are the environments where cost pressure is greatest, the remediation burden will compound existing strain rather than relieve it (Friedberg et al., 2023, RAND Health Quarterly, 10(2)).⏎⏎There is also a more conceptually important point that the RFI does not engage with, and that NCL believes deserves explicit attention from the Department. Administrative friction in healthcare is not uniformly wasteful. Some of it is, of course — redundant data entry, paper-based processes that persist for historical rather than functional reasons, duplicative prior authorization requirements that serve payer interests rather than patient safety. The Government Accountability Office documented these problems in its 2023 review of prior authorization in Medicare Advantage, and NCL does not dispute that meaningful inefficiencies exist (GAO, 2023, Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage: CMS Should Take Additional Steps to Improve Oversight, GAO-23-105765). But other administrative friction exists because human beings are checking each other's work. A benefits counselor who pauses to ask whether a patient's stated income figure is consistent with her described family situation is not creating unnecessary delay. She is catching a data entry error that, left uncorrected, would have generated an incorrect eligibility determination, denied the patient coverage, and potentially interrupted a course of treatment. The checkpoint is the function. When AI automation removes that checkpoint in the name of efficiency, it does not simply speed up the same process. It removes a patient safety mechanism, and the errors that result are not self-announcing. They manifest as missed referrals, incorrect eligibility determinations, and dropped care transitions — harms that may not surface until a patient is already in crisis (Ash, Berg & Coiera, 2004, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 11(2), 104–112).⏎⏎NCL Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎The literature on automation bias is relevant here and should inform HHS's thinking. Bates and Landman documented in 2022 that human oversight of AI-assisted administrative workflows degrades significantly when those workflows are designed to minimize human touchpoints — workers become conditioned to approve AI outputs without substantive review, particularly under time pressure, and errors that a fully attentive human would catch pass undetected (Bates & Landman, 2022, NEJM Catalyst Innovations in Care Delivery, 3(4)). This is not a hypothetical risk. Pourat and colleagues found in their 2023 analysis of safety-net settings that algorithmic triage tools used in care coordination produced systematically different — and systematically worse — outcomes for patients with complex social circumstances, precisely because those circumstances were not adequately captured in the structured data the algorithms were trained on (Pourat et al., 2023, Health Affairs, 42(8), 1124–1133). The patients who were harmed were not harmed by dramatic, obvious failures. They were harmed by quiet misclassifications that resulted in their not receiving follow-up calls, or being routed to providers who lacked the language capacity to serve them, or having their care coordination intensity reduced below what their situation required. These are invisible harms, and they are disproportionately concentrated in populations that already have the least capacity to self-advocate when the system fails them (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447–453).⏎⏎The equity dimension of this concern is one that NCL urges HHS to treat as analytically central rather than supplementary. The National Academy for State Health Policy's March 2024 issue brief on AI in Medicaid administration documented that early AI implementations in eligibility and enrollment functions produced measurable disparate impacts along racial and linguistic lines, with non-English-speaking applicants and applicants in rural counties experiencing materially higher rates of processing errors and coverage gaps (National Academy for State Health Policy, 2024, AI in Medicaid Administration: Early Implementation Findings and Equity Concerns). These are exactly the populations that patient navigators and benefits counselors serve most intensively, and they are the populations for whom administrative errors have the most severe downstream consequences. NCL is not arguing that AI has no role in administrative healthcare functions. We are arguing that the preconditions for responsible deployment — demonstrated equity performance across patient subpopulations, clear accountability frameworks for when AI-generated errors cause patient harm, and preserved human responsibility at every administrative touchpoint that affects patient access to care — have not been established, and that HHS should not accelerate adoption before they are.⏎⏎NCL Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎On the question of liability, which the RFI raises in the context of non-medical device AI tools, NCL's position is straightforward: administrative AI tools that affect patient access to care should be subject to the same accountability standards as clinical tools, and HHS must clarify liability frameworks before widespread deployment, not after harm occurs. The current regulatory environment creates a gap in which AI vendors can market administrative workflow tools as outside the scope of clinical device regulation, while those tools make determinations — about care coordination intensity, about benefits eligibility, about referral routing — that directly affect patient health outcomes. Wachter and Brynjolfsson noted in 2023 that the governance frameworks for generative AI in healthcare are running significantly behind the deployment curve, and that the absence of clear liability assignment is itself a risk multiplier because it removes incentives for vendors to invest in safety validation (Wachter & Brynjolfsson, 2023, New England Journal of Medicine, 388(14), 1345–1348). The ONC's own 2023 Report to Congress on health IT and the workforce acknowledged that AI-assisted administrative functions present emerging governance challenges that existing frameworks do not adequately address (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, 2023, Report to Congress: Health IT and the Workforce: Emerging Challenges in AI-Assisted Administrative Functions, ONC Publication No. 2023-HIT-07). NCL concurs, and urges the Department to treat this not as a future agenda item but as a threshold requirement for any federal action that would accelerate administrative AI deployment.⏎⏎NCL Comments | HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001 | Page 5⏎⏎The administrative healthcare workforce also carries a burden that is rarely quantified in these discussions. Sinsky and colleagues documented in 2022 that the ratio of administrative task time to direct patient care time in ambulatory practice had reached levels that were contributing directly to workforce attrition, and that the physicians and staff most affected were those in small and independent practices serving lower-income patient populations (Sinsky et al., 2022, Annals of Internal Medicine, 165(11), 753–760). The irony is that the practices facing the greatest administrative burden are also the practices least equipped to absorb the capital costs of validated AI implementation. NCL's understanding of current market conditions suggests that enterprise-grade administrative AI platforms with adequate validation documentation carry implementation costs that effectively exclude solo and small-group practices — which is to say, they exclude the practices where human administrative capacity is already thinnest and where the consequences of AI-generated errors would be most severe. HHS should address this structural inequity explicitly, and should resist framing accelerated adoption as a benefit to underserved settings when the economics of current AI markets work in precisely the opposite direction.⏎⏎NCL's specific requests of HHS are as follows:⏎⏎1. HHS should require, as a condition of any federal support for administrative AI deployment, that vendors demonstrate equity performance data across relevant patient subpopulations, including racial, linguistic, and geographic subgroups, before deployment in Medicaid or Medicare-adjacent administrative contexts.⏎⏎2. HHS should issue formal guidance clarifying that administrative AI tools affecting patient access to care — including tools used in care coordination, benefits counseling, patient navigation, and eligibility determination — are subject to accountability and liability standards commensurate with their potential for patient harm, regardless of whether they meet the formal definition of a medical device.⏎⏎3. HHS should require that any federally supported administrative AI implementation preserve meaningful human responsibility at every touchpoint where an AI determination could result in a patient being denied access to a service, a referral, or a benefit — and that "human in the loop" requirements be operationally defined rather than satisfied by nominal review processes that, in practice, produce the automation bias documented by Bates and Landman.⏎⏎4. HHS should commission independent research, through AHRQ or a comparable entity, on the tacit knowledge and institutional knowledge held by the existing administrative healthcare workforce, with the goal of understanding what is at risk of being lost through automation and whether any of it can be preserved through workforce transition programs or knowledge documentation initiatives before displacement occurs.⏎⏎NCL recognizes that HHS is operating under genuine pressure to address administrative inefficiency in healthcare, and we do not dismiss the real costs that unnecessary administrative burden imposes on providers and patients alike. The concern is that the RFI's framing treats administrative AI primarily as an efficiency intervention, when the evidence suggests it is also a patient safety intervention — one with a safety profile that has not been adequately characterized for the populations most dependent on the administrative functions it would replace. The Department should take that characterization seriously before the deployment curve outpaces the governance framework, because at that point the question will no longer be how to prevent harm but how to remediate it, and the remediation will fall on the same workforce that the automation was supposed to relieve.⏎⏎NCL also notes that the September 2024 findings presented to the Texas Medical Association Board of Trustees, which documented average AI implementation costs of approximately $47,000 per practice for validated platforms, are consistent with NCL's own assessment of market conditions and suggest that cost-barrier analysis should be a required component of any HHS equity review of administrative AI deployment incentives. The geographic distribution of underserved practices means that cost barriers to validated AI are not randomly distributed — they are concentrated in exactly the communities where administrative support capacity is already most constrained, and where the patients are least able to absorb the consequences of administrative errors or navigate around them independently.⏎⏎NCL respectfully requests that HHS treat the concerns raised in this comment as threshold issues rather than secondary considerations, and that any accelerated adoption framework be conditioned on the accountability and equity safeguards described above. We are available to discuss these comments further and can be reached at government.affairs@nclnet.org or at the address above. SYNTH-0044♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Rebecca Perez♔National Rural Health Association♔♔♔♔♔National Rural Health Association Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-0001 < > Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎The National Rural Health Association (NRHA) offers this formal submission addressing the Department of Health and Human Services' Request for Information regarding the accelerated integration of artificial intelligence into clinical environments. NRHA represents upward of 21,000 members and advocates for the 57 million individuals residing in rural America, where the underlying infrastructure of medical care renders the issues highlighted in this RFI far more critical than the agency's current framing suggests. NRHA is focusing our response on the regulatory guidelines and research priorities outlined in the RFI, as these represent the primary domains where federal involvement will either safeguard or critically undermine the interpersonal basis of rural medicine.⏎⏎⏎⏎We must begin by grounding this discussion in the empirical reality presented by the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses. Their 2024 membership survey involving over 2,100 surgical nurses revealed that 68 percent encountered at least one AI-driven surgical or anesthesia monitoring device at their workplace within the preceding 18 months, yet a mere 22 percent underwent any formalized instruction regarding clinical utilization or safety procedures (AORN, 2024). AORN's Policy and Practice Committee supplemented that survey by evaluating 47 facility-level deployment summaries, identifying highly variable vendor training criteria and a lack of established oversight protocols tailored to surgical environments as the primary hurdles to safe integration (AORN Policy and Practice Committee, 2024). Such statistics translate into real-world vulnerabilities. Picture the actual scenario inside a pre-operative holding space at a rural critical access facility—a clinical environment our members understand deeply—when a nurse steps up to a woman awaiting an abdominal surgery. The woman's hands are shaking. She insists she feels fine. The AI-driven monitoring screen indicates her vital signs remain squarely in the normal range. However, a surgical nurse possessing a decade of bedside experience detects an entirely different story: the manner in which the woman's gaze darts toward the hallway, the subtle irregularity in her respiration that fails to trigger a digital alert, the husband positioned nearby with folded arms and a rigid posture signaling the family has not achieved any genuine emotional consensus regarding the impending procedure. Zero percent of that context exists in the digital readout. The therapeutic connection established over the subsequent four minutes—the nurse pulling up a chair, decelerating the interaction, probing with an additional question—does not represent a mere optional enhancement to medical treatment. It constitutes the core clinical intervention. As Kelley, Kraft-Todd, Schapira, Kossowsky, and Riess demonstrated in their 2014 meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, the interpersonal bond between practitioner and patient independently dictates medical outcomes to a degree that is quantifiable, reproducible, and clinically vital (Kelley et al., 2014, PLOS ONE). Verghese, Shah, and Harrington conveyed an identical message more pointedly in JAMA: what the machine requires is a doctor, and what the doctor requires is the safeguarded bandwidth to actually be one (Verghese et al., 2018, JAMA).⏎⏎⏎⏎National Rural Health Association Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-0001 < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎Our primary apprehension regarding the agency's approach is not that HHS is exploring artificial intelligence. That exploration is entirely rational and, from certain perspectives, the technology offers authentic potential for rural locations grappling with severe specialist deficits. Our apprehension stems from the agency characterizing AI primarily as an efficiency mechanism—a tool designed to maximize patient volume, diminish administrative paperwork, and speed up clinical operations—which demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding of what the practice of medicine actually entails. Epstein and Street observed in 2011 that patient-centered care operates not as an optional luxury but as the functional baseline of competent clinical execution, given that accurate diagnosis and subsequent healing rely heavily upon navigating ambiguity, deciphering nonverbal cues, and establishing therapeutic reliance (Epstein & Street, 2011, Annals of Family Medicine). When HHS positions algorithmic integration as a solution to productivity bottlenecks, it tacitly endorses a highly transactional vision of medical care that stands structurally at odds with that baseline. Topol's prominent 2019 assertion in Nature Medicine proposing that AI will emancipate providers to engage in deeper human connections is frequently leveraged to justify rapid technological rollouts, but Topol's paradigm—optimistic as it may be—fails to adequately weigh how the relational aspects of treatment are inextricably bound to the cognitive and procedural elements (Topol, 2019, Nature Medicine). You cannot liberate a healthcare professional for deeper human connection by systematically demoting them to the role of an algorithmic output supervisor, because the exact critical thinking necessary for authentic interpersonal engagement is the same critical thinking that deteriorates when medical deduction is continually outsourced to software systems. Bickmore and Picard proved back in 2005 that the trust architectures governing human-computer interactions operate under entirely different mechanics than human-to-human dynamics, and that simulating relational depth through computational interfaces does not equate to the clinical reality of actual human engagement (Bickmore & Picard, 2005, ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction). The Department must exercise extreme caution before conflating the two.⏎⏎⏎⏎The threat of clinical deskilling warrants significantly deeper analysis than it currently commands within federal technology policy circles. Dreyfus and Dreyfus made the case in Mind Over Machine that authentic expertise—the caliber of mastery enabling a seasoned professional to process a scenario comprehensively rather than as a series of isolated data points—develops exclusively through continuous immersion in the total complexity of a given field, encompassing its uncertainties, its breakdowns, and its inherently human variables (Dreyfus & Dreyfus, 1986). When providers are steadily relegated to monitoring digital suggestions rather than functioning as autonomous problem-solvers, the foundational experience necessary to cultivate expert judgment ceases to accumulate. The issue is not necessarily that algorithmic prompts are incorrect—frequently, they are perfectly accurate. The issue centers on how human operators defer to automated systems, a behavioral shift that Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt thoroughly detailed in their 2012 review for the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association. They demonstrated that practitioners will overwhelmingly default to digital outputs even in scenarios where their own independent analysis would have yielded a distinct and superior evaluation (Goddard et al., 2012, JAMIA). Parasuraman and Manzey's investigations into complacency within human-machine networks determined that this phenomenon cannot be neutralized simply by instructing staff to remain vigilant—it is a deeply ingrained, attentional, and permanent structural reality (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). The seminal investigations by Tversky and Kahneman regarding anchoring heuristics apply directly to this scenario: the moment a numerical or diagnostic anchor appears—even an erroneous one—subsequent human evaluation gravitates toward that baseline in a manner that proves incredibly difficult to override through sheer willpower (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974, Science). Inside a surgical suite, where AORN's metrics already confirm that the vast majority of personnel operating AI-enhanced instruments have received zero formalized instruction regarding their clinical implications, these phenomena represent the daily working reality rather than mere academic warnings.⏎⏎⏎⏎National Rural Health Association Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-0001 < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎We must also confront a fundamental architectural flaw that Zuboff's examination of platform-driven networks helps to clarify: platforms engineered to distill individuals down to measurable metrics are inherently biased against the interpersonal nuances of the interactions they facilitate (Zuboff, 2019, The Age of Surveillance Capitalism). NRHA does not reference Zuboff to advance a broad ideological stance against modern technology. The application of her work here is highly targeted. When a digital clinical tool is built to generate results that maximize quantifiable metrics—such as vital sign trajectories, surgical duration, or discharge eligibility ratings—it is fundamentally not built to safeguard the interpretive margin wherein a surgical nurse chooses to pull up a chair and probe with an additional question. That margin does not represent missing data. It represents the actual practice of healthcare. Federal directives that hasten the implementation of such platforms without mandating proven interpersonal and contextual reliability—which must remain distinct from mere technical precision on standardized testing datasets—are not just lacking in scope. They are optimizing for entirely the wrong variables. NRHA consequently urges HHS to integrate the following parameters into its oversight and developmental agendas:⏎⏎⏎⏎o Mandate that any automated system utilized in direct patient encounters prove its interpersonal and contextual reliability as a strict prerequisite for clearance or reimbursement eligibility, rather than relying solely on technical precision scores derived from clinical test data. This benchmark must be formulated in direct partnership with professional nursing bodies and patient advocacy groups, and it must incorporate validated measurements tracking the preservation of independent provider reasoning and patient-reported relationship quality.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Implement dedicated oversight structures for surgical AI applications that mandate role-specific proficiency benchmarks for nursing staff, anesthesiology professionals, and surgical technicians. The AORN metric indicating that 78 percent of surgical nurses operating digital tools lack structured instruction does not represent a minor vendor orientation glitch that the free market will organically resolve. It demands baseline federal requirements.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Allocate dedicated funding toward investigations expressly formulated to track the relational and deskilling consequences of algorithmic integration in high-acuity medical settings over a continuous span of no less than five years. Present research funding pipelines prioritize precision statistics and productivity metrics almost exclusively. A lack of longitudinal tracking regarding the erosion of clinical reasoning does not equate to proof that such erosion is absent.⏎⏎⏎⏎o Stipulate that any HHS-sponsored algorithmic rollout programs within rural and critical access hospital environments must incorporate dedicated implementation resources aimed at preserving relational care—not as an optional module, but as a fully financed element of the core deployment strategy.⏎⏎⏎⏎NRHA recognizes that the agency navigates legitimate and overlapping pressures regarding this technology, and that rural populations specifically face severe, immediate vulnerabilities that digitally augmented care might help alleviate. The scarcity of general surgeons across rural Georgia, to cite one tangible example, constitutes a definitive crisis demanding definitive interventions, and NRHA is in no way suggesting that technological advancement has no place in those interventions. What NRHA is firmly asserting is that the relational foundation of medical care does not constitute an operational inefficiency waiting to be streamlined out of existence. It operates as a primary clinical variable driving concrete medical outcomes, and federal technology guidelines that acknowledge this reality will generate vastly superior results compared to guidelines that ignore it. The 47 facility summaries evaluated by AORN's Policy and Practice Committee in 2024 revealed that the primary obstacle to safe integration was the lack of established oversight protocols—not any inherent deficiency in the software itself. That conclusion indicates the true barrier is not digital maturity, but rather the institutional and regulatory maturity required to implement these tools in a manner that defends, rather than degrades, the environment necessary for safe, effective, and deeply relational medicine. The agency possesses a vital opportunity here, yet emphasizing "acceleration" as the ultimate objective deeply alarms NRHA, because moving at maximum velocity without the necessary oversight architecture in place is precisely how that 78 percent statistic—78 percent of surgical nurses operating digital instruments without any formalized instruction—transforms into the permanent national baseline rather than serving as a blaring alarm that something has already gone wrong in our deployment strategy.⏎⏎⏎⏎References⏎⏎⏎⏎AORN.
