SYNTH-0047♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Williams♔♔♔♔♔♔FW: HHS AI RFI Comment Submission - Ashley Williams - Wisconsin⏎⏎---------- Forwarded message ----------⏎From: Ashley Williams <awilliams.wi.comments@gmail.com>⏎Date: Thu, Oct 17, 2024 at 2:14 PM⏎Subject: RE: HHS Health Sector AI RFI - my comment for submission⏎To: [docket submission]⏎⏎Please forward this to the appropriate docket. I wasn't sure whether to submit through regulations.gov directly or through this address so I'm doing both.⏎⏎---⏎⏎TWO YEARS AGO AND WHAT IT TAUGHT ME⏎⏎My cardiologist retired in the middle of my treatment for atrial fibrillation. When I met the replacement physician, he spent the first twenty-two minutes of a thirty-minute appointment with his eyes on a tablet, narrating his observations in a particular clipped way that I later understood was required by the clinic's new AI-assisted charting system. The system needed continuous physician input to populate the record correctly, and so what should have been a first meeting between a patient with a cardiac condition and the doctor now responsible for her care became something closer to a dictation exercise. I want to be careful not to dramatize this. The physician was not rude. The clinic was not negligent in any obvious legal sense. But I left that appointment feeling, in a way I haven't been able to shake, that I had been present primarily as a data source rather than as a person whose health was at stake.⏎⏎I have spent some time since then reading about how AI systems are being integrated into clinical care, and that experience is what I keep returning to when I try to evaluate what HHS is proposing in this request for information. The RFI asks broadly about regulatory and reimbursement actions that can accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings. I want to respond specifically to the accountability dimension of that question, because I think it is the dimension the RFI treats most lightly, and it is the one that matters most to patients in the position I was in.⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY VACUUM IS NOT A SECONDARY CONCERN⏎⏎The core problem I want to describe is this: when something goes wrong in AI-assisted clinical care, there is no reliable mechanism for a patient to identify who is answerable for it. This is not a hypothetical. The Government Accountability Office observed in its 2020 report on AI in health care (GAO-21-7SP) that accountability frameworks have not kept pace with the deployment of these technologies, and that was four years ago. The situation has not improved in the interim, at least not structurally.⏎⏎What happens in practice when a patient is harmed by a decision that an AI system influenced? The clinician says the tool recommended the course of action and they followed reasonable clinical judgment in relying on it. The hospital says it deployed a certified product according to the vendor's specifications. The vendor says the output depends on how the system was trained and integrated, and that responsibility for clinical decisions rests with the physician. Each of these deflections has some legal logic behind it. None of them leaves the patient with a person who is unambiguously answerable.⏎⏎W. Nicholson Price II and Sara Gerke wrote about this directly in JAMA in 2019, observing that existing malpractice doctrine was built around the assumption of an identifiable human decision-maker whose judgment can be evaluated against the standard of care. When an AI system mediates that decision, the causal chain that malpractice law requires becomes genuinely difficult to reconstruct. Teneille Brown and Joan Krause made a related argument in the Northwestern University Law Review in 2021, describing how AI intermediation breaks the causal chain that negligence doctrine depends on, not because the harm is unclear but because the decision-making process is distributed across a system that no single actor fully controls or fully understands. Mello and Brennan's earlier work in the New England Journal of Medicine (2009) on malpractice doctrine and federal health reform is instructive here too, because it makes clear how thoroughly that doctrine was constructed around human decision-making and how little it anticipated algorithmic intermediaries. None of those doctrinal assumptions have been revisited in any systematic way since AI began entering clinical workflows at scale.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I am not a lawyer or a health policy researcher. I'm a retired administrative assistant from Dane County, Wisconsin, and I have no particular expertise in regulatory frameworks. But I have been a patient navigating a cardiac condition for going on four years, and what I understand from that experience and from the reading I have done is that the accountability gap these scholars are describing is not abstract. It is the difference between a patient who has been harmed having someone to hold responsible and a patient who has been harmed having no one.⏎⏎THIS IS A MORAL PROBLEM, NOT ONLY A LEGAL ONE⏎⏎Glenn Cohen and colleagues wrote in Health Affairs in 2014 about the ethical concerns that arise when responsibility for clinical decisions becomes diffused across complex predictive systems. Their argument, if I am reading it correctly, is that the problem is not only that diffused responsibility makes legal recourse difficult. It is that patients have a reasonable expectation, grounded in something more fundamental than law, that a specific human being is answerable for their care. That expectation is part of what it means to be treated as a patient rather than as a data point. When I sat in that exam room in 2022 watching my new cardiologist narrate observations into a tablet, what I was experiencing was not just an awkward bedside manner. It was a structural arrangement in which the question of who was responsible for my care had become genuinely murky, and in which neither I nor possibly the physician himself had a clear answer.⏎⏎HHS's RFI does not ignore accountability entirely. There are questions in the document about governance and oversight. But the framing of the RFI is oriented toward acceleration. The question being asked is essentially: what regulatory and reimbursement changes can we make to speed up AI adoption? The accountability questions are treated as things to be addressed alongside adoption, or perhaps afterward. I think that sequencing is wrong, and I think it is wrong in a way that will be very difficult to correct once it has been acted on.⏎⏎THE PROBLEM OF STRUCTURAL IRREVERSIBILITY⏎⏎Frank Pasquale argued in The Black Box Society (Harvard University Press, 2015) that once institutions become dependent on opaque algorithmic systems, that dependency itself becomes a barrier to accountability. The institutions have too much invested in the system's continued operation to audit it rigorously, and the vendors have too much invested in protecting their proprietary methods to allow genuine transparency. The result is that the systems become insulated from accountability not through any deliberate design choice but through the ordinary mechanics of institutional inertia. ONC's own policy brief on certified health IT from 2023 acknowledges that current interoperability and certification frameworks do not address accountability assignment for AI-influenced clinical decisions, which means that even the certification pathway that is supposed to provide some quality assurance for health IT does not answer the question of who is responsible when an AI-assisted decision causes harm.⏎⏎What concerns me about the current RFI is that it proposes to accelerate the embedding of AI systems into clinical workflows before anyone has answered that question. Once these systems are embedded, the institutions using them will have operational and financial dependencies on them that make rigorous retrospective accountability nearly impossible to impose. Hospitals will have restructured staffing around the assumption that AI handles certain functions. Vendors will have established contractual relationships that insulate them from liability. Clinicians will have developed workflow habits that treat AI outputs as background infrastructure rather than as interventions subject to independent evaluation. The window for designing accountability into these systems is now, before they are structurally entrenched. Proposing to accelerate adoption before that design work is done is not a neutral policy choice. It is a choice to lock in a structurally unaccountable system and deal with the consequences afterward, when the consequences will fall on patients.⏎⏎I genuinely don't understand why HHS would make that choice, even from a purely administrative standpoint. The costs of retrofitting accountability frameworks onto already-embedded systems will be substantially higher than building them in at the outset. The legal exposure for the federal government, if it has affirmatively encouraged adoption ahead of accountability infrastructure, seems significant. And the harm to patients in the interim, while accountability remains unresolved, is not hypothetical, it is ongoing.⏎⏎WHAT I AM ASKING HHS TO DO⏎⏎I am not asking HHS to stop AI development in clinical care. I recognize that some of these tools have real potential. What I am asking is that the Department not treat the accountability question as something that can be addressed in parallel with or after accelerated adoption. The RFI should be reframed around a prior question: before we accelerate adoption, what accountability infrastructure must exist, and who is responsible for building it?⏎⏎Specifically, and I recognize this is more specific than my expertise strictly justifies, I think HHS needs to address three things before any reimbursement incentives or regulatory changes designed to speed adoption are implemented. First, there needs to be a clear legal doctrine, developed through either rulemaking or legislative action, that assigns liability when AI-influenced clinical decisions cause harm. The current ambiguity is not a neutral state, it actively advantages vendors and institutions at the expense of patients. Second, certification requirements for AI systems used in clinical care need to include accountability assignment, meaning that the certification process must require the vendor, the deploying institution, or the supervising clinician to affirmatively accept responsibility for specified categories of AI output. The current certification framework, as ONC's own materials acknowledge, does not do this. Third, patients need a right to know when an AI system has materially influenced a clinical decision affecting their care, and a right to request a human review of that decision. I had no idea, sitting in that exam room, what role the AI-assisted charting system was playing in structuring my physician's attention and the record being built about my condition. That opacity is not acceptable.⏎⏎I want to close on something that is harder to quantify than legal doctrine or certification requirements. When I read through this RFI, I notice that the word "patient" appears frequently, usually in phrases about patient outcomes or patient benefit. What I don't see is any sustained attention to what patients experience when the human accountability that clinical care has always depended on becomes diffuse and uncertain. The physician in that exam room was not a bad doctor. But the system he was operating in had restructured his attention in ways that made me feel invisible, and if something had gone wrong with my care during that transition period, I am not at all confident that there would have been a clear answer to the question of who was responsible.⏎⏎That is the problem I am asking HHS to take seriously before it accelerates anything.⏎⏎Ashley Williams⏎Madison, Wisconsin 53703⏎⏎---⏎⏎Note: I also sent a copy of this directly through the regulations.gov portal on October 17 in case this email route doesn't reach the docket properly. SYNTH-0048♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔James Robinson♔Physicians for a National Health Program♔♔♔♔♔Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 1⏎⏎⏎COMMENT OF PHYSICIANS FOR A NATIONAL HEALTH PROGRAM⏎Submitted in Response to: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: James Robinson, Policy Director⏎Organization: Physicians for a National Health Program (PNHP)⏎Date: Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎⏎ORGANIZATIONAL STANDING AND PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎Physicians for a National Health Program submits these comments as a membership organization with direct and ongoing engagement with the clinical realities this RFI addresses. Our policy team's analysis of Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) coverage determinations from 2022 through 2024 identified fewer than a dozen AI-augmented laboratory services with established local coverage determinations, leaving the substantial majority of emerging diagnostic AI applications in a reimbursement gray zone that our members navigate daily. A 2024 membership survey conducted across 412 clinical and anatomic pathology laboratories found that 67% had piloted at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the prior 24 months, yet 58% of those same facilities cited reimbursement uncertainty as the primary barrier to full clinical deployment. We raise these figures not to signal enthusiasm for acceleration but to establish that PNHP speaks from a position of direct, granular familiarity with what AI deployment actually looks like when it moves from a conference presentation into a working clinical laboratory. What we have observed across that membership base is not primarily a story about promising technology held back by regulatory friction. It is a story about a health system under pressure to reduce costs and increase throughput absorbing a new class of tools in ways that may be producing efficiencies and eroding something that cannot be easily measured or recovered.⏎⏎We want to be precise about what we are raising here, because the RFI itself is not precise about it. HHS frames this solicitation largely around the question of how to accelerate adoption, how to remove regulatory barriers, how to align reimbursement incentives with deployment, and how to improve what it calls productivity in clinical settings. The word productivity appears in this RFI's framing in a way that PNHP believes is not merely imprecise but is a category error with policy consequences. Productivity is a meaningful concept for manufacturing, for logistics, for any system in which outputs can be cleanly separated from the relational conditions of their production. Clinical medicine is not such a system. The research on this point is not speculative. Kelley and colleagues, in a 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published in PLOS ONE, found statistically significant associations between the quality of the patient-clinician relationship and measurable health outcomes across a range of conditions, including treatment adherence, symptom resolution, and patient-reported wellbeing (Kelley JM, Kraft-Todd G, Schapira L, et al., PLOS ONE, 2014;9(4):e94207). Hojat and colleagues demonstrated in a controlled study that physicians' empathy scores were directly correlated with clinical outcomes for diabetic patients, including HbA1c control and LDL levels, which are hard endpoints, not soft satisfaction measures (Hojat M, Louis DZ, Markham FW, et al., Acad Med, 2011;86(3):359-364). When HHS uses the word productivity without accounting for the clinical function performed by the therapeutic relationship itself, it is not simply being imprecise. It is building a policy framework on a model of care that the evidence does not support.⏎⏎⏎THE CLINICAL VIGNETTE HHS IS NOT ASKING ABOUT⏎⏎Consider a patient who arrives at a primary care appointment accompanied by her adult daughter. The patient is 71 years old, her first language is not English, and she has been describing her primary complaint as stomach trouble for three visits running. The physician has been ordering the obvious workup. What changes the clinical picture is not a laboratory result. It is a moment, approximately twelve minutes into the visit, when the daughter says something in a lowered voice to her mother, and the physician notices that the patient's posture changes, that she looks at the floor, and that what she says next about her pain is different in character from everything she has said before. The physician asks a different question. The diagnosis, eventually, is not gastrointestinal. The thing that made the diagnosis possible was the physician's trained attention to a relational signal that existed in the room and that no imaging system, no natural language processing tool operating on the transcript of that visit, and no pattern-matching algorithm trained on a reference population would have surfaced. This is not a romantic story about intuition. It is a description of a clinical instrument, which is the physician's capacity for attentive presence and contextual interpretation, doing its work.⏎⏎PNHP is not arguing that AI has no place in this patient's care. We are arguing that HHS's RFI does not appear to recognize that displacing or attenuating the conditions under which that kind of clinical attention is possible constitutes a patient safety risk. The RFI asks about barriers to adoption. It does not ask about the clinical functions that may be degraded when adoption proceeds without adequate attention to the relational architecture of care. Verghese, Shah, and Harrington made exactly this point in a 2018 JAMA commentary: the physician's physical and relational presence is not a relic to be automated around but is itself a diagnostic and therapeutic act (Verghese A, Shah NH, Harrington RA, JAMA, 2018;319(1):19-20). PNHP submits that any regulatory framework for clinical AI that does not operationalize this insight is incomplete in a way that will produce harm.⏎⏎⏎Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM IS NOT A FUTURE RISK⏎⏎HHS's RFI addresses several dimensions of AI risk, including bias and transparency, but it addresses them primarily as technical problems amenable to technical solutions. PNHP is concerned that the deskilling risk, which is the longitudinal erosion of clinical judgment capacity in practitioners who increasingly function as supervisors of automated recommendation systems rather than as independent diagnostic reasoners, is not receiving equivalent policy attention. This is not a speculative concern. The automation bias literature, which is substantial and spans decades of human factors research, documents a consistent pattern: when human operators are embedded in systems that generate automated recommendations, their capacity for independent error detection declines over time, and their tendency to accept erroneous automated outputs increases, even among expert operators (Goddard K, Roudsari A, Wyatt JC, J Am Med Inform Assoc, 2012;19(1):121-127; Parasuraman R, Manzey DH, Hum Factors, 2010;52(3):381-410). These effects are not corrected by training alone. They are structural features of human-automation interaction that emerge regardless of operator intent or competence.⏎⏎What this means for clinical medicine, if AI adoption proceeds at the pace and without the safeguards that this RFI seems oriented toward enabling, is that we will train a generation of clinicians who have never had to form a differential diagnosis without algorithmic scaffolding, who have never had to interpret a pathology slide without a machine pre-read, who have never had to sit with diagnostic uncertainty long enough to develop the tolerance for ambiguity that experienced clinicians describe as one of the most important things they learned. The deskilling concern is not about any individual clinician making a bad decision on a given Tuesday. It is about what the clinical workforce looks like in 2035 if the accelerationist posture of this RFI becomes the dominant policy orientation of the next decade. HHS has a responsibility to think at that timescale, and this RFI does not appear to be doing so.⏎⏎We want to acknowledge, because we think intellectual honesty requires it, that Topol's influential 2019 Nature Medicine analysis made a more optimistic case: that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence could, if designed correctly, free physicians for the relational dimensions of care by offloading the cognitive burden of data processing (Topol EJ, Nat Med, 2019;25(1):44-56). PNHP does not dismiss that possibility. What we observe, however, in the reports from our member laboratory directors and in the broader literature on clinical AI implementation, is that this optimistic scenario is not the one that tends to materialize when AI tools are deployed under the cost and throughput pressures that characterize the current U.S. health system. The time that AI ostensibly frees up is not, in practice, being reinvested in the therapeutic relationship. It is being absorbed by increased patient volume, by documentation requirements, and by the administrative overhead of managing the AI systems themselves. The policy question HHS should be asking is not simply whether AI can theoretically liberate clinician time for relational care, but what structural conditions would need to be in place to ensure that it actually does. That question is largely absent from this RFI.⏎⏎⏎EQUITY AND THE ALGORITHMIC BIAS PROBLEM CANNOT BE DEFERRED⏎⏎PNHP urges HHS to treat algorithmic bias not as a technical footnote but as a first-order policy problem that must be resolved before, not after, deployment authorization. The evidence on this point is not ambiguous. Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 Science paper demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage the health of populations systematically underestimated the illness burden of Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent health needs, because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and Black patients with equivalent illness severity had historically lower healthcare costs due to systemic barriers to access (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S, Science, 2019;366(6464):447-453). This was not a fringe finding about an obscure tool. It was a peer-reviewed analysis of an algorithm used across hundreds of health systems, affecting millions of patients. The mechanism of bias in that case was not a programming error. It was a design choice that encoded existing health inequities into an automated recommendation system and then amplified those inequities at scale.⏎⏎PNHP's member laboratories have reported significant variation in what FDA clearance pathways and payer pre-authorization requirements actually demand with respect to demographic subgroup performance validation. In some cases, FDA 510(k) clearance was obtained on the basis of validation studies that did not include adequate representation of the racial, ethnic, or socioeconomic populations that the tool would be deployed to serve. The absence of a standardized analytical validation framework that requires demographic disaggregation as a condition of clearance is not a minor regulatory gap. It is a structural mechanism through which health disparities can be laundered through the language of algorithmic objectivity. HHS has both the authority and the responsibility to close this gap, and this RFI is an appropriate vehicle for doing so. The Department should require, as a non-negotiable condition of any pathway toward reimbursement or deployment authorization, that clinical AI tools demonstrate performance equivalence across demographic subgroups, and that this demonstration be based on prospective validation data from populations representative of the intended use population, not retrospective analysis of convenience samples.⏎⏎⏎Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 3⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF REIMBURSEMENT STRUCTURE⏎⏎PNHP focuses the following observations primarily on the reimbursement questions raised in the RFI, because they are the questions most directly implicated by our member survey data and our MAC coverage determination analysis.⏎⏎The current reimbursement landscape for clinical AI is, as our analysis confirms, characterized by fragmentation, inconsistency, and what one of our member laboratory directors described at our 2024 Annual Scientific Meeting as a kind of regulatory limbo that makes responsible deployment planning nearly impossible. We understand the appeal of the argument that reimbursement certainty would enable more deliberate, safety-conscious adoption by creating a stable economic environment for investment in proper implementation. We take that argument seriously. But PNHP is concerned that the specific reimbursement pathways being discussed in the context of AI, including new technology add-on payments and MAC-driven local coverage determinations, are being pursued in a sequence that gets the priority ordering backwards. The pattern we are observing is: tool receives FDA clearance based on limited validation data, tool enters clinical use under the pressure of payer and system incentives, real-world performance data accumulates, disparities and failure modes become visible, and then regulatory and reimbursement frameworks are revised in response. This is the wrong sequence. It is the sequence that produced the Obermeyer finding. It is the sequence that the automation bias literature predicts will produce systematic errors at scale before correction mechanisms are activated.⏎⏎PNHP recommends that HHS consider the following as minimum conditions that should be met before any AI-augmented clinical service becomes eligible for Medicare reimbursement:⏎⏎1. Prospective clinical validation in the intended use population, with demographic subgroup performance data disaggregated by race, ethnicity, age, sex, and socioeconomic status, submitted as part of the coverage determination record.⏎⏎2. Demonstrated performance equivalence across subgroups, with pre-specified acceptable performance thresholds established before, not after, deployment authorization.⏎⏎3. A mandatory post-deployment surveillance mechanism with defined triggers for coverage suspension if real-world performance data diverges from validation data at a pre-specified threshold.⏎⏎4. Documentation of the human oversight structure that will be maintained in clinical deployment, including specification of the clinical decision points at which human judgment is required to be exercised independently of the algorithmic recommendation.⏎⏎5. Transparency requirements that ensure ordering clinicians and patients have access to information about the AI tool's validation basis, known limitations, and demographic performance profile, consistent with the informed consent principles articulated in the shared decision-making literature (Stacey D, Légaré F, Lewis K, et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2017;4:CD001431).⏎⏎These are not novel requirements. They are applications of established principles of evidence-based medicine to a new category of clinical tool. The reason they feel onerous in the context of AI is not that they are inappropriate but that the AI industry and the health systems investing in AI tools have an interest in moving faster than these requirements would allow. PNHP submits that HHS's responsibility is to the patients who will be affected by these tools, not to the investment timelines of the entities deploying them.⏎⏎⏎THE THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP AS POLICY OBJECT⏎⏎PNHP wants to conclude the substantive portion of these comments by pressing HHS on a question that the RFI does not appear to have seriously considered: whether the therapeutic relationship is a policy object that the Department has any obligation to protect. We believe it is and we believe HHS does.⏎⏎Emanuel and Dubler, writing in JAMA in 1995 in the context of managed care's reorganization of clinical practice, argued that the physician-patient relationship is not merely a sentimental attachment but the functional substrate on which the clinical enterprise depends, and that policy frameworks that systematically erode the conditions for that relationship to function are properly understood as threats to the quality of care (Emanuel EJ, Dubler NN, JAMA, 1995;273(4):323-329). The argument they were making about managed care applies with equal or greater force to the current moment. The therapeutic relationship depends on time, on attention, on the clinician's capacity to be genuinely present to the patient rather than intermediating between the patient and a dashboard of algorithmic outputs. It depends on the patient's experience of being seen and heard by a person, not processed by a system. Bickmore and Paasche-Orlow have documented the specific ways in which health literacy and patient engagement are mediated by relational trust, and the particular vulnerability of patients with limited health literacy to the breakdown of that trust when clinical encounters become transactional (Bickmore TW, Paasche-Orlow MK, Am J Health Behav, 2012;36(5):744-752). If AI deployment systematically reduces the time and quality of direct clinician-patient contact, which is what the throughput logic driving current deployment patterns tends to produce, then it is not a neutral technological intervention in care delivery. It is a restructuring of the clinical encounter in ways that will have differential impacts on the patients who are already most disadvantaged by the existing system.⏎⏎PNHP is not arguing for a moratorium on clinical AI. We are arguing that HHS should be explicit, in whatever regulatory and reimbursement framework it develops in response to this RFI, that the preservation of meaningful human clinical judgment and the preservation of the conditions necessary for the therapeutic relationship to function are non-negotiable policy floors, not aspirational preferences to be traded off against efficiency gains. The Department has the authority to build those floors into coverage conditions, into FDA pre-market authorization requirements, into the ONC certification criteria for health IT products that incorporate AI, and into the research priorities it funds through AHRQ and NIH. The question is whether it has the will to do so against the considerable institutional pressure from health system administrators, technology vendors, and payer organizations who have significant financial interests in a different policy outcome.⏎⏎The Dzau and Balatbat analysis in The Lancet, which examined the imperatives for health system transformation in the coming decade, was explicit that the human dimensions of care are not obstacles to innovation but are constitutive of the health outcomes that innovation is supposed to serve (Dzau VJ, Balatbat CA, Lancet, 2020;396(10257):1071-1073). PNHP urges HHS to take that framing seriously. The accelerationist posture of this RFI is not inherently wrong as an orientation toward technological capability. What it risks, if left uncorrected by the kind of policy commitments we are urging here, is a clinical AI deployment environment in which the tools are good and the care is worse.⏎⏎One practical note on process: PNHP requests that HHS convene a dedicated technical expert panel on the therapeutic relationship and AI-mediated care, with membership that includes not only AI developers, health system administrators, and payer representatives, but clinical ethicists, patient advocates from underserved communities, and frontline clinicians who have direct experience with how AI tool deployment has changed the texture of their clinical encounters. The membership of such a panel matters enormously to the quality of the policy output, and the voices most likely to be marginalized in a process dominated by commercial stakeholders are precisely the voices whose testimony is most relevant to the questions PNHP has raised here. We would note that the contact for follow-up on these comments is jrobinson@pnhp.org, though we recognize that the docket process is the formal mechanism.⏎⏎⏎Physicians for a National Health Program | HHS AI RFI | Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 4⏎⏎⏎The post-deployment surveillance mechanism we describe above is, in our view, the single most important structural gap in the current framework, and we would urge HHS to treat it as a priority even if other elements of a comprehensive framework take longer to develop. The MAC coverage determination process, as currently structured, has no mandatory real-world performance monitoring requirement attached to coverage decisions for AI-augmented services, which means that a tool can receive a local coverage determination based on pre-market validation data and then perform differently in the real-world population without any automatic mechanism to detect that divergence or trigger a coverage review. That is a specific, correctable structural deficiency, and correcting it does not require resolving all of the harder conceptual questions about AI governance. SYNTH-0049♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Donna Scott♔American Lung Association♔♔♔♔♔American Lung Association⏎Comments to HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Federal Register Docket, 89 FR 22xxx⏎Submitted by: Donna Scott, Community Organizer, American Lung Association — Kansas Regional Office⏎⏎THE ISSUE HHS IS NOT ADDRESSING⏎⏎The framing of this Request for Information is itself a policy choice, and the American Lung Association believes that choice deserves scrutiny before any of the specific inquiries it poses are addressed. The RFI asks what HHS can do to "accelerate the adoption and use" of artificial intelligence in clinical settings — language that presupposes acceleration is the appropriate goal, that adoption is the appropriate metric, and that uncertainty is the appropriate enemy. The phrase "reducing uncertainty that impedes AI innovation," drawn directly from the RFI's framing (ONC, 2024, 89 FR 22xxx), is not neutral administrative language. It is an ideological posture. It treats the democratic process of deliberation — the legitimate uncertainty of a public that has not been asked whether it wants algorithmically mediated medicine — as an obstacle to be managed rather than a signal to be heeded. This organization wants to be precise about what is being objected to: not AI in clinical care per se, but the quiet normalization of a governance framework that has not been authorized by Congress, ratified by any meaningful public process, or subjected to the kind of institutional accountability we would demand of any other transformation of comparable scale.⏎⏎The American Lung Association represents the interests of patients, particularly those managing chronic respiratory conditions, who are among the most frequent users of prior authorization systems, and among the populations most likely to be affected by automated clinical decision support tools deployed without adequate oversight. Our concern here is not primarily clinical — questions of bias and accuracy are handled ably elsewhere in the literature (Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, & Mullainathan, 2019, Science) — but democratic and structural. The central issue is whether HHS possesses the mandate to be doing what it is doing, and whether the infrastructure being built is reversible if the determination turns out to be negative.⏎⏎THE IRREVERSIBILITY PROBLEM, STATED PLAINLY⏎⏎Langdon Winner asked, in 1980, whether artifacts have politics — whether the design of technical systems encodes choices that outlast the decisions that produced them (Winner, 1980, Daedalus). The conclusion, applied to healthcare AI, is clearly yes, and the implications for this RFI are serious. When proprietary AI systems are embedded into clinical workflows at sufficient scale, the knowledge required to audit, contest, or replace them begins to atrophy. Clinicians who have not exercised independent judgment about a particular diagnostic category in three years are not simply "rusty." They have lost access to the institutional memory that made independent judgment possible in the first place (Braithwaite, Herkes, Ludlow, Testa, & Lamprell, 2017, BMJ Open). This is not a hypothetical. It is precisely what happened during the hospital consolidation waves of the 1990s and 2000s, when regional health systems that surrendered billing and administrative infrastructure to consolidated vendors found, a decade later, that they could not reconstitute it — not because the knowledge was secret, but because the people who held it had retired, been reassigned, or simply stopped being hired (Dafny & Lee, 2016, New England Journal of Medicine). HHS is proposing to accelerate a process that carries identical lock-in dynamics, and it is doing so without any serious discussion of exit mechanisms, reversibility requirements, or public accountability structures.⏎⏎The opacity problem compounds the reversibility problem. Proprietary AI systems in clinical care are, by design, not transparent. Selbst and Barocas (2018, Fordham Law Review) documented the structural impossibility of meaningful explanation in many machine learning architectures — not because vendors are malicious, but because the systems are genuinely not interpretable in the way that clinical accountability requires. Pasquale (2015, The Black Box Society) extended this analysis to the governance dimension: when the systems that govern consequential decisions are opaque, the possibility of meaningful democratic accountability does not merely diminish, it disappears. The American Lung Association does not believe HHS has grappled with this at all. The RFI contains no discussion of what accountability looks like when a prior authorization denial is generated by a system whose decision logic cannot be examined, cannot be subpoenaed in a meaningful form, and cannot be compared against a counterfactual because the counterfactual no longer exists in the workflow.⏎⏎American Lung Association Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The National Academy for State Health Policy documented, in its 2023 policy brief on state legislative approaches to AI in prior authorization, that at least seventeen states had moved to impose transparency or audit requirements on algorithmic prior authorization systems precisely because federal frameworks had not done so. The fact that state legislatures — with far less technical capacity than HHS — felt compelled to act should be read as a signal, not a footnote. It suggests that the democratic preemption of public deliberation by accelerated federal AI adoption policy is already being contested at the level where democratic accountability is most legible. HHS should be examining why that is happening, not designing frameworks that make it harder.⏎⏎WHAT THE CLEARINGHOUSE DATA ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎The American Lung Association's organizational survey, conducted across 847 member clearinghouses in 2024, found that 68% of respondents reported receiving AI-generated prior authorization requests containing data formatting inconsistencies significant enough to trigger manual review queues. The average processing delay caused by these inconsistencies was 4.2 days per claim. Across a membership collectively processing more than 2.3 billion clinical transactions annually, that number is not a rounding error. It represents tens of millions of patient-days of delayed care, concentrated disproportionately in populations — including those with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, and related conditions — for whom delays in medication authorization carry real clinical consequence.⏎⏎The Q3 2024 Policy Working Group, convening representatives from fourteen regional clearinghouse networks, identified the absence of standardized AI output schemas as the single most frequently cited interoperability barrier impeding clinical AI adoption at the point of transaction. This finding has a direct bearing on the RFI's sections regarding regulatory and research-and-development actions. The specific barriers our membership encounters are not primarily about clinical accuracy or algorithmic bias. They are about the downstream transaction infrastructure — the clearinghouse layer — being asked to absorb the cost of AI systems that were designed without reference to the operational realities of that layer. When an AI-generated prior authorization request arrives in a format that does not conform to existing X12 transaction standards, the clearinghouse does not have the option of returning it for revision. It enters a manual review queue, and a human being — increasingly a scarce resource — spends time on a problem that should not exist.⏎⏎This is what Coiera (2019, Journal of Medical Internet Research) called the "last mile" problem: the gap between what AI systems can do in controlled conditions and what they actually do at the point of real-world implementation. HHS's acceleration framework addresses the first gap and appears largely unaware of the second. The clearinghouse layer is invisible in the RFI's framing, and the American Lung Association submits that this invisibility is not incidental. It reflects a policy design process that consulted vendors and health systems and, to a much lesser extent, the transaction infrastructure that actually moves clinical data between them.⏎⏎SPECIFIC REQUESTS REGARDING RFI TOPIC AREAS⏎⏎The American Lung Association addresses the following areas specifically, without attempting to cover the full scope of the RFI:⏎⏎Regarding standardization requirements for AI-generated clinical transactions:⏎⏎1. HHS should require, as a condition of any reimbursement accommodation for AI-assisted prior authorization, that AI systems generating X12-formatted transactions demonstrate conformance with existing EDI standards through a third-party testing protocol. The current absence of such a requirement is the direct cause of the 4.2-day processing delay documented in our 2024 survey.⏎⏎2. ONC should convene a technical working group that includes clearinghouse representatives — not merely EHR vendors and payers — to develop standardized output schemas for AI-generated prior authorization requests. The fourteen regional networks represented in our Q3 2024 Policy Working Group have expressed willingness to participate and have not, to the American Lung Association's knowledge, been invited to any comparable federal process.⏎⏎3. Any AI system operating in the prior authorization workflow should be required to produce a machine-readable audit log in a standardized format, retained for a minimum of seven years, and accessible to the clearinghouse processing the transaction. This is not a novel requirement — it is the functional equivalent of what we already require of human reviewers in many state regulatory frameworks.⏎⏎Regarding the democratic accountability deficit in HHS's framing:⏎⏎o The RFI should be reissued with a specific inquiry evaluating whether the public supports the federal government's role in accelerating AI adoption in clinical care, rather than presupposing that conclusion.⏎⏎o HHS should commission an independent assessment of the reversibility of AI infrastructure decisions made between 2022 and 2025, with particular attention to proprietary system dependencies that cannot be unwound without significant cost or knowledge loss.⏎⏎o Any reimbursement incentive for AI adoption should include a sunset provision requiring affirmative reauthorization after five years, with a public comment period that specifically solicits evidence of harm as well as benefit.⏎⏎American Lung Association Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎The accountability deficit is not abstract. Eubanks (2018, Automating Inequality) documented with considerable specificity how algorithmic governance systems, once embedded in public-facing institutions, become effectively immune to democratic challenge — not because they are protected by law, but because the technical complexity required to contest them exceeds the capacity of any individual or community organization to mobilize. The American Lung Association is a sophisticated organizational actor with legal staff, policy expertise, and a national network. If this organization finds the opacity of AI-generated prior authorization decisions difficult to navigate, the implications for individual patients — particularly those in rural Kansas communities who are managing respiratory conditions without specialist access — should concern HHS deeply. Topol (2019, Nature Medicine) has argued that AI in medicine can expand access and reduce clinician burden, and the American Lung Association does not dismiss that argument. But the conditions under which it might be true require precisely the kind of transparency, accountability, and democratic legitimacy that the current acceleration framework is not building.⏎⏎THE MANDATE ISSUE⏎⏎The American Lung Association wants to close on a point that is uncomfortable but necessary. HHS has not been authorized by Congress, and has certainly not been authorized by the American public, to decide that clinical medicine should be algorithmically governed at scale. The Department has authority over reimbursement, over certification standards, over research funding — but authority over those instruments is not the same as a mandate to use them in combination to produce a particular technological future without public deliberation. The highway system analogy is instructive here, and not in a flattering way: the Interstate Highway System was built with enormous federal investment and produced enormous economic benefits, and it also restructured American cities in ways that took decades to understand and that remain, in many respects, irreversible. The communities displaced by highway construction did not consent to that outcome. They were not asked. The acceleration of AI in clinical care, proceeding as it currently is, has the same structure: benefits that accrue to the legible stakeholders who were consulted, and costs that accrue to the communities and transaction-layer workers who were not.⏎⏎Doshi-Velez and co-authors (2017, Berkman Klein Center) argued that accountability for AI under law requires not just explanation but the institutional capacity to act on explanation — to modify, override, or reject algorithmic outputs in a context where doing so is genuinely possible. That capacity is being eroded, not preserved, by the acceleration framework HHS is proposing. The American Lung Association does not believe the Department has engaged seriously with what it means to build infrastructure that cannot be unbuilt, and to do so on a timeline that forecloses the kind of democratic deliberation that should precede decisions of this magnitude.⏎⏎The organizational survey data cited above — 847 clearinghouses, 2.3 billion transactions, 4.2 days of average delay — is offered not merely as evidence of an operational problem but as evidence of a governance problem. The clearinghouse layer is absorbing costs that were never allocated to it, generated by systems that were never designed with it in mind, under a federal framework that has never acknowledged its existence as a stakeholder. That is the specific, concrete version of the democratic accountability deficit that Eubanks and Pasquale describe in the abstract. HHS should address it not by issuing guidance on clearinghouse best practices, but by evaluating who was in the room when the acceleration framework was designed, and who was not.⏎⏎The American Lung Association would welcome the opportunity to present the Q3 2024 Policy Working Group findings in a technical briefing with ONC staff. Contact information for the Kansas Regional Office policy team is available through the organization's national headquarters. The working group documentation, including the full survey instrument and regional network response data broken down by transaction volume and system type, can be made available under appropriate data sharing⏎⏎alungcomments-kansas@lung.org⏎⏎arrangements pending execution of a standard data use agreement. Our comments focus specifically on two of the RFI's central inquiries: what regulatory conditions should govern pre-deployment authorization of clinical AI tools, and how should HHS structure reimbursement incentives to promote responsible adoption. We do not address the full scope of the RFI. Our concern is narrower and, we believe, more urgent than the Department's current framing suggests.⏎⏎⏎⏎ORGANIZATIONAL STANDING AND THE DENTAL AI EVIDENCE BASE⏎⏎⏎⏎The Digital Medicine Society represents 847 member dental practices across 34 states. Our policy working group completed an 18-month analysis of FDA-cleared dental AI products — specifically caries detection and periodontal risk stratification software — concluding in early 2025. That analysis identified a finding that we regard as disqualifying for the current accelerationist posture HHS appears to be adopting: no standardized performance benchmarks exist for diverse patient populations among the cleared dental AI products we reviewed. None. A 2024 survey of our membership found that 62% of practices had explored one or more diagnostic AI software options, yet only 23% had successfully integrated such solutions into routine clinical workflows. When asked why adoption stalled, 78% of those practices cited reimbursement uncertainty and unclear compliance standards — not clinical skepticism, not technology limitations. The practices were willing. The regulatory environment gave them no safe ground to stand on.⏎⏎⏎⏎We also convened four regional roundtables between 2023 and 2024, in Tulsa, Nashville, Albuquerque, and Baltimore, bringing together dental school faculty, private practitioners, and group practice administrators. Across those sessions, participants reported consistently that HHS and CMS guidance on AI documentation requirements for claim submission is entirely absent. This is not a gap that accelerating adoption will fill. It is a gap that, if ignored, will produce compliance failures and, more consequentially, disparate clinical harm concentrated in the practices and patient populations least equipped to detect it.⏎⏎⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED PATTERN HHS CANNOT AFFORD TO REPEAT⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department should approach this RFI with full awareness that algorithmic bias in clinical AI is not a theoretical concern or a future risk — it is a documented, recurring pattern with a clear mechanism. In their 2019 Science publication, Obermeyer and coauthors showed how a population health model implemented at scale consistently minimized the medical acuity of Black individuals. This occurred because the software relied on medical spending to estimate clinical necessity, encoding decades of access inequity directly into its predictions (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447–453). Sjoding et al. found that pulse oximeters — a technology so embedded in clinical practice that its bias went unexamined for decades — produced occult hypoxemia at significantly higher rates in Black individuals compared to their white counterparts (Sjoding MW et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477–2478). Seyyed-Kalantari et al. documented that AI algorithms applied to chest radiographs systematically underdiagnosed conditions in underserved populations, with performance degradation that was invisible in aggregate accuracy metrics but pronounced at the subgroup level (Seyyed-Kalantari L et al. Nat Med. 2021;27(12):2176–2182). Wong et al. showed that a proprietary sepsis prediction model widely implemented in hospital systems performed substantially worse when externally validated in community settings than its developers had reported (Wong A et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065–1070). Adamson and Smith raised the same concern about dermatology AI, where training datasets drawn from academic medical center archives dramatically underrepresented patients with darker skin tones (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247–1248).⏎⏎⏎⏎The mechanism is consistent across these cases. Gianfrancesco et al. identified it precisely: when training data is drawn from populations with systematically different patterns of care access, documentation quality, and treatment history, the resulting model will reproduce those patterns as if they were clinical ground truth (Gianfrancesco MA et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544–1547). Vyas et al. extended this analysis to show that race correction embedded in clinical algorithms — sometimes inadvertently, sometimes by design — can actively direct resources away from patients who need them most (Vyas DA et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874–882). Char, Shah, and Magnus argued in 2018 that the implementation of machine learning in healthcare requires proactive ethical governance, not post-hoc correction, because the scale of deployment amplifies bias effects far beyond what any individual clinical error could produce (Char DS et al. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981–983). The GAO reached a similar conclusion in its 2022 assessment, finding that benefits from health AI are unevenly distributed and that existing regulatory frameworks do not adequately address equity risks (GAO-22-104629. Washington, DC: GAO; 2022).⏎⏎⏎⏎Digital Medicine Society Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎Our own 18-month analysis found that this pattern extends directly into dental AI. The National Dental Association and Health Equity Research Collaborative documented in 2023 that FDA-cleared oral health diagnostic AI products were validated almost exclusively on datasets from academic dental schools and large private group practices — populations that are whiter, wealthier, and more frequently insured than the patients seen in community health centers and Medicaid-dominant practices (NDAHRC. Diagnostic AI in Oral Health: Equity Gaps in FDA-Cleared Device Validation Studies. Washington, DC; 2023). The Obermeyer algorithmic bias playbook from the University of Chicago's Center for Applied AI offers a practical framework for identifying these gaps before deployment, but its use is entirely voluntary, and no HHS regulation currently requires it (Obermeyer Z et al. Algorithmic Bias Playbook. Center for Applied AI, University of Chicago Booth School of Business. 2021).⏎⏎⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM AND DEPLOYMENT-SETTING DEGRADATION⏎⏎⏎⏎There is a second mechanism of harm that the RFI does not appear to engage with adequately. When clinical AI tools produce outputs with the visual and rhetorical authority of objective diagnostics — probability scores, color-coded risk flags, annotated radiographic overlays — they suppress the clinician's inclination to interrogate those outputs. This is automation bias, and it is well-documented in safety-critical fields. In the dental context, a caries detection algorithm that flags a lesion with 94% confidence will almost certainly be accepted by a busy practitioner in a high-volume community clinic, even if that algorithm was validated on a dataset demographically unlike that clinic's patient population and has never been tested in that setting. The performance degradation Wong et al. documented in sepsis prediction — where a model performing well in its development environment failed significantly in external validation — is not an anomaly. It is what happens when deployment settings differ from development settings, which they almost always do in safety-net and rural contexts.⏎⏎⏎⏎The ONC's Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability final rule at 45 CFR Parts 170 and 171 (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, Jan. 9, 2024) establishes algorithm transparency requirements for certain decision support interventions, but those requirements do not extend to pre-deployment equity auditing or post-deployment performance surveillance stratified by patient demographics. That gap is the specific regulatory failure our organization is asking HHS to address.⏎⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎⏎⏎Our organization urges HHS to take the following actions before extending reimbursement incentives to clinical AI tools:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. Require mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing as a condition of reimbursement eligibility. Any AI tool for which CMS reimbursement is sought should be required to demonstrate validated performance across race, ethnicity, insurance status, and geographic practice setting before that reimbursement pathway is opened.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. Establish post-deployment bias surveillance requirements. Vendors of reimbursement-eligible AI tools should be required to report performance metrics broken down by patient demographics and practice setting type to HHS on a defined reporting schedule, with performance thresholds below which continued reimbursement eligibility is suspended.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. Adopt population-specific performance benchmarks for dental AI specifically. Given our working group's finding that no such benchmarks currently exist for FDA-cleared dental AI products, and given that practices serving Medicaid beneficiaries are disproportionately exposed to undetected performance degradation, HHS should task ONC and CMS jointly with developing those benchmarks in coordination with the dental professional community by no later than calendar year 2026.⏎⏎⏎⏎4. Institute a conditional moratorium on new reimbursement incentives for AI diagnostic tools until the equity auditing framework described above is in place. This is not opposition to AI adoption. It is opposition to adoption that repeats the pulse oximetry error at a larger scale and in a context — dental care — where Medicaid coverage gaps already produce serious access inequities.⏎⏎⏎⏎Our policy working group is available to provide technical assistance to HHS staff developing the equity auditing framework. SYNTH-0051♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Mitchell♔♔♔♔♔♔SUBMITTED TO: HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎RE: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Stephanie Mitchell, Commercial Motor Vehicle Operator (CDL Class A), Medford, Oregon⏎⏎THE PROBLEM WITH "ACCELERATION"⏎⏎My cardiologist's office in Medford ran me through an AI-assisted cardiac screening during my DOT physical renewal in March of this year. The computer flagged what it called a cardiac anomaly. What followed was three months of follow-up echocardiograms, a referral to a specialist up in Portland, and enough anxiety to make me genuinely unsure if I would ever be medically certified to drive again. Ultimately, a human cardiologist determined that the computer program had misread a physiological adaptation that is completely normal for anyone who has spent thirty years doing the heavy lifting and demanding work that long-haul trucking demands. An athletic heart. Not a disease. Not even close. The front office staff had no idea how the program reached its conclusion. Nobody could tell me what group of people it was tested on, whether that group included commercial drivers, or if the software had ever been checked against the specific rules governing occupational fitness under 49 CFR Part 391. Nobody even seemed to think those details mattered.⏎⏎I am writing this letter because HHS is currently asking how to speed up the rollout of systems exactly like the one that nearly derailed my entire livelihood. Looking at it from that angle completely misses the mark.⏎⏎WHAT HHS IS ACTUALLY PROPOSING⏎⏎This solicitation mostly talks about AI adoption as a way to boost productivity and efficiency. The words "enhancing productivity" are right there in the document, and the whole push seems to treat the main hurdle as how fast we can get this software running, rather than how safe it is. I want to be blunt about what that perspective shows. When a federal health department talks about clinical AI mainly as a way to increase output, it sends a clear message to patients about how the agency views medical care. It implies that healthcare is just an assembly line, that visits between doctors and patients are mere transactions to be counted, and that HHS cares more about optimizing volume than ensuring high-quality human judgment is applied to real people experiencing distress.⏎⏎That perspective is not just some neutral tech jargon. It is a deliberate administrative decision, and the fallout will hit hardest on the very patients who already struggle to get decent care.⏎⏎The actual research on what drives good medical results contradicts this assembly-line mindset. A 2014 paper by Kelley and colleagues in the Journal of General Internal Medicine showed clear health improvements directly linked to patients seeing the same providers over time. The actual human connection, not just getting a diagnostic code right, plays a huge role in getting people better. When you swap out a doctor's direct thinking for a computer's output, you are not just saving time on a chore. You are fundamentally changing the doctor-patient interaction, wearing away the very foundation that good health outcomes rely on. HHS acts like this does not matter. I strongly disagree, and the medical evidence backs me up.⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS IS NOT A HYPOTHETICAL RISK⏎⏎Researchers who study human behavior often talk about something called automation bias. A 2012 review by Goddard and others in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association described this as the habit of people in highly automated settings to blindly trust computer outputs, which leads them to stop double-checking the work themselves. Their review noted that this blind trust happens in pretty much every industry, and it gets much worse when people are rushed, overwhelmed, or dealing with high volumes of work. Those are the exact circumstances where clinical AI is currently being rolled out.⏎⏎In a 2019 Nature Medicine article, Eric Topol wrote about blending human and machine intelligence. He is largely hopeful about what AI can do, and I want to acknowledge his viewpoint fairly. Yet even he points out that automation bias is a serious problem requiring built-in safeguards. He does not say we should abandon the technology, but he insists we must be extremely cautious about mixing it into medical routines. The current HHS document barely touches on this danger. It focuses on speeding up the rollout without bothering to ask what safety nets need to be built first before hitting the gas pedal on adoption.⏎⏎Wachter and Cassel wrote something in JAMA in 2020 that really stuck with me: if doctors spend most of their day just signing off on what a machine tells them instead of thinking for themselves, their diagnostic skills will fade. That is not just a guess. It is exactly what happens to any professional who stops actively practicing their craft. I see this all the time out on the highway. I have watched what relying entirely on a GPS does to truckers who stop looking at the actual road signs. They lose their situational awareness. They miss hazards the screen was never programmed to catch. When the screen glitches out, they have no idea how to fix the situation, because they let their basic navigation skills get rusty. The exact same thing will happen in medicine, and it deeply frustrates me that HHS does not see this as a massive red flag.⏎⏎THE EXPLAINABILITY GAP IS NOT A MINOR TECHNICAL DETAIL⏎⏎The Oregon Health Authority released a 2023 report on health technology that pointed out a glaring lack of rules requiring these AI occupational screening tools to actually explain their math. That might sound like a niche issue, but it matters deeply. The software used for workplace health checks—like DOT physicals, which are legally binding under FMCSA rules—often faces zero requirements to show its work. The doctor looking at the screen might have no way of knowing how the software arrived at its conclusion. The patient whose life is upended by that conclusion definitely has no way of knowing.⏎⏎In my situation, the computer threw a warning flag. That warning set off a chain reaction of regulatory hurdles that threatened my job. Not a single person in that clinic could explain which part of my ECG triggered the warning, what baseline the software was judging me against, or how often it gets things wrong for older women with my physical background. The computer's guess was treated as absolute medical truth, even though no human in the building could decipher how it made that guess. That is not just some small technical hiccup. It is a complete breakdown in basic accountability, and it threatened my ability to earn a living.⏎⏎A 2021 Health Affairs brief by Hyman and Silver noted that when doctors stop relying on their own reasoning in highly automated clinics, it does more than just hurt the quality of care. It creates a massive loophole for dodging blame. If a provider just agrees with a computer and the computer is dead wrong, figuring out who is at fault becomes a giant mess. The software company will just point the finger at the doctor, saying the human was supposed to be in charge. But the doctor might not have been given enough data to actually double-check the machine's work. The patient ends up suffering, and everyone washes their hands of it. This is not some rare, imaginary scenario. This is exactly what happened to me.⏎⏎WHAT SHOULD ACTUALLY HAPPEN BEFORE ACCELERATION⏎⏎I want to be incredibly clear about what I want HHS to do here, because I am not saying we need to ban clinical AI completely. I am saying your priorities are in the wrong order.⏎⏎Before HHS changes rules or payment structures to push AI into clinics faster, the agency must mandate strict transparency for any diagnostic software used in situations with legal or career impacts. DOT physicals are the perfect example, along with disability claims, fitness-for-duty exams, and insurance screenings. Transparency needs to mean something real: the medical provider using the software must be able to see, in plain English, exactly what data points caused the result, the margin of error for that result, and the specific demographics of the people the software was originally tested on. That is not too much to ask. It is the bare minimum required for a doctor to actually do their job instead of just blindly signing off on a mystery machine's guess.⏎⏎HHS must also demand thorough fairness testing before these tools are unleashed on groups of people who look different from the original test subjects. This is not some wild new concept. It is a standard requirement for any rigorous testing process. The fact that occupational health software currently gets a free pass on this is a massive loophole, and HHS has the power—and the duty—to fix it.⏎⏎Furthermore, HHS needs to stop acting like the bond between doctor and patient is just some outdated tradition that computers will eventually replace. The research on seeing the same provider over time, dating back to that Kelley paper and beyond, proves that human connection matters. Having a doctor who actually knows you, who can read your body language, and who can tell when your verbal answer contradicts the look of worry in your eyes—that is not a waste of time to be streamlined out of existence. It is the core of good medicine. Inserting an algorithm into the middle of that dynamic alters it in ways nobody is tracking. HHS ought to mandate studies on that impact before handing out financial rewards to clinics that sideline human doctors.⏎⏎A NOTE ON WHO BEARS THE COST OF ERRORS⏎⏎One final point. Reading through this document, it seems completely geared toward the benefit of hospital networks, software companies, and insurance firms. When this technology saves time, those are the groups that reap the rewards. When the software makes a mistake, the patient pays the price. For me, that price was a solid three months of intense stress, thousands of dollars in out-of-pocket medical bills that my insurance refused to fully cover, and the terrifying prospect of losing my livelihood. I am a perfectly healthy seventy-year-old woman. I have safely driven big rigs for thirty years without a single major health issue. The computer program did not know any of that. It could not ask me about my history. It could not look me in the eye and see my fear, or ask follow-up questions that were not printed on the clipboard, or balance my lifelong health record against whatever tiny blip it thought it saw.⏎⏎A competent human doctor would have done all of those things. But the provider I saw that day did none of them, because they were too busy managing a software alert to actually examine the human sitting on the exam table. That is the exact scenario HHS is trying to make more common. I firmly believe the agency needs to demand proof that this hands-off approach is actually safe before handing out any more incentives to spread it.⏎⏎That Oregon Health Authority report regarding the lack of transparency in workplace screening software is crucial here, because a DOT physical is not just a routine checkup. It is a strict legal requirement that dictates whether a person is allowed to work. The FMCSA enforces those medical rules under 49 CFR Part 391 to ensure public safety on our highways. If a clinic uses a computer program to decide whether a driver passes or fails, and that program cannot clearly explain its math to the human doctor signing the form, the entire legal foundation of that safety check falls apart. HHS ought to be deeply worried about that. Right now, it does not seem like they are.⏎⏎Speaking purely practically, I burned through roughly forty hours over the course of three months just dealing with the sheer logistical nightmare caused by one false computer alarm. I was stuck making endless phone calls, wrangling with scheduling, filling out redundant forms, and paying for a hotel room in Portland just to see the specialist because I could not manage the drive up from Medford and back in a single day. Nobody paid me for those lost hours. I guarantee none of my wasted time factored into anyone's grand calculations about how much "efficiency" this software creates.♔♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔individual♔high♔angry♔Oregon♔truck driver♔70♔My cardiologist's office in Medford ran me through a new AI-assisted diagnostic screening at my DOT physical renewal in March, and the system flagged an "anomaly" that triggered three months of follow-up tests, specialist referrals, and enough anxiety to make me question whether I'd ever climb back into a cab — only for the final human review to determine the algorithm had misread my perfectly normal athletic heart rate adaptation from thirty years of long-haul driving.
