SYNTH-0054♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Hernandez♔Boston Scientific♔♔♔♔♔Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 1⏎⏎Barbara Hernandez, MD, MBA⏎Chief Medical Officer⏎Boston Scientific / Tapestryhealth Affiliated Network⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎February 2025⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Tapestryhealth's affiliated network of 47 care sites has deployed AI-assisted clinical decision support tools at meaningful scale, and our internal data confirm real efficiency gains: a 23% reduction in average diagnostic turnaround time and measurable reductions in clinician cognitive burden as documented in structured post-implementation surveys completed by 892 providers across the network. We are not opposed to AI adoption. We have invested in it. We have seen it work.⏎⏎What we have also seen, and what this RFI conspicuously fails to address, is the systematic failure of these tools when deployed outside the academic medical center environments where they were trained and validated. We have watched the same tools that performed well in our larger urban facilities produce outputs of materially degraded quality in our rural sites and safety-net institutions. We have documented clinician automation bias developing over time in our own post-implementation surveys, with providers reporting, in their own words, that they question AI recommendations less as familiarity increases. And we have read the peer-reviewed literature that demonstrates, across multiple clinical domains, that AI systems trained on historical healthcare data do not merely reflect existing disparities in care but amplify them in ways that are measurable and, if left unsurveilled, will compound with each new deployment.⏎⏎HHS is proposing to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. That is a policy choice with real consequences. The Department has not proposed mandatory pre-deployment equity auditing. It has not proposed post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting requirements. It has not proposed that performance stratification by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, or care setting be a condition of reimbursement eligibility. These are not minor technical omissions. They are structural gaps that will produce predictable harm to the patients least positioned to absorb it.⏎⏎This comment addresses two specific areas of the RFI: the regulatory framework for AI deployment in clinical settings, and the reimbursement conditions HHS should attach to AI-augmented services. We have not attempted to address every question in the RFI. The equity concerns documented below are sufficiently serious that they warrant focused attention rather than broad coverage.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 2⏎⏎SECTION I: THE EQUITY FAILURE MODES THIS RFI DOES NOT ADDRESS⏎⏎The published literature on AI bias in healthcare is not speculative. It is not a collection of theoretical concerns raised by academic ethicists. It is a body of peer-reviewed findings documenting specific, measurable harm to specific patient populations, and HHS is proposing to scale the systems responsible for that harm without requiring the safeguards that would detect it.⏎⏎The most widely cited finding is probably Obermeyer and colleagues' 2019 analysis in Science, which demonstrated that a commercial algorithm used to manage the health of populations systematically assigned lower risk scores to Black patients than to white patients with equivalent levels of illness, effectively directing resources away from patients who needed them more (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). The mechanism was straightforward: the algorithm used healthcare costs as a proxy for health needs, and because Black patients had historically received less care, their costs were lower, so the algorithm rated them as healthier. This is not a design flaw that was subsequently corrected and can now be treated as a closed chapter. It is a demonstration of what happens when AI systems are trained on data that encodes decades of discriminatory care patterns. The data reflects the disparity. The model learns the disparity. The model then reproduces and, at scale, amplifies it.⏎⏎The pulse oximetry findings reported by Sjoding and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 document a different but equally serious failure mode (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Pulse oximeters, which have been in clinical use for decades and which clinicians treat as reliable, overestimate oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin tones. The implication for AI systems that incorporate pulse oximetry data in their training is direct: any model trained on that data has learned from systematically incorrect measurements for a subset of the patient population. When those models are then used to make or support clinical decisions about oxygenation, deterioration risk, or ventilator management, the bias is not introduced by the AI. It was already there in the training data, invisible, and the AI operationalizes it at scale.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 3⏎⏎Dermatology AI presents a third documented pattern. Adamson and Smith's 2018 analysis in JAMA Dermatology found that publicly available dermatology image datasets used to train machine learning models were heavily weighted toward images of lighter skin tones, with darker skin tones substantially underrepresented (Adamson AS, Smith A. JAMA Dermatol. 2018;154(11):1247-1248). The diagnostic performance of models trained on those datasets is, predictably, worse for patients with darker skin. This is not a surprising finding. It is the expected result of training a pattern-recognition system on an unrepresentative sample. What is surprising is that it remains an unaddressed regulatory gap five years after publication, and that HHS is now proposing to accelerate the adoption of AI diagnostic tools without requiring any demonstration that the training data was representative of the patient populations who will be subject to those tools' outputs.⏎⏎The sepsis prediction literature is where Tapestryhealth's internal experience most directly intersects with the published findings. Wong and colleagues' 2021 external validation study in JAMA Internal Medicine examined a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found that its performance in external validation was substantially worse than the performance reported in the original development studies, with the AUROC metrics that vendors cite in their marketing materials masking a downstream burden of false alerts that in real-world settings consumes nursing and physician attention at significant cost (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). Our own experience at Tapestryhealth sites mirrors this finding precisely. The same sepsis prediction tool that performed acceptably in our larger facilities with robust nursing ratios and well-resourced rapid response infrastructure generated alert fatigue at our rural and safety-net sites, where staffing constraints meant that the false-positive burden was not merely an inconvenience but a direct contributor to delayed response to genuine deterioration events. We are not in a position to share site-specific performance data in a public comment, but the pattern is consistent with what Wong et al. documented and with what Wiens and colleagues described in their 2019 Nature Medicine roadmap for responsible machine learning in healthcare, which specifically identified external validation in diverse care settings as a prerequisite for responsible deployment rather than an optional post-market activity (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340).⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 4⏎⏎The National Academy of Medicine's 2019 report on artificial intelligence in healthcare identified this validation gap as one of the most significant barriers to equitable AI deployment, noting that performance benchmarks established in academic medical centers routinely fail to generalize to community hospitals and rural settings where patient populations, documentation practices, and care infrastructure differ substantially from the training environment (National Academy of Medicine. Artificial Intelligence in Health Care: The Hope, the Hype, the Promise, the Peril. Washington, DC: National Academies Press; 2019). This is not a new concern. It was documented and published before the current wave of AI deployment accelerated. HHS is aware of this literature. The RFI's silence on mandatory community-setting validation is therefore a choice, not an oversight.⏎⏎We want to be precise about what we mean by "silence." The RFI asks broad questions about how to accelerate adoption and reduce barriers. It does not ask how to ensure that the tools being adopted perform equitably across the patient populations who will be subject to them. It does not ask what surveillance mechanisms should accompany deployment to detect performance degradation before patients are harmed. The framing of the RFI is, throughout, one of facilitation. Our concern is that facilitation without equity conditions is not a neutral posture. It is an active policy choice to externalize the risk of AI failure onto the patients who are already most harmed by inequitable care.⏎⏎Gianfrancesco and colleagues' 2018 analysis in JAMA Internal Medicine identified several specific sources of bias in machine learning models using electronic health record data, including differential data completeness across patient populations, differential rates of healthcare utilization that affect which patients appear in training datasets, and the encoding of socioeconomic proxies in clinical variables (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). Each of these bias sources is structural. None of them can be addressed after deployment. They require intervention at the point of model development and validation, and they require verification before clinical deployment, not after a harm event has prompted a retrospective review.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 5⏎⏎SECTION II: AUTOMATION BIAS IS A DOCUMENTED CLINICAL PHENOMENON AND HHS HAS PROPOSED NO MECHANISM TO ADDRESS IT⏎⏎The efficiency gains we have documented at Tapestryhealth are real. A 23% reduction in diagnostic turnaround time is clinically meaningful. We are not arguing against AI deployment. What our post-implementation data also show, however, is a pattern that the clinical literature identifies as automation bias: over time, clinicians exposed to AI decision support tools report reduced inclination to question the tool's recommendations. In our Q3 2024 structured post-implementation surveys, providers across the network described, in response to open-ended questions, that they had become less likely to seek additional clinical information when the AI output was consistent with an initial impression, and less likely to question AI recommendations when they were uncertain. This is not a failure of training or of individual clinical judgment. It is a documented cognitive phenomenon that occurs when clinicians interact with systems that appear authoritative and that have, in the clinician's experience, generally been reliable.⏎⏎The problem is that automation bias is most dangerous precisely when the AI is most wrong. And the literature documents that AI clinical tools are most wrong for patients with atypical presentations, incomplete medical records, and demographic profiles underrepresented in training data. These are, systematically, the patients who face the greatest barriers to equitable care in the first place. Char, Shah, and Magnus addressed this dynamic directly in their 2018 New England Journal of Medicine analysis of ethical challenges in healthcare machine learning implementation, noting that the populations most likely to be harmed by AI failure are frequently the same populations whose data is least well represented in training sets and whose care contexts differ most from the environments where models were validated (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). When a clinician's automation bias reduces their likelihood of questioning an AI recommendation, and that AI recommendation is degraded because the patient is Black, rural, elderly, or has an atypical presentation, the result is a compounding failure: the tool fails the patient and the clinician's modified behavior reduces the probability that the failure will be caught.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 6⏎⏎HHS has proposed no surveillance mechanism to detect this pattern in deployed systems. There is no proposed requirement for post-deployment performance monitoring stratified by patient demographics. There is no proposed threshold for performance degradation that would trigger review or suspension of reimbursement eligibility. The HTI-1 final rule's algorithm transparency provisions under 45 CFR Parts 170 and 171 represent a genuine regulatory step: requiring that developers of clinical decision support software subject to certification disclose the data used to train their algorithms and the performance metrics measured during development (Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. HTI-1 Final Rule. 45 CFR Parts 170 and 171. 2024). We support those provisions. But transparency about what happened during development does not create accountability for what happens after deployment. A vendor can disclose that their sepsis prediction model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 in a development cohort drawn from three academic medical centers, and that disclosure is fully compliant with HTI-1 requirements, and it tells a rural safety-net hospital almost nothing about how the model will perform in their patient population. The transparency framework is necessary. It is not sufficient.⏎⏎Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones' 2020 New England Journal of Medicine analysis of race correction in clinical algorithms is relevant here in a way that goes beyond dermatology or pulse oximetry (Vyas DA, Eisenstein LG, Jones DS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882). Their argument is that the use of race as a variable in clinical algorithms, even when intended to account for biological differences, frequently encodes social rather than biological determinants of health and thereby perpetuates rather than corrects disparities. The implication for AI systems is that models which include race as a feature variable, or which are trained on data that encodes race as a proxy for other variables, require specific scrutiny of whether race is functioning as a biological adjustment or as a proxy for differential care access. This is a question that pre-deployment equity auditing could address. Without a mandatory auditing requirement, it is a question that will go unasked in most commercial AI deployments.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 7⏎⏎SECTION III: THE REGULATORY GAP AND WHAT HHS MUST DO⏎⏎We want to be specific about what is missing from the current regulatory framework, because the RFI questions about regulatory actions HHS can take are where we have the most concrete recommendations to offer.⏎⏎The current framework has three structural gaps that must be addressed before reimbursement pathways for AI-augmented services are established:⏎⏎1. No mandatory pre-deployment equity audit requirement. AI clinical tools are currently validated by developers, and while FDA clearance for Software as a Medical Device addresses certain performance thresholds, it does not require stratified performance analysis by race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, or care setting as a condition of clearance or certification. HTI-1 requires disclosure of training data and performance metrics but does not require that performance be demonstrated to be equitable across patient subgroups. HHS should require, as a condition of reimbursement eligibility for AI-augmented clinical services, that developers provide pre-deployment equity audits conducted by independent third parties, stratified by race, ethnicity, language preference, socioeconomic status proxy variables, and care setting type (academic medical center, community hospital, rural health clinic, federally qualified health center). The audit methodology should be standardized and publicly available, not proprietary.⏎⏎2. No post-deployment bias surveillance mandate. Even a well-validated model can degrade when deployed in a new environment or when the patient population shifts. Pierson and colleagues' 2021 Nature Medicine analysis of algorithmic approaches to pain disparity documented how algorithmic systems that appear equitable in aggregate can produce systematically different outcomes for underserved populations when examined at the subgroup level (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140). Post-deployment surveillance is not optional. HHS should require that any care site receiving reimbursement for AI-augmented services implement ongoing performance monitoring stratified by the same demographic variables required in pre-deployment auditing, with results reported to a federal or federally designated registry on a defined schedule, not less than annually.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 8⏎⏎3. No performance degradation thresholds tied to reimbursement eligibility. The absence of a defined threshold for unacceptable performance means that a tool can fail systematically for a subset of patients without triggering any regulatory response. HHS should establish, through notice-and-comment rulemaking, performance degradation thresholds below which a clinical AI tool's reimbursement eligibility is automatically suspended pending review. These thresholds should be specific to clinical domain and patient subgroup, not aggregate performance metrics that can mask subgroup failures.⏎⏎We recognize that the administrative burden of these requirements is real. Our Q3 2024 policy review found that documentation overhead associated with AI tool utilization compliance was already consuming an estimated 1.4 hours per provider per week across the network, effectively offsetting a meaningful portion of the efficiency gains we had achieved. Additional reporting requirements will impose additional costs. We are not dismissing that concern. But the alternative, which is deploying tools at scale without equity guardrails and discovering the harm retrospectively, is not a cost-free option. It is a choice to externalize the cost onto patients who have no visibility into how the tools affecting their care are performing for people like them.⏎⏎The reimbursement uncertainty that 68% of our site medical directors cited as the primary barrier to sustained AI adoption is a legitimate policy problem that HHS should address. We support the development of clear coverage pathways for AI-augmented services. But coverage pathways that do not condition reimbursement eligibility on demonstrated equitable performance will create financial incentives for the deployment of tools that have not been validated for the patient populations they will be used on. That is the predictable consequence of separating the reimbursement question from the equity question, and the RFI's structure, which treats them as separate topics, reflects exactly that separation.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 9⏎⏎SECTION IV: SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The following recommendations address the two RFI topic areas this comment focuses on: regulatory framework and reimbursement conditions.⏎⏎Regarding the regulatory framework for AI deployment in clinical settings:⏎⏎o HHS should issue guidance requiring pre-deployment equity auditing as a condition of certification under the ONC Health IT Certification Program for clinical AI tools that generate or inform clinical decisions. Audit standards should be developed through a transparent stakeholder process that includes patient advocates, clinicians from safety-net settings, and health equity researchers, not only technology developers.⏎⏎o HHS should work with FDA to ensure that Software as a Medical Device clearance pathways for clinical AI tools require stratified performance analysis by race, ethnicity, and care setting as a condition of 510(k) clearance or De Novo authorization where the intended use includes diverse patient populations.⏎⏎o HHS should establish a post-deployment surveillance registry for clinical AI tools receiving reimbursement under Medicare and Medicaid, modeled on existing adverse event reporting frameworks, with public-facing reporting of performance data stratified by patient demographics and care setting.⏎⏎o HHS should direct ONC to strengthen HTI-1 enforcement provisions to include equity-specific performance thresholds as a condition of maintaining certification, not merely as a disclosure requirement. Disclosure without accountability is not a safety mechanism.⏎⏎Regarding reimbursement conditions for AI-augmented clinical services:⏎⏎o CMS should not finalize coverage pathways for AI-augmented services until pre-deployment equity audit requirements are established and enforceable. Reimbursement without equity conditions will create deployment incentives that outpace the regulatory framework's capacity to detect harm.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 10⏎⏎o Where CMS does establish coverage pathways in advance of comprehensive equity auditing requirements, those pathways should include sunset provisions requiring that tools demonstrate equitable performance within a defined period or lose reimbursement eligibility.⏎⏎o CMS should require that claims for AI-augmented services include data elements sufficient to support post-deployment performance monitoring by patient demographic characteristics, consistent with the stratification variables required in pre-deployment equity audits.⏎⏎o HHS should fund, through AHRQ or a designated research mechanism, the development of standardized equity audit methodologies for clinical AI tools, with particular attention to the performance of tools in rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, and critical access hospitals, which are the settings most likely to be underrepresented in commercial validation studies and most likely to serve patient populations with the greatest burden of health disparities.⏎⏎These recommendations are not offered as a complete framework. They are the minimum conditions that Tapestryhealth believes must be in place before HHS's proposed acceleration of AI adoption in clinical care can proceed without creating predictable, systematic harm to patients who are already underserved.⏎⏎APPENDIX NOTE⏎⏎A technical appendix documenting Tapestryhealth's internal AI deployment analysis across 47 affiliated care sites, including site-level performance data, provider survey results, and administrative burden calculations, is referenced in this submission but has not been attached due to data governance review requirements currently in process. We anticipate that the appendix will be available for submission to HHS upon request within 60 days of this comment's filing date. Inquiries may be directed to:⏎⏎policy@tapestryhealth-network.org⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 11⏎⏎A final observation that we keep returning to in our internal discussions about this RFI: the framing of federal AI policy as "acceleration" is not ideologically neutral. Acceleration implies that the primary problem is speed, that the existing barriers to AI adoption are obstacles to be removed, and that the appropriate federal posture is facilitation. That framing may be accurate for some of the barriers the RFI identifies, including the reimbursement uncertainty that is genuinely limiting sustained deployment at sites that have already demonstrated AI can work. But it is precisely the wrong framing for the equity barriers, because the equity barriers are not obstacles to good AI deployment. They are, in several documented cases, the mechanism by which existing deployment is already producing harm. Removing barriers to the deployment of tools that amplify racial disparities in pain management, as Pierson and colleagues documented (Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140), is not acceleration toward better care. It is acceleration toward a specific and documented failure mode.⏎⏎We are not arguing that HHS should stop. We are arguing that the Department cannot in good conscience frame this as a straightforward facilitation problem when the literature it is aware of documents that the tools being facilitated fail systematically for the patients who most need them to work. The National Academy of Medicine put it clearly in 2019: the hope and the peril of AI in healthcare are not separate questions that can be addressed sequentially, with adoption first and equity later. They are the same question, and the answer to one determines the answer to the other.⏎⏎The 892 providers in our post-implementation survey who reported reduced cognitive burden are real. The efficiency gains are real. The bias findings in the literature are also real, and the automation bias our own providers described in open-ended survey responses, the gradual reduction in clinical skepticism toward AI outputs, is real and is documented and is exactly the mechanism by which a tool that fails for a specific patient population will fail silently, without triggering the clinical override that might otherwise catch the error before it reaches the patient.⏎⏎Tapestryhealth Network | HHS Health Sector AI RFI Comments | Page 12⏎⏎HHS should require pre-deployment equity auditing, post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting, and performance degradation thresholds tied to reimbursement eligibility. These are not novel concepts. They are standard elements of any responsible post-market surveillance framework, applied to a context where the evidence of harm is already published and peer-reviewed. The question of whether to require them is therefore not a question about what is technically feasible. It is a question about whether the Department considers the patients most harmed by AI failure to be within the scope of the policy problem it is trying to solve.⏎⏎We believe they are. We are asking HHS to make the same determination and to reflect it in the regulatory and reimbursement conditions attached to the adoption pathway it is building.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Barbara Hernandez, MD, MBA⏎Chief Medical Officer⏎Boston Scientific / Tapestryhealth Affiliated Network⏎⏎The administrative overhead calculation cited in this comment (1.4 hours per provider per week) is derived from Tapestryhealth's Q3 2024 policy review and reflects self-reported time allocation data from providers at 47 affiliated care sites. SYNTH-0056♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Scott♔Society of Hospital Medicine♔♔♔♔♔Society of Hospital Medicine⏎16000 Commerce Parkway, Suite 101⏎Mount Laurel, NJ 08054⏎⏎Barbara Scott, Community Organizer and Policy Representative⏎Oklahoma Regional Affiliate⏎⏎June 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Attention: ASTP/ONC Health Sector AI Request for Information⏎Re: HHS RFI — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎---⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎THE FRAMING OF THIS REQUEST FOR INFORMATION IS THE PROBLEM⏎⏎The Society of Hospital Medicine (SHM) submits these comments not to help HHS refine the terms of acceleration, but to challenge the premise that acceleration is the appropriate federal posture at this time. The Department has issued a request that asks how it can move faster. SHM's answer is that the question itself represents an intentional administrative decision to treat documented, measurable harm to marginalized patients as an acceptable cost of deployment speed. We are not willing to accept that framing, and we do not believe the patients we serve — disproportionately those admitted to local county medical centers, non-urban facilities, and resource-constrained public facilities across Oklahoma and the broader country — are in a position to absorb the consequences of a federal agency that has decided urgency matters more than equity. Our present feedback centers around two discrete questions raised by the RFI: what regulatory preconditions should govern AI deployment in clinical care settings, and what post-deployment oversight mechanisms are necessary to detect and correct algorithmic harm once a system is in use. We will not be addressing the full scope of the RFI's questions because the most important thing we can say is narrow and specific: no AI system should be permitted to operate in clinical care, insurance authorization, or healthcare administration until it has completed compulsory algorithmic fairness evaluations before launch and demonstrated safety across the full spectrum of patient populations, not just the university-affiliated research hospital cohorts where most validation studies are currently conducted.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED HARM RECORD IS NOT BACKGROUND CONTEXT⏎⏎HHS's RFI characterizes AI adoption as an opportunity to be accelerated. SHM's members, who care for hospitalized patients every day in facilities where AI tools are already being deployed without federal equity standards, characterize it differently. The literature on algorithmic bias in healthcare is not a collection of theoretical concerns about future risk. It is a record of observed, measured, replicated harm that the Department has chosen not to treat as a regulatory emergency. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan published in Science in 2019 a landmark analysis demonstrating that a proprietary calculation tool employed to manage care for tens of millions of patients systematically assigned lower risk scores to Black patients with identical or greater illness burden when compared against Caucasian individuals possessing similar health profiles, because the formula relied upon medical cost as a proxy for healthcare need — a substitution that encoded decades of racially discriminatory access into the tool's predictive architecture (Obermeyer et al., 2019, Science, 366(6464), 447–453). That study was not a warning. It was a forensic account of a system already running, already making decisions, already producing racially disparate outputs in production environments. The Department was aware of that literature when it drafted this RFI. The decision not to require equity auditing as a precondition for deployment is therefore a choice, not an oversight.⏎⏎The pulse oximetry literature makes the same point more viscerally. Sjoding, Dickson, Iwashyna, Gay, and Valley published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 a study demonstrating that pulse oximeters — a device so ubiquitous in clinical settings that its failure had gone largely unnoticed for decades — systematically artificially inflated blood gas readings for individuals possessing deeper complexions, meaning those patients were assessed as less hypoxic than they actually were and were consequently less likely to receive supplemental oxygen or escalated care at the moment they needed it most (Sjoding et al., 2020, NEJM, 383(25), 2477–2478). This is not algorithmic bias in some abstract computational sense. This is a measurement device producing racially stratified errors in the middle of clinical encounters, and the healthcare system absorbed those errors for years before anyone was required to account for them systematically. Computational tools developed using the clinical records generated by that same measurement environment inherit those errors as ground truth. The bias is not introduced by the algorithm alone; it is embedded in the data the algorithm is trained on, and any validation study that does not explicitly correct for that upstream distortion will produce accuracy estimates that are inflated for white patients and depressed for patients of color, without the study's authors necessarily knowing it.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎Dermatology AI is another documented site of harm that has received far less regulatory attention than it warrants. Adamson and Smith published in JAMA Dermatology in 2018 an analysis of machine learning tools for skin condition classification and found that the training datasets for most commercially available systems were overwhelmingly composed of images of light-skinned patients, producing tools that performed substantially worse on darker skin tones — precisely the patient populations with the highest rates of delayed diagnosis for melanoma and other conditions where early detection determines survival outcomes (Adamson & Smith, 2018, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247–1248). The research regarding systemic infection forecasting adds yet another data point. Wong, Otles, Donnelly, Krumm, and Singh published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2021 an external validation of an extensively adopted corporate systemic infection forecasting tool and discovered that its performance degraded significantly when applied outside the university-affiliated research hospital environment where it was originally developed — a finding with direct implications for the local county medical centers and non-urban facilities where SHM's Oklahoma-based members practice (Wong et al., 2021, JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065–1070). The system was already running in those hospitals when the validation study found it wasn't working the way its developers claimed. That is the regulatory environment HHS is now proposing to accelerate.⏎⏎SHM does not cite these studies as background context. They are prosecutorial evidence. Each one represents a class of patients who received worse care because a tool was deployed without adequate equity validation and without post-deployment surveillance capable of detecting the disparity before it caused harm. The question before HHS is not how to accelerate more of this. The question is what mandatory preconditions will prevent it from continuing.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎---⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AS A MECHANISM OF HARM, NOT A NEUTRAL FEATURE⏎⏎One of the aspects of this RFI that concerns SHM most is what it does not say. The Department discusses AI outputs as informational tools that will support clinical decision-making, but it does not grapple with the substantial literature on automation bias — the well-documented tendency of human decision-makers to over-rely on algorithmic outputs and to reduce independent critical evaluation precisely in the situations where that evaluation is most necessary. Cabitza, Rasoini, and Gensini published in JAMA in 2017 a systematic analysis of unintended consequences in machine learning applications in medicine, arguing that the authoritative appearance of AI-generated outputs actively suppresses the clinical skepticism that functions as a safety mechanism in complex cases (Cabitza et al., 2017, JAMA, 318(6), 517–518). Sendak and colleagues, in their 2020 paper presented at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, found that clinicians frequently described deep learning tools as operating on a logic they could not interrogate — the phrase "the human body is a black box" appearing as a kind of resigned epistemic surrender to algorithmic authority (Sendak et al., 2020, ACM FAT*). That surrender is not evenly distributed across the patient population. It is most likely to occur in precisely the cases where the algorithm is least reliable: atypical presentations, patients with incomplete records, patients whose clinical histories contain gaps produced by prior encounters with a healthcare system that documented their care less thoroughly. Those patients are disproportionately poor, disproportionately non-white, and disproportionately concentrated in the local county medical centers and government-supported community clinics where SHM's members see them.⏎⏎Char, Shah, and Magnus published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 a careful analysis of the ethical challenges in executing advanced computational modeling within medicine, specifically noting that algorithms trained on historical data will reproduce the clinical decisions embedded in that data — including decisions that reflected the biases, resource constraints, and structural inequities of the environments in which they were made (Char et al., 2018, NEJM, 378(11), 981–983). When a clinician in a rural Oklahoma hospital is presented with an AI-generated risk score, the authoritative formatting of that output does not come with a footnote explaining that the model was validated on patients at a large urban university-affiliated research hospital and has not been tested in populations with the demographic and socioeconomic profile of the patients in front of them. The clinician sees a number. The number looks precise. Precision is persuasive. And the patients most likely to be harmed when that precision is false are the ones the system was never designed to serve accurately in the first place.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE VALIDATION STUDY GAP IS A NAMED STRUCTURAL FAILURE⏎⏎SHM wants to be specific about something the RFI treats as a general concern but which is actually a named structural failure with predictable victims. The overwhelming majority of AI validation studies in healthcare are conducted within large teaching institutions with relatively complete electronic health records, relatively stable patient populations, and relatively well-resourced informatics infrastructure. Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 a systematic analysis of potential biases in machine learning algorithms using digitized medical charts, finding that EHR-based training datasets systematically underrepresent patients with limited healthcare access, patients who receive care across multiple disconnected systems, and patients whose records contain documentation gaps produced by financial barriers to care (Gianfrancesco et al., 2018, JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544–1547). Those are not marginal populations in the American healthcare system. In Oklahoma, they are the majority of the patients SHM's community hospital members see. A validation study conducted at a major university-affiliated research hospital in a large metropolitan area is structurally incapable of predicting how a tool will perform at a critical access hospital in the Oklahoma Panhandle, and HHS's silence on this gap is not a technical oversight. It represents an intentional administrative decision about whose safety counts as a precondition for deployment.⏎⏎The TMA survey data that informs this comment provides additional evidence of the disparity in deployment conditions. Among physicians in rural and government-supported community clinic-affiliated settings, fewer than 30% reported access to vendor-supported AI implementation resources — meaning these tools are being introduced into resource-constrained environments without the technical support infrastructure that might catch performance failures before they reach patients. Meanwhile, 74% of physicians across practice settings cited the absence of clear federal standards as the primary barrier to responsible integration. The absence of those standards is not neutral. It advantages large health systems with the legal and technical resources to conduct their own evaluations, and it disadvantages the local county medical centers and resource-constrained public facilities that serve the patients most likely to be harmed by unvalidated tools.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎Celi and colleagues, in their 2022 global review of sources of bias in artificial intelligence that perpetuate healthcare disparities, published in PLOS Digital Health, documented how the combination of biased training data, unrepresentative validation cohorts, and deployment in low-resource settings creates a compounding disparity effect where algorithmic errors are largest precisely in the settings where the capacity to detect and correct them is smallest (Celi et al., 2022, PLOS Digital Health, 1(3), e0000022). Mittermaier, Raza, and Kvedar published in npj Digital Medicine in 2023 a synthesis of mitigation strategies for AI bias in health care, noting that even well-intentioned bias correction efforts at the model development stage may not translate to equity in deployment if the deployment environment differs substantially from the development environment — a point that applies with particular force to the local county medical centers and non-urban clinic settings that receive almost no attention in this RFI (Mittermaier et al., 2023, npj Digital Medicine, 6(1), 1–6).⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE RACE CORRECTION PROBLEM HAS NOT BEEN RESOLVED⏎⏎Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 an analysis regarding demographic adjustments within clinical algorithms that deserves more attention in this regulatory proceeding than it has received. Their paper documented how dozens of widely used clinical decision support tools embed race as a biological variable — adjusting predicted kidney function, lung capacity, and other physiological measures based on a patient's self-reported or clinician-assigned racial category — in ways that systematically underestimate disease severity and reduce treatment recommendations for Black patients (Vyas et al., 2020, NEJM, 383(9), 874–882). This is not a legacy problem that AI will correct. It is a problem that AI will amplify if AI systems are trained on the outputs of those racially corrected tools. An algorithm that learns to predict appropriate treatment intensity from a training dataset that systematically underprescribed treatment to Black patients will learn to undertreat Black patients, not as a malfunction but as a feature — as the behavior the training data encoded as correct. The compulsory algorithmic fairness evaluations before launch that SHM is demanding would require developers to trace this kind of upstream distortion explicitly and to demonstrate that their training data does not encode racially stratified clinical decision errors as ground truth. The current regulatory environment requires no such demonstration.⏎⏎SHM recognizes that race correction and racially biased training data are distinct problems that require distinct technical responses. But they share a common regulatory failure: there is no federal requirement that AI developers or deploying institutions document either the presence of these distortions in their training data or the steps taken to correct them before a tool is used in clinical care. The National Academy for State Health Policy published a 2023 policy brief on algorithmic accountability in Medicaid managed care that documented several state-level attempts to require equity auditing and vendor oversight in managed care contracting, but noted that the absence of federal standards has created a fragmented landscape in which the stringency of oversight depends on which state a patient happens to live in (NASHP, 2023, Algorithmic Accountability in Medicaid Managed Care). Oklahoma has not been among the states moving aggressively on this front. The patients in this state's local county medical centers and non-urban clinics are therefore operating under a regulatory framework that currently provides them no protection against rolling out applications that have never been validated in populations that resemble them.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎---⏎⏎SPECIFIC REGULATORY DEMANDS⏎⏎SHM is not submitting these comments to register general concern. The following are specific regulatory actions the Department must take before any further acceleration of AI adoption in clinical care settings can be considered responsible:⏎⏎1. Compulsory algorithmic fairness evaluations before launch. Any AI system used in clinical diagnosis, treatment recommendation, risk stratification, or insurance authorization must complete a documented equity audit prior to deployment. That audit must assess performance disaggregated by demographic background, financial standing, insurance status, and geographic setting. Performance thresholds must be established for each demographic subgroup, not just for the overall population. A tool that performs acceptably on average but performs significantly worse for Black patients or Medicaid beneficiaries should not be permitted in clinical use until the disparity has been corrected or the tool has been restricted to the populations in which it has demonstrated acceptable performance.⏎⏎2. External validation in local county and non-urban settings. Validation studies conducted exclusively within large teaching institutions must not be accepted as sufficient evidence of generalizability for deployment in local county medical centers, critical access hospitals, or government-supported community clinics. HHS must establish a requirement that any AI system intended for broad clinical deployment be validated in at least one non-academic community setting and one rural or safety-net setting before receiving approval for general use.⏎⏎3. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance. Deploying institutions must be required to implement ongoing monitoring of AI system outputs disaggregated by patient demographic characteristics. That monitoring must include defined triggers for automatic suspension of a tool when performance disparities exceed specified thresholds. The absence of post-deployment surveillance requirements is not a gap in the regulatory framework; it is the regulatory framework's most dangerous feature, because it means that the only way a disparity currently gets detected is if someone happens to be looking for it, which is exactly what did not happen with pulse oximetry for decades.⏎⏎4. Transparency about training data demographics. Developers must be required to publish documentation of the demographic composition of training and validation datasets, including information about the clinical settings in which the training data was generated. A tool trained predominantly on data from within large teaching institutions should be required to disclose that fact prominently, and deploying institutions should be required to assess whether their patient population is adequately represented in that training data before deployment.⏎⏎5. Prohibition on deploying race-corrected outputs as training data. No AI system should be permitted to use as training data the outputs of clinical decision support tools that have been identified by HHS or published academic research as embedding racially biased corrections. HHS should maintain and publish a list of such tools and prohibit their use as training data sources without documented correction.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 9⏎⏎---⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF WHO BEARS THE COST OF THE CURRENT FRAMEWORK⏎⏎SHM wants to be direct about something that tends to get lost in regulatory proceedings like this one. The patients who will bear the cost of deploying AI systems without adequate equity validation are not the patients at well-resourced facilities within large teaching institutions who will have access to the latest tools and the most thoroughly validated implementations. They are patients in hospitals like Integris Baptist Medical Center in Oklahoma City's north side, or in critical access facilities in counties where the nearest specialist is two hours away and the electronic health records are years behind the systems in which most AI tools were developed and validated. They are patients whose records are incomplete because they could not afford consistent healthcare access. They are patients who have already experienced the consequences of a healthcare system that was not designed with them in mind, and who are now being asked to absorb the additional risk of AI systems that underwent initial development and testing without them.⏎⏎The Society of Hospital Medicine does not believe HHS is indifferent to these patients. But the framing of this RFI as a question about how to accelerate adoption, rather than a question about what preconditions must be met before adoption is responsible, reflects an institutional orientation toward the interests of the health systems and technology vendors who are most eager to deploy these tools, and away from the interests of the patients who are most likely to be harmed when those tools fail. The 68% of physicians in the TMA survey who are already piloting AI tools are doing so in a regulatory vacuum. Some of them are in community hospitals in Oklahoma. The patients in front of them are not test subjects. They are people who deserve the same level of protection that would be demanded if these tools were being deployed in the university-affiliated research hospital environments where the validation studies were done.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 10⏎⏎---⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 10 (cont.)⏎⏎SHM would like to add one point that is perhaps somewhat tangential to the main regulatory argument but that has come up repeatedly in conversations with member hospitalists in Oklahoma and that the Department should understand. The experience of practicing clinicians with AI tools in community settings is not primarily an experience of tools that malfunction obviously and catastrophically. It is an experience of tools that produce outputs that look reasonable, that fit within the range of what a clinician might have expected, and that are therefore accepted without the scrutiny they would receive if they produced obviously wrong answers. The most dangerous AI failures are the ones that are small enough and plausible enough to be invisible. A sepsis prediction score that is slightly too low for a Black patient with an atypical presentation will not trigger an alarm. It will just be a number that looks about right, and the clinician will move on, and the patient will deteriorate, and nobody will ever connect the outcome to the algorithm. That is what the literature on automation bias is describing. That is what the post-deployment surveillance requirements SHM is demanding are designed to catch. And that is what the existing compliance structure, as described in this RFI, has no mechanism to detect.⏎⏎The Department should also be aware that the state-level landscape on algorithmic accountability is moving, however unevenly. The NASHP 2023 brief documents several states that have begun requiring equity auditing in Medicaid managed care contracting, and SHM supports those efforts. But state-level action cannot substitute for federal standards, because the tools being deployed cross state lines, the vendors selling them operate nationally, and the patients most likely to be harmed are in states that have been least aggressive in developing their own oversight frameworks. Oklahoma is one of those states. The patients in Oklahoma's community hospitals are not going to be protected by California's algorithmic accountability requirements.⏎⏎Society of Hospital Medicine Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 11⏎⏎SHM strongly encourages HHS to reframe the central question of this regulatory proceeding. The question is not how to accelerate adoption. The question is what the minimum conditions are under which adoption does not constitute a federally sanctioned harm to the patients the healthcare system is obligated to protect. Those conditions include, at minimum, compulsory algorithmic fairness evaluations before launch with disaggregated performance thresholds, external validation in local county and non-urban settings, mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance with defined suspension triggers, transparency requirements for training data demographics, and a prohibition on deploying race-corrected outputs as clean training data. None of those requirements are technically infeasible. Several of them are already being implemented voluntarily by responsible developers. The reason they are not universal is that the Department has not required them, and the vendors who benefit from the absence of requirements have not volunteered to comply with standards that would slow their time to market.⏎⏎SHM respectfully requests that HHS treat the documented evidence of algorithmic bias in clinical AI systems not as a concern to be managed in the course of accelerating adoption, but as a disqualifying defect that must be remediated before deployment. SYNTH-0059♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Barbara Scott♔National Disability Rights Network♔♔♔♔♔NATIONAL DISABILITY RIGHTS NETWORK⏎Comments Submitted to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP-ONC⏎Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎89 Fed. Reg. 22,071 (March 2024)⏎⏎Submitted by: Barbara Scott, Campaign Director⏎National Disability Rights Network⏎⏎ndrncomments@ndrn.org⏎⏎---⏎⏎ACCOUNTABILITY BEFORE ACCELERATION: WHY THE HHS AI REQUEST FOR INFORMATION GETS THE SEQUENCE WRONG⏎⏎The National Disability Rights Network (NDRN) offers this submission responding to HHS's call for input regarding regulatory, reimbursement, and research initiatives meant to speed up artificial intelligence integration within clinical care environments. Our organization's interest in this request for information (RFI) stems from one strictly documented issue: the Department intends to structurally expedite the rollout of AI in medical settings before putting the necessary liability architecture in place. Getting this sequence backward is hardly a minor procedural snag. Rather, it represents the foundational flaw of the RFI as currently drafted, forming the entire basis of our remarks here.⏎⏎A 2024 landscape analysis by the Global Liver Institute, which gathered data from 214 hepatology centers and patient advocacy groups spanning 38 states, determined that 67% of these sites currently operate without standardized protocols for bringing AI-assisted diagnostics into their liver disease screening processes (Global Liver Institute, 2024). This statistic highlights a widespread structural reality regarding clinical AI rollouts: medical facilities are bringing systems online much faster than they are figuring out who exactly holds the liability if a software recommendation leads to patient harm. In that same survey, 78% of hepatology practices pointed to reimbursement uncertainty as their main hurdle to adoption. NDRN certainly agrees that misaligned payment structures present a real issue that needs fixing. However, addressing financial compensation without concurrently fixing the liability gap does nothing to mitigate danger. Instead, it simply funnels the danger directly onto the clinicians and patients who have the fewest resources to manage it.⏎⏎NDRN Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > 89 Fed. Reg. 22,071 < > Page 2⏎⏎THE THREE-WAY BLAME-DEFLECTION DYNAMIC AND WHY DOCTRINE CANNOT RESOLVE IT⏎⏎Liability issues in medical AI do not simply stem from missing regulations. They originate from a structural design defect baked into the three-way dynamic connecting health systems, AI developers, and frontline clinicians. If an AI-assisted diagnostic application generates an output contributing to patient injury, the resulting cycle of finger-pointing is entirely predictable and heavily documented by legal scholars. The treating physician blames the software. The hospital administration points to the developer's specifications, insisting the application was operated according to the manual. The developer then blames either user error or limitations inherent to the training data. Taken one by one, each excuse sounds reasonable enough. Together, they create a phenomenon legal experts term "accountability diffusion." This is a scenario where no specific party holds identifiable liability for an adverse event, leaving the injured individual without any straightforward avenue for recourse.⏎⏎In a 2019 JAMA article, Price, Gerke, and Cohen observed that our traditional liability structures were simply never built to handle the muddy causation issues generated by AI-supported medical choices. They pointed out that we still do not know if a doctor relying on an erroneous algorithmic prompt is demonstrating reasonable clinical judgment or abandoning their professional duty (Price, Gerke, & Cohen). That point was raised half a decade ago, yet the RFI seemingly brushes right past it. Similarly, a 2020 JAMA piece by Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert detailed how medical malpractice liability serves as an essential quality-control lever in patient care. They concluded that for malpractice doctrine to deter negligent behavior, the legal system must be able to link causation to a distinct entity (Mello et al., 2020). Once causation gets scattered across a complex human-and-machine network involving multiple players, that deterrent effect collapses completely. The acceleration route proposed by this RFI would weave algorithmic systems further into medical operations at the exact time this loss of deterrence poses the greatest threat.⏎⏎Traditional legal doctrines like respondeat superior—which makes an employer vicariously responsible for an employee's negligence—fail to translate cleanly to AI-guided medicine. The software is obviously not an employee, and its generated prompts do not qualify as acts under standard legal definitions. Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo highlighted this exact mismatch in a 2014 Health Affairs paper examining predictive analytics in healthcare. They explained that our ethical and legal structures for assigning blame were constructed for human beings making distinct decisions, requiring major overhauls before they could ever work properly in algorithmic medical settings (Cohen et al., 2014). Those overhauls never took place. The RFI does not suggest undertaking them now. Rather, the document seeks to push software adoption forward into a liability void that our current laws simply cannot govern.⏎⏎Writing in a 2020 Academic Press volume covering healthcare artificial intelligence, Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen framed this not as an accidental byproduct, but as a structural reality. The very way these applications are developed and sold intentionally fosters diffused liability. Developers are highly incentivized to label their software as "decision support" rather than "decision making," effectively pushing the legal burden onto the physician who follows the prompt (Gerke, Minssen, & Cohen, 2020). This framing should fundamentally change how HHS views the reimbursement ideas laid out in the RFI. Should CMS establish payment channels for AI-guided medical choices without explicitly naming which party holds absolute, non-transferable liability for the outcomes, the developers' strategy of dodging responsibility will only become more deeply rooted.⏎⏎NDRN Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > 89 Fed. Reg. 22,071 < > Page 3⏎⏎INSTITUTIONAL DEPENDENCY AND THE PATH DEPENDENCY PROBLEM⏎⏎Another structural layer to this dilemma goes entirely unmentioned in the RFI. Once a hospital weaves an algorithmic application into its daily operations, the financial and logistical barriers to extracting that software result in institutional dependency. In a 2019 Nature Medicine piece exploring the intersection of human and machine intelligence in medicine, Topol documented how deeply these applications alter clinical procedures, making it increasingly agonizing for facilities to untangle themselves later (Topol, 2019). We are not criticizing the mere act of adopting technology. We are pointing out the path dependency generated by institutional reliance. Practically speaking, this dependency shields developers even further from legal consequences. Once a hospital relies on a specific application to function, administrators are far less likely to file liability claims against the creator, fearing they might lose their software access or rupture a vendor relationship they cannot quickly substitute.⏎⏎Dworkowitz and Kesselheim noted in a 2022 Health Affairs Forefront article that the FDA's developing approach to software-as-a-medical-device completely failed to tackle post-market liability. They warned that heavily prioritizing pre-market clearance gave users a false sense of security, implying these applications remained universally safe regardless of where or how they were implemented (Dworkowitz & Kesselheim, 2022). Furthermore, a 2023 review by the National Academy for State Health Policy examining jurisdictional approaches to medical algorithms revealed that very few states have passed mandatory liability rules. Instead, most state governments have merely issued voluntary guidelines or formed study groups lacking any real enforcement teeth (NASHP, 2023). The federal terrain is equally barren. Yet, the RFI suggests pouring financial rewards and regulatory shortcuts directly into this void. The inevitable outcome will be a rushed rollout accompanied by a massive dilution of legal responsibility.⏎⏎While obviously not legally binding in the United States, the European Parliament's 2023 AI Liability Directive draft provides a highly relevant template. It suggests that organizations utilizing high-risk algorithms in critical sectors should face a rebuttable presumption of causality if an injury happens. This shifts the evidentiary burden, maintaining liability without forcing an injured patient to somehow untangle the complex web of algorithmic causation on their own (European Parliament, 2023). HHS does not have to copy this exact directive, but the foundational logic applies perfectly. The RFI should put forward a parallel concept: a strict federal rule mandating that a named institutional party holds non-transferable liability at every distinct AI-guided decision juncture in a patient's care. Securing CMS payment eligibility must depend entirely on having this designation firmly established.⏎⏎NDRN Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > 89 Fed. Reg. 22,071 < > Page 4⏎⏎WHAT HHS MUST DO BEFORE ACCELERATING DEPLOYMENT⏎⏎NDRN holds a very specific position on this matter. HHS has to make any new algorithmic adoption pathway contingent upon first establishing strict, non-transferable liability assignments at every single juncture where software informs a medical choice. We are not asking for a complete halt to medical technology integration. We are insisting on a foundational prerequisite for safe progress. In a 2016 New England Journal of Medicine piece, Obermeyer and Emanuel asserted that integrating predictive software into medicine demanded more than mere technical testing. It required solid administrative structures dictating exactly how doctors would oversee, dispute, and ultimately override computer-generated prompts (Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016). That warning has only grown more urgent as these applications become more sophisticated and deeply ingrained in hospital operations. Hoffman and Podgurski raised a similar alarm regarding biomedical databases in the 2013 American Journal of Law and Medicine. They argued that failing to assign definite administrative responsibility for data-informed medical choices ultimately creates an environment where mistakes are routinely buried instead of being exposed and fixed (Hoffman & Podgurski, 2013).⏎⏎The liability framework NDRN advocates for would function in the following manner. Before any algorithmic application is integrated into a CMS-funded medical process, the hospital or clinic must proactively name a distinct individual or administrative entity who accepts full legal and regulatory liability for choices made using that software. This assignment cannot be delegated. A hospital could not use a vendor contract to offload the risk, and the named responsible party could not evade blame by pointing fingers at the computer's output. Holding this designation would act as a strict prerequisite to bill CMS, and failing to uphold it would trigger immediate payment clawbacks. While this approach might not settle every single legal puzzle surrounding medical algorithms—and NDRN understands the statutory mechanics need careful drafting—it directly neutralizes the primary structural flaw. It eliminates the current environment where all three parties can successfully pass the buck to someone else.⏎⏎As currently drafted, the RFI asks HHS to brainstorm ways to speed up technology adoption. NDRN's definitive response is that the single most impactful step HHS can take is to halt any acceleration until a robust liability architecture is fully operational. The Global Liver Institute's 2024 data showing that 67% of hepatology clinics operate without standardized integration procedures is not just proof of an adoption lag. It is glaring evidence of a liability void. Facilities lacking proper integration rules inherently lack a methodology for deciding who is at fault if an algorithmic screening tool returns a false negative, causing a patient's fibrosis to remain hidden until it worsens into cirrhosis. Yes, the reimbursement hurdle exists. But the liability hurdle is vastly more dangerous, and these two issues cannot be handled sequentially by pushing responsibility down the road until after the rollout is already moving at top speed.⏎⏎NDRN strongly urges HHS to overhaul the regulatory and financial concepts stemming from this RFI, ensuring that assigning definitive liability serves as a mandatory first step rather than an afterthought. The exact operational mechanics of making these assignments will require deeper policy discussions with stakeholders, and NDRN would gladly contribute to those conversations. However, the sequence itself is not up for debate. The liability structure must be finalized before we press the gas pedal on adoption. The RFI in its present form fails to recognize this necessary order of operations, and NDRN respectfully yet firmly insists that HHS fix this fundamental oversight.♔♔2026-02-03T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-03T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔urgent♔Iowa♔campaign director♔62♔A 2024 landscape analysis conducted by the Global Liver Institute, drawing on input from 214 hepatology care centers and patient advocacy partners across 38 states, found that 67% of facilities lack standardized protocols for integrating AI-assisted diagnostic tools into liver disease screening workflows, despite growing evidence that early-stage fibrosis detection rates improve by up to 34% when such tools are deployed. SYNTH-0060♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Robinson♔AARP Public Policy Institute♔♔♔♔♔AARP Public Policy Institute Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 1⏎⏎The AARP Public Policy Institute submits these comments with a degree of institutional frustration that, after decades of watching administrative modernization initiatives produce outcomes that systematically disadvantage older adults and low-income beneficiaries, has become very difficult to modulate into the register of collegial regulatory dialogue. The Department's Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care is framed as a question about efficiency and innovation, and the AARP Public Policy Institute does not dispute that AI tools, deployed with appropriate safeguards, could reduce the administrative burden that Himmelstein et al. (2020) estimated at $812 billion annually in the United States — a figure that dwarfs comparable expenditures in Canada and represents a genuine, ongoing harm to patients, providers, and payers alike. The problem is not the aspiration. The problem is that HHS is soliciting comment on acceleration before it has established the precautionary architecture that would make acceleration anything other than reckless.⏎⏎AARP Public Policy Institute Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 2⏎⏎THE WORKFORCE DISPLACEMENT QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎Before engaging with the specific reimbursement and regulatory questions the Department poses, the AARP Public Policy Institute finds it necessary to name what this RFI conspicuously does not ask: what happens to the human workforce whose tacit knowledge and institutional memory currently constitute the connective tissue of care coordination for older adults? The Department asks how to accelerate adoption. It does not ask what is lost in that acceleration, or who bears the cost of that loss. Care coordinators, patient navigators, and benefits counselors — the specific administrative roles the Department's efficiency calculus tends to render invisible — do not merely process information. They hold relationships. A benefits counselor at a federally qualified health center in Clark County, Nevada, who has worked the same caseload for eleven years knows that a particular 72-year-old patient with early-stage dementia will not call back if her prior authorization is denied; she knows to call the patient's daughter instead, and she knows the daughter's number by heart because it is not in the system. That knowledge is not in any database. It cannot be extracted into a training set. Fernandez et al. (2023) documented precisely this phenomenon — the irreplaceable role of tacit knowledge and institutional memory in patient navigation — and found that algorithmic substitution of navigation functions produced measurable increases in care discontinuity among patients with complex social needs, which is to say, the patients AARP most directly represents.⏎⏎The Department should understand that when AI systems are deployed to automate prior authorization workflows, benefits coordination, or eligibility determination, the errors those systems produce are not evenly distributed. They concentrate among patients who are least equipped to detect, document, and appeal them. These are what the AARP Public Policy Institute would call invisible errors — harms that never register as errors in any feedback loop because the patient who was harmed either accepted the denial, lost contact with the system, or died before the administrative record caught up with what happened to them. Eubanks (2018) traced this structural dynamic across multiple public-sector automation deployments and found that algorithmic systems consistently produce outcomes that are facially neutral but operationally discriminatory against low-income and elderly populations. Obermeyer et al. (2019) established how a prominent predictive modeling tool chronically misjudged the medical requirements of Black individuals by equating financial expenditures with actual clinical necessity — a methodological choice that appeared technically defensible until its racial consequences were made visible. The AARP Public Policy Institute does not believe HHS intends to reproduce these outcomes. The AARP Public Policy Institute does believe that acceleration without precaution will reproduce them regardless of intent.⏎⏎AARP Public Policy Institute Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 3⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING ADMINISTRATIVE AI AND PRIOR AUTHORIZATION⏎⏎The Government Accountability Office documented in 2022 that prior authorization processes already impose substantial, documented harms on Medicare Advantage beneficiaries, including treatment delays and denials that are subsequently overturned on appeal at rates that suggest systematic initial error (GAO-22-104536). The Department is now soliciting comment on how AI can be integrated into these same workflows. The AARP Public Policy Institute's concern is not theoretical. Bates et al. (2021) acknowledged the potential for AI to reduce administrative errors while simultaneously warning that poorly governed deployment could amplify existing systematic biases in ways that are difficult to audit after the fact. The National Partnership for Women and Families (2023) documented specific instances in which AI-assisted insurance administration tools produced denial rates that correlated with beneficiary age and disability status in ways that the deploying institutions could not explain because the models were proprietary and the audit trails were incomplete.⏎⏎The AARP Public Policy Institute therefore demands — and this organization uses that word deliberately — that HHS condition any reimbursement incentives or regulatory accommodations for administrative AI on the following precautionary requirements:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment bias audits for any AI system used in prior authorization, eligibility determination, or benefits coordination, with specific demographic disaggregation for age, race, disability status, and dual-eligible status.⏎⏎2. Prohibition on the use of financial-expenditures-as-proxy-for-need methodologies in any AI system deployed in Medicare or Medicaid administrative contexts, consistent with the evidentiary findings in Obermeyer et al. (2019).⏎⏎3. Preservation of human review rights: no administrative AI determination affecting a beneficiary's access to care may be finalized without a documented human review step, and that review must be performed by a credentialed professional with relevant training, not a clerical worker operating under time pressure.⏎⏎4. Public disclosure requirements for any AI system used in Medicare Advantage or Medicaid managed care administrative functions, including model architecture summaries, training data provenance, and ongoing performance monitoring results disaggregated by the demographic categories listed above.⏎⏎5. Explicit workforce protection provisions ensuring that the deployment of administrative AI does not result in the elimination of care coordinator, patient navigator, or benefits counselor positions without a documented transition plan approved by the relevant state Medicaid agency or CMS regional office.⏎⏎AARP Public Policy Institute Comments | HHS AI RFI Docket | Page 4⏎⏎The administrative burden on clinicians is real. Sinsky et al. (2022) documented that physicians in ambulatory practice spend roughly twice as much time on administrative tasks as on direct patient care, and the AARP Public Policy Institute does not dismiss the genuine appeal of tools that could rebalance that proportion. The American Hospital Association (2023) has argued that administrative simplification through AI could free significant clinical capacity, and that argument has surface plausibility. But the AARP Public Policy Institute has watched enough "simplification" initiatives produce complexity for the patients those initiatives were nominally designed to help that it is no longer willing to extend good-faith deference to efficiency arguments that do not account for distributional consequences. Ash, Berg, and Coiera (2004) documented nearly two decades ago that health information technology deployments consistently produce unintended consequences that are invisible to the deploying institution and disproportionately harmful to patients with limited health literacy or limited access to advocacy resources. The structural conditions that produced those findings have not materially changed. Bhatt and Bathija (2018) documented the specific dependency of vulnerable community populations on human navigation infrastructure — the kind of infrastructure that is first to be defunded when institutions believe they have an algorithmic substitute.⏎⏎The AARP Public Policy Institute also notes, with some concern about the framing of this RFI itself, that the Department's questions consistently assume that the goal is acceleration and ask how to achieve it, rather than asking whether acceleration is appropriate in specific contexts and under what conditions. That framing is not neutral. It encodes a policy preference that this organization believes has not been adequately justified by the evidence base currently available. The ONC's own working paper on non-clinical AI classification gaps (ONC, 2023) acknowledged that accountability frameworks for administrative AI remain underdeveloped relative to the pace of deployment, which means that HHS is soliciting comment on how to go faster in a domain where its own technical staff have documented that the governance architecture is not yet adequate to manage the risks of current deployment speeds, let alone accelerated ones.⏎⏎The AARP Public Policy Institute requests that HHS publish a supplemental RFI specifically addressing the workforce and beneficiary protection dimensions of administrative AI deployment, and that no final regulatory or reimbursement actions incentivizing administrative AI adoption be taken before that supplemental process is complete.
