SYNTH-0063♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Gonzalez♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via the Federal eRulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎ADMINISTRATIVE AUTOMATION IS NOT A NEUTRAL INTERVENTION⏎⏎My name is Sharon Gonzalez. I am 77 years old, I live in Sparks, Nevada, and I have driven long-haul freight on I-80 between Reno and Salt Lake City for the better part of four decades. I want to say something about what happened to me in February of this year, and then I want to say something more general that I think is worth HHS actually reading.⏎⏎In February, I flagged an irregular heartbeat reading from my home cardiac monitor through my cardiologist's patient portal. My cardiologist retired in 2022 and the practice that absorbed his patients uses some kind of automated triage system to sort incoming messages before a human ever looks at them. The algorithm classified my message as a "non-urgent general inquiry." I waited eleven days for a callback. Eleven days is not a close call I am comfortable describing as acceptable. I am not a medical professional, but I have spent forty years managing equipment on a route where a missed warning indicator at the wrong moment can put a truck through a guardrail at 65 miles per hour. I know what it looks like when a system has too many decision points and not enough redundancy. What I experienced is exactly what Ash, Berg, and Coiera described back in 2004 in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association: health IT systems generate errors that are invisible to the system itself. The algorithm that classified my message as non-urgent did not flag that classification as a potential error. Nothing in the system knew it was wrong.⏎⏎THE SPECIFIC PROBLEM WITH ADMINISTRATIVE AUTOMATION⏎⏎The framing in this RFI treats administrative burden reduction as an unambiguous good. I am skeptical of that framing, and I want to name why.⏎⏎Administrative work in clinical settings is not just paperwork. A significant portion of what gets labeled "administrative burden" is actually judgment work performed by people who have developed what Michael Polanyi, in The Tacit Dimension, called tacit knowledge: knowledge that cannot be fully articulated, formalized, or transferred through written rules. When a medical assistant reads a portal message and decides it sounds off, she is doing something that a classification algorithm cannot replicate by design. Himmelstein and colleagues documented in the Annals of Internal Medicine in 2020 that U.S. healthcare spends an extraordinary share of its resources on administrative functions relative to comparable systems. That finding is often cited as evidence that automation would free up resources. What it actually shows is that the system is already structurally overloaded, and that the people doing administrative work are already compensating for that overload in ways that are not visible in the data.⏎⏎The Sinsky et al. time-and-motion study from 2016 in the same journal found that doctors working in outpatient settings spend roughly two hours on EHR and desk work for every one hour of direct patient contact. HHS and others cite this as a reason to automate. I read it differently. If physicians are spending that much time on administrative functions, some portion of that time is load-bearing in ways that are not captured by the category label. Automating the category does not mean automating only the genuinely mechanical parts. It means automating everything the label contains, including the parts that require judgment.⏎⏎There is also a distributional problem that this RFI does not appear to take seriously. Obermeyer and colleagues published a study in Science in 2019 showing how a prominent software program consistently downplayed the care needs of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need. The errors were not random. They followed the existing gradients of disadvantage. Automated insurance approvals have produced a similar pattern: the National Academy for State Health Policy documented in 2023 that automated clearance systems generate denial rates that fall disproportionately on patients with complex, atypical, or underdocumented conditions, which is to say patients who are already harder to serve.⏎⏎So here is what I would ask HHS to consider:⏎⏎1. Any financial or rule-based push for clinical AI adoption should require, as a condition, that the system generate auditable logs of every classification or routing decision it makes, with mandatory human review of any case that results in a delay of more than 72 hours in patient contact.⏎⏎2. HHS should not treat administrative efficiency metrics as a proxy for care quality. A system that routes messages faster is not ipso facto a system that routes messages correctly.⏎⏎3. The RFI asks about research priorities. I would suggest that one underinvestigated question is how much tacit clinical judgment currently lives inside administrative workflows, and what happens to patient outcomes when that judgment is removed.⏎⏎I recognize there is no mechanism in this RFI for me to opt out of the Medicare Advantage marketing mail that started arriving at my address after my cardiologist's practice changed hands, but if there is a place to note that the data sharing that makes that mail possible is part of the same infrastructure being discussed here, I am noting it.♔♔2026-02-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-17T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔2♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Nevada♔truck driver♔77♔My cardiologist retired in 2022, and the practice that absorbed his patients uses some kind of AI triage system to route messages through a portal before a human ever sees them — I've been driving long-haul routes between Reno and Salt Lake for forty years and I know what it means when a system has too many decision points and not enough redundancy. SYNTH-0064♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Andrew Jones♔American Psychological Association♔♔♔♔♔American Psychological Association — Georgia Advocacy Division⏎Comments Submitted to HHS Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎RE: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL⏎Submitted by: Andrew Jones, Community Organizer, APA Georgia Advocacy Division⏎⏎APA Georgia Advocacy Division Comments | HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE RELATIONAL FOUNDATION OF CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎The American Psychological Association's Georgia Advocacy Division submits these comments with specific concern for two dimensions of the proposed RFI that have received insufficient attention in the broader policy conversation: the measurable clinical value of the therapeutic relationship itself, and the structural risk that AI intermediation poses to that relationship over time. Our comments draw on empirical work conducted through our member network, as well as a substantial body of peer-reviewed literature that we believe HHS has not adequately weighed in framing this inquiry.⏎⏎Before turning to the relational argument, the Division notes that a 2024 policy review conducted across 847 member clearinghouses in our network found that 68% of participating organizations reported receiving AI-generated or AI-assisted claims submissions containing coding anomalies that existing adjudication systems were not designed to detect. This finding, presented formally to the Cooperative Exchange Technology and Standards Working Group in September 2024 in Washington, D.C., generated consensus recommendations that federal reimbursement policy must address AI validation requirements at the clearinghouse layer, not solely at the point-of-care level (Cooperative Exchange Technology and Standards Working Group, 2024). We raise this not to dwell on reimbursement mechanics, but because it illustrates a consistent pattern in how HHS has framed this RFI: the Department's questions are organized around adoption speed, productivity gains, and workflow integration — and the implicit assumption is that friction is a problem to be solved rather than, in some cases, a feature of responsible clinical practice.⏎⏎The RFI's repeated invocation of "enhanced productivity" as a primary goal is worth pausing on. Productivity is a reasonable concern in manufacturing. In clinical care, it is a category error. A clinician who moves faster through more patients is not, by definition, providing better care — and the framing of efficiency as the organizing value of AI adoption signals a transactional model of medicine that the peer-reviewed literature has spent two decades arguing against. Epstein and Street (2011) documented that patient-centered care, which depends on attentiveness to the patient as a whole person, produces measurably better outcomes across a range of conditions — and that attentiveness requires time, relational presence, and the kind of interpretive engagement that cannot be delegated to a pattern-matching system. Zulman and colleagues (2020) found that specific practices of physician presence — making eye contact, sitting rather than standing, explicitly acknowledging patient concerns — were independently associated with improved patient-reported outcomes and reduced physician burnout. These are not soft findings. They are clinical data, and the HHS framing does not engage with them.⏎⏎APA Georgia Advocacy Division Comments | HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE DIAGNOSTIC VALUE OF WHAT AI CANNOT SEE⏎⏎Consider a scenario that any experienced clinician in community-based practice will recognize. A patient presents to a primary care appointment complaining of fatigue and mild headaches. The electronic record shows nothing alarming. The AI-assisted diagnostic support tool, drawing on pattern recognition across thousands of similar presentations, surfaces the most statistically probable explanations and recommends a standard workup. The clinician, under pressure to move through a full schedule, accepts the recommendation. What the AI did not register — because it cannot — is that the patient sat down slowly, avoided eye contact when asked about sleep, and answered questions about home life in a way that was technically complete but tonally flat. The clinician who is fully present, and who has not outsourced interpretive attention to a machine, might have paused. Might have asked one more question. Might have identified the depression, or the domestic situation, or the medication interaction that no pattern-matching system would have surfaced. Verghese (2011) wrote with characteristic precision about the diagnostic information carried in the physical encounter — in gesture, posture, and the thousand small signals that constitute what he called "the patient's presence." That information is not captured in any dataset. It never will be.⏎⏎Ridd and colleagues (2009), in their synthesis of qualitative literature on patients' perspectives of the doctor-patient relationship, found that patients consistently identified the quality of that relationship — specifically, feeling known and understood as a person — as both intrinsically valuable and independently associated with better health behaviors and outcomes. The relationship is not a delivery mechanism for care. In many cases, it is the care. Bickmore and Picard (2005) demonstrated, in a different context, that even sustained human-computer interactions can generate something resembling relational rapport — but their work also makes clear how fragile and shallow that rapport is compared to genuine human connection, and how quickly it degrades when the interaction becomes transactional. The argument is not that AI has no place in clinical settings. Topol (2019) made a thoughtful case that AI can free clinicians from administrative burden and allow them to spend more time in relational engagement with patients — and that framing, notably, treats AI as subordinate to the therapeutic encounter rather than as a replacement for clinical judgment. HHS would do well to return to that framing rather than the productivity-centered model implicit in this RFI.⏎⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM⏎⏎There is a structural concern here that the Division believes has not received adequate attention in the regulatory literature, though it has been documented in adjacent fields. Hoff (2011) studied primary care physicians adapting to two work innovations and found measurable patterns of deskilling — a gradual atrophy of independent clinical reasoning as clinicians became habituated to relying on system-generated recommendations. This is not a character failing. It is a predictable cognitive adaptation. When a system reliably produces a recommendation, and when the clinician's role is increasingly to review and approve rather than to generate independent judgment, the capacity for independent judgment erodes. Tversky and Kahneman (1974) documented the underlying cognitive mechanism — the tendency to anchor on available information, including machine-generated outputs — and Goddard and colleagues (2012) conducted a systematic review confirming that automation bias is a consistent, measurable phenomenon in clinical decision support contexts, not an edge case.⏎⏎The concern is not that any individual clinician will become incompetent. The concern is that a system-wide shift toward AI-mediated clinical decision-making will, over time, produce a clinical workforce whose independent reasoning capacity has systematically atrophied — and that this workforce will be less able to catch the errors that AI systems inevitably make, precisely because they have become habituated to trusting those systems. Hartzband and Groopman (2020) argued that the administrative and technological burdens already placed on physicians have eroded the cognitive space necessary for genuine clinical reasoning, contributing to burnout and diagnostic error. Adding another layer of AI intermediation — particularly under the productivity-centered framing HHS has adopted — will not reverse that trend. It will accelerate it.⏎⏎APA Georgia Advocacy Division Comments | HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 3⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS FOR HHS CONSIDERATION⏎⏎The Division respectfully urges HHS to reframe the organizing question of this RFI. Rather than asking how AI adoption can be accelerated, the Department should ask how AI can be deployed in ways that strengthen rather than erode the relational foundations of clinical care. Concretely, this means:⏎⏎1. Any reimbursement or certification pathway for AI clinical tools should require demonstrated evidence that the tool preserves, rather than displaces, meaningful clinician-patient interaction time. The ONC Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024-2030 articulates goals around safety and equity; those goals are not served by adoption metrics alone (ONC, 2024).⏎⏎2. AI validation requirements should operate at the clearinghouse layer as well as the point-of-care level, consistent with the September 2024 consensus recommendations of the Cooperative Exchange Technology and Standards Working Group. Our Q2 and Q3 2024 interoperability analysis found that 54% of smaller community-based clearinghouses — those processing fewer than 500,000 transactions annually — cited the absence of standardized data exchange protocols as their primary integration barrier. Smaller organizations serving underresourced communities bear disproportionate compliance costs under the current framework, and that inequity will deepen if AI adoption policy continues to be written around the operational capacity of large health systems.⏎⏎3. HHS should require prospective, not merely retrospective, evidence of clinical safety before any AI clinical decision support tool qualifies for federal reimbursement pathways. The current framework, as described in this RFI, does not make that requirement explicit.⏎⏎4. Any framework for AI adoption in clinical care should include mandatory mechanisms for preserving clinician accountability and independent judgment — not as a rhetorical commitment, but as a structural requirement with defined standards and enforcement mechanisms.⏎⏎The Division acknowledges that these recommendations will slow the adoption timeline that HHS appears to prefer. We do not regard that as a cost. We regard it as the appropriate price of responsible deployment in settings where errors have irreversible consequences for real patients.⏎⏎APA Georgia Advocacy Division Comments | HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL | Page 4⏎⏎The Division would welcome the opportunity to discuss these comments further with the relevant HHS program offices. For follow-up, please contact the APA Georgia Advocacy Division at:⏎⏎advocacy-ga@apa-georgia.org⏎404-555-0183⏎⏎One additional point that we did not fully develop above but that we believe warrants further inquiry: the RFI does not address how AI intermediation in behavioral health settings — where the therapeutic relationship is not merely supportive but is the primary treatment mechanism — will be evaluated differently from AI use in, say, radiology or pathology. The distinction matters enormously, and the absence of any differentiation in the RFI's framing suggests that HHS has not yet fully grappled with the heterogeneity of "clinical care" as a category. SYNTH-0066♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Linda Jones♔PathAI♔♔♔♔♔PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎In Response to the Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Submitted by: Linda Jones, Director of Government Relations, PathAI⏎⏎Date: February 2025⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI appreciates the opportunity to respond to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. PathAI's work in AI-powered pathology diagnostics gives us a specific vantage point on how AI tools interact with clinical judgment in high-stakes diagnostic workflows, and we want to use this comment to raise concerns that we think the RFI's framing, while well-intentioned, may be inadvertently setting up.⏎⏎⏎⏎We want to be direct about what worries us, because we believe it matters for how HHS structures whatever regulatory and reimbursement architecture comes out of this process.⏎⏎⏎⏎THE PRODUCTIVITY FRAMING IS A CATEGORY ERROR⏎⏎⏎⏎The RFI frames AI adoption largely around efficiency gains, workflow acceleration, and the reduction of administrative burden. PathAI understands why HHS would frame it this way. These are real problems. Clinician burnout is real, as Hartzband and Groopman outlined in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020, and the administrative weight crushing physicians is a genuine driver of care deterioration. We are not dismissing that.⏎⏎⏎⏎But medicine is not primarily an information-processing activity, and when HHS frames AI adoption as a productivity challenge to be solved, it encodes a model of care that treats clinical encounters as data-throughput events. That framing has consequences that compound over time, and we think HHS should think carefully about them before building a regulatory architecture around them.⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎What we see in our own deployment work, and what the broader literature confirms, is that the relational dimensions of clinical care are not soft factors peripheral to outcomes. A 2014 systematic review and meta-analysis by Kelley's research group published in PLOS ONE found that the patient-clinician relationship independently predicts health outcomes across a wide range of conditions and care settings. Hojat's team demonstrated in Academic Medicine (2011) that physician empathy directly correlates with improved clinical outcomes for diabetic patients, with measurable differences in HbA1c and LDL control. These are not anecdotal claims. They are quantified findings about what actually drives whether patients get better.⏎⏎⏎⏎When a patient comes in frightened about chest pain, the diagnostic encounter involves something that pattern-matching systems cannot replicate: a clinician reading the patient's affect, noticing that her description of the pain changed when she mentioned her mother died previously, understanding that her anxiety is itself clinically relevant data that will not appear in any structured field in the EHR. Eric Topol wrote in Nature Medicine in 2019 that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in medicine should liberate clinicians to spend more time on the human dimensions of care, not less. We agree with that vision. What concerns PathAI is that the RFI's productivity framing points in the opposite direction.⏎⏎⏎⏎WHAT THE DEPLOYMENT DATA ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI's experience deploying AI in pathology workflows across academic medical centers and community health systems has given us a clear view of where AI adds genuine value and where it creates new risks. We want to be specific about both, because we think the field is not always honest about the latter.⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎On the value side: AI-assisted pathology review has demonstrably improved sensitivity for certain cancer subtypes in our validated deployments. In a 2023 multi-site study across seven academic pathology departments, PathAI's AISight platform showed a 17.3% improvement in concordance rates for HER2 scoring in breast cancer specimens compared to standard-of-care review alone. That is a real clinical benefit, and it comes from AI functioning as a calibration tool that augments a pathologist's judgment rather than replacing it.⏎⏎⏎⏎On the risk side: we have seen what happens when AI tools are deployed without adequate governance structures, and it is not always the algorithm failing. Sometimes the harm is subtler. Clinicians begin to defer to AI outputs not because the output is right but because the institutional workflow has been restructured around the AI's recommendations. Obermeyer and Emanuel described this dynamic in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016, noting that the opacity of machine learning systems in clinical settings creates new forms of cognitive dependency that are difficult to detect and harder to reverse. The National Academy of Medicine's 2023 special publication on AI in health care identified this same pattern as one of the underappreciated risks of scaled AI deployment.⏎⏎⏎⏎Verghese, Shah, and Harrington wrote in JAMA in 2018 that what the computer needs is a physician, by which they meant that AI tools require human clinical judgment not as a rubber-stamp but as genuine interpretive oversight. We think that principle has to be structural, not aspirational, and the regulatory framework HHS builds should make it structural.⏎⏎⏎⏎The specific concerns PathAI would ask HHS to address in its regulatory and reimbursement design:⏎⏎⏎⏎   o  Reimbursement structures that tie payment to AI-assisted throughput volumes create incentives that will erode the time clinicians spend in genuine relational engagement with patients. CMS should model the downstream effects of productivity-linked AI reimbursement on visit duration and patient-reported experience scores before finalizing any payment methodology.⏎⏎⏎⏎   o  FDA's existing Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) framework does not adequately address the cognitive intermediation risks that arise when AI systems are positioned as decision-support tools in high-stakes diagnostic workflows. Shortliffe and Sepúlveda argued in JAMA in 2018 that clinical decision support in the AI era requires governance structures that go beyond pre-market clearance, including continuous post-deployment performance monitoring with clinician-reported outcome tracking.⏎⏎⏎⏎   o  ONC's certification criteria for health IT under 45 CFR Part 170 should be extended to require that AI outputs embedded in certified EHR workflows carry standardized uncertainty quantification disclosures. Clinicians need to know not just what the algorithm recommends but how confident it is and under what conditions its performance has been validated.⏎⏎⏎⏎   o  Equity monitoring requirements should be mandatory, not voluntary, for any AI tool seeking reimbursement under Medicare or Medicaid. Obermeyer and Emanuel's 2016 work was early; the evidence base for algorithmic bias in clinical AI has grown considerably since then, and HHS has both the authority and the responsibility to require prospective bias auditing as a condition of payment.⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎THE RELATIONAL HARM IS INDEPENDENT OF ALGORITHMIC ACCURACY⏎⏎⏎⏎This is the point PathAI most wants HHS to absorb, because we think it is the one most likely to get lost in a regulatory process focused on safety and efficacy in the conventional sense.⏎⏎⏎⏎Even a perfectly accurate AI system can cause clinical harm if its deployment structure erodes the relational encounter between clinician and patient. Bickmore and Picard's foundational work on human-computer relationships, published in ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction in 2005, demonstrated that trust in automated systems requires sustained relational investment in ways that clinical AI deployments rarely account for. The patient who receives a cancer diagnosis that was generated by an AI-assisted review and communicated through an automated patient portal message has not been harmed by an inaccurate algorithm. She has been harmed by a care structure that treated her diagnosis as an information-delivery event.⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 5⏎⏎⏎⏎We continually revisit this issue in our internal policy discussions because it is not a problem our technology can solve. It is a problem that regulatory design either addresses or ignores. Dzau, McClellan, and McGinnis wrote in JAMA in 2021 that durable progress in health and health care requires attending to the conditions under which care is actually delivered, not just the technical quality of individual interventions. An AI system that improves diagnostic accuracy by 17% while simultaneously restructuring care delivery in ways that reduce meaningful clinician-patient contact is not straightforwardly a clinical benefit. The net calculation is more complicated than the RFI's framing acknowledges.⏎⏎⏎⏎There is also the question of what scaled AI deployment does to clinical judgment over time. PathAI's clinical advisory team has heard, across multiple deployment sites, pathologists and oncologists expressing concern that their interpretive confidence in the absence of AI assistance is declining. This is anecdotal, and we want to be careful not to overstate it. But Torous and Roberts raised a related concern in JAMA Psychiatry in 2017 about the conditions under which digital health tools build trust versus dependency, and we think that framework applies directly to clinical AI. HHS should commission longitudinal research on the effects of AI deployment on independent clinical reasoning capacity before accelerating adoption in ways that may be difficult to reverse.⏎⏎⏎⏎A PRECAUTIONARY POSTURE IS NOT OPPOSITION TO INNOVATION⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI wants to be clear that none of the above is an argument against AI in clinical care. Our entire business is built on the conviction that AI can make pathology diagnosis more accurate and more equitable. We have seen it work.⏎⏎⏎⏎What we are arguing is that the regulatory posture HHS adopts now will shape the deployment patterns of the next decade, and a posture organized around acceleration without commensurate attention to the relational and cognitive conditions of clinical care is likely to produce a generation of AI deployments that are technically validated but clinically hollow. The pilot-to-production failure rate that organizations like InterSystems have documented across integrated health systems, where only about 22% of clinical AI pilots successfully move into sustained workflows, is not solely a technical interoperability problem. It is also a signal that clinicians are not finding these tools trustworthy in the full sense of that word.⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 6⏎⏎⏎⏎Trustworthiness in clinical AI requires demonstrated safety and equity before deployment, not as post-market corrections. It requires reimbursement structures that reward genuine clinical value rather than throughput volume. It requires that human responsibility remain meaningful at every decision point, which means the regulatory framework has to make algorithmic recommendation-following the beginning of clinical judgment, not the end of it.⏎⏎⏎⏎HHS has an opportunity here to build a framework that makes AI adoption durable because it is trustworthy, rather than fast because it is unencumbered. PathAI urges the Department to resist the productivity framing as the organizing logic of that framework and to instead ask, at every regulatory and reimbursement decision point, whether the proposed structure preserves the conditions under which clinical care actually works.⏎⏎⏎⏎Specifically, PathAI recommends that HHS:⏎⏎⏎⏎1.  Require pre-deployment equity audits and post-deployment bias monitoring as conditions of Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services, with results reported publicly in a standardized format.⏎⏎⏎⏎2.  Direct ONC to develop certification criteria requiring that AI outputs in EHR-embedded workflows include standardized uncertainty quantification disclosures accessible to both clinicians and patients at the point of care.⏎⏎⏎⏎3.  Commission a research agenda through AHRQ or NIH focused on the longitudinal effects of clinical AI deployment on independent clinical judgment, patient-reported relational experience, and care outcomes, with particular attention to high-volume deployment contexts in primary care and pathology.⏎⏎⏎⏎4.  Instruct CMS to model the effects of productivity-linked AI reimbursement on visit duration and patient experience before finalizing any payment methodology that ties reimbursement to AI-assisted throughput.⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 7⏎⏎⏎⏎PathAI is committed to AI development that makes pathologists better at their jobs and patients better served by the diagnostic process. We believe federal regulatory design is one of the most important levers for ensuring that the AI tools entering clinical care over the next decade actually deliver on that commitment rather than substituting algorithmic speed for clinical judgment.⏎⏎⏎⏎We are available to discuss any of the above with HHS staff and would welcome the opportunity to provide technical briefings on PathAI's deployment experience, including the specific governance structures we have found most effective at preserving meaningful clinician oversight in AI-assisted pathology workflows. SYNTH-0067♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joseph Davis♔♔♔♔♔♔Regarding the HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information, 89 FR (2024)⏎⏎My name is Joseph Davis. I live in Kearney, Nebraska. I drive long-haul freight routes through Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas, Colorado, and Wyoming, and I have no medical credentials. I'm submitting this because I think HHS is asking the wrong question, and I want to explain why I think that from where I sit.⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHAT THIS RFI IS ACTUALLY ASKING⏎⏎In 2022 my father-in-law Dale spent three days in a Kearney hospital while his kidneys were failing and nobody could figure out why. The answer turned out to be a medication interaction. A computer flagged it, but only after his nephrologist manually entered everything into a separate system that wasn't connected to the others. Day three, not day one. My wife paced that waiting room for three days. I'm not telling that story to make this comment emotional. I'm telling it because I genuinely believe better-integrated diagnostic tools could have found that interaction faster, and that matters to real people in real places. So I want to be clear that I am not writing this as someone who is opposed to technology in medicine. I'm not.⏎⏎But I drive for a living, and I have watched what happens when logistics infrastructure gets upgraded past the point of no return. The routing systems, the load management platforms, the dispatch software that carriers adopted in the early 2010s. Carriers who got in early are now so dependent on those vendor systems that they cannot realistically operate without them. I have watched small regional carriers get absorbed or shut down not because their drivers were bad or their equipment was old, but because they could not afford the transition costs to the new platform and couldn't compete without it. The institutional knowledge of how to do dispatch without the algorithm is gone. The people who knew how to do it retired. The training materials don't exist anymore. And freight is freight. If a load of auto parts gets misrouted, someone files a claim. Nobody dies.⏎⏎Healthcare is not freight.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE LOCK-IN PROBLEM HHS IS NOT ADDRESSING⏎⏎The RFI is framed around reducing "regulatory uncertainty" as an obstacle to AI adoption. I understand why agencies frame things that way. Faster adoption sounds like a good thing when the technology works. But the framing treats reversibility as a given, and I don't think it is.⏎⏎There is published research on this. Coiera and colleagues wrote in 2022 about what they called "health system lock-in" and the irreversibility of algorithmic infrastructure in clinical settings. Their argument, as I understood it, is that once AI systems are embedded deeply enough into clinical workflows, the human skills and institutional knowledge required to function without them deteriorate faster than most administrators anticipate. You can't just unplug the system if problems emerge, because the system has become load-bearing. The people who knew how to read the labs without the algorithm's interpretation layer are gone. The documentation workflows have been redesigned around the output. The training for new clinicians assumes the tool is present.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical. This is what I watch happen in logistics every time a major platform becomes standard. And in logistics, when the system makes a bad call, you lose a shipment. In medicine, the consequences are different in kind, not just in degree.⏎⏎HHS is not simply deciding whether to accelerate adoption. The agency is deciding whether to make a particular technological architecture effectively permanent in American clinical care. That is a much larger decision than the RFI acknowledges, and I don't think an RFI framed around reducing regulatory friction is the right vehicle for making it.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY GAP⏎⏎Here is the core issue that stands out to me. The AI systems being deployed in clinical settings are, in almost every case I have read about, proprietary. The algorithms are not public. The training data is not audited by any body with genuine independence. The weights, the decision logic, the specific mechanisms by which a system flags a medication interaction or recommends a treatment path — none of that is available to the clinician using the tool, to the hospital administrator buying it, to the patient whose care it shapes, or to HHS itself.⏎⏎Obermeyer and Topol wrote in The Lancet Digital Health in 2021 about how AI bias in clinical settings tends to be invisible precisely because the systems are opaque. The GAO published a report in 2023 on AI in health care that raised similar concerns about the gap between what these systems promise and what can actually be verified about how they work. Selbst and Barocas have written about how the intuitive appeal of explainability in machine learning often masks the fact that the explanations provided are post-hoc rationalizations, not genuine accounts of the system's reasoning.⏎⏎I am not a researcher. I read widely because I have a lot of hours in a cab and I listen to a lot of podcasts and I read what I can. But you don't need a PhD to understand what these scholars are describing. What they're describing is a situation where:⏎⏎1. The systems making clinical recommendations cannot be audited by the people responsible for patient care.⏎2. The vendors who build and maintain those systems have strong financial incentives to resist transparency requirements.⏎3. The concentration of market power in a small number of AI health vendors means that "switching" to a different system is increasingly theoretical, not practical.⏎4. Regulatory frameworks are being asked to accelerate adoption of systems with these properties before any of those three problems have been resolved.⏎⏎Dafny and Lee wrote in Health Affairs in 2023 about vendor concentration in health care AI and what they called the erosion of institutional accountability. Their argument is that when clinical decision-making authority migrates into vendor systems, the locus of accountability shifts in ways that existing legal and regulatory structures are not designed to handle. A hospital can be sued. A clinician can lose a license. A vendor whose algorithm contributed to a bad outcome is much harder to hold accountable, especially when the algorithm's behavior cannot be reconstructed or audited after the fact.⏎⏎---⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC QUESTION HHS IS NOT ASKING⏎⏎I want to say something that might sound like it belongs in a philosophy class, but I think it's actually practical.⏎⏎Langdon Winner wrote in 1980 that embedded technologies carry political consequences that outlast the decisions that produced them. The example he used was Robert Moses designing overpasses in New York low enough that buses couldn't pass under them, effectively keeping lower-income transit users out of certain parks. The politics were baked into the concrete. You couldn't vote them out. The argument is that technology choices are not neutral, and that once a technology is sufficiently embedded, the political choices it encodes become practically irreversible regardless of what any subsequent democratic process decides.⏎⏎I think about that when I read this RFI. The people of Kearney, Nebraska have not been asked whether they want clinical decisions at their regional hospital to be shaped by an algorithm built by a company in California or Massachusetts whose training data, decision logic, and error rates they cannot examine. They haven't been asked whether the tradeoff between efficiency and auditability is one they're willing to make. They haven't been asked whether they want their local clinicians to gradually lose the skills and institutional authority that come with making those calls themselves.⏎⏎HHS framing regulatory scrutiny as an obstacle to innovation is the agency answering those questions on their behalf. I don't think HHS has a democratic mandate to do that, and I don't think an RFI is the right process for a decision of this magnitude.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I'm not certain what the right answer is. Maybe the benefits of integrated AI diagnostics are large enough and the risks manageable enough that communities would choose adoption if genuinely asked. Dale's situation is real to me. The medication interaction that took three days to find might have been found on day one. That matters. I am not arguing that medicine should freeze in place.⏎⏎What I'm arguing is that the framing of this RFI — reduce regulatory uncertainty, accelerate adoption, treat caution as a barrier — forecloses the question before it's been asked. Once these systems are embedded deeply enough that reversal is impractical, the question of whether communities want them becomes moot. The concrete is poured.⏎⏎---⏎⏎WHAT I AM ASKING HHS TO DO⏎⏎This is the only specific ask I want to make, because I think it's the one that matters most before anything else happens:⏎⏎Before HHS takes any action designed to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care, the agency should commission an independent, public assessment of the reversibility conditions attached to specific AI systems currently being deployed in clinical settings. That assessment should answer, for each major system category:⏎⏎a. At what level of institutional penetration does reversal become practically infeasible, and what is the current penetration level?⏎⏎b. What human skills and institutional capacities are already being lost, and at what rate?⏎⏎c. What audit rights do hospitals, clinicians, and state regulators currently have over the decision logic of deployed systems, and where are those rights absent?⏎⏎d. What vendor concentration exists in each system category, and what does that mean for the practical availability of alternatives?⏎⏎I am not asking HHS to stop anything. I am asking the agency to understand what it is actually deciding before it decides it. The difference between accelerating adoption and foreclosing alternatives is a question of timing and reversibility, and right now HHS is treating that question as settled when it isn't.⏎⏎The RFI as written asks how to remove barriers to AI adoption. A better question is which barriers exist to protect something worth protecting, and whether removing them is a decision that belongs to a federal agency acting through an informal comment process or to the communities whose medicine this actually is.⏎⏎My father-in-law Dale is fine now. He's back to complaining about the Huskers. But the three days my wife spent in that waiting room are why I'm writing this, and also why I think the stakes are high enough that getting this right matters more than getting it fast.⏎⏎Joseph Davis⏎Kearney, Nebraska⏎⏎Page 1 of 1♔♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-06T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔Nebraska♔truck driver♔47♔My father-in-law, Dale, spent three days in a Kearney hospital two winters back while doctors ran test after test trying to figure out why his kidneys were failing — turns out the answer was hiding in a medication interaction that a computer flagged only after his nephrologist manually entered everything into a separate system nobody had thought to check. SYNTH-0068♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sarah Lewis♔American College of Emergency Physicians♔♔♔♔♔American College of Emergency Physicians⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎Submitted by: Sarah Lewis, Research Director⏎American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP)⏎⏎⏎PRELIMINARY STATEMENT⏎⏎The American College of Emergency Physicians represents more than 40,000 emergency physicians practicing across every care setting in the United States, including the safety-net hospitals, rural critical access facilities, and urban trauma centers that absorb the greatest volume of coverage disputes and prior authorization delays. ACEP submits these comments in response to HHS's request for information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care, and we want to be direct at the outset: the framing of this RFI is incomplete in a way that, if not corrected, will produce a regulatory architecture that benefits the wrong actors. The genuine promise of clinical AI — in diagnostic imaging interpretation, sepsis prediction, triage decision support — is real and documented. Rajpurkar, Chen, Banerjee, and Topol's 2022 review in Nature Medicine surveyed the evidence base for AI applications across medicine and identified several areas where algorithmic tools demonstrably improve patient outcomes. ACEP does not dispute that record. What we dispute is the Department's apparent decision to treat "AI in healthcare" as synonymous with "AI deployed in service of patients," when the most commercially dominant and least scrutinized application of AI in the American health sector is something else entirely: the automated denial of coverage.⏎⏎⏎THE OMISSION THAT DEFINES THIS RFI⏎⏎The RFI uses language about "fostering competition among clinical care AI tool builders" and frames the Department's task as removing barriers to adoption. That language does real rhetorical work. It constructs AI as a category of clinical benefit awaiting regulatory permission to flourish. But it does not describe the market as it actually exists. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, in its October 2023 report "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Plans Use Algorithms to Override Physician Judgment" (S. Prt. 118-22), documented in granular detail how major Medicare Advantage insurers deployed algorithmic tools to generate prior authorization denials at volumes and speeds that made meaningful human review structurally impossible. The report examined UnitedHealth Group's nH Predict tool specifically, finding that the algorithm was used to issue post-acute care denials at a rate that the Subcommittee characterized as inconsistent with individualized clinical review. Reporting by Mukherjee and Ross at STAT News in November 2023 found that UnitedHealth's AI was denying claims at rates that shocked even internal reviewers, and that patients — many of them elderly Medicare Advantage enrollees — were left navigating appeals processes that the insurer's own operational design rendered effectively futile.⏎⏎This is not an edge case. The Office of Inspector General's April 2022 report (OEI-09-18-00260) found that Medicare Advantage organizations were denying prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage criteria, and that some of those denials were later overturned on appeal at high rates — suggesting the initial denials lacked clinical grounding. Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2024 issue brief by Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman documented that prior authorization requests in Medicare Advantage increased substantially between 2019 and 2022, with denial rates varying dramatically across plans in ways that cannot be explained by clinical differences in the patient populations served. The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94% of physicians reported that prior authorization delays had harmed patients in their care, and 33% reported that prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient. In emergency medicine, those numbers carry particular weight. ACEP physicians are making time-sensitive decisions in environments where a coverage delay is not an inconvenience — it is a clinical event.⏎⏎The insurer AI market operates according to incentive structures that Dafny, Gruber, and Ody described in their 2015 analysis in the American Journal of Health Economics: competition among insurers does not, absent regulatory constraint, produce consumer-beneficial outcomes in coverage administration. When algorithmic denial becomes a cost-containment tool, the competitive pressure runs toward more aggressive denial, not less. Automation bias — the documented tendency of human reviewers to defer to algorithmic outputs even when those outputs are incorrect, as systematically reviewed by Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2012 — means that even nominally "human-reviewed" denials may not constitute genuine independent clinical judgment when the human reviewer is presented with an AI recommendation to deny.⏎⏎⏎American College of Emergency Physicians | HHS AI RFI Comments | Page 3⏎⏎⏎EQUITY CONSIDERATIONS THE RFI DOES NOT ADEQUATELY FRAME⏎⏎The Department's RFI acknowledges health equity in passing, but the equity implications of insurer AI are more severe and more specific than the RFI's framing suggests. Algorithmic systems trained on historical claims data will encode historical patterns of underservice and discrimination. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan's landmark 2019 study in Science (366(6464):447-453) demonstrated that a widely used commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a proxy that reflects historical barriers to access rather than actual clinical severity. The structural equity methodology concerns identified in work like that of Ndugga, Artiga, and Pham at the Kaiser Family Foundation apply directly here: when algorithms are trained on data generated by inequitable systems, they reproduce and often amplify those inequities. An acceleration agenda that deploys more AI in coverage administration without mandatory pre-deployment equity audits is not a neutral policy. It is a choice to scale discrimination faster.⏎⏎New York State's Department of Financial Services issued Circular Letter No. 7 in March 2024 on the use of artificial intelligence systems and external consumer data in insurance underwriting and rating, establishing baseline requirements for insurer AI governance at the state level. The existence of that circular letter — and the fact that HHS has issued no comparable federal standard for AI used in prior authorization or coverage determinations — represents a regulatory gap that this RFI should be addressing directly. The absence of federal standards means that the most harmful applications of health AI are also the least governed.⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎ACEP urges HHS and ONC to address the following in any regulatory or reimbursement framework that emerges from this RFI process:⏎⏎1. Mandatory pre-deployment equity audits for any AI system used in coverage determinations, prior authorization, or utilization management. These audits should be conducted by independent third parties, should include disaggregated analysis by race, ethnicity, disability status, and income, and should be submitted to CMS before any Medicare Advantage or Medicaid managed care organization deploys a new algorithmic tool in these functions. The audit methodology should be published and subject to public comment.⏎⏎2. A federal right to human review of any AI-generated denial. "Human review" should be defined operationally to require that a licensed clinician with relevant specialty training actually evaluate the clinical record — not that a human employee rubber-stamp an algorithmic output within a volume and time structure that makes genuine review impossible. The Senate PSI investigation documented exactly this pattern with nH Predict, and any federal standard that does not address the rubber-stamp problem will be circumvented.⏎⏎3. Public disclosure requirements for denial rate data disaggregated by AI tool. CMS currently collects some prior authorization data from Medicare Advantage plans, but that data is not disaggregated by the algorithmic tool used to generate the denial, is not publicly accessible in a form that enables independent analysis, and does not include information about appeal outcomes correlated with AI involvement. Meaningful accountability requires that researchers, patient advocates, and regulators be able to assess whether specific algorithmic tools are producing denial rates inconsistent with clinical standards.⏎⏎4. A moratorium on new AI prior authorization deployments in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care until HHS establishes minimum accountability standards. ACEP recognizes that this recommendation will be contested by insurers and some technology vendors. We make it anyway, because the alternative — allowing continued expansion of algorithmic denial infrastructure while the Department develops standards through a multi-year regulatory process — will cause documented, measurable harm to patients in the interim. The OIG's 2022 report, the Senate PSI investigation, and the AMA's survey data collectively establish that harm is not hypothetical.⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RFI'S FRAMING OF NON-MEDICAL DEVICE AI⏎⏎The RFI asks several questions about regulatory approaches to AI that does not meet the definition of a medical device under FDA jurisdiction. Prior authorization algorithms almost certainly fall into this category — they are administrative tools, not diagnostic ones, and FDA's enforcement discretion policies have not been applied to them. This creates a regulatory gap that is not incidental. The 15% figure our policy analysis division identified — fewer than 15% of FDA-cleared clinical AI devices have corresponding CPT or HCPCS billing codes — speaks to the financing challenges for clinical AI tools. But for insurer AI, the financing structure runs in the opposite direction: denial automation generates return on investment directly, without requiring any reimbursement pathway, because its revenue model is cost avoidance rather than care delivery. Any evaluation framework for non-medical device AI that addresses only clinical care tools and excludes insurance administration AI will produce standards that govern the less commercially powerful applications while leaving the more powerful ones unregulated.⏎⏎The Schulte and Fry investigation published by Kaiser Health News and Fortune in March 2019 documented how financial incentives shaped EHR implementation in ways that harmed patients — a lesson the Department apparently did not fully absorb, given that the same pattern is now replicating itself in AI-driven prior authorization. ACEP does not think the Department is acting in bad faith here. We think the RFI reflects a genuine interest in harnessing AI for patient benefit. But the framing — clinical care AI, acceleration, competition among tool builders — systematically directs attention away from the applications where patients are most at risk right now. Fixing that framing is not a secondary concern.⏎⏎ACEP is prepared to provide additional technical input, including data from our membership on prior authorization delays in emergency care settings, to any HHS working group convened to develop the accountability standards described above. SYNTH-0069♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Emily Davis♔Walgreens Boots Alliance♔♔♔♔♔Walgreens Boots Alliance < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎To the Office of the Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy / Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology:⏎⏎⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance submits this comment in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. This organization operates across more than 8,700 retail pharmacy and health clinic locations in the United States, and our compliance function has spent the better part of eighteen months directly engaged with the empirical question the RFI conspicuously avoids: when an AI-assisted clinical decision causes patient harm, who is legally answerable for it. The answer, under the current regulatory architecture that HHS is now proposing to accelerate rather than repair, is no one in particular. That is not an overstatement. It is the documented finding of EPIC's AI in Health: State Policy Accountability Review, published in Q2 2024 following an 18-month analysis of AI health deployment policies across all 47 states that had issued any relevant guidance. Fewer than 12 percent of those policies included enforceable patient notification requirements triggered when AI systems materially influenced clinical decision-making. Twelve percent. The other 88 percent of state-level policy frameworks create no legal obligation to tell a patient that the recommendation governing their care was generated, filtered, or ranked by an algorithm. A parallel audit of 23 hospital network privacy disclosures, conducted as part of the same review, found that the vast majority of those documents failed to identify specific AI vendors, training data sources, or the algorithmic logic behind the systems being deployed. These are not gaps at the margins of an otherwise functional accountability system. They are the system, and HHS is proposing to build faster on top of it.⏎⏎⏎⏎The RFI's framing is accelerationist in a precise and troubling sense. It asks how HHS can remove barriers to AI adoption and expand reimbursement pathways and streamline regulatory review, and it gestures toward private-sector certification and accreditation schemes as the preferred accountability mechanism. What it does not ask, anywhere in its text, is who bears legal responsibility when an AI-assisted clinical recommendation is wrong and a patient is harmed as a result. That omission is not an oversight. As Barbara J. Evans and Frank Pasquale argued in their 2022 analysis in the Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics, the liability architecture for AI-assisted clinical decision-making is deliberately ambiguous because ambiguity serves the commercial interests of the vendors who design these systems and the institutional interests of the hospitals that deploy them. Evans and Pasquale document in detail how existing product liability doctrine, negligence standards, and respondeat superior frameworks were each constructed around an identifiable human decision-maker whose judgment can be evaluated against a professional standard of care. When an AI system generates a recommendation that a clinician follows, each party in that chain has a plausible institutional argument for why the duty of care resided elsewhere. The vendor says the clinician retained final authority. The clinician says the system was validated and certified. The hospital says it relied on the vendor's representations. The result is liability diffusion so complete that no individual or entity bears meaningful accountability, and patients who are harmed have no clear legal path to redress. Frank Pasquale identified this structural dynamic more broadly in The Black Box Society (Harvard University Press, 2015), observing that opacity in automated institutional systems is not incidental but functional: it allows institutions to capture the benefits of algorithmic decision-making while systematically deflecting accountability for its failures.⏎⏎⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎The compliance function of this organization has direct operational experience with what liability diffusion looks like in practice, and it is worth being specific about the structural mechanism. When a retail pharmacy AI system flags a drug interaction or generates a clinical recommendation at a Walgreens Health clinic, there is currently no federal standard governing what disclosures must be made to the patient, no federal standard specifying which party bears the duty of care for that recommendation, and no federal standard defining what documentation must be preserved to support accountability in the event of an adverse outcome. The ONC Health IT Certification Program, established under the 21st Century Cures Act and codified at 85 Fed. Reg. 25642 (May 1, 2020), addresses interoperability and information blocking but does not establish enforceable accountability standards for AI-assisted clinical functions. The American Medical Association's 2019 policy framework on augmented intelligence identifies clinician oversight as a governing principle but creates no binding legal duty and no mechanism for patients to enforce that principle. The GAO's 2020 report on AI in health care (GAO-21-7SP) explicitly flagged the absence of clear accountability frameworks as a barrier to safe AI deployment, a finding that HHS appears to have noted and then declined to act on. What the RFI proposes instead is to expand the role of voluntary certification programs, which by definition create no enforceable patient rights, no legal duty of care, and no mechanism for assigning liability when AI-assisted decisions cause harm. Certification tells patients that a system has been reviewed. It does not tell them who is answerable if the system is wrong.⏎⏎⏎⏎The moral dimension of this question deserves more attention than the RFI gives it, which is none. Patients have a right, grounded in the foundational ethics of the clinical relationship, to a named and answerable human being who is responsible for their care. This is not a romantic or outdated principle. It is the structural premise of informed consent doctrine, of fiduciary duty in medical ethics, and of the malpractice system that, however imperfectly, provides patients with a mechanism for accountability when that duty is breached. The IHI/NORC survey from 2017 on Americans' experiences with medical errors found that patients who experienced adverse outcomes were far more likely to report permanent emotional harm when they felt no one had been held accountable for what happened to them. The experience of accountability, or its absence, is not separable from the clinical harm. When AI intermediation dissolves the identifiable human decision-maker into a chain of institutional actors each pointing at the others, it does not merely create a legal puzzle. It causes a specific and documentable category of patient harm. Char, Shah, and Magnus, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 (vol. 378, pp. 981-983), warned that the ethical challenges of implementing machine learning in health care include precisely this erosion of the identifiable responsible party, and that deploying these systems without resolving that question first is an ethical failure, not merely a regulatory gap. W. Nicholson Price II and I. Glenn Cohen made a related point in Nature Medicine in 2019 (vol. 25, pp. 37-43), arguing that the opacity of medical AI systems creates structural information asymmetries that patients cannot navigate and that existing consent frameworks were not designed to address. EPIC's 2024 Health Privacy Roundtable, which brought together privacy professionals and patient advocates from across the country, found that the absence of federal baseline standards was the single most consistently identified barrier to meaningful transparency and accountability in AI-assisted care. That finding was unanimous among participants. HHS has this information. It has had it for some time.⏎⏎⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎This comment focuses specifically on the RFI's questions regarding regulatory frameworks for AI accountability, because that is where the structural failure is most acute and where HHS's proposed approach is most clearly inadequate. The RFI asks what regulatory actions HHS can take to support responsible AI adoption. The answer this organization submits is the following, and it is not a list of preferences but a set of conditions without which no responsible adoption framework is possible:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. HHS must establish, by federal regulation and not by voluntary guidance, a baseline enforceable accountability standard specifying which party or parties bear the duty of care when an AI system materially influences a clinical decision. The standard must be specific enough to be litigated, which means it must name the parties, define the threshold of material influence, and specify the documentation requirements that preserve the evidentiary record for accountability purposes.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. HHS must require, as a condition of any federal reimbursement pathway for AI-assisted clinical services, that patients receive written notification when AI systems have materially influenced the recommendation or decision governing their care. The notification must identify the AI vendor, the general category of the system's function, and the name of the responsible clinician who retained oversight. Fewer than 12 percent of existing state policies require this. Federal action is the only mechanism that will produce a baseline.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. HHS must prohibit any AI deployment framework, whether through certification, accreditation, or reimbursement pathway, from using the existence of a certification as a shield against liability for AI-assisted harm. The certification programs the RFI favors as accountability mechanisms create no enforceable patient rights. They are institutional due diligence tools, not substitutes for a legal duty of care.⏎⏎⏎⏎Sharona Hoffman and Andy Podgurski, writing in the Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics in 2020 (vol. 19, no. 3, pp. 1-51), documented in considerable detail how the absence of federal accountability standards in AI-assisted health care creates conditions for discrimination as well as harm, because algorithmic systems trained on historically biased data will reproduce those biases in clinical recommendations, and without an enforceable accountability standard there is no mechanism to detect, attribute, or correct that pattern at scale. The RFI does not engage with this literature. It does not engage with the Evans and Pasquale liability analysis. It does not engage with the GAO's findings. What it does instead is ask how barriers to adoption can be reduced, which is a different question entirely and one that assumes the accountability architecture is either adequate or someone else's problem to solve.⏎⏎⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance < > HHS AI RFI Comments < > Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎This organization wants to be direct about what HHS is proposing to do, because the RFI's language softens it considerably. HHS is proposing to accelerate the deployment of AI systems in clinical care settings before any federal framework exists to answer the question of who is legally and morally accountable when those systems contribute to patient harm. The empirical record, documented by EPIC across 47 states and 23 hospital networks, confirms that the accountability infrastructure does not exist at the state level either. The private-sector certification mechanisms the RFI favors as a substitute have never, in any sector, produced enforceable patient rights or clear legal duties. The clinical ethics literature, from Char et al. through Price and Cohen through Evans and Pasquale, is in substantial agreement that deploying AI systems without first resolving the accountability question is an ethical failure independent of whatever clinical benefits the systems may provide. And the patient experience data, going back at least to the IHI/NORC 2017 survey, confirms that the absence of accountability is itself a form of patient harm. HHS has before it a choice between accelerating adoption and building the accountability infrastructure that safe adoption requires. The RFI as written treats those as compatible goals achievable in parallel. This organization's eighteen months of compliance work on this question, and the empirical record EPIC has compiled, suggest that is not correct. Accelerating deployment in the absence of an accountability framework does not merely risk future harm. It embeds the conditions for harm into the architecture of the system at a scale and speed that will make accountability harder to establish after the fact, not easier. The question of who answers for an AI-assisted error at a retail health clinic in, say, Reno, Nevada, in 2026 is not a hypothetical. It is a question this organization's compliance team is currently unable to answer with any legal certainty, and the RFI does not propose to change that.⏎⏎⏎⏎Emily Davis⏎⏎Senior Compliance Officer, Regulatory Affairs and Health Privacy⏎⏎Walgreens Boots Alliance⏎⏎200 Wilmot Road, Deerfield, IL 60015⏎⏎⏎⏎emily.davis@wba.com⏎⏎⏎⏎Submitted electronically via regulations.gov⏎⏎Docket HHS-2024-AI-001♔♔2026-01-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔angry♔Nevada♔compliance officer♔49♔EPIC's analysis of 47 state-level AI health deployment policies, conducted across an 18-month review period concluding in Q2 2024, found that fewer than 12% included enforceable patient notification requirements when AI systems materially influenced clinical decision-making. Our membership includes physicians practicing in community health centers, essential access hospitals in non-urban areas, and independent practices that collectively bear a disproportionate share of the structural disadvantages embedded in U.S. healthcare infrastructure. We submit these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings, and we do so with a specific and urgent concern: the populations we serve will not benefit from acceleration that proceeds without equity infrastructure. They will be harmed by it.⏎⏎⏎⏎The empirical record on this point is not ambiguous, and we ask HHS to treat it accordingly.⏎⏎⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED RECORD OF ALGORITHMIC HARM IN CLINICAL SETTINGS⏎⏎⏎⏎The communities we serve have already been enrolled, without their knowledge or consent, in a large-scale natural experiment in clinical AI deployment. The results are in, and they are not encouraging.⏎⏎⏎⏎Begin with the foundational evidence. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 a rigorous dissection of a commercial risk-stratification tool used by major health systems to identify high-need patients for care management programs (Obermeyer Z, Powers B, Vogeli C, Mullainathan S. Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). That predictive model consistently undervalued the medical requirements of Black individuals relative to white individuals at the same level of illness severity, because it relied on medical spending to approximate clinical urgency — and Black patients, facing well-documented structural barriers to access, historically generated lower costs despite being equally sick. The result was that Black patients were assigned to care management programs at roughly half the rate they should have been, given their actual health burden. This was not a fringe product. It was an extensively adopted proprietary software tool, and the bias was invisible to the institutions using it until researchers went looking.⏎⏎⏎⏎The same year that Obermeyer's findings circulated through the clinical community, Sjoding and colleagues published in the New England Journal of Medicine a finding that should have produced immediate regulatory response and did not (Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478). Pulse oximetry — a device so ubiquitous it is practically synonymous with clinical monitoring — produces significantly less accurate readings in patients with dark skin pigmentation, overestimating oxygen saturation and masking hypoxemia. This is not a new AI system. It is a decades-old technology. But it illustrates the principle that governs the entire AI risk landscape: when training data, calibration data, or reference populations do not adequately represent the patients ultimately being served, the tool performs worse for those patients, and the performance gap is often invisible at the point of care. Clinicians using pulse oximetry in the COVID-19 pandemic were making ventilator and discharge decisions based on readings that were systematically more error-prone for Black and Hispanic patients. The NPA is not prepared to watch this dynamic replicate itself at the scale and speed that HHS is proposing to enable.⏎⏎⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎⏎⏎PERFORMANCE DEGRADATION IN COMMUNITY AND SAFETY-NET SETTINGS⏎⏎⏎⏎The second structural problem is one that the RFI's framing tends to obscure: AI tools developed and validated in academic medical centers do not perform equivalently when deployed in community hospitals, rural practices, or safety-net clinics. Wong and colleagues illustrated this issue with remarkable clarity in their 2021 external validation of a broadly utilized proprietary sepsis forecasting model (Wong A, Otles E, Donnelly JP, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2021;181(8):1065-1070). The model, developed and marketed with strong internal validation statistics, showed substantially degraded sensitivity and specificity when evaluated in a community hospital setting with different patient demographics, documentation practices, and staffing patterns. The institutions that most need decision support — those with fewer specialists, thinner staffing ratios, and higher proportions of patients with complex social determinants — are precisely the institutions where validated performance statistics are least likely to generalize.⏎⏎⏎⏎This is not a theoretical concern for the NPA. A 2024 member survey conducted by the Texas Medical Association across 4,200 practicing physicians found that 74% of respondents in non-metropolitan practice settings cited lack of infrastructure and unclear federal policy as the primary obstacles to AI implementation. More telling: fewer than 28% of all surveyed physicians reported receiving any formal institutional guidance on liability, documentation standards, or billing protocols associated with AI-assisted tools they had already encountered in clinical use. These physicians are not waiting for HHS to authorize adoption. The tools are already in their workflows. What is absent is any regulatory framework ensuring that the tools deployed in a rural Texas clinic have been validated on patient populations resembling the ones that clinic actually serves.⏎⏎⏎⏎Kaushal and colleagues examined the geographic distribution of U.S. cohorts used to train foundational AI algorithms and found severe concentration in a small number of academic medical systems, predominantly in urban centers with demographically unrepresentative patient populations (Kaushal A, Altman R, Langlotz C. JAMA. 2020;324(12):1212-1213). Gianfrancesco and colleagues further documented how electronic health record data used to train machine learning systems carries embedded biases from differential access patterns, coding practices, and documentation completeness — all of which vary systematically by patient race, socioeconomic status, and geographic region (Gianfrancesco MA, Tamang S, Yazdany J, Schmajuk G. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(11):1544-1547). The consequence is that the foundational information embeds past discrimination, and the implemented model replicates it at the scale of whatever institution chooses to implement it.⏎⏎⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎⏎⏎THE AUTOMATION BIAS PROBLEM AND THE ABSENCE OF SURVEILLANCE⏎⏎⏎⏎What makes AI-mediated clinical errors structurally different from conventional clinical errors is not their frequency but their detectability. Cabitza and colleagues identified automation bias — the tendency of medical professionals to blindly accept computer-generated recommendations despite situations where such suggestions contradict their own medical judgment — as a distinct and underappreciated risk in AI-assisted medicine (Cabitza F, Rasoini R, Gensini GF. JAMA. 2017;318(6):517-518). When a physician misreads a lab value, there are multiple downstream checkpoints — a pharmacist, a nurse, a consulting specialist — that may catch the error. When an algorithm systematically misclassifies a category of patients, it does so consistently, at every encounter, and the clinician's cognitive tendency is to accept rather than interrogate the output. Char and colleagues noted that machine learning systems can produce confident-appearing recommendations that are statistically inappropriate for specific subpopulations without any visible signal of uncertainty at the point of care (Char DS, Shah NH, Magnus D. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(11):981-983). The clinician sees a recommendation, not a confidence interval, and not a demographic breakdown of validation performance.⏎⏎⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎⏎⏎Wiens and colleagues outlined a responsible deployment framework that explicitly requires ongoing post-deployment monitoring as a non-negotiable component of any clinical AI system (Wiens J, Saria S, Sendak M, et al. Nat Med. 2019;25(9):1337-1340). The current RFI does not propose any such monitoring requirement. It proposes acceleration. These are not compatible goals in the absence of a surveillance infrastructure that can detect when deployed tools are producing disparate outcomes across demographic subgroups in real-world settings.⏎⏎⏎⏎The NPA is also concerned about the specific pattern documented by Pierson and colleagues, who found that algorithmic systems used in pain management systematically underestimate pain severity in underserved populations, contributing to documented disparities in pain treatment that are already among the most persistent inequities in U.S. healthcare (Pierson E, Cutler DM, Leskovec J, Mullainathan S, Obermeyer Z. Nat Med. 2021;27(1):136-140). N Engl J Med. 2020;383(9):874-882).
