Specifically, we request the following:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. Obligatory fairness evaluations before implementation. Any clinical AI tool seeking reimbursement, regulatory authorization, or federal procurement eligibility should be required to demonstrate performance equivalence across demographic subgroups — including racial background, cultural heritage, sex, age, socioeconomic status, and geographic location. Performance statistics derived exclusively from academic medical center validation cohorts should not be accepted as sufficient for tools intended for deployment in community, safety-net, or rural settings. Subgroup-stratified performance data should be submitted to HHS and made publicly accessible.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. Mandatory post-deployment bias surveillance with public reporting. AI tools in active clinical use should be subject to ongoing monitoring requirements, with participating institutions required to report outcome data stratified by demographic subgroup on a regular reporting cycle. Significant performance divergence between subgroups should trigger mandatory review and, where indicated, suspension of the tool pending investigation. HHS should designate a specific office with authority and resources to receive, analyze, and act on this surveillance data. This is not a novel regulatory concept; it is the post-market surveillance model applied to pharmaceutical products, extended to software functioning as a medical device.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. A moratorium on AI use in high-stakes clinical and insurance decisions pending establishment of the above safeguards. The NPA recognizes that this is a significant ask. We make it because the alternative — accelerating deployment into the communities we serve without any mechanism to detect whether those tools are producing racially or socioeconomically disparate outcomes — is a policy choice to accept harm as a condition of innovation. That is not a tradeoff the NPA can support, and we do not believe it is one HHS intends to endorse, though the current RFI framing risks implying exactly that.⏎⏎⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎⏎⏎National Physicians Alliance Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎─────────────────────────────────────────────────────⏎⏎⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE QUESTION OF PROCESS⏎⏎⏎⏎The NPA notes, with some frustration, that the RFI format is a limited vehicle for the kind of substantive engagement this topic warrants. SYNTH-0072♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Betty Lee♔CVS Health♔♔♔♔♔CVS Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎COMMENT OF CVS HEALTH⏎Submitted to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP/ONC⏎Re: Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Betty Lee, Practice Manager, CVS Health⏎Date: October 15, 2024⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎CVS Health offers these remarks regarding HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care. Our organization operates across a substantial footprint of retail health clinics, pharmacy care settings, and affiliated imaging workflow partnerships, and our Q2 2024 internal policy review, drawing on operational metrics from over 2.1 million imaging studies conducted across 47 clinical sites utilizing Harrison.ai's diagnostic support tools, places us in a position to speak with some specificity about what AI integration looks like on the operational side. That review found that AI-assisted diagnostic workflows reduced mean radiologist reporting turnaround time by 38 percent. We are not disputing that finding, and we are not here to argue against AI adoption in the abstract.⏎⏎What this comment argues, and what we want HHS to take seriously before moving further down the path this RFI describes, is that the efficiency gains documented in our review and in the broader literature do not resolve a structural problem that the Department appears to be accelerating past rather than through. That problem is the diffusion of legal accountability that occurs when AI systems are embedded in clinical decision pathways, and it is a problem that existing medical malpractice doctrine, reimbursement architecture, and federal regulatory frameworks are not currently equipped to handle. Our concern is not that AI will fail technically. Our concern is that when it does cause harm, no identifiable human being or institution will carry definitive legal liability for that harm, and HHS is proposing to scale these systems before the requisite liability structures to contain that risk have been established.⏎⏎CVS Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL LIABILITY PROBLEM HHS IS NOT ADDRESSING⏎⏎The classical framework of medical malpractice liability, as Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert described in their 2020 JAMA analysis, presupposes a specific individual practitioner whose choices may be assessed using established clinical benchmarks. Respondeat superior doctrine assigns institutional liability through an employment or agency relationship that connects a specific act to a specific actor. Proximate causation analysis traces harm back through a chain of decisions to a point where human judgment either failed or succeeded. These doctrinal mechanisms were never intended for a clinical environment in which a radiologist reviews an AI-flagged finding, a hospital procurement office approved the AI system under vendor indemnification provisions that limit downstream liability, and the AI vendor's terms of service disclaim responsibility for any clinical outcome that involved human override or acceptance of the system's output. Each of those parties possesses what we would describe as a plausible deflection narrative: the radiologist will say the AI recommended it, the hospital will say the radiologist accepted it, and the vendor will point to the contract language and the FDA clearance letter as evidence that their product performed within specification.⏎⏎Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified this exact problem in their 2019 JAMA piece on physician liability for AI use, noting that standard negligence analysis struggles to assign fault when an AI system is neither the treating physician nor an instrument fully under the physician's control in the way that a scalpel or an infusion pump is. The AI occupies an intermediate space, and that intermediate space is, at present, a liability vacuum. Delvaux, Picard, Meunier, and colleagues conducted a systematic review of liability frameworks across seven jurisdictions and found that none of the frameworks reviewed, including those with more developed AI regulatory architectures than the United States currently has, provided a coherent mechanism for assigning proximate liability in AI-assisted harm scenarios where the AI output was accepted by a clinician who then documented that acceptance in the medical record (Health Policy and Technology, 2023). That is not a gap that can be patched by clarifying CPT codes or streamlining FDA clearance pathways. It is a structural design flaw in how accountability is assigned when human and machine judgment are co-mingled in a single clinical act.⏎⏎CVS Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎WHY ACCELERATION BEFORE ACCOUNTABILITY IS THE WRONG SEQUENCE⏎⏎The RFI asks, in substance, what HHS can do to move faster. Our answer is that moving faster on deployment without moving at all on the accountability architecture makes the problem progressively harder to solve, not easier. Once AI-assisted workflows are embedded in clinical operations at scale, the institutional and financial incentives to maintain those workflows become substantial. Procurement investments have been made. EHR integrations have been built. Staffing models have been redesigned around the assumption that AI will handle certain triage or flagging functions. The practical consequence is that a system deployed without a mandatory accountability framework becomes, over time, a system that is very difficult to audit, challenge, or remove, because doing so would require acknowledging that it was deployed without adequate accountability architecture in the first place.⏎⏎Sendak, Elish, Gao, and colleagues echoed this sentiment in their 2020 ACM FAT* proceedings paper, observing that clinical decision support systems acquire institutional legitimacy through use rather than through validation, and that this legitimacy then insulates the systems from the kind of scrutiny that would have been applied at the deployment decision stage. Obermeyer and Emanuel noted in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2016 that the opacity of machine learning models in clinical settings means that errors may be systematically invisible until they manifest at scale. The GAO reached a similar conclusion in its November 2020 report on AI in health care (GAO-21-7SP), finding that a lack of definitive post-market performance monitoring requirements for AI-based clinical decision support tools created conditions in which model drift and systematic error could accumulate undetected across large patient populations.⏎⏎CVS Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎Our Q2 2024 policy review identified reimbursement ambiguity and the absence of standardized FDA-payer alignment pathways as the two most frequently cited barriers to broader AI integration among our partner health systems, and we recognize that these are real operational problems. Fewer than one-third of the 47 sites in the Harrison.ai deployment cohort had received any reimbursement recognition for AI-augmented reads under existing CPT coding structures. We understand why practice managers at those sites are frustrated, because we share that frustration. But the correct response to reimbursement ambiguity is to build a reimbursement framework that is coupled to an accountability framework, not to clear the reimbursement pathway while leaving accountability unresolved. The American Medical Association's augmented intelligence policy (H-480.940, adopted 2018, updated 2023) explicitly states that AI tools in clinical settings must be subject to meaningful physician oversight and that the locus of accountability for AI-assisted decisions must remain with an identifiable human professional. HHS has not yet operationalized what that means in practice, and the RFI does not propose to do so before accelerating adoption.⏎⏎The European Parliament's Artificial Intelligence Act, specifically Article 22's human oversight requirements for high-risk AI systems, provides a reference point that HHS has not seriously engaged with in this RFI (Regulation EU 2024/1689). We are not arguing that the EU framework should be adopted wholesale. What we are pointing to is that a major regulatory jurisdiction has concluded that high-risk AI applications, including clinical diagnostic support, require mandatory human oversight provisions that are legally enforceable, not aspirational. The ONC's own clinical decision support fact sheet, updated February 2023, acknowledges that CDS tools vary significantly in the degree to which they support versus supplant clinical judgment, and that this variation has implications for accountability, but stops short of prescribing any binding accountability assignment mechanism. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen, writing in the Academic Press volume on AI in healthcare in 2020, argued that the moral and legal dilemmas surrounding AI-driven healthcare cannot be resolved through voluntary vendor commitments or soft guidance, and that the absence of mandatory accountability frameworks in the United States creates conditions where regulatory safe harbor provisions, originally designed to encourage innovation, effectively function as liability shields for vendors whose systems result in adverse medical outcomes.⏎⏎CVS Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD DO INSTEAD⏎⏎This comment does not argue that HHS should halt AI adoption in clinical settings. That would be both impractical and, given the documented efficiency gains, potentially harmful to patients who benefit from faster diagnostic turnaround. What this comment argues is that HHS should condition any regulatory, reimbursement, or R&D acceleration on the prior establishment of a mandatory accountability assignment framework with the following operational characteristics.⏎⏎First, every AI-assisted clinical decision should be associated with a named accountable party, either a specific licensed clinician or a specifically designated institutional officer, who accepts legal accountability for that decision as documented in the patient's medical record. This is not a requirement that the named party must have independently derived the clinical conclusion without AI assistance. It is a requirement that a human being with identifiable professional credentials and enforceable professional obligations is on record as the decision-maker, such that standard proximate causation analysis can function as designed.⏎⏎Second, vendor indemnification provisions in AI procurement contracts should not be permitted to operate as categorical liability shields in cases where the vendor's system produced the output that the clinician accepted. HHS should work with CMS and with state insurance commissioners to develop a framework that allocates liability proportionally among the clinician, the hospital, and the vendor based on the degree to which each party's conduct contributed to the harm, including the vendor's responsibility for model performance and the clinician's responsibility for appropriate oversight. The current practice of embedding broad liability disclaimers in vendor terms of service, and then treating FDA clearance as evidence that the system performed within specification regardless of patient outcome, is not consistent with the accountability principles that Keskinbora articulated in the Journal of Clinical Neuroscience in 2019 or with the AMA's own policy framework.⏎⏎CVS Health < > HHS AI RFI Comment < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎Third, and this is perhaps the point where we feel the strongest, HHS should not treat reimbursement pathway clarification as separable from accountability framework construction. The reason fewer than one-third of the sites in our deployment cohort received reimbursement recognition for AI-augmented reads is partly a CPT coding problem and partly a payer-alignment problem. But it is also, in some cases, a problem of payers appropriately declining to reimburse for services where the accountability chain for the AI-assisted component is not documentable. Resolving the reimbursement ambiguity without resolving the accountability ambiguity may increase adoption rates in the short term while creating a much larger liability exposure for health systems, clinicians, and patients when harms occur. The accountability framework should come first, or at minimum should be constructed in parallel, not deferred to a subsequent rulemaking cycle.⏎⏎Our organization is prepared to share the full operational data from the Q2 2024 policy review, including site-level detail on indemnification contract structures and reimbursement documentation gaps, with HHS or ONC staff upon request. The relevant contact information is included as Appendix A to this submission (not attached to the public docket version per our organization's data governance policy; available upon direct request to the policy contacts listed below).⏎⏎We recognize that what we are asking for is harder than what the RFI proposes. Building a mandatory accountability assignment framework requires coordination across HHS, CMS, ONC, state medical boards, malpractice insurers, and AI vendors, and there is no obvious existing regulatory vehicle that covers all of those actors simultaneously. We are not under any illusion that this is a simple administrative task. But the alternative, scaling AI adoption across clinical workflows before the accountability architecture exists to contain the liability diffusion that AI creates, is a choice to make the problem larger and harder to fix at a later date, and the patients who will bear the consequences of that choice will have no specific human being they can hold accountable for⏎⏎blee@cvshealth.com⏎Policy Contacts, CVS Health Government Affairs⏎One CVS Drive, Woonsocket, RI 02895♔♔2026-02-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-19T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔supportive♔South Carolina♔practice manager♔59♔A 2024 analysis of Harrison.ai's deployment data across 47 clinical sites found that AI-assisted diagnostic workflows reduced mean radiologist reporting turnaround time by 38%, yet fewer than one-third of those sites had received any reimbursement recognition for AI-augmented reads under existing CPT coding structures. SYNTH-0073♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Ashley Flores♔Association for Molecular Pathology♔♔♔♔♔Association for Molecular Pathology⏎1120 Route 73, Suite 200⏎Mount Laurel, NJ 08054⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎⏎RE: Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care; Comments of the Association for Molecular Pathology⏎⏎AMP Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 1⏎⏎The framing of this Request for Information contains a structural omission that, if left unaddressed, will cause the Department's acceleration agenda to function as regulatory cover for the most consequential and already-deployed AI application in American healthcare: automated denial of coverage. HHS has framed this RFI around clinical care improvement — imaging diagnostics, predictive risk stratification, clinical decision support — and those applications deserve rigorous governance attention. But "AI in healthcare" is not a monolithic category, and the Department's failure to distinguish between AI that serves patients and AI that is deployed against patients is not merely an oversight. It is a policy choice with foreseeable consequences. The Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP), whose members include clinical laboratory professionals and senior policy staff with direct visibility into how coverage determinations affect access to molecular diagnostic testing and surgical care, submits these comments to place that omission on the record and to request that HHS issue supplemental guidance that directly addresses insurer-deployed AI in utilization management before extending any reimbursement incentives to health technology adoption.⏎⏎The evidence base documenting the harms of AI-assisted prior authorization is no longer preliminary. The HHS Office of Inspector General's April 2022 audit (OEI-09-18-00260) found that Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests at rates that, upon independent review, were found to meet Medicare coverage criteria — meaning denials were not clinically justified but were algorithmically generated and effectively final for the majority of beneficiaries who lacked the capacity or resources to appeal. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations subsequently documented, in S. Prt. 118-42 (2024), how named insurers including UnitedHealth Group's NaviHealth subsidiary and Cigna deployed AI models that generated denial recommendations with what internal communications described as minimal clinician review, processing claim volumes that no human reviewer could have independently evaluated. Humana's utilization management practices received similar scrutiny in that same investigation. The Kaiser Family Foundation's March 2023 issue brief by Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman documented that Medicare Advantage beneficiaries faced prior authorization requirements for services that would have been covered without review under traditional Medicare, with denial rates that have increased in correlation with the adoption of automated review tools. What the OIG audit found, what the Senate investigation confirmed, and what the KFF analysis contextualized is that the insurer AI market is not a future risk to be anticipated — it is an existing harm operating at scale, today, in the same Medicare and Medicaid programs that this Department administers.⏎⏎AMP Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 2⏎⏎The regulatory framework governing this conduct already exists in partial form, which makes HHS's silence on the matter more difficult to explain. The Medicare Advantage utilization management requirements codified at 42 C.F.R. Part 422 establish that coverage determinations must be made by qualified health professionals applying clinical criteria, and CMS's own guidance has repeatedly affirmed that AI-generated recommendations do not satisfy the physician review requirement for adverse determinations. The proposed rule published at 88 Fed. Reg. 47,968 (July 25, 2023), addressing prior authorization processes for certain hospital outpatient department services, acknowledged the systemic burden that utilization management places on providers and patients but stopped short of addressing the AI-specific acceleration of that burden. The ACA's medical loss ratio requirements, which mandate that a defined percentage of premium revenue be spent on clinical care rather than administrative functions, theoretically constrain the profitability of denial automation — but insurers have successfully argued that AI-driven utilization management qualifies as a care coordination expenditure, effectively reclassifying a financial instrument as a clinical service. AMP submits that HHS has both the statutory authority and the administrative record to close that reclassification gap, and the Department's decision to issue a broad AI acceleration RFI without engaging this question suggests either that the gap has not been prioritized or that the political economy of insurer relationships has made it inconvenient to address.⏎⏎The equity dimensions of this problem are not speculative. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan demonstrated in their 2019 Science paper (366(6464), 447–453) that widely deployed health algorithms systematically underestimated the care needs of Black patients by using cost as a proxy for health need — a methodological choice that produced discriminatory outputs from facially neutral inputs. The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in their 2024 Health Justice Policy Brief No. 7 that AI prior authorization tools exhibit analogous patterns, generating higher denial rates for patients of color in ways that are obscured by the opacity of vendor models and the absence of mandatory demographic disaggregation in denial reporting. The California Department of Managed Health Care's 2023 Independent Medical Review Annual Report (DMHC Publication No. 2023-IMR-04) found that independent medical reviewers overturned AI-assisted utilization management denials at rates substantially higher than historical baselines for human-reviewed denials — which is to say, the denials being generated by these systems are not simply more efficient versions of the denials that preceded them. They are a qualitatively different category of determination, one that is less clinically grounded and more systematically biased, and the appeals processes nominally available to aggrieved patients are structurally designed to produce attrition rather than review. The AMA's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94 percent of physicians reported prior authorization delays that adversely affected patient care, and that a substantial proportion of patients who received denials ultimately abandoned recommended treatment — not because the treatment was determined to be medically unnecessary, but because the administrative burden of appeal exceeded what patients in acute need could reasonably sustain.⏎⏎AMP Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 3⏎⏎This last point connects directly to the perioperative context that AMP's senior policy staff have observed in their collaboration with surgical nursing colleagues. Surgical procedure authorizations — including those for procedures that depend on molecular pathology results to establish medical necessity — are among the most frequently denied categories in Medicare Advantage utilization management data. When an AI system generates a denial for a colorectal resection or a diagnostic thoracoscopy, the downstream consequence is not an administrative inconvenience. It is a perioperative nursing team that has prepared for a patient who does not arrive, a surgeon who has blocked time for a case that is cancelled at forty-eight hours, and a patient who is told to resubmit documentation that an algorithm has already reviewed and rejected. The Blumenthal, Fowler, Abrams, and Collins analysis published in the New England Journal of Medicine (383(15), 1483–1488, 2020) documented the particular vulnerability of low-income and elderly patients to systemic disruptions in care access, and the pattern they described in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic maps with uncomfortable precision onto the pattern that denial automation is producing in surgical access today. Papanicolas, Woskie, and Jha's 2018 JAMA analysis (319(10), 1024–1039) established that the United States spends substantially more per capita on healthcare administration than comparable high-income countries, and the expansion of AI-assisted utilization management is a mechanism for increasing that administrative burden on providers while reducing it for insurers — a redistribution of administrative cost that the value-based care frameworks described by Teisberg, Wallace, and O'Hara in Academic Medicine (95(5), 682–685, 2020) would recognize as antithetical to the alignment of incentives around patient outcomes. AMP is not opposed to efficiency in healthcare administration. The Association is opposed to efficiency that is achieved by making denials faster and appeals slower, and to federal policy that subsidizes that tradeoff without acknowledging it.⏎⏎The vendor accountability parallel that Schulte and Fry documented in their Kaiser Health News and Fortune investigation on electronic health records — the pattern of technology being adopted at institutional scale before clinical staff had the training, governance infrastructure, or regulatory protection to manage it safely — is precisely what is now occurring in insurer AI deployment, and the absence of federal standards is the common thread. HHS's reimbursement incentive proposals, if extended to health plan technology adoption without explicit carve-outs, will subsidize denial automation in the same way that meaningful use incentives subsidized EHR adoption without adequate attention to clinical workflow consequences. AMP therefore requests that HHS take the following actions in any final guidance or rulemaking that follows this RFI: first, that the Department issue a formal interpretation clarifying that AI-generated adverse determinations in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care do not satisfy the qualified health professional review requirements under 42 C.F.R. Part 422, and that any adverse determination generated or materially influenced by an AI model requires mandatory human clinical review by a licensed clinician in the relevant specialty before it becomes effective; second, that HHS prohibit the use of AI models trained on cost-containment outcomes as a primary input in coverage determinations, requiring instead that any model used in utilization management be validated against clinical necessity criteria and subject to independent demographic bias auditing prior to deployment; third, that CMS establish algorithmic transparency requirements for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care organizations that mandate disclosure of the AI tools used in utilization management, the denial rates attributable to those tools disaggregated by race, age, and disability status, and the reversal rates for appeals of AI-assisted denials; and fourth, that HHS impose a moratorium on the deployment of new AI prior authorization systems in federally funded programs pending completion of independent equity audits by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality or a designated independent body. AMP recognizes that these requests go beyond the clinical care framing of the RFI as published. That is precisely the point. The Department cannot accelerate responsible AI adoption in clinical care while simultaneously failing to regulate AI deployment in coverage determination, because the two domains interact directly — a diagnostic AI that correctly identifies a patient's need for surgery is rendered irrelevant by a prior authorization AI that denies the surgery before it occurs. The acceleration agenda, as currently framed, addresses half of the system and ignores the half that is already causing documented harm. AMP requests that HHS acknowledge this gap in any public response to these comments and commit to a supplemental process specifically addressing insurer AI governance, with a timeline and a mechanism for public participation that is not limited to⏎⏎AMP Comments | HHS AI RFI 2024 | Page 4⏎⏎industry stakeholders with financial interests in the current deployment trajectory.⏎⏎Respectfully submitted,⏎⏎Ashley Flores⏎Senior Policy Analyst⏎Association for Molecular Pathology⏎aflores@amp.org⏎(856) 439-0500♔♔2026-01-08T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-08T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Louisiana♔senior policy analyst♔49♔A 2024 AORN member survey encompassing more than 2,100 perioperative registered nurses across acute care, ambulatory surgery, and outpatient settings found that 68% reported their facilities had introduced or piloted at least one AI-assisted clinical decision support tool within the preceding 18 months, yet only 29% indicated their institutions had established formal governance frameworks to evaluate these tools for patient safety, workflow integration, or nursing scope-of-practice implications. SYNTH-0074♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Emily Wilson♔♔♔♔♔♔Two years ago, my supervisor at the distribution center where I work in Florida had a cardiac event on the floor during a shift. The on-site first responder spent nearly eight minutes on hold trying to reach someone at the ER who could read his EKG over the phone. Eight minutes. He survived, but his cardiologist told his wife that a faster triage decision at that initial moment would have changed his prognosis in ways that cannot now be undone. I work ten-hour shifts alongside people whose bodies are absorbing the same kind of wear, and I have thought about that phone call more than I let on to anyone.⏎⏎That is why I read this RFI. Or tried to. I want to say something about that first, because it matters: I spent a significant amount of time with the Federal Register notice and I genuinely could not follow large portions of it. The language is written for lawyers and health IT executives, not for the people whose care is actually being discussed. I understand there are legal constraints on how federal notices get written, but I do not think those constraints require the level of inaccessibility present here. When HHS says it wants public comment, it should mean public comment, not just comment from the organizations that can afford someone to decode the document. I am doing my best, but I want to be honest that I am working with incomplete comprehension of what is actually being proposed, and I think that is a problem HHS created, not one I created.⏎⏎What I did understand, clearly enough to concern me, is that the framing of this RFI is an acceleration agenda. The question being asked is not whether AI deployment in clinical settings serves patients. The question is how to make deployment faster. Those are not the same question, and the difference is not semantic. When a federal agency takes as given that the goal is speed and asks only about the mechanisms, it has already made a substantive policy choice before receiving a single comment. I have read enough about how these processes work to know that this kind of framing tends to benefit the parties who have the most to gain from the policy direction already embedded in the question. Dafny, Gruber, and Ody wrote in the Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law in 2023 about vendor influence in federal health technology rulemaking, and the pattern they describe, where the acceleration agenda gets laundered through the public comment process as if it were still an open question, is exactly what I see here. I am not saying HHS is acting in bad faith. I am saying the structure of this RFI makes it very hard to submit a comment that challenges the premise, because the premise is not listed as one of the things being commented on.⏎⏎The specific question I want to address is the one about industry-driven accreditation and credentialing for AI tools in clinical settings. I want to be direct: letting the vendors who profit from deployment also shape the standards used to evaluate whether deployment is safe and appropriate is a structural conflict of interest. I understand the argument for it, that industry has the technical knowledge and that government agencies lack the capacity to build credentialing infrastructure from scratch. But technical knowledge and financial interest are not separable here. According to KLAS Research data from 2023, the clinical decision support AI market is heavily concentrated among a small number of vendors, with Epic, Oracle Health, and Microsoft/Nuance together accounting for the majority of EHR-integrated AI deployments. These are not neutral technical experts. They are companies with significant lobbying operations. Open Secrets' summary of health technology lobbying disclosures for 2023 shows substantial expenditure from exactly these firms directed at federal health IT rulemaking. The idea that they can simultaneously be the subject of accreditation standards and the architects of those standards is not a partnership model. It is regulatory capture with extra steps.⏎⏎There is a related problem that I want to name, even though I am not sure I have the full picture. Kesselheim, Cresswell, and Sheikh published work in BMJ Health and Care Informatics in 2021 on vendor lock-in in hospital procurement of clinical decision support systems, and the switching costs they describe are enormous. Adler-Milstein and Pfeifer documented similar dynamics in EHR adoption as far back as 2017 in Health Services Research, showing that once a health system adopts a platform, the institutional and contractual barriers to switching become so high that the initial procurement decision is effectively permanent. What this means for AI credentialing is that if the standards get written in a way that advantages the current dominant vendors, and those vendors are the ones writing the standards, the market will freeze around the incumbents in a way that is very difficult to reverse. Smaller health systems, rural hospitals, safety-net providers, the ones serving people like my coworkers, will end up locked into whatever the big vendors decide to offer, with no meaningful ability to demand something different. I do not think HHS has fully grappled with this in the way the RFI is framed.⏎⏎The Obermeyer et al. study from Science in 2019 showed that a widely deployed commercial algorithm used to manage care for millions of patients systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health status, and Black patients had historically been given less access to care, so they had lower costs, so the algorithm ranked them as healthier than they were. The vendor produced this tool. The vendor deployed it. The vendor was not the one who found the problem. Independent academic researchers found it. This is not an argument against AI in healthcare. It is an argument against the specific governance model where the industry being regulated is also the primary body responsible for validating what it produces. If HHS moves forward with an industry-led accreditation process without independent technical review that is genuinely insulated from vendor financial interest, the Obermeyer finding is not a historical cautionary tale. It is a preview.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I am not certain what the right structure for independent oversight looks like, and I am aware that I am a warehouse worker in Broward County, not a health policy researcher. But I do not think you need a graduate degree to recognize a conflict of interest, and I do not think the complexity of the technical domain is a reason to hand governance over to the parties with the most financial stake in the outcome. What I am asking is this: reject the acceleration framing long enough to ask whether demonstrated safety should be a precondition for deployment rather than a post-market concern. Require that any accreditation or credentialing process for clinical AI include independent technical reviewers who do not have financial relationships with the vendors being reviewed. Publish the standards-development process in language that non-specialists can actually read, because the people whose care is at stake deserve to understand what is being decided about them. I also want to say that the GAO's 2022 report on machine learning technologies for medical diagnostics, GAO-22-104629, raised concerns about the lack of transparency in how these tools are validated before deployment, and I have not seen evidence that HHS has substantively responded to those concerns in the design of this RFI. That report came out more than two years before this notice, and the questions it raised about pre-market validation standards are still, as far as I can tell, unanswered. The structural problem it identified is:⏎⏎1. Most clinical AI tools enter deployment through regulatory pathways that were not designed for continuously learning software.⏎2. Post-market surveillance requirements are weak relative to the pace at which these tools are updated after initial clearance.⏎3. The burden of identifying performance failures falls disproportionately on clinical staff and patients rather than on vendors.⏎4. There is no standardized mechanism for requiring vendors to disclose when a tool's performance degrades in a specific patient population.⏎⏎None of those four problems are addressed by accelerating adoption. They are made worse by it. And the people most likely to be harmed by undetected performance failures are not the administrators who sign the procurement contracts. They are the patients in underfunded facilities who have no other options, and the workers like the people I spend ten hours a day with, whose access to quality care is already thin enough that an algorithm error could be the difference between a diagnosis and a missed one. I keep thinking about those eight minutes on hold, and I keep thinking that the answer to that problem is not to deploy faster. The answer is to deploy better.⏎⏎I genuinely do not know if this comment will be read by anyone who has the power to change the framing of what HHS is doing here. But I am submitting it because the process said public comment was open, and I took that at face value, even if the document itself made that harder than it needed to be. I would ask that HHS consider publishing a plain-language summary of this RFI and any subsequent proposed rules that touch on AI in clinical care, not as a courtesy but as a basic condition of meaningful public participation. The Federal Register notice for this RFI runs to a length and a register that effectively excludes the majority of the people it affects, and that exclusion is not neutral. It shapes whose concerns get heard and whose get filtered out before the comment period even opens. I noticed, for instance, that the notice does not include a plain-language summary section, even though HHS has the technical capacity to produce one and has done so for other rulemakings. I don't know if that was an oversight or a resource constraint or something else, but it is worth fixing before the next notice goes out, whatever gets decided about the substance.♔♔2026-02-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-09T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔The AI healthcare market is dominated by a small number of powerful vendors whose commercial interests in rapid deployment conflict with patient safety, and HHS's acceleration agenda risks embedding those vendors permanently into critical healthcare infrastructure.♔individual♔high♔resigned♔Florida♔warehouse worker♔58♔When my supervisor at the distribution center had a cardiac event on the floor two years ago, the on-site first responder spent nearly eight minutes on hold trying to reach someone at the ER who could interpret his irregular EKG reading over the phone — eight minutes that felt like watching sand fall through a closed fist. SYNTH-0075♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Anthony Lopez♔Consumer Reports♔♔♔♔♔Consumer Reports | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 1⏎⏎COMMENT OF CONSUMER REPORTS IN RESPONSE TO THE HHS HEALTH SECTOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REQUEST FOR INFORMATION: ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Submitted by: Anthony Lopez, Community Organizing Division⏎Consumer Reports, Washington State Office⏎Contact: alopez@cr.org⏎⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-001⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Consumer Reports submits this comment in response to HHS's request for information on regulatory, reimbursement, and research-and-development actions the Department might take to accelerate artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. Our organization draws on survey data collected from 847 community health organizations affiliated with our national network, policy analysis of fourteen federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) currently deploying AI diagnostic support tools, and feedback gathered at our 2024 national convening, which brought together more than 200 community health advocates from across the country. We are not opposed to AI adoption in healthcare. We are concerned, however, that the accelerationist framing of this RFI — its emphasis on speed of adoption over conditions of adoption — will predictably harm the frontline workforce on which equitable care depends. The Department is being asked to endorse and fund tools whose primary market positioning is efficiency and burnout reduction, but whose operational deployment in resource-constrained settings has repeatedly produced the opposite: heavier caseloads, algorithmic performance monitoring, and the systematic sidelining of clinical judgment. This comment addresses specifically the workforce implications of AI deployment in clinical labor contexts and offers concrete policy recommendations that HHS should adopt before extending any reimbursement pathway or federal endorsement to AI tools used in those settings.⏎⏎Consumer Reports | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 2⏎⏎THE GAP BETWEEN MARKETING CLAIMS AND OPERATIONAL REALITY⏎⏎The RFI asks respondents to identify barriers to AI adoption. Our network's experience suggests a more pressing question: barriers to what kind of adoption, and beneficial for whom. The AI tools currently being marketed to hospital systems and community health administrators are overwhelmingly positioned as solutions to clinician burnout — a real and serious problem that Shanafelt et al. (2022) documented across physician populations between 2011 and 2020, finding persistently elevated rates of emotional exhaustion and professional dissatisfaction that predated and outlasted the COVID-19 pandemic. Bates et al. (2021) acknowledged the genuine potential for AI to reduce documentation burden and administrative friction, while also issuing a warning that deserves far more attention in this RFI than it has received: the same tools can, under conditions of misaligned administrative incentives, increase cognitive load on clinicians rather than reduce it. That warning has not aged well as merely an abstract worry. It has aged as a prediction that has come true.⏎⏎The MITRE Corporation and Accenture Federal Services prepared a workforce displacement risk assessment for HHS's own Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation in 2022, which identified significant risk that AI deployment in federal health programs would be used to rationalize staffing reductions rather than to support existing workers (Accenture Federal Services / MITRE Corporation, 2022). The Government Accountability Office reached a related conclusion in its 2023 review of AI in health care, noting that workforce impact assessment frameworks remain largely absent from procurement and deployment standards (GAO, 2023, GAO-23-105980). Our own policy analysis of fourteen FQHCs found an average nine-month delay between AI tool implementation and any formal reimbursement determination — meaning these facilities were absorbing both the financial risk of deployment and the operational disruptions to their clinical staff, with no federal guidance on either front. That is not a minor administrative inconvenience. For a federally qualified health center operating on thin margins in an underserved community, nine months of reimbursement uncertainty while simultaneously managing a new AI system imposed on clinical workflows is a structural threat to organizational survival.⏎⏎Wachter and Goldsmith (2018) made a point about digital medical records that applies with equal force to AI tools: technology designed around administrative and billing priorities, rather than around the actual work of clinical care, creates cognitive friction for the clinicians who must use it, and that friction accumulates into burnout, errors, and attrition. Friedberg et al. (2022) at the RAND Corporation documented the relationship between loss of professional autonomy and physician dissatisfaction in terms that should inform any federal AI policy: when clinicians feel that technology is being used to monitor their performance, constrain their judgment, or justify reductions in staffing, the downstream effects on care quality are measurable and significant.⏎⏎Consumer Reports | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 3⏎⏎SURVEILLANCE, AUTONOMY EROSION, AND THE EXCLUSION OF FRONTLINE WORKERS⏎⏎National Nurses United's 2023 research report on AI surveillance tools in hospital settings documented the growing deployment of productivity-monitoring applications that track nurse movement, task completion rates, and response times — tools that are categorically different from clinical decision support but are being bundled into the same "AI in healthcare" policy conversation (National Nurses United, 2023). The American Nurses Association's 2023 position statement on AI and nursing practice called explicitly for frontline nurse involvement in AI procurement decisions, noting that tools designed without nursing input routinely fail to account for the actual complexity of bedside care and instead optimize for metrics that are administratively legible but clinically meaningless (American Nurses Association, 2023). Dyrbye et al. (2019) documented the relationship between work-unit safety climate and burnout among hospital nurses, finding that environments characterized by reduced autonomy and increased performance surveillance were associated with significantly elevated burnout rates — which should give the Department pause before endorsing any AI deployment pathway that includes workforce monitoring components.⏎⏎Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020) provide perhaps the most analytically rigorous framing of what is actually happening when AI is deployed in labor contexts: these tools are not neutral productivity aids but instruments in an ongoing contest over workplace control, one in which workers with less institutional power — including nurses, patient navigators, and community health workers — are systematically disadvantaged (Kellogg et al., 2020). The National Partnership for Women and Families documented in 2023 how algorithmic management tools deployed in health and human services settings have been used to intensify work pace, reduce discretionary time, and erode the informal relational labor that is particularly important in community health settings (National Partnership for Women & Families, 2023). Obermeyer and Emanuel (2016) cautioned that machine learning tools in clinical medicine will encode the priorities of whoever designs and deploys them — and if procurement decisions are made by hospital administrators optimizing for cost reduction rather than by clinicians optimizing for care quality, the tools will reflect those priorities regardless of how they are marketed.⏎⏎What our member organizations report, consistently, is that frontline workers are not at the table when AI tools are selected. The 2024 national convening feedback was unambiguous on this point: clinical staff at community health centers learn about new AI deployments when the tools arrive, not during the procurement process. This is not an accident. It reflects a structural feature of how healthcare administration works, in which clinical labor is treated as a cost variable to be managed rather than as a source of expertise to be consulted. Accelerating AI adoption without addressing this structural feature will accelerate harm, not care improvement.⏎⏎Consumer Reports | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 4⏎⏎POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎Consumer Reports urges the Department to condition any HHS endorsement, reimbursement pathway, or federal funding stream for AI tools deployed in clinical labor contexts on the following demonstrated preconditions:⏎⏎1. Mandatory workforce consultation documentation. Vendors and health systems seeking federal reimbursement for AI clinical tools must demonstrate, through a structured attestation process, that frontline clinical staff — including nurses, care coordinators, and patient navigators — were meaningfully consulted during the procurement and design process. "Meaningful consultation" should be defined in regulation to require more than informational sessions; it should require documented input, response to that input, and worker ability to raise safety concerns without retaliation.⏎⏎2. Pre-deployment workforce impact assessment. Prior to any AI tool deployment in a clinical setting that receives federal funding, the deploying organization must complete a workforce impact assessment examining: (a) projected effects on staffing levels and caseloads; (b) any productivity monitoring or performance tracking functions embedded in the tool; (c) the degree to which the tool is designed to constrain or support clinical judgment; and (d) mechanisms for ongoing worker feedback after deployment. The assessment methodology should be developed with input from nursing and allied health professional organizations, not solely from technology vendors or hospital administrators.⏎⏎3. Separation of clinical decision support from workforce surveillance tools in any reimbursement or endorsement framework. The current policy conversation conflates AI tools that assist clinicians with diagnostic or treatment decisions with AI tools that monitor and manage clinical labor. These are categorically different interventions with categorically different workforce implications, and federal policy should treat them as such.⏎⏎4. Reimbursement continuity protections for FQHCs during AI implementation periods. Given the nine-month average reimbursement determination delay our analysis identified, HHS should establish an interim reimbursement bridge mechanism for federally qualified health centers that have implemented AI tools in good faith while awaiting formal determination. The current gap imposes disproportionate financial risk on the facilities serving the most vulnerable patient populations.⏎⏎Our network is aware that these recommendations will be characterized by some commenters as obstacles to innovation. We would suggest, more precisely, that they are conditions for innovation that does not consume the workforce it depends on. The Department has an opportunity here to set standards that distinguish between AI adoption that strengthens clinical capacity and AI adoption that extracts value from clinical labor while degrading the conditions under which good care is possible. The evidence base for making that distinction is available; what has been missing is the regulatory will to apply it.⏎⏎See Appendix A: Survey Instrument and Aggregated Results from 2024 Community Health Organization Network Survey (not attached to electronic submission; available upon request).⏎⏎See Appendix B: FQHC Case Study Summaries, Policy Analysis of AI Reimbursement Delays, Consumer Reports Community Health Policy Program, 2024 (available upon request).⏎⏎alopez@cr.org | Consumer Reports, 1101 17th Street NW, Washington, D.C. 20036⏎⏎Consumer Reports | HHS AI RFI Comment | Docket HHS-2024-AI-001 | Page 5⏎⏎Note: The pagination above reflects the formatting of the original Word document submission. SYNTH-0077♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kenneth Torres♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via the Federal eRulemaking Portal: regulations.gov⏎Docket ID: HHS-2024-AI-RFI⏎RE: HHS Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Kenneth Torres, LMSW, Bolivar County, Mississippi⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Thirty-one years of child welfare and community health casework in the Mississippi Delta has given me a particular vantage point on what happens when systems designed elsewhere get rolled out into communities like the ones I serve. I want to be precise about that vantage point, because I think it matters for how HHS reads this comment. I am not writing as someone opposed to technology in clinical care. I have watched rural clinic closures accelerate over the past decade in ways that make remote monitoring and automated triage genuinely compelling options for my clients, who are predominantly Black, predominantly low-income, and who are driving past closed facilities to reach care that used to be twenty minutes away. The core issue for me is not whether these advanced tools belong in these settings. It is whether HHS intends to implement them without any compulsory framework for detecting the harm they will cause when they fail in predictable, documented ways. The RFI as written proposes no required equity auditing before rollout and no bias surveillance after rollout as conditions of any reimbursement or approval pathway the Department creates. That gap is not an oversight I can let pass without comment.⏎⏎The evidence that algorithmic systems trained on historical healthcare data reproduce existing racial and socioeconomic disparities is not theoretical at this point. It is peer-reviewed, replicated, and in some cases concerns tools already in widespread clinical use. Obermeyer and colleagues (2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453) demonstrated that a widely used commercial model for managing population health consistently undervalued the medical needs of Black patients, because it utilized healthcare expenditures as a stand-in for actual wellness requirements, encoding decades of differential access into its predictions. Sjoding and colleagues (2020, NEJM, 383(25), 2477-2478) documented that pulse oximeters, a technology so routine it barely registers as artificial intelligence, produced clinically significant overestimates of blood oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin, meaning that Black patients were less likely to be flagged for hypoxemia during COVID-19 hospitalization. In dermatology, Adamson and Smith (2018, JAMA Dermatology, 154(11), 1247-1248) found that machine learning diagnostic tools for skin conditions were built almost entirely using images from lighter-skinned populations, raising documented concerns about performance across skin tones. Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones (2020, NEJM, 383(9), 874-882) identified race-correction factors embedded in clinical formulas for kidney function and pulmonary assessment that routinely routed Black patients away from certain diagnoses and interventions. What these examples share is that none of them were hypothetical risks identified before implementation. They were harms identified after the tools were already in use, often at massive scale.⏎⏎The sepsis prediction literature adds a dimension that is particularly relevant to the institutional gap I want HHS to consider. Wong and colleagues (2021, JAMA Internal Medicine, 181(8), 1065-1070) externally validated a widely implemented proprietary sepsis prediction model and found that its performance degraded substantially when applied outside the academic medical center environment where it was developed. Sensitivity was poor, specificity was poor, and the tool's clinical utility in community hospital settings was not supportable. This is the geographic and institutional validation gap that Kaushal, Altman, and Langlotz (2020, JAMA, 324(12), 1212-1213) documented more broadly: the cohorts used to train foundational deep learning algorithms in U.S. healthcare are concentrated in a small number of large academic medical centers, primarily in California, New York, and Massachusetts. Bolivar County, Mississippi is not in those datasets. The community health clinics and safety-net hospitals serving my clients are not in those datasets. Gianfrancesco and colleagues (2018, JAMA Internal Medicine, 178(11), 1544-1547) identified the specific mechanisms through which EHR-derived training data introduces bias: missing data patterns that correlate with race and coverage levels, differential coding practices across institution types, and selection effects in who receives certain diagnostic workups in the first place. The point is not that these advanced systems cannot be made to work in underserved settings. The point is that they will not work equitably in those settings unless fair performance is a strict prerequisite for rollout, rather than an aspiration expressed in a preamble.⏎⏎What concerns me about the RFI's framing is the automation bias problem that sits downstream of all of this. When a medical professional makes a racially disparate treatment decision, there is at least a theoretical possibility that a supervisor, a patient advocate, or a quality review process will identify it as an error attributable to a human judgment that could have been different. When an algorithm produces the same disparate output, the authoritative appearance of a computed score makes that error harder to identify and harder to challenge. Practitioners who might push back against a colleague's recommendation often do not push back against a risk score with three decimal places. I have seen this dynamic in non-clinical contexts across my career, and the health literature on automation bias in clinical decision support is consistent with what I would have predicted from practice. The implication for underserved communities is that algorithmic failure will not surface the way human failure does. It will surface in outcome data, months or years after implementation, if anyone is tracking the right outcomes in the right populations. HHS's RFI does not propose requiring anyone to track those outcomes as a condition of the reimbursement and adoption incentives the Department is considering. That is the regulatory gap I am asking HHS to close.⏎⏎My specific requests are addressed primarily to the RFI's questions about what regulatory and reimbursement actions HHS should take to support responsible technology adoption. I am not addressing vendor certification economics or liability allocation, both of which deserve separate treatment. What I am asking HHS to require, as a condition of any reimbursement pathway or regulatory approval mechanism the Department creates for clinical algorithmic tools, is the following:⏎⏎1. Compulsory equity auditing prior to launch, conducted on data that is demographically and institutionally representative of the intended patient population, not solely on the academic medical center cohorts where most tools are currently validated. This evaluation should assess performance stratified by race, ethnicity, coverage type, and geography, and results should be publicly reported before authorization is granted.⏎⏎2. Required bias surveillance after rollout as an ongoing condition of continued reimbursement eligibility. This means requiring healthcare facilities to track clinical outcome data stratified by the same demographic dimensions, at intervals sufficient to detect emerging disparate harm before it compounds. The specific interval and data reporting format should be developed with input from community health organizations in underserved areas, not solely from health system informatics departments.⏎⏎3. A requirement that validation cohorts used prior to release be disclosed as part of any regulatory submission, with explicit documentation of geographic and institutional distribution. Kaushal and colleagues' 2020 finding that foundational algorithm training is concentrated in a handful of ZIP codes is not a minor methodological footnote. It is information that healthcare administrators in the Delta need to have before they adopt a tool.⏎⏎4. A threshold requirement that any algorithmic tool seeking reimbursement eligibility demonstrate performance parity across racial and socioeconomic subgroups within the margin of clinical significance, not just aggregate accuracy. A tool that performs well on average while performing poorly for Black patients in rural Mississippi is not an acceptable tool for the communities I work in, regardless of its overall AUC.⏎⏎I want to be honest that I am not certain about the right institutional mechanism for all of this. Whether these requirements belong in a pre-market review process, in conditions of participation for hospitals receiving federal reimbursement, or in a separate certification pathway through ONC is a question I do not have the technical expertise to resolve. What I am confident about is that the current RFI does not propose any of these requirements in a compulsory form, and that the communities bearing the greatest historical burden of healthcare system failure are also the communities least likely to generate the public leverage that would force a correction after the fact. Bolivar County had four rural hospital closures or service reductions between 2012 and 2022. The clients I see are not in a position to wait for a retrospective analysis of algorithmically generated disparate harm to work its way through a federal comment cycle.⏎⏎Another related concern involves a tension I have not fully resolved in my own thinking. The RFI asks about accelerating adoption, and I understand why speed matters, particularly for remote monitoring applications that could genuinely improve access for patients who cannot reach a provider. I am not asking HHS to intentionally delay rollout across the board. I am asking HHS to make fairness a prerequisite rather than an afterthought, because the two goals are not in conflict unless the Department designs them to be. A reimbursement pathway that conditions eligibility on demonstrated fair performance does not prevent adoption. It shapes what gets adopted and in what form.⏎⏎A more detailed technical discussion of proposed audit methodologies, including specific performance stratification frameworks and surveillance data standards, is included in Appendix A, which is available upon request and will be submitted as a supplemental document to this docket.⏎⏎The RFI asks what HHS can do to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. My answer is that the Department should accelerate the adoption of computational tools that have been shown to work equitably across the populations they will actually serve, and it should build the regulatory infrastructure to tell the difference before patients in places like Bolivar County bear the cost of finding out.♔♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-20T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔individual♔high♔supportive♔Mississippi♔social worker♔70♔When my colleague Darlene retired from our county's child welfare office after thirty-two years, she told me the thing she regretted most wasn't a case she'd lost — it was the sheer volume of documentation that had consumed hours she could have spent actually sitting with families in crisis.
