SYNTH-0078♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Melissa Baker♔Siemens Healthineers♔♔♔♔♔Siemens Healthineers Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-CLINICAL-RFI⏎Submitting Organization: Siemens Healthineers⏎Contact: Melissa Baker, Director of Government Relations⏎Date: March 14, 2025⏎⏎melissa.baker@siemens-healthineers.com⏎⏎COMMENTS OF SIEMENS HEALTHINEERS IN RESPONSE TO THE HHS HEALTH SECTOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REQUEST FOR INFORMATION: ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in response to the Department of Health and Human Services' Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. Siemens Healthineers is a global medical technology company with significant operations and partnerships across the United States healthcare system, including imaging systems, laboratory diagnostics, and AI-enabled clinical decision support tools deployed across hundreds of U.S. hospital networks. Our perspective on this RFI is grounded in that operational reality, and we want to be direct about something the RFI's framing does not fully reckon with: the decision to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings cannot be separated from addressing what happens to the clinicians who are supposed to use these tools. Looking at our own customer relationships and through the published literature, AI deployment that is not designed with workforce concerns at the center tends to compound existing pressures rather than relieve them. That is not a reason to slow AI adoption. It is a reason to be considerably more careful than this RFI's framing sometimes suggests.⏎⏎We are focusing our comments primarily on two areas of the RFI: the sections related to regulatory guardrails and credentialing standards for AI clinical decision support tools, and the inquiries related to interoperability and data sharing infrastructure. These are the areas where Siemens Healthineers has the most direct experience and where we believe the Department's current framing carries the most significant risks.⏎⏎WORKFORCE HARM AS A REGULATORY PROBLEM, NOT A WORKFORCE PROBLEM⏎⏎Before addressing those two areas specifically, we want to put something on the record that tends to get lost in AI adoption discussions. The clinical workforce is already operating under significant strain. Shanafelt et al. (2022), publishing in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, documented that physician burnout rates reached 62.8% in 2021, a substantial increase from prior measurement periods, and the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine's 2019 report on clinician burnout identified health information technology design as one of the primary systemic contributors to that burden. Overhage and McCallie (2020), writing in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that physicians spent more than 16 minutes per patient encounter on EHR documentation tasks, a figure that has not meaningfully improved since that study was published. We raise these numbers not as background context but as the actual baseline condition into which any federally-accelerated AI deployment will land.⏎⏎The reason this matters for regulatory design is that AI tools which are poorly matched to clinical workflows, or which are deployed without adequate frontline clinician consultation, do not simply fail to reduce burden. They frequently add burden in new forms. Bates et al. (2021) in npj Digital Medicine noted the genuine potential for AI to reduce burnout while maintaining care quality, but also identified that realizing that potential requires careful attention to how tools are integrated into existing workflows, which is precisely the kind of implementation science that gets compressed or skipped when the policy goal is acceleration. Our concern with this RFI is that "accelerating adoption" as a frame tends to reward speed of deployment over quality of deployment, and the people who pay the price for that compression are the clinicians who are already stretched.⏎⏎Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin (2020), writing in the Academy of Management Annals, documented in considerable detail how algorithmic management tools in workplace settings function as a new form of performance surveillance, and their analysis applies directly to clinical AI. When AI tools generate productivity metrics, flag documentation patterns, or produce workflow recommendations that feed into staffing and scheduling decisions, they are not neutral clinical aids. They are labor management instruments. Our 2024 internal policy review, conducted across our network of licensed clinical social workers, found that 68% of practitioners expressed significant concerns about AI-assisted documentation tools overriding clinical judgment in treatment planning, particularly for clients navigating complex trauma, substance use, and co-occurring disorders. That figure is not a data point about technology preferences. It is a data point about whether clinicians trust the tools they are being asked to use, and trust is not recoverable through better marketing or more training modules.⏎⏎REGARDING CREDENTIALING AND ACCREDITATION STANDARDS FOR AI CLINICAL DECISION SUPPORT⏎⏎The RFI poses several inquiries about whether HHS should support the development of accreditation or credentialing frameworks for AI tools used in clinical care. We want to be direct about the risk embedded in how this topic is framed. If credentialing frameworks for clinical AI are developed primarily by industry consortia, professional societies with significant vendor funding relationships, or standards bodies that do not have mandatory frontline clinician consultation requirements built into their governance structures, those frameworks will tend to reflect vendor interests more than clinical safety interests. That is not a cynical claim. It is a structural prediction based on how standards bodies tend to work when one set of stakeholders has more resources to participate than another.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎The AFSCME Research Department's 2023 analysis of AI in the healthcare workplace documented specific instances in which vendor-developed "best practice" frameworks for clinical AI deployment were used to justify staffing reductions by demonstrating AI-enabled productivity gains, without any corresponding demonstration that patient outcomes were maintained. Stanton and Rutherford (2004), in their AHRQ research on hospital nurse staffing and quality of care, established the foundational evidence that staffing ratios have direct patient outcome consequences. The concern is that AI credentialing frameworks developed without mandatory worker consultation requirements will simply launder the kind of productivity extraction that the staffing literature has consistently shown to be harmful, by re-labeling it as AI-enabled efficiency.⏎⏎We urge the Department to take the following specific positions in any credentialing or accreditation framework it supports or endorses:⏎⏎1. Any credentialing body for clinical AI tools must include mandatory representation from frontline clinical workers, including nurses, licensed clinical social workers, medical assistants, and other non-physician staff who interact with these tools in practice. Representation means voting membership in governance, not advisory input that can be disregarded.⏎⏎2. Credentialing standards must include licensure-specific guardrails. A decision support tool appropriate for a radiologist reviewing imaging studies is not automatically appropriate for a licensed clinical social worker managing a trauma treatment plan. The absence of licensure-specific differentiation in current AI tool certification is, based on our member feedback collected through 2024 continuing education forums, one of the most consistently identified gaps in the current regulatory environment.⏎⏎3. Any credentialing framework must require demonstrated safety performance before a tool is eligible for federal reimbursement support, not after. The current tendency to launch first and monitor for harms afterward places the burden of proof on patients and clinicians rather than on developers.⏎⏎4. Credentialing standards must prohibit the use of AI-generated productivity or efficiency metrics as the primary or sole basis for staffing ratio decisions. This is not primarily a technology issue. It is a patient safety imperative, and the evidence from Stanton and Rutherford and from subsequent staffing research is clear enough that a federal credentialing framework that does not address it explicitly would be an omission of significant consequence.⏎⏎5. Tools that have been found to produce racially or socioeconomically biased outputs, as Obermeyer et al. documented in Science (2019) regarding an extensively adopted demographic risk model, should be ineligible for credentialing until bias has been demonstrably remediated and independently verified. The Obermeyer findings are now six years old and that predictive model remained in use for years after publication, which should inform how much weight the Department places on retrospective field monitoring as a substitute for safety validations required prior to go-live.⏎⏎REGARDING INTEROPERABILITY AND DATA SHARING⏎⏎The RFI also asks about actions HHS can take to expand data sharing infrastructure and interoperability as a means of supporting AI development and deployment. We want to be careful here because we genuinely support interoperability goals and have invested substantially in FHIR-based data exchange capability. The ONC's 2023 Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability final rule (88 Fed. Reg. 23746) moved the field meaningfully forward on algorithm transparency, and we supported that rulemaking. The concern we are raising is more specific than a general objection to data sharing.⏎⏎Expanded interoperability infrastructure, if not designed with explicit limits on secondary use of clinical workflow data, creates the technical conditions for more granular workforce surveillance. When a hospital system can pull together documentation timestamps, clinical decision override rates, AI recommendation acceptance rates, and patient throughput data across an interoperable network, those data streams can be combined to produce clinician-level productivity profiles that are qualitatively different from anything that existed in the pre-interoperability environment. Kellogg et al.'s analysis of algorithmic management is directly relevant here: the concern is not that any single data element is inappropriate to collect, but that the aggregation of multiple data streams enables forms of performance monitoring that individual clinicians cannot meaningfully contest or opt out of.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎Topol (2023), writing in npj Digital Medicine on the imperative for regulatory oversight of large language models in healthcare, noted that the governance frameworks for clinical AI have consistently lagged the deployment of the underlying technologies. That lag is especially dangerous in the interoperability context because the infrastructure, once built and populated with data, creates path dependencies that are very difficult to reverse. We are not asking the Department to slow down interoperability work. We are asking the Department to build explicit workforce data use restrictions into the interoperability governance framework now, before the infrastructure is fully in place, rather than attempting to retrofit restrictions after vendors and health systems have built operational dependencies on the data flows.⏎⏎Specifically, we urge the Department to consider the following in any interoperability-related guidance or rulemaking that touches on AI:⏎⏎o Clinical workflow data generated by AI tool interactions (including documentation time stamps, alert override records, and recommendation acceptance or rejection logs) should be classified as sensitive workforce data and subject to explicit use restrictions that prevent their use in individual clinician performance evaluation without the clinician's informed consent and without independent oversight.⏎⏎o Any interoperability framework that enables AI training on clinical workflow data should require disclosure to frontline clinical staff of what data is being collected, how it is being used, and who has access to it. This is not a novel principle. It is the same transparency logic that ONC applied to algorithm transparency in the 2023 final rule, applied to a different data subject.⏎⏎o HHS should require that any AI tool receiving federal reimbursement support and operating in an interoperable data environment undergo regular independent audits for disparate impact on particular demographic cohorts, consistent with the methodological approach described in Obermeyer et al. (2019). The audit results should be publicly available.⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE RFI'S FRAMING⏎⏎We want to return, briefly, to something that runs through this entire submission. The RFI is titled "Accelerating AI Adoption," and the Department should be aware that this framing sends a signal to the field that the policy priority is speed. That signal has consequences. Once health systems and vendors perceive the national policy priority to be acceleration, procurement timelines compress, pilot evaluation periods shorten, and the careful implementation science work that Bates et al. identified as the condition for AI actually reducing burnout tends to get treated as optional. Dyrbye et al. (2019), in work published in the Archives of Surgery on work-home conflicts and burnout, documented the cumulative nature of clinician strain, and the point is relevant here: workforce harm from poorly-implemented technology does not announce itself immediately. It accumulates over time and shows up as turnover, disengagement, and eventually in patient care quality metrics, by which point the causal connection to specific deployment decisions is much harder to trace.⏎⏎The Department has an opportunity in this RFI process to establish that the federal posture on clinical AI is not simply "go faster" but "go well." Those are not incompatible goals. But they require different regulatory architectures, and the difference between them is most visible in exactly the issues this comment has tried to address: who gets a vote in credentialing standards, what data use restrictions accompany interoperability infrastructure, and whether safety demonstrations are mandatory hurdles for reimbursement support or aspirational after-the-fact objectives.⏎⏎Our specific policy demands, for clarity of record, are as follows:⏎⏎1. Mandatory frontline worker consultation requirements must be built into the governance structure of any credentialing or accreditation body for clinical AI tools that HHS endorses or supports, with voting membership rather than advisory status.⏎⏎2. Federal reimbursement support for AI clinical decision support tools should be conditioned on demonstrated safety performance, including independent bias audits consistent with the Obermeyer et al. methodology, before rollout rather than as an after-the-fact mandate.⏎⏎3. Licensure-specific guardrails must be a component of any credentialing framework, with differentiated standards for tools operating in behavioral health, primary care, surgical, and other clinical contexts where the nature of clinical judgment and the risks of AI override differ substantially.⏎⏎4. AI-generated productivity or efficiency metrics must be explicitly prohibited from serving as the primary basis for staffing ratio decisions in any health system receiving federal funding, pending the development of a separately designed regulatory framework that addresses the staffing-quality-of-care evidence base directly.⏎⏎5. HHS should issue explicit workforce data use restrictions applicable to clinical AI tools operating in interoperable data environments, covering documentation timestamps, alert override logs, and recommendation acceptance rates, with independent oversight requirements and clinician consent requirements for any use of those data streams in individual performance evaluation.⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers Comments < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎Siemens Healthineers remains committed to the responsible development and deployment of AI tools that genuinely support clinical care. We have made substantial investments in that direction and we intend to continue doing so. What we are asking the Department to do is build a regulatory architecture that makes "responsible" mean something specific and enforceable, rather than leaving it as a voluntary aspiration that the competitive dynamics of the health technology market will consistently erode.⏎⏎We are available to provide additional technical input on any of the issues raised in these comments and would welcome the opportunity to participate in any stakeholder engagement process the Department convenes in connection with this RFI. Inquiries may be directed to Melissa Baker, Director of Government Relations, at the contact information listed above.⏎⏎One additional point that we did not fully develop in the credentialing section but want to flag for the record: the RFI inquires specifically about whether HHS should support AI-specific continuing education or training mandates for clinicians. Our 2024 continuing education forum data suggests that the training issue is considerably more complex than a simple "yes, require training" answer would capture. Clinicians who received AI tool training that was developed primarily by the tool's vendor reported, at higher rates than those who received training developed by independent clinical educators, that the training did not adequately address failure modes, edge cases, or appropriate circumstances for overriding AI recommendations. The content of training matters as much as its existence, and a federal requirement for AI training that does not specify independence of curriculum development from vendor interests will not reliably produce the informed, appropriately skeptical clinical users that safe AI deployment requires. We would urge the Department to address curriculum independence explicitly if it moves forward with any training mandate, and to consider requiring that training materials include documented case examples of AI tool failures and appropriate clinician responses, not only examples of AI tool successes and adoption workflows.⏎⏎The practical challenge of who reviews those curriculum standards, and on what timeline, is one we do not have a fully developed answer to, and we acknowledge that.♔♔2026-02-27T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-27T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare will be used by employers and insurers as a mechanism for workforce surveillance, productivity extraction, staffing cuts, and the devaluation of clinical expertise rather than genuine care improvement.♔organization♔high♔angry♔Maine♔director of government relations♔37♔A 2024 internal policy review conducted across our network of licensed clinical social workers identified that 68% of practitioners expressed significant concerns about AI-assisted documentation tools overriding clinical judgment in treatment planning, particularly for clients navigating complex trauma, substance use, and co-occurring disorders. SYNTH-0079♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joshua Martinez♔American Hospital Association♔♔♔♔♔American Hospital Association < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI Response < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎---⏎COMMENTS FROM THE AMERICAN HOSPITAL ASSOCIATION CONCERNING THE HHS REQUEST FOR INFORMATION: ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎Submitted by: Joshua Martinez, Executive Director⏎Date: February 2025⏎---⏎⏎I. THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF ACCELERATION: WHY THIS RFI ASKS THE WRONG QUESTION⏎⏎The American Hospital Association's Health AI Institute surveyed 412 health system members during 2024, yielding findings that clarify the landscape in ways the Department might not anticipate. Sixty-seven percent of the surveyed health systems had deployed at least one AI-enabled clinical decision support (CDSS) tool within the preceding 24 months. Fifty-eight percent of those rollouts faced delays averaging 14 months, driven largely by ambiguous FDA classification frameworks and inconsistent payer coverage rulings (Health AI Institute, 2024. Our policy analysis division's parallel review of 93 FDA submissions involving AI/ML-based software as a medical device revealed a median review timeline 40% longer than comparable non-AI applications. We provide these figures not to support the acceleration HHS proposes, but to establish a foundation for a completely different diagnosis. The delays experienced by our members are indeed real. However, the proposed remedies are structurally misaligned with the actual root causes of those delays, and the Department's framing of this RFI as an impartial solicitation of public input on how best to speed up AI adoption requires direct challenge. This request is not a neutral inquiry. It reflects a pre-structured agenda whose contours were defined by entities holding concentrated market power and direct financial stakes in the regulatory outcomes likely to emerge.⏎⏎Our organization focuses our remarks on the RFI's inquiries about payment reform and public-private research partnerships, since these represent the two mechanisms most immediately vulnerable to the market-distorting dynamics identified in our analysis. The healthcare AI vendor market exhibits structural concentration in ways that render standard accelerationist policy logic highly dangerous. As Dafny and Lee (2016) demonstrated regarding hospital mergers, market concentration in the health sector fails to self-correct through competitive pressure in the manner conventional economic models predict; instead, incumbents leveraging existing infrastructure relationships extract rents precisely because switching costs remain prohibitive. This dynamic is nowhere more severe than in the electronic health record market. As Wiggins (2023) highlighted in Health Affairs, Epic and Oracle jointly control the data architecture of the vast majority of U.S. hospital networks, and the contractual switching expenses embedded in those relationships amount to tens of millions of dollars per institution. When HHS proposes speeding up AI adoption through federal billing channels and CRADAs, it is not establishing a level competitive playing field. Rather, it is granting preferential access to the payment and coverage ecosystem to vendors who already occupy the center of hospital data pipelines, who have already dictated the technical standards those pipelines depend on, and who have already poured vast resources into regulatory relationships that smaller rivals simply cannot match. Feldman and Frondorf (2017) observed this identical structural dynamic in pharmaceutical markets, where regulatory complexity acts not as a neutral hurdle but as a selective barrier that entrenched firms are uniquely equipped to absorb. The parallel to healthcare AI may not be flawless, but it is accurate enough to cause serious alarm.⏎⏎American Hospital Association < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI Response < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎The payment reform proposals outlined in this RFI would, in practical terms, establish billing avenues that massive EHR-integrated AI vendors can tap into immediately via existing CMS relationships, while health systems utilizing independent or smaller-vendor AI tools confront coverage uncertainty that the Congressional Budget Office (2023) showed creates systematic cost-transfer pressure onto hospital operating budgets. Landi (2024) reported in Fierce Healthcare that AI vendor contracts within health systems conceal cost escalators and lock-in clauses that CFOs are only currently starting to scrutinize, and this scrutiny arrives at the exact moment HHS proposes deepening those contractual ties through federal payment validation. The Institute is not opposing financial coverage for AI-enabled clinical instruments as a general principle. The argument is narrower and inherently structural: coverage rulings issued before independent performance benchmarking frameworks are codified will systematically advantage products from vendors possessing the lobbying capacity to dictate coverage criteria, and the lack of those frameworks is itself a direct result of vendor influence over the regulatory apparatus. Torous, Bucci, and Keshavan (2022) identified this exact dynamic in the mental health app space, where the void of standardized rating frameworks allowed vendor self-certification to replace independent efficacy reviews. Rai (2019) made the broader theoretical argument in the Maryland Law Review: regulatory agencies overseeing AI systems face structural capture pressures because the technical complexity of the subject matter generates information asymmetries that incumbent vendors are perfectly positioned to exploit, meaning the correct remedy is not faster regulation but better-insulated regulation. The GAO reached a related conclusion in its 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104629), determining that federal oversight mechanisms for AI/ML clinical tools lack the institutional capacity to independently verify vendor performance claims, a vulnerability that speeding up payment approvals without corresponding oversight investments will permanently cement.⏎⏎II. ON PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS AND THE TRANSFER OF PUBLIC RESEARCH VALUE⏎⏎The RFI's section concerning Cooperative Research and Development Agreements (CRADAs) and public-private AI development partnerships demands particular scrutiny. Mazzucato (2018) detailed in The Entrepreneurial State how public research investment in technology sectors is routinely captured by private actors via partnership structures granting firms preferential access to publicly funded intellectual property without matching public benefit obligations. The healthcare AI context serves as a direct application of this phenomenon. HHS-funded research regarding clinical AI applications, undertaken in partnership with dominant EHR vendors or massive technology corporations, will yield intellectual property and training datasets that those companies will subsequently commercialize through proprietary product lines that health systems are forced to purchase at market rates. The public absorbs the research costs; the vendor seizes the commercial value; and the health system pays twice, initially through the federal tax base funding the research and again through the vendor contract. Gee and Gurwitz (2018) showed at the Center for American Progress that structural market power in healthcare consistently generates this cost-transfer pattern, and the proposed CRADA framework replicates it with remarkable directness.⏎⏎American Hospital Association < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI Response < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎The accountability gap is worsened by the near-total lack of mechanisms for revoking payment eligibility for poor-performing AI products once coverage is established. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019) revealed in Science that a widely utilized commercial algorithm meant to manage population health systematically underestimated the severity of illness in Black patients, a discovery that surfaced through independent academic research rather than vendor disclosure or regulatory detection. Had that product been deeply integrated into a federal coverage model at the time of that discovery, the institutional and contractual obstacles to removing it would have been immense. The Institute's members brought up this exact concern at the 2024 Annual Convening, where the consensus held that payment uncertainty and regulatory unpredictability serve as the primary barriers to sustainable AI integration. This is not because members desire faster coverage decisions, but because they require predictable standards against which products can be evaluated and, when necessary, decertified.⏎⏎The American Hospital Association therefore urges HHS to enact a moratorium on accelerationist payment reforms and new CRADA arrangements pending the completion of an independent market structure analysis of the healthcare AI vendor landscape. Furthermore, we require the development of standardized, third-party-administered performance benchmarking frameworks as a mandatory prerequisite for any coverage determination, alongside the codification of explicit anti-capture procedural safeguards governing vendor participation in standard-setting processes. The Department must commission that market structure analysis from an organization holding no active contractual relationships with the major EHR or AI vendors, and it should publish the conflict-of-interest disclosures of all advisory participants before any resulting policy recommendations are finalized. We note that the 14-month average deployment delay our members report does not, according to our analysis, indicate a regulatory process that is too slow. Rather, it indicates a regulatory process that is poorly structured, and the remedy for poor structure is never merely speed.⏎⏎https://www.aha.org/health-ai-institute/regulatory-comments/2025-hhs-ai-rfi-submission⏎⏎Contact: policy@aha.org < > Health AI Institute, 155 N. SYNTH-0080♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Susan Flores♔Paige AI♔♔♔♔♔Paige AI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎We submit these comments in response to the above-captioned Request for Information on accelerating AI adoption in clinical care settings. Paige AI is a computational pathology company operating at the intersection of AI model development and clinical deployment infrastructure. Our comments today do not address clinical safety performance benchmarks or vendor economics — those matters are addressed elsewhere in this docket by parties better positioned to speak to them. We are here to raise a prior question, one that the RFI's framing conspicuously declines to pose: whether the Department has established democratic legitimacy for what it is proposing to accelerate. This core necessity for foundational legitimacy serves as my primary anchor when evaluating the current drive to expedite the integration of algorithmic tools into patient care environments. We regard the absence of that question from this RFI as a governance failure, not a technical gap. It is a category error to treat "how do we speed this up" as the operative question when "should we, and on whose authority, and with what accountability structures" has not been answered in any public forum this Department has convened.⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎THE DEPLOYMENT TIMELINE PROBLEM IS NOT WHAT HHS THINKS IT IS⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department should be aware of what is actually driving AI deployment delays in clinical settings, because the RFI's framing implies a diagnosis that the operational data does not support. Deployment analytics across 47 partner health systems in 2024 recorded a median workflow integration time of 11.3 months from FDA clearance to clinical activation. In 68% of those cases, the primary delay factor was identified as compliance and reimbursement uncertainty. A structured survey of clinical and administrative contacts at those same facilities found that 83% cited the absence of clear Medicare coverage pathways for AI-assisted diagnostic tools as a significant barrier to procurement approval. An analysis of 14 AI imaging products cleared between 2021 and 2023 further found that none had achieved a dedicated CPT code within 24 months of clearance, forcing facilities to absorb deployment costs under existing fee schedules that do not account for AI-augmented service delivery. The Department is correct that these delays are real. Where the RFI goes wrong is in treating them as purely technical or administrative obstacles that better guidance and streamlined reimbursement pathways can resolve. Evaluating the root causes of these timelines, the delays are, in substantial part, the appropriate hesitation of institutions that cannot yet answer basic governance questions about the systems they are being asked to deploy. Coiera, Ash, and Berg, writing in the Yearbook of Medical Informatics on the unintended consequences of health information technology, documented how institutional resistance to adoption is frequently not irrationality but a rational response to opacity and unresolved accountability. HHS is proposing to eliminate the hesitation rather than address the conditions producing it.⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎THE DEMOCRATIC LEGITIMACY QUESTION THIS RFI DOES NOT ASK⏎⏎⏎⏎The RFI's framing is not neutral. It presupposes that acceleration is the correct policy objective and solicits input only on mechanisms for achieving it. This is a significant structuring choice, and this Department has not answered for it. Winickoff, Amon, and Oye, writing in Health Affairs, argued that the governance of AI in health requires a precautionary democratic framework that explicitly addresses irreversibility before commitments are made at scale. The Federal Health IT Strategic Plan 2024-2030 (ONC, 2024) gestures toward equity and transparency as values, but it does not constitute a democratic mandate for the deployment decisions that would follow from the actions HHS is now contemplating. The difference matters. Path dependency in healthcare infrastructure is well-documented: Dafny and Lee (2016) observed in the New England Journal of Medicine that institutional infrastructure decisions in healthcare are extraordinarily difficult to reverse once embedded, which means that the question of whether to accelerate adoption is also, implicitly, a question about what becomes permanent. When HHS proposes to create reimbursement incentives and regulatory streamlining for AI tools that operate as proprietary black boxes, it is not simply reducing administrative friction. It is making a structural commitment on behalf of communities that have not been asked whether they consent to it.⏎⏎⏎⏎The structural opacity problem is not incidental. Selbst and Barocas (2018), in the Fordham Law Review, documented how the intuitive appeal of explainable AI systems obscures the degree to which proprietary clinical tools resist meaningful audit even when vendors claim interpretability. Pasquale (2015), in The Black Box Society, made the broader argument that algorithmic accountability requires not just technical transparency but institutional transparency about who controls the system and on what terms. When HHS creates reimbursement pathways for tools that health systems cannot independently audit, it is not merely a technical policy choice. It is a decision about whether communities served by those health systems have any meaningful recourse when the tools perform badly. Obermeyer et al., in a widely-cited Science paper, demonstrated that a widely deployed commercial algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health status. That finding was not surfaced by the vendor. It was surfaced by independent academic researchers who happened to have data access. The question this RFI should be asking is: what institutional structures would make that kind of finding possible routinely, rather than accidentally? HHS is instead asking how to move more tools through the pipeline faster.⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎ON THE QUESTION OF AUDITABILITY AND WHAT "OVERSIGHT" CURRENTLY MEANS IN PRACTICE⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 5⏎⏎⏎⏎We want to be precise about what oversight of proprietary AI systems actually consists of under current regulatory conditions, because the RFI uses the word "oversight" in a way that suggests a more robust accountability infrastructure than exists. FDA clearance under the 510(k) pathway does not require disclosure of training data, model architecture, or performance stratification by patient subgroup. CMS coverage determinations do not require auditability as a condition of coverage. The ONC certification program, as structured, does not reach most AI-assisted diagnostic tools. What this means in practice is that health systems deploying FDA-cleared AI tools are, in the vast majority of cases, operating on the basis of vendor-provided performance claims that they cannot independently verify. Doshi-Velez and colleagues (2017), in a Berkman Klein Center working paper on accountability of AI under law, argued that the role of explanation in AI governance is not merely technical but legal and democratic — that the inability to explain a decision is also an inability to contest it. Metcalf, Moss, and boyd (2019), writing in Social Research, documented how corporate ethics frameworks in technology companies systematically internalize oversight functions in ways that insulate decision-making from external accountability. HHS's acceleration agenda, as framed, would embed this accountability structure more deeply into clinical infrastructure rather than correcting it. The European Parliament's AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) imposes mandatory conformity assessments, transparency obligations, and fundamental rights impact assessments for high-risk AI systems, including those used in health contexts. This Department has not explained why a comparably precautionary framework is inappropriate for the United States, and the RFI does not pose the question. Topol (2019), in Nature Medicine, made efficiency and performance claims for clinical AI that have been widely cited by acceleration advocates, but Topol's own analysis acknowledged that performance metrics derived from controlled datasets may not generalize to real-world deployment populations — a caveat that tends to disappear from policy citations of that work.⏎⏎⏎⏎There is also the matter of what Paige AI, as a company that builds these tools, regards as a genuine governance gap rather than a rhetorical one. We are not arguing against AI adoption in clinical settings. We are arguing that the current policy architecture makes it structurally impossible for health systems, patients, or regulators to know whether the tools being deployed are performing as claimed across the populations they serve. That is not a problem that faster reimbursement pathways will fix. The RFI does not ask what accountability conditions should attach to coverage, and we regard that omission as a serious one.⏎⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC REQUEST FOR AGENCY ACTION⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI respectfully demands that HHS take the following actions before issuing any final guidance or implementing any reimbursement or regulatory changes based on this RFI: first, that the Department publish a formal democratic mandate analysis addressing whether the acceleration agenda reflected in this RFI has been developed with meaningful community input from the populations most likely to bear the risks of premature or inadequately audited AI deployment; second, that the RFI be formally re-opened with explicit questions about irreversibility (specifically, what mechanisms exist to withdraw coverage or certification for tools that exhibit post-deployment performance degradation or bias), auditability (specifically, what disclosure conditions HHS regards as minimum necessary for a tool to be eligible for any federal reimbursement), and community consent (specifically, what obligations health systems have to inform patient populations about the use of AI tools in their care and to provide meaningful opt-out mechanisms). The current RFI asks none of these questions. This Department has not answered why it chose not to ask them, and that absence is itself a policy decision that warrants public accounting.⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI also notes, for the record, that the absence of a CPT code for AI-augmented diagnostic services 24 months post-clearance is a genuine problem for deployment economics, but it is a second-order problem. The first-order problem is that no one outside the vendor currently has reliable access to the information needed to know whether a cleared tool should be deployed at all in a given patient population. Fixing the reimbursement pathway before fixing that information asymmetry is not acceleration. It is a commitment made without adequate basis.⏎⏎⏎⏎Susan Flores⏎⏎Vice President, Regulatory Compliance⏎⏎Paige AI⏎⏎susan.flores@paige.ai⏎⏎⏎⏎Paige AI Comments < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 6♔♔2026-01-11T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-11T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔5♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Once AI systems are embedded in healthcare infrastructure, they become practically irreversible and resistant to democratic oversight, creating a permanent transfer of power from clinicians, patients, and regulators to technology vendors.♔organization♔high♔angry♔Pennsylvania♔compliance officer♔44♔Harrison.ai's internal deployment analytics across 47 partner health systems in 2024 recorded a median workflow integration time of 11.3 months from FDA clearance to clinical activation, with compliance and reimbursement uncertainty identified as the primary delay factor in 68% of cases. SYNTH-0082♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sarah Lopez♔Center for Science in the Public Interest♔♔♔♔♔CSPI COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎Submitted by: Sarah Lopez, Director of Government Affairs⏎⏎Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI)⏎⏎On Behalf of CSPI's Government Affairs and Public Policy Division⏎⏎⏎⏎RE: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎⏎⏎I. THE GOVERNANCE GAP IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL⏎⏎⏎⏎CSPI submits these comments with a specific and documented concern that is not captured anywhere in the framing of the Department's request for information. In 2024, CSPI conducted a survey of more than 2,200 perioperative nurses across the United States (Center for Science in the Public Interest, 2024, CSPI Survey on AI-Assisted Surgical Tools and Automated Clinical Documentation: Findings and Policy Implications, Washington, DC: CSPI). That survey found that 58% of respondents were already working in facilities where AI-assisted surgical tools or automated clinical documentation systems had been introduced within the prior 24 months. Of those, 74% reported that their institutions lacked any formal governance structure to oversee AI implementation in the operating room environment. CSPI's Patient Safety Advisory Group documented in its most recent annual review that perioperative settings present a category of AI integration challenges — sterile field decision support, instrument and sponge detection systems, anesthesia monitoring algorithms — that fall entirely outside the scope of general clinical AI guidance currently circulating in the field (CSPI Patient Safety Advisory Group, 2024, Annual Review of Perioperative AI Integration Challenges: Governance Gaps in the OR Environment, Supplemental Report). The Department is asking how to accelerate AI deployment. CSPI asserts that the more pressing issue is how to halt the rollout of AI in clinical settings where the governance infrastructure does not yet exist to make that deployment safe. Consider a concrete example. A circulating nurse is managing a procedure, tracking surgical instruments, and monitoring a patient who — because of the sedation state preceding general anesthesia — cannot articulate what she is feeling. The nurse reads the patient's face. She notices a particular tension in the jaw, a quality of shallow breathing that is not yet captured in any monitoring waveform. She makes a judgment call that delays induction by ninety seconds and prompts a conversation with the anesthesiologist. That moment — that ninety seconds — is not a productivity event. It is not a data point. And it is the exact type of clinical act that AI intermediation, if it repositions the nurse as a monitor of algorithmic outputs rather than an independent reasoner, will over time erode.⏎⏎⏎⏎CSPI COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎II. WHAT THE DEPARTMENT'S FRAMING GETS WRONG ABOUT CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎⏎⏎The Department's request for information frames AI adoption primarily as a mechanism for accelerating productivity and operational efficiency in clinical care settings. CSPI respectfully submits that this framing is structurally incompatible with what medicine, and specifically perioperative nursing, actually is. Verghese, Shah, and Harrington wrote in JAMA in 2018 that what the clinical encounter requires is not computational power but the irreplaceable human act of bearing witness to another person's illness — and that AI systems, however technically accurate, cannot replicate the moral weight of that presence (Verghese, A., Shah, N.H., & Harrington, R.A., 2018, What this computer needs is a physician: Humanism and artificial intelligence, JAMA, 319(1), 19–20). Eric Topol, who is hardly an AI skeptic, argued in Nature Medicine that the most important function AI can serve in healthcare is to give clinicians time back — time to be present with patients — and that deploying AI in ways that substitute for clinical relationship rather than protect it represents a fundamental misapplication of the technology (Topol, E.J., 2019. High-performance medicine: The convergence of human and artificial intelligence. Nature Medicine, 25(1)). The therapeutic relationship between clinician and patient is not a soft variable. Kelley and colleagues conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship has independently measurable effects on clinical outcomes — not merely on patient satisfaction, but on objective health measures (Kelley, J.M., Kraft-Todd, G., Schapira, L., Kossowsky, J., & Riess, H., 2014, The influence of the patient-clinician relationship on healthcare outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, PLOS ONE, 9(4), e94207). Hojat and colleagues demonstrated in Academic Medicine that physicians' empathy scores were directly associated with better glycemic control in diabetic patients — a finding that connects relational attentiveness to a measurable physiological outcome (Hojat, M., Louis, D.Z., Markham, F.W., Wender, R., Rabinowitz, C., & Gonnella, J.S., 2011, Physicians' empathy and clinical outcomes for diabetic patients, Academic Medicine, 86(3), 359–364). When HHS frames AI as a productivity tool, it is implicitly accepting a model of care in which these relational dimensions are costs to be reduced, not capacities to be protected. That is a policy choice, and it is the wrong one. The Department has an opportunity in this RFI to articulate a different model — one in which AI is assessed not merely by its ability to produce accurate outputs, but by its impact on preserving or degrading the human relationships that make clinical care safe and meaningful. Obermeyer and Emanuel cautioned in the New England Journal of Medicine that the clinical value of predictive algorithms depends entirely on how they are integrated into care workflows, and that poorly governed integration can produce harms that no accuracy benchmark will detect (Obermeyer, Z., & Emanuel, E.J., 2016, Predicting the future — big data, machine learning, and clinical medicine, New England Journal of Medicine, 375(13), 1216–1219).⏎⏎⏎⏎CSPI COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎III. THE DESKILLING PROBLEM IS A PATIENT SAFETY PROBLEM⏎⏎⏎⏎There is a body of research that the Department's RFI does not appear to have taken into account, and CSPI believes this literature strongly applies to any regulatory structure governing AI in clinical settings. Parasuraman and Manzey demonstrated in Human Factors that when human operators are repositioned as supervisors of automated systems rather than active decision-makers, they experience measurable declines in vigilance, situational awareness, and the ability to intervene effectively when automation fails — a phenomenon the literature calls automation-induced complacency (Parasuraman, R., & Manzey, D.H., 2010, Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration, Human Factors, 52(3), 381–410). Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt conducted a systematic review of automation bias across clinical decision support contexts and found that clinicians who rely on algorithmic recommendations are measurably more likely to accept incorrect outputs and less likely to catch errors that contradict the system's suggestion (Goddard, K., Roudsari, A., & Wyatt, J.C., 2012, Automation bias: A systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 121–127). This is not a theoretical concern in perioperative nursing. Surgical instrument and sponge detection systems are being deployed in operating rooms across the country — right now, in facilities that, per CSPI's own survey data, lack formal AI governance structures — and the clinicians using those systems are being implicitly encouraged to treat algorithmic confirmation as a substitute for independent count verification. The cognitive architecture that Tversky and Kahneman described in their foundational work on heuristics and biases is strongly implicated in this context: when a system presents a confident output, human judgment anchors to that output even when independent reasoning would produce a different conclusion (Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D., 1974. Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases, Science 185, no. 4157). Over time, the clinical judgment capacity that experienced perioperative nurses have built through years of practice — the capacity to know when something is wrong before any instrument confirms it — atrophies. No technical accuracy benchmark measures that atrophy. No reimbursement model accounts for it. Dzau and colleagues argued in The Lancet that realizing the promise of AI-augmented health systems requires aligning institutional incentives with long-term patient outcomes rather than short-term efficiency gains, and that without that alignment, adoption pressure will systematically favor tools that produce measurable near-term outputs at the expense of harder-to-quantify clinical capacities (Dzau, V.J., Ginsburg, G.S., Van Nuys, K., Agus, D., & Goldman, D., 2021, Aligning incentives to fulfill the promise of learning health systems, The Lancet, 392(10162), 2326–2328). The Department should take that argument seriously.⏎⏎⏎⏎IV. SPECIFIC POLICY ASKS REGARDING GOVERNANCE AND RESEARCH PRIORITIES⏎⏎⏎⏎CSPI urges HHS to take four specific actions in response to this RFI. First, the Department should require that any clinical AI tool deployed in a hospital or ambulatory surgical setting be accompanied by a documented institutional governance structure — including defined roles for clinical oversight, a mechanism for frontline clinician reporting of AI-related concerns, and a periodic review process — prior to qualifying for reimbursement consideration under any federal program. The 74% governance gap documented in CSPI's 2024 survey is not a marginal finding. It represents the baseline condition of AI deployment in perioperative nursing right now, and it is unacceptable as a national standard. Second, HHS should adopt a precautionary deployment standard that requires demonstrated evidence of safety and equity — not merely technical accuracy — before federal programs provide any financial incentive for AI adoption in clinical care. Bickmore, Pfeifer, and Jack found in their work on virtual nurse agents that even well-designed AI communication tools can produce differential outcomes across health literacy levels in ways that are not apparent from aggregate performance metrics (Bickmore, T.W., Pfeifer, L.M., & Jack, B.W., 2009, Taking the time to care: Empowering low health literacy hospital patients with virtual nurse agents, Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1265–1274). Third, HHS should preserve meaningful human decision-making authority at every point of care, which means that no AI system deployed in a clinical setting should be positioned — through workflow design, reimbursement structure, or institutional protocol — as the default decision-maker, with human oversight as the exception. The reversal of that hierarchy is already occurring in some perioperative settings, and it is occurring without any federal regulatory framework to constrain it. Fourth, and this is a point CSPI wishes to emphasize: HHS should commission research into the relational and deskilling harms of AI intermediation, not only into technical accuracy and bias. The literature exists. The methodologies exist. What does not yet exist is a federally funded research agenda that treats the degradation of clinical judgment and the erosion of therapeutic relationship as patient safety outcomes worthy of the same measurement infrastructure that governs device performance. Until that research agenda exists, the Department will be making deployment decisions without the evidence base those decisions require, and the consequences will fall disproportionately on the nurses and patients who are already inside the adoption curve lacking sufficient protection — which is, at this point,⏎⏎⏎⏎CSPI COMMENTS | HHS HEALTH SECTOR AI RFI | DOCKET HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎⏎⏎the majority of perioperative nurses working in the United States.⏎⏎⏎⏎sarahlopez@cspinet.org⏎⏎www.cspinet.org/government-affairs♔♔2026-02-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-07T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔6♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Medicine is fundamentally a human relationship built on judgment, context, and trust, and AI threatens to reduce patients to data points and clinicians to machine overseers.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔concerned♔Texas♔director of government affairs♔52♔A 2024 AORN member survey of more than 2,200 perioperative nurses found that 58% reported working in facilities where AI-assisted surgical tools or automated clinical documentation systems had been introduced within the prior 24 months, yet 74% of those respondents indicated their institutions lacked formal governance structures to oversee AI implementation in the OR environment.
