SYNTH-0083♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Sharon Scott♔Connected Health Initiative♔♔♔♔♔The Cooperative Exchange — Member Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-001⏎Submitted by: Sharon Scott, Senior Policy Analyst, Connected Health Initiative / The Cooperative Exchange⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 1⏎⏎⏎THE FRAMING PROBLEM IN THIS RFI⏎⏎The Cooperative Exchange represents a network of healthcare clearinghouses that collectively process approximately 14 billion healthcare administrative transactions annually. Our member organizations occupy an unusual vantage point in the healthcare data ecosystem: positioned between providers, payers, and patients, they see claim flows, prior authorization request volumes, denial rates, routing failures, and adjudication patterns in aggregate that most individual stakeholders cannot observe. It is from that position — not from a posture of opposition to AI — that The Cooperative Exchange submits these comments, and it is from that position that we must register serious concern about the framing choices embedded in this RFI.⏎⏎The Department has structured this solicitation around the concept of acceleration. The RFI asks how HHS can "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders," how reimbursement structures can be redesigned to reward AI-assisted care, and how regulatory friction can be reduced to speed deployment. These are reasonable questions in a context where AI genuinely has not yet reached patients who might benefit. The problem is that AI has already reached patients — extensively, at scale, in operational deployment — and the application that has reached them most aggressively is not clinical decision support, not diagnostic imaging analysis, not medication reconciliation. It is automated prior authorization denial. The RFI's framing of AI adoption as a future opportunity to be unlocked treats the most consequential current deployment of AI in the health sector as though it does not exist, and that omission is not neutral. It is a choice that will shape what HHS incentivizes, what it monitors, and what harms it fails to anticipate.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2⏎⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED RECORD OF AI-DRIVEN DENIAL AUTOMATION⏎⏎The evidentiary record on AI-driven prior authorization and claims adjudication systems is no longer speculative. In March 2023, an investigation published jointly by ProPublica and KFF Health News (Schulte & Fry, 2023, "Death by a Thousand Clicks: How Insurers Are Using AI to Deny Health Claims") documented the operational deployment of AI denial systems by major Medicare Advantage insurers, including specific instances in which post-acute care and rehabilitation approvals were systematically curtailed by algorithmic tools processing thousands of cases per day with review periods averaging under two seconds per case. The article reported that one insurer's AI system, nH Predict, was used to override physician-ordered care for elderly patients, generating denials at a rate that the company's own internal data showed was inconsistent with historical physician review outcomes. The patients affected were predominantly elderly, often recently hospitalized, and in many cases lacked the functional capacity or family support infrastructure to navigate multi-step appeals processes.⏎⏎This is not an isolated anecdote. In April 2022, the HHS Office of Inspector General published OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260, "Some Medicare Advantage Organization Denials of Prior Authorization Requests Raise Concerns About Beneficiary Access to Medically Necessary Care," which found that Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage criteria in a statistically significant share of reviewed cases, and that a substantial proportion of those denials were overturned on appeal — suggesting that the initial denial, whether generated by algorithm or by a human reviewer following algorithmic guidance, was clinically unjustified. The OIG's findings were reinforced by the Government Accountability Office in March 2023 (GAO-23-105556, "Medicare Advantage: CMS Should Use Data on Prior Authorization Denials and Appeals to Ensure Beneficiary Access to Care"), which found that CMS was not systematically collecting or analyzing denial and appeal data in ways that would allow the agency to identify patterns of inappropriate denials across Medicare Advantage plans.⏎⏎Then, in October 2024, the U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations released "Denial, Delay, Disappear: How Medicare Advantage Organizations Use Prior Authorization to Limit Care," a report that named specific insurers, documented internal communications indicating awareness of denial rate targets, and presented data showing that prior authorization denial rates had increased in correlation with the adoption of AI-assisted review tools. The Subcommittee found that three of the largest Medicare Advantage insurers collectively issued hundreds of thousands of prior authorization denials annually, with appeal overturn rates in some categories exceeding 75 percent — meaning that the majority of algorithmically-supported denials that patients actually challenged were found to be wrong. The Subcommittee report is the most detailed congressional documentation to date of what The Cooperative Exchange's own transaction-volume data has shown in aggregate: denial rates are rising, appeal rates are not keeping pace, and the gap between those two numbers represents patients who received medically necessary care late, received it at personal expense, or did not receive it at all.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎⏎THE COST-CONTAINMENT OPTIMIZATION PROBLEM⏎⏎What is particularly important for HHS to understand — and what the RFI's framing of AI as a tool for clinical improvement systematically obscures — is that AI denial systems are not malfunctioning. They are performing exactly as designed. These systems are trained on financial objectives. The optimization target is not clinical appropriateness; it is cost containment, and more specifically, it is the identification of denial opportunities that will not generate successful appeals. A system trained on historical approval and denial data, in an environment where appeal rates are low and appeal success rates are lower, will learn that certain patient profiles, certain procedure codes, and certain clinical contexts can be denied with low reversal risk. That is not a bug in the algorithm. It is the algorithm doing what it was built to do.⏎⏎The research literature on algorithmic bias in healthcare risk models supports this interpretation. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453) proved that a heavily utilized proprietary software system built to coordinate care for large demographic groups chronically undervalued the medical necessities of Black individuals. This occurred because the software was trained on healthcare cost as a proxy for health need — a proxy that reflects historical inequities in access rather than actual clinical burden. The lesson from this discovery, which has been widely cited in the policy literature, is that when AI systems are trained on financial outcomes in a healthcare environment already shaped by structural inequities, the resulting models will encode and amplify those inequities. Prior authorization AI systems trained on payer cost data face the same structural problem. Patients who have historically received less care — including elderly patients, low-income Medicaid enrollees, and patients with disabilities — generate training data that makes lower-cost interventions appear clinically sufficient, because the system has no reliable way to distinguish "this patient received less care because less was appropriate" from "this patient received less care because their access was constrained."⏎⏎The National Health Law Program documented this dynamic specifically in the Medicaid managed care context in its February 2023 report, "Automated Injustice Redux: How Algorithmic Decision-Making in Medicaid Managed Care Harms Enrollees" (NHeLP,  2023), which catalogued state-level deployments of automated prior authorization and level-of-care determination systems that generated mass denials for personal care services, home health, and behavioral health, disproportionately affecting enrollees with complex disabilities. In several of the states NHeLP examined, the automated systems were implemented without adequate notice to enrollees, without transparent disclosure of the criteria being applied, and without meaningful pathways for human review — a pattern that raises serious questions under existing regulatory frameworks, including the due process and notice requirements embedded in 42 C.F.R. § 422.568 and § 422.590 governing Medicare Advantage organization determinations and reconsiderations.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎⏎WHAT ACCELERATION WILL PRODUCE WITHOUT PRECAUTIONARY REQUIREMENTS⏎⏎The RFI asks how HHS can use reimbursement policy to "foster competition among clinical care AI tool builders." The Cooperative Exchange does not object to competition in AI development as a general principle. The concern is with what competition in this specific market has already produced and what HHS's proposed incentive structures will deepen if deployed without precautionary requirements.⏎⏎The market for AI-assisted prior authorization and claims adjudication is already competitive. Multiple vendors offer payers AI-driven denial optimization tools, and the competitive pressure in that market runs in the direction of more aggressive denial, not less — because payers select vendors based in part on the financial outcomes those vendors produce. Ledford (2023, "AI tools for prior authorization are already in use — and already raising alarms," Nature Medicine, 29(8), 1876-1878) documented that as of the date of publication, multiple major insurers had deployed AI prior authorization tools in live operational environments, and that physician and patient advocacy organizations were already raising alarms about denial rates, lack of transparency, and the absence of any federal regulatory framework governing the use of these tools. The American Medical Association's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey found that 94 percent of responding physicians reported that prior authorization burdens had increased over the previous five years, that 33 percent reported prior authorization had led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care, and that the majority of respondents described the prior authorization process as having a significant negative impact on patient outcomes (AMA, "AMA Prior Authorization Physician Survey: 2023 Survey Results," AMA Policy Research Perspectives, 2023). These findings predate what the Senate PSI documented in October 2024 as a further escalation of AI-driven denial rates.⏎⏎If HHS uses reimbursement incentives to accelerate AI adoption in clinical settings without simultaneously establishing mandatory requirements for AI systems operating in the prior authorization and claims adjudication space, the predictable outcome is that payers will use the same incentive structures to further entrench denial automation while providers use reimbursement-supported AI tools to generate clinical documentation — and those two AI systems will interact in ways that systematically disadvantage patients. The provider's AI will generate a prior authorization request; the payer's AI will deny it; the patient will receive a denial letter that may or may not accurately describe the basis for the denial; and the patient will face an appeals process that, as the Kaiser Family Foundation's 2023 issue brief documented, most Medicare Advantage beneficiaries do not successfully navigate (Koma, Cubanski, & Neuman, 2023, "Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage: Trends and Beneficiary Experiences," KFF Issue Brief, March 2023). KFF found that fewer than one percent of Medicare Advantage beneficiaries who received a prior authorization denial filed an appeal, despite the fact that appeal overturn rates for those who did appeal were substantial. The gap between denial rates and appeal rates is not evidence that most denials are appropriate. It is evidence that most patients, particularly elderly patients and those with limited health literacy or family support, cannot effectively exercise their statutory rights under 42 C.F.R. § 422.590.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5⏎⏎⏎EQUITY OBLIGATIONS AND THE DIFFERENTIAL BURDEN ON VULNERABLE POPULATIONS⏎⏎The equity dimensions of this problem are not peripheral — they are central, and HHS has existing regulatory obligations that bear on them directly. The populations most affected by AI-driven prior authorization denial are precisely the populations that federal health programs exist to protect. Medicare Advantage enrollees are elderly and often functionally dependent. Medicaid managed care enrollees are disproportionately low-income, members of racial and ethnic minority groups, and individuals with disabilities. These populations face compounded barriers to navigating denial and appeal processes: limited health literacy, limited digital access, limited capacity to obtain supporting documentation from physicians, and in many cases limited time — because the care being denied is time-sensitive post-acute care, home health, or rehabilitation services.⏎⏎The Obermeyer et al. (2019) findings on racial bias in healthcare algorithms are directly relevant here, and The Cooperative Exchange is concerned that HHS's RFI does not engage with them. When AI systems trained on cost-proxy data are used to determine care eligibility for populations whose historical healthcare utilization reflects constrained access rather than lower clinical need, the resulting determinations will systematically underserve those populations. Geruso and Layton (2020, "Upcoding: Evidence from Medicare on Squishy Risk Adjustment," Journal of Political Economy, 128(3), 984-1026) documented related dynamics in risk adjustment, showing that financial incentives in Medicare Advantage lead to systematic manipulation of diagnostic coding — a finding that, taken together with the OIG's 2022 report and the Senate PSI's 2024 findings, suggests a pattern of financial optimization behavior by Medicare Advantage organizations that AI tools are accelerating rather than correcting.⏎⏎The Cooperative Exchange's member organizations process claims and prior authorization transactions across all major payer types and all patient populations. Our transaction data, aggregated across approximately 14 billion annual transactions, shows that claim rejection rates are highest in transaction categories associated with complex, multi-step prior authorization requirements — exactly the categories where AI denial tools are most actively deployed. A 3 to 5 percentage point reduction in claim rejection rates, which our internal modeling suggests is achievable through AI-assisted routing accuracy improvements, would represent substantial administrative savings. But those savings will not materialize, and the administrative burden on providers will not decrease, if AI-driven prior authorization denial continues to generate rejection rates that offset routing efficiency gains. The two dynamics cannot be analyzed in isolation from each other, and HHS's RFI treats them as though they belong to entirely separate policy domains.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 6⏎⏎⏎SPECIFIC POLICY DEMANDS⏎⏎The Cooperative Exchange urges HHS to take the following specific regulatory and administrative actions, which are not alternatives to the AI adoption agenda in the RFI but preconditions for it:⏎⏎1.   Mandatory human review thresholds before AI denial issuance. HHS should establish, through rulemaking under the Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care programs, that no prior authorization denial may be issued on the basis of AI-generated review alone. Any AI-assisted denial determination must be reviewed and affirmatively approved by a licensed clinician with relevant specialty expertise before issuance. The clinician reviewer must document, in a manner auditable by CMS, that the denial reflects independent clinical judgment rather than algorithmic output. This requirement should apply to all Medicare Advantage organizations and Medicaid managed care organizations regardless of whether their AI tools are developed in-house or procured from third-party vendors.⏎⏎2.   Algorithmic auditability requirements tied to CMS certification. Any AI system used in prior authorization or claims adjudication by a Medicare Advantage or Medicaid managed care organization should be subject to CMS certification requirements analogous to the requirements governing digitized medical charting platforms under the ONC Health IT Certification Program. Certification should require disclosure of training data sources, optimization objectives, validation methodology, and demographic performance disaggregation. Payers should be required to demonstrate, prior to deployment and at regular intervals thereafter, that their AI systems do not generate statistically significant disparities in denial rates across race, ethnicity, disability status, and income level. CMS should have authority to decertify AI tools that fail these requirements and to prohibit their use in federal health programs.⏎⏎3.   Standardized federal AI governance framework for payer-clearinghouse data interchange agreements. The Cooperative Exchange's policy review committee, meeting across four quarterly sessions in 2024, documented a consistent finding: payer-clearinghouse data interchange agreements are being renegotiated to include AI governance provisions, but there is no federal framework to anchor those negotiations. Individual clearinghouses lack the market power to impose adequate AI accountability requirements on major payers through bilateral contract negotiations. HHS should establish minimum federal standards for AI governance provisions in payer-clearinghouse agreements, including requirements for auditability, data lineage documentation, and notification obligations when AI models are retrained or updated. These standards should be developed in coordination with ASTP/ONC and should be compatible with existing de-identification and data use frameworks under 45 C.F.R. § 164.514.⏎⏎4.   Moratorium on new AI-driven prior authorization deployments pending equity impact assessment. HHS must enact a temporary halt regarding the deployment of new AI prior authorization and claims adjudication systems by Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care organizations until those organizations have completed and submitted to CMS a standardized equity impact assessment for each proposed system. The assessment should evaluate the system's projected impact on denial rates disaggregated by beneficiary demographics, document the clinical validation methodology used to establish that the system's outputs are consistent with evidence-based coverage criteria, and include an independent third-party audit. This is not a permanent prohibition on AI in prior authorization; it is a requirement that the evidence base for deployment meet a minimum standard before patients are affected.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 7⏎⏎⏎THE CLEARINGHOUSE PERSPECTIVE ON ADMINISTRATIVE AI⏎⏎The Cooperative Exchange does want to be direct about one thing that the RFI gets partially right: there is genuine potential for AI to reduce administrative burden in healthcare transactions, and The Cooperative Exchange's member organizations are actively exploring that potential. Seventy-three percent of our member clearinghouses were, as of our 2024 survey, piloting or evaluating AI-driven claims adjudication and routing workflows. The promise of those applications — faster routing, reduced rejection rates, more accurate eligibility verification — is real. The problem is not AI in administrative workflows per se. The problem is AI in denial determination, where the optimization target is financial rather than clinical and where the downstream consequences fall on patients who have no visibility into the algorithmic process being applied to their care.⏎⏎The 68 percent of our member organizations that cited the lack of uniform HHS directives on AI auditability and liability allocation as their primary barrier to full-scale deployment are not asking HHS to slow down AI adoption. They are asking HHS to give them a federal framework within which responsible AI deployment is legally and contractually legible. Right now, a clearinghouse that processes a prior authorization transaction through an AI-assisted routing system has no way to know whether the payer on the other end of that transaction is applying its own AI denial system in a manner that is auditable, clinically validated, or compliant with any federal standard — because no such standard exists. The absence of that framework is not just an equity problem. It is a liability problem for every organization in the transaction chain, and it is producing exactly the kind of contractual fragmentation that HHS's RFI should be trying to address.⏎⏎Dafny and Lee (2022, "The Good News About Health Care Consolidation — and the Risks We're Ignoring," New England Journal of Medicine, 386(10), 901-904) noted that market consolidation in healthcare creates conditions in which dominant players can impose data and process standards on smaller participants, and that the absence of federal guardrails in such environments tends to entrench the preferences of the most powerful actors. The market for AI-driven prior authorization is not a market of equally-positioned competitors where HHS can simply "foster competition" and expect beneficial outcomes to emerge. It is a market in which a small number of very large Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care organizations have already deployed AI tools optimized for cost containment, and in which the clearinghouses, providers, and patients on the other side of those transactions have no federal framework for challenging or auditing those tools.⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 8⏎⏎⏎REGARDING THE RFI'S QUESTION ON REGULATORY BARRIERS⏎⏎The RFI asks specifically about regulatory barriers to AI adoption that HHS might consider reducing. The Cooperative Exchange's response to that question is: the more pressing regulatory gap is not excess restriction but rather the almost complete void of any federal accountability framework for AI systems already deployed in prior authorization and claims adjudication. There is no federal requirement that a Medicare Advantage organization disclose to a beneficiary or a provider that a denial was generated by an AI system. There is no federal requirement that the AI system's outputs be clinically validated before deployment. There is no federal requirement that denial rates be disaggregated by race, ethnicity, or disability status and reported to CMS. There is no federal requirement that a payer notify its clearinghouse partners when it retrains or updates an AI model that affects transaction routing or adjudication outcomes. These are not theoretical gaps. They are operational gaps that our member organizations encounter in the course of processing 14 billion transactions per year, and they are gaps that the Senate PSI, the OIG, the GAO, and multiple peer-reviewed research teams have documented as producing measurable patient harm.⏎⏎The Cooperative Exchange is not asking HHS to halt AI development in healthcare. The member organizations of The Cooperative Exchange are themselves investing in AI. What The Cooperative Exchange is asking is that HHS not use the language of innovation and competition to avoid the harder regulatory work of establishing accountability standards for AI systems that are already operating, already affecting patient care, and already generating a documented record of disproportionate harm to the populations that Medicare and Medicaid exist to serve. The RFI's question about "reducing regulatory barriers" should be read alongside the Senate PSI's October 2024 finding that the absence of regulatory requirements for AI auditability and human review in prior authorization is itself the barrier — the barrier to patients receiving the care they are entitled to under their coverage.⏎⏎There is one additional operational detail that The Cooperative Exchange's member organizations have flagged as requiring specific HHS attention: the liability allocation question for AI-generated denial determinations in multi-party transaction chains is currently unresolved, and it is producing paralysis. When a clearinghouse routes a prior authorization request, a payer's AI system denies it, and the patient suffers a harm, who bears regulatory and legal liability? The payer? The AI vendor? The clearinghouse that facilitated the transaction? The physician who submitted the request? Current federal guidance does not answer that question, and the bilateral contract negotiations that our member organizations are engaged in with payers are producing inconsistent, idiosyncratic liability allocations that will not hold up to regulatory scrutiny once HHS or CMS begins examining AI-related patient harm at scale. HHS should address liability allocation in any forthcoming AI governance rulemaking, and it should do so in consultation with clearinghouses, not just with payers and provider organizations, because clearinghouses are the operational infrastructure through which most of these AI-assisted transactions actually flow. The Cooperative Exchange requests that HHS convene a specific working group on AI liability in administrative transactions, with clearinghouse representation, no later than the first quarter of fiscal year 2026.⏎⏎sharon.scott@connectedhealthinitiative.org⏎The Cooperative Exchange / Connected Health Initiative⏎Raleigh, NC 27601⏎⏎   Connected Health Initiative | Cooperative Exchange Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 9♔♔2026-01-27T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-27T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔12♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI-powered insurance decision-making automates prior authorization denials and coverage restrictions in ways that are opaque, unappealable, and systematically biased against vulnerable patients.♔advocacy_organization♔high♔supportive♔North Carolina♔senior policy analyst♔41♔A 2024 survey of The Cooperative Exchange's 214 member clearinghouses found that 73% are actively piloting or evaluating AI-driven claims adjudication and prior authorization workflows, yet 68% of those organizations cited the absence of standardized HHS guidance on AI auditability and liability allocation as their primary barrier to full-scale deployment. SYNTH-0084♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Thomas White♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via the Federal eRulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎WHAT MADE THAT MOMENT WORK⏎⏎Eighteen months ago, a retired mill worker came into the Eau Claire branch where I work. He was managing three chronic conditions and had just been discharged from a local hospital. He had a stack of paperwork he could not parse — medication schedules, follow-up instructions, a prior authorization form he did not know was a prior authorization form. We had recently piloted an AI-assisted reference tool, and I watched him use it to ask questions he had never known how to formulate before. By the end of that session, he understood his medication schedule in a way he had not when he left the hospital. I have thought about that afternoon a great deal since then, and I want to be honest about what I took from it, because I think my conclusion is different from the one HHS seems to be drawing.⏎⏎What made that interaction work was not the AI tool. The tool was useful, genuinely. But what made it work was that I knew this patron. I knew he had transportation constraints that meant the follow-up appointment listed on his paperwork was effectively inaccessible without intervention. I knew the community health worker program at the Chippewa Valley clinic sometimes had openings and sometimes did not. I knew he was proud and would not easily ask for help with things he felt he should already understand. None of that knowledge was in any database. None of it could have been retrieved by a system that did not already know him, and know the local ecosystem of care, in the way that a librarian who has worked the same branch for eleven years knows it. The AI tool gave him a better question. I knew what to do with the answer.⏎⏎Michael Polanyi spent a career arguing that skilled practice depends on knowledge that cannot be fully articulated, let alone encoded, and his 1966 work on the tacit dimension is not a historical curiosity. It is a direct challenge to any regulatory framework that treats knowledge work as though it is primarily about information retrieval. As I read the HHS request for information, I find myself asking if the Department has truly reckoned with this reality. The push toward "accelerating adoption" appears to assume the tasks targeted for automation are far simpler than they are in practice.⏎⏎THE COST QUESTION IS NOT A SIDE ISSUE⏎⏎The RFI asks broadly about reimbursement and regulatory barriers to AI adoption, and I want to address this directly, because I think it is where the stakes are most concrete for the people I serve. My patron from that afternoon is on a fixed income. He does not know what AI adoption in clinical settings will cost him. Neither, frankly, do I. But I have been paying attention, and what I have read does not reassure me.⏎⏎When a health system invests in AI infrastructure, that cost gets recovered somewhere. It may appear in facility fees. It may appear in the administrative complexity that already, according to a 2021 study by Sinsky and colleagues in the Annals of Internal Medicine, consumes a disproportionate share of physician time in ambulatory practice, time that was supposed to go to patients. It may appear in the slow erosion of the human workers who currently do the coordination work that AI systems are being positioned to replace. The GAO reported in 2023 (GAO-23-105412) that administrative and coordination roles in rural and underserved settings are already understaffed, persistently so, and that the workers who fill those roles are often the primary navigators for patients who cannot advocate for themselves. If AI adoption accelerates in ways that further reduce those positions, the efficiency gains accrue to the health system, and the cost is paid by patients who no longer have anyone to call when the portal does not work or the prior authorization is denied for the third time.⏎⏎I am not saying AI cannot help. I am saying that "accelerating adoption" as a regulatory goal, without a parallel commitment to protecting the human infrastructure that serves vulnerable patients, is a choice with distributional consequences HHS has not fully named in this RFI.⏎⏎WHAT THE LIBRARY ANALOGY ACTUALLY SUGGESTS⏎⏎Libraries went through a version of this. When catalog systems were digitized, when reference databases came online, when search engines made it possible for anyone to find a citation without asking a librarian, there was a period of institutional enthusiasm that looked a lot like what I see in this RFI. The technology was real. The efficiency gains were real. And a generation of library administrators concluded, not unreasonably but incorrectly, that the skilled work of reference librarians could be substantially automated.⏎⏎What actually happened is well documented in library science literature and does not need extensive rehearsal here. The patrons who had always been able to navigate information systems continued to do so, now faster. The patrons who had depended on human mediation, who needed someone to understand not just their question but their situation, found themselves without adequate support. The gap between information-rich and information-poor did not close. In many settings, it widened. The parallel to clinical care seems to me close enough to be worth taking seriously.⏎⏎Friedman and colleagues, in a 2022 mixed-methods study in the Journal of General Internal Medicine, found that patient navigation in safety-net settings depends heavily on contextual knowledge that algorithms are not designed to hold: knowledge about which specialist will actually see a Medicaid patient on short notice, which community organizations have current capacity, how to talk to a particular patient about a sensitive diagnosis given what the navigator already knows about that patient's history. Their finding that algorithmic triage tools frequently failed to account for these contextual factors, and that this failure fell disproportionately on the most vulnerable patients, is not a minor caveat to an otherwise positive efficiency story. It is the main story for the people I am thinking about when I write this comment.⏎⏎STRUCTURED DATA ENCODES WHAT WAS ALREADY THERE⏎⏎There is a technical point that I think deserves more attention in HHS's framing than it has received. AI systems trained on administrative and clinical data do not produce neutral outputs. They produce outputs shaped by the data they were trained on, and that data encodes the inequities already present in the system. In 2019, Ziad Obermeyer and his co-authors published research in Science that ought to be mandatory reading for anyone shaping health care AI rules. They showed how a major commercial tool built for population health management consistently undervalued the medical requirements of Black individuals. This happened not by malicious design, but because the model relied on past medical spending to estimate medical necessity, ignoring the reality that Black individuals historically receive less care for the same level of sickness. The model was, in a formal sense, working correctly. The problem was upstream, baked into the training information.⏎⏎I raise this not to argue against AI adoption but to argue that deciding what gets accelerated, and for whom, is inseparable from understanding what the underlying data reflects. A system that accelerates triage for patients whose data is rich and whose histories are well-documented in electronic records will produce different outcomes than a system serving patients who have moved frequently, who have used safety-net providers with fragmented records, who have avoided the health system for reasons that do not appear anywhere in a structured data field. The Eau Claire patron I mentioned at the beginning of this comment had a twenty-year gap in his medical records because he had not had insurance for most of his working life. An AI system that had access to his structured clinical history would have had access to very little. What it would have missed is precisely what a human navigator, working in context, would have known to ask about.⏎⏎THE ADMINISTRATIVE EFFICIENCY FRAMING DESERVES SCRUTINY⏎⏎HHS's request for information treats administrative burden reduction as an unambiguous good, and I understand why. Prior authorization delays kill people. Eligibility errors strand patients. Documentation requirements consume physician time that could go to care. These are real problems. But the National Partnership for Women and Families published a 2022 report on automated prior authorization and eligibility systems that found a consistent pattern: automation reduced processing time for straightforward cases and increased error rates for complex ones, with the errors concentrated among patients with multiple conditions, non-standard coverage situations, or limited capacity to appeal. The efficiency gain was real. So was the harm. The two did not cancel out; they fell on different people.⏎⏎Ash, Berg, and Coiera wrote in a 2004 paper in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association about unintended consequences of health information technology, and their observation that new systems tend to create new categories of error even as they eliminate old ones seems to me still accurate and still underweighted in policy discussions. The errors that humans make in administrative coordination are visible and attributable. The errors that automated systems make are often invisible until they accumulate into a pattern, and by then, the human workers who might have caught individual errors early have been reduced or eliminated.⏎⏎I genuinely do not know how to weigh these tradeoffs in the abstract. I suspect HHS does not either, which is perhaps why the RFI is framed as broadly as it is. What I would ask is that the Department resist the pressure to treat acceleration as the metric. Speed of adoption is not the same as quality of adoption, and in health care, the cost of a bad adoption is not borne by the institution that made the decision.⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD ACKNOWLEDGE BEFORE MOVING FORWARD⏎⏎The framing of this RFI assumes a baseline where the primary barriers to AI adoption are regulatory and reimbursement-related, and where removing those barriers will produce broadly positive outcomes. That assumption may be correct in some settings and for some applications. For the patients I have in mind, the retired mill worker and the many others who come to the Eau Claire branch because they do not know where else to go, I am not confident the assumption holds.⏎⏎Before HHS moves to accelerate adoption, I would ask the Department to do something more basic: map what administrative and coordination workers actually do, in the granular sense that Polanyi would have recognized as prerequisite to any serious automation project. Not what their job titles say. Not what their workflows produce on paper. What knowledge they hold that is not recorded anywhere, what relationships they maintain that make the system navigable for patients who cannot navigate it alone, what exceptions and workarounds they manage that would not appear in any training dataset. The GAO workforce report I cited earlier gestures at this but does not go far enough; the shortage data it documents is real, but shortage data does not capture the qualitative dimension of what is being lost when these positions go unfilled or get eliminated.⏎⏎I am genuinely hopeful about what AI can do in clinical settings, including for the patients who have the least. The interaction I described at the beginning of this comment was real, and the clarity it gave one man about his own care was not trivial. But that moment was possible because a human being with contextual knowledge was present to scaffold it. If HHS's regulatory and reimbursement actions produce a clinical environment where artificial intelligence is heavily integrated and the human workers who know how to use it in context have been systematically reduced, the technology will have been deployed and the patients who most needed help will be worse off than before.⏎⏎There is also the cost question I raised earlier, which I want to return to because I do not think it got a complete answer above. My patron is on a fixed income. When new technology gets adopted in health settings, someone pays for it, and it is rarely the health system absorbing the cost indefinitely. Whether that cost shows up in premiums, in facility fees, in reduced access as smaller safety-net providers find they cannot afford compliant systems, or in some other form I have not anticipated, I would ask HHS to model it explicitly before accelerating anything. The people who will be harmed by a poorly designed adoption process are not the people who will be in the room when these decisions get made, and they are not well-positioned to appeal after the fact.⏎⏎I recognize this comment does not fit neatly into the RFI's question structure, and I apologize for that. I am a librarian, not a health policy professional. But I have spent enough time watching people try to navigate a system that was not designed with them in mind to feel that this comment was worth submitting, even if the framing is imperfect. SYNTH-0085♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Paul Allen♔American Physical Therapy Association♔♔♔♔♔American Physical Therapy Association⏎1111 North Fairfax Street⏎Alexandria, VA 22314⏎⏎Paul Allen, Senior Policy Analyst⏎Government Affairs and Health Policy⏎⏎April 14, 2025⏎⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary⏎U.S. Department of Health and Human Services⏎200 Independence Avenue, S.W.⏎Washington, D.C. 20201⏎⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎---⏎⏎APTA COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI — CLINICAL CARE ADOPTION | Page 1⏎⏎TO THE OFFICE OF THE DEPUTY SECRETARY:⏎⏎The American Physical Therapy Association (APTA) submits these comments in response to the Department's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. APTA represents more than 100,000 physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, and students practicing across every care setting in the United States, including outpatient clinics, acute care hospitals, post-acute rehabilitation facilities, and school-based programs. The Department's RFI raises questions that are directly relevant to that membership, particularly regarding reimbursement pathways and regulatory clarity for AI-assisted clinical decision support tools. However, the framing of the RFI — which treats acceleration as the primary policy objective — inverts what APTA regards as the correct sequencing. Before the Department moves to accelerate anything, it must first construct the accountability infrastructure that makes acceleration responsible.⏎⏎APTA's position is grounded in data that predates this RFI by nearly a year. A 2024 member survey conducted by the Association for Diagnostics and Laboratory Medicine (ADLM 2024) found that fewer than one in five responding institutions reported that existing reimbursement pathways adequately accounted for the validation and quality-oversight infrastructure that AI-assisted diagnostic tools require. The median time from AI platform procurement to clinical integration exceeded 14 months, with regulatory ambiguity and payer coverage uncertainty identified as the two primary bottlenecks. APTA's own member feedback from 2024 reflects an almost identical pattern in rehabilitation settings: physical therapists are being asked to adopt AI-assisted movement analysis tools, gait assessment platforms, and clinical decision support systems (CDSS) for post-surgical rehabilitation planning, and they are doing so without any coherent federal guidance about who bears legal responsibility when those tools contribute to a patient harm event.⏎⏎---⏎⏎APTA COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI — CLINICAL CARE ADOPTION | Page 2⏎⏎THE ACCOUNTABILITY VACUUM — WHY THIS IS AN ARCHITECTURAL PROBLEM⏎⏎The Department's RFI asks, among other things, whether private-sector accreditation and certification schemes could serve as a primary mechanism for ensuring AI tool quality and safety in clinical environments. APTA regards this as a category error, and the Association wants to be direct about that characterization. Accreditation can certify that a tool performs as specified under defined conditions. It cannot assign moral or legal responsibility when a patient is harmed by a clinical decision that no single identifiable human being owned. The problem is not a gap that credentialing organizations can fill, because the problem is structural: AI intermediation severs the causal chain between decision and decision-maker that all existing liability doctrines presuppose.⏎⏎Price, Gerke, and Cohen (JAMA 2019) identified this problem with considerable precision, noting that the standard negligence framework requires a plaintiff to demonstrate that a specific defendant breached a specific duty of care, and that AI-assisted decisions distribute that duty across tool developers, institutional deployers, clinician users, and the opaque algorithmic logic of the system itself in ways that existing respondeat superior doctrine cannot cleanly resolve. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020) extended that analysis to observe that the learned intermediary doctrine — which historically has shielded manufacturers from direct liability when a licensed professional exercises independent clinical judgment — may not apply when the AI system's recommendation is presented in a format that forecloses meaningful independent review. Sendak et al. (2020) documented exactly that dynamic in a clinical deployment study, finding that clinicians frequently could not articulate why a deep-learning system had generated a particular recommendation, which raises obvious questions about whether any "intermediary" judgment was occurring at all.⏎⏎The Department should also consider what peer jurisdictions have concluded about this problem. The European Parliament's AI Liability Directive (2022/0303(COD), 2023) represents a legislative acknowledgment that existing tort frameworks are insufficient to handle AI-mediated harms, and that burden-shifting mechanisms — requiring AI developers and deployers to disclose system outputs and demonstrate compliance — are necessary precisely because the opacity of these systems makes traditional causation proof nearly impossible for injured patients. The United States has no equivalent framework. The GAO documented this gap in its 2022 report on AI in health care (GAO-22-104629), noting that federal oversight of AI-enabled clinical tools remains fragmented across FDA, ONC, and CMS with no unified accountability standard. That fragmentation has not been resolved in the three years since that report was published.⏎⏎---⏎⏎APTA COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI — CLINICAL CARE ADOPTION | Page 3⏎⏎SPECIFIC CONCERNS REGARDING REIMBURSEMENT AND PHYSICAL THERAPY PRACTICE⏎⏎APTA wishes to address the Department's questions regarding reimbursement pathways with particular specificity, because the current coding environment creates a perverse incentive structure that the RFI does not appear to recognize. The existing Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) framework does not include codes that adequately capture AI-assisted clinical workflows in physical therapy. When a physical therapist uses an AI-enabled gait analysis platform — the kind now being marketed by at least a dozen vendors to outpatient rehabilitation practices, including practices with fewer than ten clinicians — the professional work involved in reviewing, validating, and potentially overriding the system's output is not separately reimbursable. The clinician absorbs that cognitive and temporal burden without any corresponding payment adjustment. This is not a theoretical concern; APTA members in Michigan, Ohio, and Pennsylvania have reported that the overhead cost of maintaining validation protocols for AI tools — including staff time for quality review, documentation of override decisions, and participation in post-market surveillance activities — is running between $3,000 and $8,000 per year per tool for small practices.⏎⏎The billing data analysis corroborating the ADLM (2024) survey findings identified a persistent gap between clinical utility demonstrated in peer-reviewed literature and the reimbursement codes available to capture AI-enabled workflows. That gap is as real in physical therapy as it is in laboratory medicine. Cohen et al. (2014) noted years ago that the legal and ethical concerns arising from complex predictive analytics in health care are inseparable from the economic structures that govern their deployment, and the reimbursement gap is itself an accountability failure: it means that the financial incentive to adopt AI tools outpaces any financial incentive to maintain the human oversight infrastructure those tools require.⏎⏎APTA's specific reimbursement recommendations are as follows:⏎⏎1. CMS should convene a technical expert panel, including rehabilitation medicine representation, to evaluate whether existing CPT codes adequately capture AI-assisted clinical workflows in physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech-language pathology settings, with a report due no later than December 31, 2025.⏎⏎2. Any new reimbursement codes or payment adjustments created to support AI tool adoption should include an explicit component for validation and oversight activities, not merely for the AI-generated output itself.⏎⏎3. CMS should require that any Medicare Advantage plan covering AI-assisted clinical decision support in outpatient rehabilitation settings disclose, in machine-readable format, the coverage determination criteria applied to those tools, consistent with the transparency principles articulated in ONC's 2023 Draft Strategy on AI in Health IT (88 Fed. Reg. 21,082).⏎⏎4. HHS should direct ONC to develop standardized application programming interface (API) specifications for AI tool output documentation in rehabilitation settings, so that clinician override decisions are captured in the electronic health record (EHR) in a form that is auditable and usable for post-market surveillance.⏎⏎---⏎⏎APTA COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI — CLINICAL CARE ADOPTION | Page 4⏎⏎THE BIAS PROBLEM CANNOT BE DEFERRED⏎⏎APTA also wants to register a concern that the RFI does not address with sufficient seriousness: the differential performance of AI tools across patient populations defined by race, ethnicity, disability status, and socioeconomic background. Obermeyer and Topol (2021) documented that AI systems trained on historically biased clinical data reproduce and in some cases amplify those biases in deployment, and that patients from marginalized groups bear a disproportionate share of the resulting harm. Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert (2020) established that malpractice liability functions as a quality signal in health care, but only when the causal chain between decision and harm is traceable. When AI intermediation obscures that chain, the liability signal weakens precisely for the patient populations least able to absorb the harm. Pasquale (2020) has argued — persuasively, in APTA's view — that the appropriate response is not to optimize algorithmic performance but to establish non-delegable human accountability for clinical decisions, regardless of the tools used to inform them.⏎⏎Physical therapy is not immune to this problem. AI tools for movement analysis and functional capacity assessment have been validated primarily on datasets that overrepresent younger, non-disabled, white male subjects. When those tools are deployed with elderly patients, patients with neurological conditions, or patients from communities with limited prior access to rehabilitation services, the performance gap is not theoretical. APTA is not in a position to quantify that gap with precision — the post-market surveillance infrastructure to do so does not currently exist, which is itself a regulatory failure the Department should address before accelerating deployment further.⏎⏎---⏎⏎APTA COMMENTS | HHS AI RFI — CLINICAL CARE ADOPTION | Page 5⏎⏎APTA's overarching position is this: the Department must not finalize any acceleration framework for AI in clinical care until it has proposed, solicited public comment on, and adopted a clear regulatory rule specifying which party bears non-delegable legal responsibility for AI-assisted clinical decisions. That rule must address the developer, the institutional deployer, and the treating clinician, and it must do so in a way that does not permit any of those parties to disclaim responsibility by pointing to another node in the chain. The EU AI Liability Directive (European Parliament 2023) demonstrates that this kind of rule is both legally feasible and politically achievable in a democratic system with a mixed public-private health care environment. The strict liability framework proposed in that directive for high-risk AI applications is a reasonable starting point for HHS to evaluate, though APTA recognizes that the U.S. legislative context differs in important respects.⏎⏎The accountability infrastructure that would make AI adoption safe in clinical settings is not a luxury to be constructed after the market has matured. Topol (2019) and the broader literature on high-performance medicine have documented the genuine clinical potential of AI tools, and APTA does not dispute that potential. What APTA disputes is the assumption embedded in this RFI that acceleration and accountability can be sequenced — that the Department can move fast on deployment and catch up on liability later. The history of health care technology adoption does not support that assumption, and the 14-month median integration lag documented in ADLM (2024) suggests that the market is already moving faster than the regulatory environment can track.⏎⏎APTA appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and requests that the Department specifically acknowledge, in any subsequent notice of proposed rulemaking arising from this RFI, the question of non-delegable liability for AI-assisted clinical decisions. SYNTH-0086♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Stephanie Moore♔Veeva Systems♔♔♔♔♔Veeva Systems Compliance Practice < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 1⏎⏎COMMENT OF VEEVA SYSTEMS COMPLIANCE PRACTICE⏎In Response to HHS Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎For the majority of the previous twenty-four months, the compliance monitoring division at Veeva Systems has been entrenched in the day-to-day operational mechanics of implementing AI-assisted clinical decision support. We collaborated with 47 health system partners between the first quarter of 2023 and the third quarter of 2024. Rather than yielding rosy adoption statistics, this initiative generated a highly detailed log of where the liability for AI-influenced medical choices ultimately lands when adverse events occur. Across 112 evaluated clinical locations, the documented reality is that responsibility lands on no one in particular. This submission challenges the underlying premise of the Request for Information, which presumes that the main hurdles to artificial intelligence integration are regulatory hurdles and payment uncertainties. We contend that the Department has diagnosed the wrong core issue. The foundational flaw in the existing implementation framework is not merely the confusion around payment channels—although that exists, with 68% of our reviewed facilities citing CMS billing code vagueness as a bottleneck. Instead, the critical failure is the absence of a legally and ethically accountable entity when an algorithm-supported suggestion leads to patient injury. The Department is attempting to fast-track an infrastructure where this liability void is fundamentally ingrained, yet the current RFI lacks any mechanism to correct this before unlocking certification and payment avenues.⏎⏎Veeva Systems Compliance Practice < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 2⏎⏎Stating the underlying legal predicament is straightforward. In the United States, medical malpractice frameworks inherently rely on a specific human actor whose medical discretion can be measured against established standards of care (Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, & Studdert, 2020, JAMA, 323(4), 352-366). Once an algorithmic platform offers a medical suggestion that a doctor follows, adjusts, or rejects while facing tight time constraints, determining who is at fault for any subsequent injury becomes deeply disputed. Current legal principles simply were not constructed to handle these disputes (Price, Gerke, & Cohen, 2019, JAMA, 322(18), 1765-1766). Software developers will claim their product functioned exactly as designed. Medical facilities will maintain that the prescribing provider held ultimate decision-making power. The provider will counter that the software's recommendation carried institutional weight, meaning any deviation demanded extensive defense. We are not describing an imagined courtroom battle; this is the exact setup of every algorithmic clinical process our oversight personnel have audited. Hoffman and Podgurski (2023, American Journal of Law and Medicine, 49(1), 5-38) refer to this phenomenon as the liability deficit in algorithm-supported healthcare, a deficit that tweaking payment codes will never bridge. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen (2020, Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare, Academic Press, pp. 295-336) note identical foundational confusion where product defect laws meet professional malpractice standards. A full ten years ago, Cohen, Amarasingham, Shah, Xie, and Lo (2014, Health Affairs, 33(7), 1139-1147) highlighted comparable worries regarding predictive modeling, yet our jurisprudence remains practically unaltered today.⏎⏎What actually has shifted is how deeply these applications have infiltrated patient care settings. The dynamic Elish (2019, Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, 5, 40-60) termed the "moral crumple zone" perfectly captures what our facility audits show: the frontline medical worker ultimately shoulders the culpability for algorithmic mistakes, despite lacking true independent control when the mistake occurred. Sendak et al. (2020, ACM FAT*, pp. 99-109) noted that medical professionals often defer to machine learning conclusions specifically because the underlying logic is hidden, creating the exact environment where this displaced blame is most hazardous. The recent HTI-1 Final Rule from ONC (89 Fed. Reg. 1192, 2024) mandated visibility standards for these support mechanisms. While helpful, knowing the internal mechanics of a model provides zero clarity to a judge or an injured individual regarding who holds legal culpability for a damaging result. Delvecchio Good and Hannah (2015, Journal of Law and the Biosciences, 2(3), 618-641) previously raised parallel arguments regarding the ethical shifting of blame that happens when software is injected into medical interactions absent defined liability frameworks.⏎⏎Veeva Systems Compliance Practice < > HHS Health Sector AI RFI < > Docket No. HHS-2024-AI-001 < > Page 3⏎⏎Within the Request for Information, the Department inquires about potential administrative maneuvers to hasten the rollout of these technologies. From the perspective of our compliance division, pushing for speed before a solid liability framework is built is an administrative route the Department must strictly avoid. We offer the following concrete directive:⏎⏎1. The Department must mandate that before any novel algorithmic payment channel or certification route is approved, the implementing organization must publish a binding liability matrix. This document must clearly name the legally answerable entity for every type of medical choice the software is intended to sway.⏎⏎2. At a bare minimum, this matrix must delineate: (a) who holds fault if the algorithmic suggestion is followed exactly and results in injury; (b) who holds fault if the suggestion is rejected and that rejection results in injury; and (c) the method for distributing fault when a provider's rejection was indirectly shaped by previous software suggestions during that specific patient visit.⏎⏎3. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services must demand that any algorithmic decision aid petitioning for payment approval submit this liability matrix during the initial coverage evaluation phase, rather than treating it as an afterthought for post-market surveillance.⏎⏎Our partner organizations faced an average of $340,000 in unforeseen regulatory costs while integrating external algorithmic components into certified electronic health records to meet ONC interoperability rules. That financial burden is entirely real, and our oversight team has dedicated immense resources to managing it. However, financial burdens can be recouped. An individual suffering physical injury due to an algorithm-influenced medical mistake, while lacking any legally accountable entity to pursue, represents a fundamentally distinct crisis. The timeline the Department currently suggests—unlocking payment avenues immediately while figuring out liability structures down the line—is completely contradicted by the operational realities we observed across these 47 institutional partners. We are prepared to supply the Department's personnel with full documentation from these audits upon inquiry.
