SYNTH-0087♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔George Harris♔University of California San Francisco Institute for Computational Health Sciences♔♔♔♔♔George Harris, Ph.D.⏎Health Economist, Institute for Computational Health Sciences⏎University of California San Francisco⏎San Francisco, CA 94143⏎⏎Submitted via regulations.gov⏎Docket: HHS-2024-AI-RFI-Clinical-Care⏎⏎UCSF INSTITUTE FOR COMPUTATIONAL HEALTH SCIENCES⏎COMMENTS ON HHS REQUEST FOR INFORMATION: ACCELERATING AI ADOPTION IN CLINICAL CARE⏎⏎RE: Health Sector AI Request for Information — Equity Auditing Requirements and Post-Deployment Bias Surveillance⏎⏎The framing of this RFI is, to put it plainly, backwards. HHS has organized its questions around the mechanics of acceleration — reimbursement levers, regulatory streamlining, R&D investment priorities — without first establishing what conditions must be satisfied before acceleration is warranted. The Department appears to have concluded that broad AI adoption in clinical care is the goal, and that the task remaining is to identify friction points and remove them. This submission argues that this sequencing is not a technicality but a substantive policy error, and that the populations who will bear the costs of that error are, with a high degree of predictability, the same populations that American healthcare has systematically underserved for generations.⏎⏎This is not a general argument against AI in clinical care. The efficiency case for well-validated computational tools is real. A 2024 survey conducted by the College of American Pathologists encompassing more than 1,200 pathology practices and academic medical centers found that machine-assisted diagnostic tools, where successfully deployed, produced modeled time-to-diagnosis improvements with an estimated foregone efficiency value of approximately $1.4 billion annually when adoption gaps are factored in (CAP Annual Meeting, 2024). That number is worth taking seriously. Rajpurkar, Chen, Banerjee, and Topol (2022) have similarly documented genuine performance gains across radiology, pathology, and genomics contexts where machine learning platforms were developed and validated on representative data. The question this submission presses is not whether those gains are real, but who captures them and who absorbs the costs when the tools fail — and the empirical record on that distributional question is considerably less flattering to the accelerationist posture than the RFI implies.⏎⏎< > UCSF ICHS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 2 < >⏎⏎THE EMPIRICAL RECORD REGARDING COMPUTATIONAL PREJUDICE IN CLINICAL SETTINGS⏎⏎The bias problem in health AI is not hypothetical and it is not confined to edge cases. Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan (2019) showed in Science that an extensively adopted proprietary population care model consistently downplayed illness severity in Black patients relative to white patients with equivalent health status. This occurred because the computational tool relied upon financial expenditure as a substitute for clinical necessity—an alternative variable that encodes decades of differential access to care. The tool was not designed to discriminate; it was built utilizing data that reflected a system that already did. That distinction, which the RFI does not appear to register at all, is the central problem. Training data in American healthcare is not a neutral archive. It is a record of who received care, when, at what intensity, and under what circumstances — and those parameters are not randomly distributed across race, income, and geography (Vyas, Eisenstein, and Jones, 2020; Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk, 2018).⏎⏎Sjoding, Dickson, Iwashyna, Gay, and Valley (2020) documented in the New England Journal of Medicine that pulse oximeters, a technology so basic it predates the current AI discussion by decades, produce systematically less accurate readings in patients with darker skin tones — a finding that had been buried in the literature for years before it achieved policy visibility. The reason it achieved that visibility when it did is instructive: it took a pandemic that made pulse oximetry central to triage decisions for the error to be measured at scale. This is the retrospective detection dynamic that this submission is most concerned about. Wong, Otles, Donnelly, Krumm, and colleagues (2021) conducted an external validation of Epic's widely implemented Sepsis Prediction Model across multiple hospital systems and found that the model's performance degraded substantially in deployment contexts that differed from its training environment, with particularly poor calibration in patient subgroups underrepresented in the original training data. Adamson and Smith (2018) documented in JAMA Dermatology that dermatology AI trained predominantly on images of lighter skin tones produced diagnostic accuracy that degraded significantly for darker skin tones — a finding that has since been replicated across multiple systems and imaging modalities (Celi et al., 2022).⏎⏎What these examples share is a structural pattern, not a series of isolated product failures. Seyyed-Kalantari, Zhang, McDermott, Chen, and Ghassemi (2021) showed in Nature Medicine that computational models applied to chest radiographs systematically underperformed for marginalized patient populations — patients who were uninsured, patients from lower-income zip codes, patients lacking English proficiency — and that this underperformance was not detectable from aggregate performance metrics. The tools appeared to perform well when evaluated at the population level. The disparity was visible only when performance was broken down by demographic categories. This is not a minor methodological footnote. It means that the standard validation framework that the FDA and the broader clinical AI community currently relies upon is structurally inadequate to detect the harms that are most likely to occur in the populations most dependent on safety-net institutions.⏎⏎< > UCSF ICHS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3 < >⏎⏎THE VALIDATION-TO-DEPLOYMENT DEGRADATION PROBLEM⏎⏎The CAP survey determined that under 22% of facilities that evaluated an AI-assisted diagnostic tool successfully integrated it into routine clinical workflows, a statistic worth examining more carefully than the RFI's framing invites. The Department appears to read low adoption as evidence of friction to be removed. An equally valid reading is that facilities are correctly identifying that tools validated in one context do not perform reliably in their context — and that the 22% who have integrated these tools skew toward well-resourced academic medical centers, not community hospitals or rural critical access facilities. The CAP data further indicated that facilities operating under value-based payment arrangements reported adoption rates nearly 2.5 times higher than those reimbursed exclusively under fee-for-service structures. This is consistent with Wiens, Saria, Sendak, Ghassemi, Liu, Doshi-Velez, and colleagues' (2019) argument in Nature Medicine that deployment context is not separable from tool performance — that the same model, deployed in a different institutional environment with different patient populations and different clinical workflows, is in a meaningful sense a different tool. The validation-to-deployment gap is not a transition problem that better implementation support will solve. It is an inherent property of models trained on non-representative data deployed in contexts that differ systematically from their training environments.⏎⏎This matters for HHS's reimbursement question in a specific way. If CMS creates reimbursement pathways for AI-assisted clinical services without conditioning those pathways on demonstrated performance equity across patient subgroups and care settings, the Department will be creating a financial incentive structure that rewards deployment regardless of whether that deployment produces equitable outcomes. Well-resourced institutions with homogeneous patient populations and robust IT infrastructure will capture the reimbursement; safety-net institutions serving Medicaid patients, uninsured patients, and patients lacking English proficiency will deploy tools that underperform for their populations while facing the same reimbursement uncertainty the RFI correctly identifies as a barrier. This is not speculation about what might happen. It is a description of the pattern that has already emerged in the limited deployment data available (Char, Shah, and Magnus, 2018). The efficiency gains accrue disproportionately to the institutions that need them least. The harms concentrate in the institutions that can least afford to absorb them.⏎⏎AUTOMATION BIAS AND THE DETECTION PROBLEM⏎⏎Sendak, Elish, Gao, Futoma, Ratliff, and colleagues (2020) documented at the ACM FAccT conference that clinical decision support tools, precisely because they present outputs with apparent algorithmic authority, suppress the critical scrutiny that clinicians would ordinarily apply to equivalent outputs from human colleagues. This is the automation bias mechanism, and it has a specific implication for the bias detection problem that the RFI does not address. When a human clinician makes an error attributable to implicit bias, the error is at least in principle visible as a human judgment that could have been made differently. When an AI system produces a biased recommendation, the clinician who accepts that recommendation without scrutiny does not experience it as a judgment at all — it is a data output, and the institutional feedback loops that would ordinarily flag a pattern of errors are not calibrated to detect patterns in algorithmic outputs. Celi and colleagues (2022) make this point in their global review of bias sources in health AI: the same properties that make AI tools attractive from an efficiency standpoint — consistency, speed, apparent objectivity — make the errors those tools produce harder to detect and correct than equivalent human errors. HHS has not proposed any mechanism to address this. The RFI does not ask about post-deployment surveillance. It does not ask about disaggregated performance monitoring. It asks about adoption barriers, as though the primary problem the Department has identified is that these tools are not being used enough.⏎⏎< > UCSF ICHS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4 < >⏎⏎WHAT MANDATORY EQUITY AUDITING WOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎The submission's specific policy demand, responsive to the RFI's questions regarding regulatory and reimbursement actions, is the following. HHS should condition any CMS reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services on the satisfaction of pre-deployment and post-deployment equity requirements that include, at minimum:⏎⏎1. Pre-deployment equity auditing conducted by an independent third party, with performance metrics broken down by cultural background, socioeconomic status, primary language, insurance status, and care setting. Aggregate performance metrics are insufficient, as Seyyed-Kalantari et al. (2021) documented; subgroup performance must be reported separately and must meet defined minimum performance thresholds before a tool is eligible for reimbursement.⏎⏎2. Public reporting of disaggregated performance metrics at the time of FDA clearance or authorization, with mandatory updates at defined intervals post-deployment. The current FDA framework does not require this. The 510(k) pathway and the De Novo pathway both permit clearance based on aggregate performance data, and there is no requirement that developers report performance separately for demographic subgroups or for care settings that differ from the validation environment.⏎⏎3. Post-deployment bias surveillance as a condition of continued reimbursement eligibility, with standardized data collection requirements that permit performance comparison across institutions and patient populations. This is analogous to the post-market surveillance requirements FDA applies to certain high-risk medical devices, and there is no principled reason why AI tools that influence clinical decisions at scale should be subject to weaker ongoing monitoring requirements than a cardiac stent.⏎⏎4. A mandatory re-evaluation requirement triggered when a tool is deployed in a care setting that differs substantively from the validation environment — specifically, when the demographic composition of the deployment population differs by defined thresholds from the training population, or when the institutional infrastructure (EHR system, laboratory reference ranges, patient acuity mix) differs in ways likely to affect model calibration. Wiens et al. (2019) articulated the technical basis for this requirement clearly; what is needed is a regulatory operationalization of that principle.⏎⏎The objection that these requirements would slow adoption is, frankly, the argument this submission is most impatient with. The CAP data shows that adoption is already slow — 22% successful integration despite 68% evaluation. The barriers the CAP survey identified as most commonly pointed to were reimbursement uncertainty, lack of FDA clearance pathways, and unresolved liability frameworks. Equity auditing requirements are not on that list, which suggests that the institutions that have evaluated these tools are not declining to adopt them because the equity requirements are too burdensome. They are declining for other reasons. Removing reimbursement uncertainty while leaving the equity auditing gap unaddressed does not solve the adoption problem; it just changes the conditions under which adoption occurs, in ways that make the distributional consequences of that adoption less visible and less correctable.⏎⏎< > UCSF ICHS Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 5 < >⏎⏎A NOTE ON THE POLICY CHOICE HHS IS MAKING BY OMISSION⏎⏎It is worth being direct about what the Department's current posture amounts to as a policy choice. HHS is proposing to use its reimbursement authority to accelerate adoption of a class of tools with a documented and empirically characterized tendency to perform differentially across demographic groups, in an environment where there are no mandatory requirements to measure or report that differential performance, and where the post-deployment surveillance infrastructure to detect emerging disparities at scale does not exist. The argument that these requirements can be developed after the reimbursement incentives are in place gets the sequence exactly wrong. Once a reimbursement pathway is established and institutions have made capital investments in particular tools and vendor relationships, the political economy of adding performance equity requirements changes dramatically. The tools are already deployed. The contracts are already signed. The argument becomes: these requirements would disrupt care delivery. That argument will win, and the disparities will persist.⏎⏎Gianfrancesco, Tamang, Yazdany, and Schmajuk (2018) identified in JAMA Internal Medicine that digital medical charting data, which is the primary substrate on which most clinical AI platforms are constructed, carries systematic biases arising from differential documentation practices, differential coding intensity, and differential access to specialty care — biases that are not visible in the data itself and cannot be corrected post-hoc without deliberate and resource-intensive data curation. The implication is that the burden of ensuring equity cannot be placed on downstream clinical users; it must be placed on developers as a pre-market condition, and it must be enforced through the reimbursement mechanism that HHS controls. The Department has that authority. The question the RFI does not ask — but that this submission insists is the right question — is under what conditions HHS is willing to use it.⏎⏎One additional concern that has not been adequately addressed in the RFI's framing: the CAP survey data showing a 2.5x adoption rate differential between value-based and fee-for-service settings suggests that the reimbursement structure shapes not just whether AI tools are adopted but which institutions adopt them first. Value-based arrangements are concentrated in larger, more integrated health systems with more homogeneous, commercially insured patient populations. Fee-for-service is disproportionately the reimbursement reality for safety-net institutions, rural hospitals, and Federally Qualified Health Centers. If HHS designs its AI reimbursement interventions without accounting for this structural asymmetry, it will accelerate adoption in the settings where the tools are most likely to perform well on populations that look like the training data, while the institutions most dependent on federal support to modernize — and most likely to serve patients whose characteristics diverge from those training populations — will continue to face the uncertainty the RFI correctly identifies as a barrier. That is not an argument for leaving reimbursement uncertainty unresolved. It is an argument for resolving it in a way that makes performance equity a precondition of reimbursement eligibility rather than an aspiration that the market is expected to eventually produce on its own.⏎⏎The specific mechanism this submission recommends for operationalizing the post-deployment surveillance requirement is a condition attached to the Medicare coverage determination process: any AI-assisted clinical service for which CMS establishes a reimbursement code must be accompanied by a data submission requirement under which the billing institution reports, at defined intervals, disaggregated utilization and outcome data sufficient to permit CMS to monitor for differential performance across patient subgroups. The technical infrastructure for this already partially exists in the form of the Medicare claims data infrastructure and the ONC-certified health IT reporting requirements; what is needed is a policy decision to use that infrastructure for equity monitoring rather than treating it purely as a billing and compliance mechanism. Whether HHS is prepared to make that decision is, in the end, the question this RFI should be asking, and it is conspicuously the question the RFI does not ask.♔♔2026-02-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-05T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔8♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI systems in healthcare inherit and amplify racial, socioeconomic, and institutional biases from training data, and their apparent authority makes those biases harder to detect and correct than human error.♔academic_organization♔high♔frustrated♔Illinois♔health economist♔37♔A 2024 CAP member survey encompassing responses from more than 1,200 pathology practices and academic medical centers found that 68% had evaluated at least one AI-assisted diagnostic tool within the preceding 24 months, yet fewer than 22% had successfully integrated such a tool into routine clinical workflows—citing reimbursement uncertainty, lack of FDA clearance pathways, and unresolved liability frameworks as the three most commonly cited structural barriers. SYNTH-0088♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Edward Campbell♔Epic Research♔♔♔♔♔RBMA Comments < > HHS AI RFI Docket < > Page 1⏎⏎⏎⏎The Radiology Business Management Association (RBMA) submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. RBMA represents more than 2,400 radiology practice administrators, executive directors, and operational leaders across the United States, and our organization occupies a specific vantage point that most AI policy discussions systematically overlook: we are neither the vendors selling these tools nor the clinicians using them, but the administrative professionals who sit at the intersection of procurement decisions, budget pressures, workforce management, and patient care outcomes. That position gives RBMA a particular view of how AI deployment decisions actually happen in practice, and what we observe on a daily basis across member organizations diverges sharply from the framing embedded in this RFI. The Department's stated goal of "accelerating adoption" presupposes that the primary barriers to AI integration are regulatory and technical.  RBMA's direct observation, and the evidence base reviewed below, suggests a different and more troubling diagnosis: the structural conditions under which AI tools are currently being deployed in health systems are generating workforce harm that will predictably translate into patient harm, and accelerating deployment without correcting those structural conditions will make outcomes worse, not better.⏎⏎⏎⏎The governance failure RBMA wishes to bring to the Department's attention is not subtle. A 2023 survey of 1,200 hospital-based physicians and nurses published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association found that fewer than 30 percent of frontline clinicians reported any meaningful involvement in the selection or evaluation of AI tools deployed in their clinical workflows (Kohn, R., et al., JAMIA, 30(8), 2023, pp. 1412–1421). The American Medical Association's 2023 Digital Medicine Practice Playbook, which RBMA member organizations have used as a governance reference since its publication, explicitly identifies clinician exclusion from procurement as among the highest-risk failure modes in health system AI adoption, noting that tools selected without frontline input routinely misalign with actual workflow requirements and generate adoption resistance that administrative responses — including performance monitoring and mandatory use policies — tend to entrench rather than resolve (AMA, 2023). What RBMA observes among its membership confirms this pattern. Procurement decisions for AI tools in radiology and adjacent clinical departments are overwhelmingly driven by CFO-level cost-reduction mandates and vendor relationships established through health system contracting channels, not by clinician-identified need. The tools that result from this process are frequently optimized for throughput metrics that make financial sense on a spreadsheet and operational sense to no one actually performing the clinical work. Eric Topol's 2023 commentary in the New England Journal of Medicine on physician presence in AI governance is worth citing here at some length: Topol argues that the absence of physician governance authority in AI deployment is not merely a procedural gap but a structural corruption of the clinical purpose these tools are supposed to serve (Topol, E.J., NEJM, 388(14), 2023). RBMA endorses that framing and urges HHS to treat clinician governance exclusion as a regulatory problem requiring a regulatory solution, not a cultural problem to be addressed through voluntary best-practice guidance.⏎⏎⏎⏎RBMA Comments < > HHS AI RFI Docket < > Page 2⏎⏎⏎⏎The workforce surveillance dimension of this issue deserves more attention than it has received in the regulatory literature to date. When health systems deploy AI-driven productivity monitoring in clinical and administrative settings — and RBMA's membership survey data indicate this is occurring at a rate that would surprise most federal policymakers — the consequences extend well beyond individual privacy concerns. The Economic Policy Institute's 2023 working paper on algorithmic productivity surveillance in healthcare settings documents how AI-derived performance metrics create a feedback loop in which clinicians are evaluated against throughput benchmarks that the artificial intelligence platforms are calibrated to produce, a circularity that systematically penalizes the contextual, time-intensive judgment calls that distinguish competent clinical care from transactional processing (EPI Working Paper, 2023). This is not a theoretical concern. Physician burnout, which Shanafelt's team documented in a 2022 Mayo Clinic Proceedings study as having reached historically elevated levels across nearly every specialty, is causally linked to electronic health record burden and algorithmic management in ways the literature has established with reasonable confidence (Shanafelt, T.D., et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2022; Dyrbye, L.N., et al., JAMA Network Open, 2021). National Nurses United's 2023 policy brief on AI in healthcare workforce settings reaches a consistent conclusion from the nursing perspective: AI tools deployed primarily to reduce labor costs generate demoralization, deskilling, and attrition among experienced clinical staff whose institutional knowledge is critical and whose departure imposes costs on patients that no efficiency metric captures (NNU Policy Brief, 2023). The Pew Research Center's October 2023 report on worker attitudes toward algorithmic management found that healthcare workers report higher levels of distrust toward AI-driven performance monitoring than workers in any other sector surveyed, a finding that RBMA believes reflects not technophobia but a professionally informed assessment of how these tools are actually being used (Pew Research Center, October 2023). RBMA is genuinely uncertain whether HHS has a clear picture of how widespread AI-derived productivity monitoring already is in the health systems this RFI is intended to serve. The Department should find out before it accelerates anything.⏎⏎⏎⏎Regarding the specific regulatory and reimbursement questions this RFI poses, RBMA focuses on two of these items specifically. On the question of what regulatory actions HHS can take to support responsible AI adoption, RBMA recommends the following:⏎⏎⏎⏎1. HHS should amend the Conditions of Participation under 42 CFR Part 482 to require that hospitals and health systems document frontline clinician consultation as a prerequisite for deploying AI tools in clinical or clinically adjacent administrative workflows. Voluntary guidance has not produced meaningful governance change; a CoP requirement would.⏎⏎⏎⏎2. HHS should direct ASTP/ONC to incorporate workforce governance requirements into the health IT certification criteria established under 45 CFR Part 170, specifically conditioning certification of AI-augmented clinical decision support systems on vendor disclosure of the workforce impact assessments conducted prior to deployment.⏎⏎⏎⏎3. HHS should condition any AI-related payment incentives — including any new reimbursement pathways developed in response to the reimbursement-gap concerns this RFI targets — on demonstrated evidence of clinician consultation in procurement, explicit prohibitions on using AI-derived productivity metrics as the sole basis for staffing decisions, and minimum staffing ratio protections in settings where AI tools are deployed as labor-substitution mechanisms. The AHRQ systematic review on nurse staffing and care quality, published in 2022, is unambiguous that staffing reductions below evidence-based thresholds produce measurable patient harm regardless of what technology is introduced to compensate (Stanton, M.W. & Rutherford, M.K., AHRQ Publication No. 22-0034, 2022).⏎⏎⏎⏎RBMA Comments < > HHS AI RFI Docket < > Page 3⏎⏎⏎⏎On the question of research and development priorities, RBMA urges HHS to fund independent evaluation of AI tools' workforce effects as a condition of any federal AI health research initiative. The GAO's 2022 report on AI in health care noted the near-total absence of independent evidence on workforce outcomes associated with clinical AI deployment, a gap the report identified as a significant barrier to evidence-based policy (GAO-22-104629, 2022). That gap has not been closed. The peer-reviewed literature detailing algorithmic bias in clinical tools illustrates that utilities reaching active deployment without adequate independent scrutiny can cause extensive harm before it is even measurable. A primary example of this is the 2019 Science publication by Ziad Obermeyer's research team, which analyzed racial bias within a broadly utilized demographic health tracking framework, proving that unchecked deployment scales up negative outcomes rapidly (Obermeyer, Z., et al., Science, 2019). RBMA does not oppose AI adoption in principle, and the Association acknowledges that specific applications in radiology workflow, prior authorization processing, and care coordination have demonstrated genuine clinical value in controlled settings. The concern is not with the technology but with the governance conditions under which it is being deployed at speed, and with the Department's apparent intention to accelerate that speed without first establishing the governance floor that would make acceleration safe. The HHS Office of Inspector General's 2023 report on Medicare Advantage organizations' use of AI in prior authorization determinations documented patterns of denial that the OIG found inconsistent with clinical necessity standards, a finding that illustrates precisely the patient harm pathway RBMA is describing: AI tools deployed to serve administrative cost objectives, without adequate clinical governance, produce outcomes that harm patients and ultimately discredit the technology itself (OIG Report OEI-09-23-00380, 2023).⏎⏎⏎⏎RBMA's formal recommendation to the Department is that HHS pause any acceleration initiatives specifically tied to AI deployment incentives until minimum workforce governance standards are established in regulation, not guidance. The distinction matters. Guidance documents are read by compliance officers and filed. Regulatory requirements with enforcement mechanisms change procurement behavior. RBMA is available to provide technical assistance to the Department in developing those standards and would welcome the opportunity to convene a working group of RBMA member organizations across the 28 states represented in our 2023 AI Reimbursement Working Group to inform that process. SYNTH-0090♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Kenneth Nguyen♔Evolent Health♔♔♔♔♔Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 1⏎⏎Response to HHS Request for Information: Health Sector Artificial Intelligence and Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎Submitted by: Kenneth Nguyen, Chief Financial Officer, Evolent Health⏎Date of Submission: March 2025⏎⏎PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS⏎⏎The financial case for AI-assisted clinical care is not theoretical. A 2024 financial impact analysis conducted across member health systems affiliated with Michigan Healthcare Freedom Network documented a 1.3-day reduction in average length-of-stay and a 9% reduction in preventable readmissions among facilities piloting AI-assisted clinical decision support tools within the first six months of deployment (Michigan Healthcare Freedom Network, 2024). Evolent Health has tracked comparable trends across its own network. The organization does not submit this comment to dispute the operational promise of clinical AI. It submits this comment because the promise, and the institutional capital already deployed in pursuit of it, is being jeopardized by a structural defect that HHS's RFI does not acknowledge, let alone propose to remedy.⏎⏎That defect is accountability diffusion. When a clinician relies on an AI-generated recommendation that plays a material role in an adverse clinical outcome, no existing legal or regulatory framework clearly identifies who is answerable. The clinician may argue the tool was defective. The hospital may argue the clinician held ultimate clinical veto power. The developer will assert that the software operated exactly as designed. All three positions can be simultaneously defensible under current law. The patient, meanwhile, has no clearly answerable responsible party. HHS is proposing to accelerate the deployment of systems that produce exactly this outcome at scale, and it has not explained how the accountability infrastructure necessary to protect patients, or the institutions caring for them, will be established before that acceleration begins.⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE LIABILITY VACUUM AS STRUCTURAL DEFECT⏎⏎The 2024 Michigan Healthcare Freedom analysis found that 68% of CFOs surveyed identified the absence of clear CMS reimbursement pathways as the primary barrier to scaling AI pilots. That finding is real and the reimbursement problem deserves federal attention. But the CFOs surveyed were describing an operational constraint, not a patient safety architecture failure. The accountability vacuum represents an entirely distinct classification of systemic failure, and in Evolent Health's assessment it is more consequential.⏎⏎Hoffman and Podgurski's 2023 analysis in the Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics is among the clearest descriptions of this problem available in the current literature. They write that clinical AI deployment has produced "accountability gaps" in which the distributed nature of AI development, validation, deployment, and clinical integration means that responsibility is structurally fragmented across actors who have no binding legal relationship with one another with respect to patient outcomes (Hoffman & Podgurski, 2023). This is not a gap waiting to be filled by incremental regulatory guidance. It is a design feature of the current deployment environment, and it will not resolve itself as adoption scales. It will compound.⏎⏎The GAO's 2022 report on artificial intelligence in health care identified a related structural problem: the absence of post-market surveillance requirements for AI-based clinical decision support tools means that model performance degradation, what the informatics literature calls model drift, can go undetected across clinical workflows for extended periods without triggering any regulatory accountability event (GAO-22-104629, 2022). Obermeyer and Emanuel observed as early as 2016 that machine learning models in clinical medicine are optimized for specific training environments and that their performance in real-world deployment conditions is a different and less predictable phenomenon (Obermeyer & Emanuel, 2016, NEJM, 375(13), 1216-1219). What the GAO and Obermeyer together describe is a system in which a tool can be causing harm, the harm can be attributable in part to model drift, and no existing regulatory mechanism compels anyone to detect, report, or accept institutional responsibility for that drift. Accelerating deployment into that environment is not a policy choice Evolent Health can characterize as responsible.⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 3⏎⏎THE INADEQUACY OF EXISTING MALPRACTICE DOCTRINE⏎⏎Medical malpractice doctrine, as it has developed across state common law and the limited federal frameworks that touch clinical liability, presupposes a specific individual acting as the clinical authority whose judgment can be evaluated using established medical baselines of acceptable practice. Price, Gerke, and Cohen identified in their 2019 JAMA analysis that AI intermediation in clinical decisions dissolves this presupposition in ways the doctrine has not addressed (Price, Gerke, & Cohen, 2019, JAMA, 322(18), 1765-1766). When a physician orders a treatment protocol after reviewing an AI-generated recommendation, the question of whether the physician exercised independent clinical judgment or effectively deferred to the tool's output is not answerable by examining the physician's conduct alone. It requires interrogating the AI system's decision logic, which is often opaque even to its developers, as Sendak and colleagues documented in their 2020 FAT* Conference paper on the clinical decision-making opacity problem (Sendak et al., 2020).⏎⏎Mello, Frakes, Blumenkranz, and Studdert's comprehensive 2020 review in JAMA of malpractice liability and health care quality documented the well-established deterrence function of malpractice liability in clinical settings: the prospect of legal accountability shapes clinical behavior in ways that, imperfectly but meaningfully, protect patients (Mello et al., 2020, JAMA, 323(4), 352-366). If AI intermediation dissolves the specific human authority that malpractice doctrine requires, it also dissolves that deterrence function. Clinicians who cannot be held accountable for deferring to an AI recommendation have less institutional incentive to exercise independent judgment when the AI recommendation is wrong. Hospitals that can point to vendor liability clauses have less institutional incentive to build internal governance mechanisms capable of catching errors. The accountability diffusion that Hoffman and Podgurski describe is not merely a legal technicality; it restructures the behavioral incentives that currently make clinical environments safer than they would otherwise be.⏎⏎Evolent Health has reviewed the standard contractual structures that AI vendors in the clinical decision support space currently use. The indemnification carve-outs and performance warranty limitations in these agreements are written to survive almost any clinical harm scenario. Gerke, Minssen, and Cohen's 2020 academic press analysis of the ethical and legal challenges of AI-driven healthcare documents the systematic way in which vendor contracts shift liability exposure toward deploying institutions (Gerke, Minssen, & Cohen, 2020). Those institutions, in turn, face malpractice frameworks that were not designed to account for AI intermediation. The patient sits at the end of this chain with no clearly answerable party. That is the structural defect.⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 4⏎⏎THE MORAL DIMENSION: PATIENTS AND THE RIGHT TO AN ANSWERABLE PARTY⏎⏎Keskinbora's 2019 analysis in the Journal of Clinical Neuroscience on medical ethics considerations in AI deployment identifies patient autonomy and the right to human accountability as foundational ethical requirements that AI deployment in clinical settings has not yet satisfied (Keskinbora, 2019, Journal of Clinical Neuroscience, 64, 277-282). This is not an abstract philosophical point. When a patient experiences harm in a clinical encounter, the patient has a reasonable expectation, grounded in centuries of medical ethics and codified in state and federal patient rights frameworks, that a human being with professional accountability is answerable for what happened. Char, Shah, and Magnus made a related argument in their 2018 NEJM paper on implementing machine learning in health care: the ethical challenges of AI deployment include the structural erosion of the human accountability relationship between clinician and patient that gives informed consent its meaning (Char, Shah, & Magnus, 2018, NEJM, 378(11), 981-983).⏎⏎Topol's 2019 Nature Medicine analysis of high-performance medicine and the convergence of human and artificial intelligence is frequently cited in support of accelerated AI adoption, and its documentation of AI's diagnostic performance capabilities is accurate (Topol, 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44-56). What Topol's analysis does not resolve, and what proponents of accelerated deployment have not resolved, is how the patient-clinician accountability relationship survives AI intermediation in a form that retains its ethical and legal integrity. The performance capabilities of a tool do not answer the question of who is responsible when the system plays a role in an adverse outcome. A system that performs at 94% accuracy is still a system that produces errors, and the patients who experience those errors are entitled to a clearly answerable responsible party.⏎⏎The RFI inquires about various regulatory actions HHS could implement to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care settings. Evolent Health's response to that question is that the regulatory predicate for acceleration is an accountability infrastructure, and HHS has not proposed one. The Department has not proposed binding liability allocation standards for AI-assisted clinical errors. It has not proposed mandatory post-market surveillance requirements that would create an institutional obligation to detect and report model drift. It has not proposed regulatory standards for the disclosure of AI intermediation to patients in ways that would allow patients to exercise meaningful informed consent. It has not proposed any mechanism by which a patient harmed by an AI-assisted clinical error could identify a legally answerable responsible party with confidence. Without those elements in place, the regulatory action HHS can most responsibly take to accelerate AI adoption is to pause and build the infrastructure first.⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 5⏎⏎THE RFI'S STRUCTURAL SILENCE ON ACCOUNTABILITY⏎⏎Evolent Health has read the RFI carefully. The Department asks about reimbursement pathways, about interoperability, about workforce training, about research priorities. These are legitimate policy questions. The 2024 Michigan Healthcare Freedom analysis documented $114 million in uncompensated implementation costs absorbed by member facilities in fiscal year 2023 alone, with critical access hospitals disproportionately constrained, and the reimbursement architecture question is real. But the RFI's silence on accountability infrastructure is not an oversight; it reflects a policy orientation in which accountability is treated as a downstream concern to be addressed after adoption has scaled. That orientation is wrong, and Evolent Health believes it is demonstrably wrong based on the current legal and regulatory environment.⏎⏎The argument that accountability frameworks can be developed in parallel with or subsequent to accelerated deployment has been advanced in other technology sectors and has consistently produced the outcome that critics predicted: harms accumulate during the period when accountability infrastructure is absent, and the regulatory response arrives after the institutional patterns that generated the harms have become entrenched. Clinical AI deployment at scale, in which AI tools are embedded in clinical workflows in ways that create workflow dependencies, is a particularly poor candidate for the "deploy first, regulate later" approach because the harms at issue are patient safety harms, not economic harms or privacy harms, though those are also present. Once a health system's clinical workflows are architecturally dependent on an AI tool, removing or fundamentally modifying that tool to comply with a subsequently enacted accountability framework becomes operationally disruptive in ways that create their own patient safety risks.⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 6⏎⏎WHAT HHS SHOULD DO BEFORE ACCELERATING DEPLOYMENT⏎⏎The Department should, before issuing any guidance or taking any regulatory action designed to accelerate clinical AI adoption, convene a formal rulemaking process focused specifically on liability allocation for AI-assisted clinical errors. That process should produce binding standards, not voluntary frameworks, that specify how liability is allocated among clinicians, deploying institutions, and AI vendors when an algorithmic recommendation plays a material role in an adverse clinical outcome. The current environment in which each party's contractual and litigation posture is to deflect liability to the other parties is not a stable or ethically defensible foundation for scaled deployment.⏎⏎The Department should also establish mandatory post-market surveillance requirements for clinical AI tools, with defined reporting obligations and institutional accountability for detecting and disclosing model drift. The GAO's 2022 report documented the current absence of such requirements in detail. Evolent Health would note that this is one area where the reimbursement question and the accountability question converge: if CMS were to condition reimbursement for AI-augmented care delivery on compliance with post-market surveillance and accountability disclosure requirements, the reimbursement pathway that 68% of surveyed CFOs identified as the primary scaling barrier could simultaneously function as an accountability enforcement mechanism.⏎⏎Finally, Evolent Health would observe that the informed consent implications of AI intermediation in clinical decisions have not been addressed in the RFI and have not, to the organization's knowledge, been addressed in any binding federal regulatory guidance. Char, Shah, and Magnus identified this in 2018 as an ethical requirement for responsible deployment. Seven years later, the gap remains. Patients who are receiving clinical recommendations that are generated or materially shaped by AI tools are, in most institutional settings, not being informed of that fact in any systematic way, and there is no regulatory requirement that they be. The patient rights dimension of this problem is not separable from the accountability dimension; a patient who does not know that AI intermediation occurred cannot meaningfully assess whether to seek accountability, from whom, or on what basis.⏎⏎The organization recognizes that these are difficult problems and that building the accountability infrastructure described here takes time and requires coordination across HHS, CMS, ONC, FDA, and potentially Congress. That coordination is precisely why HHS should begin building it now rather than after deployment has scaled to the point where retrofitting accountability mechanisms becomes operationally and politically difficult.⏎⏎Evolent Health | HHS AI RFI Response | Docket HHS-2024-AI-RFI | Page 7⏎⏎Contact for follow-up inquiries regarding this submission:⏎Kenneth Nguyen, CFO⏎Evolent Health⏎policy-comments@evolenthealth.org♔♔2026-02-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-02-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔7♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔AI in healthcare diffuses responsibility across clinicians, hospitals, and vendors in ways that leave patients without a clear accountable party when errors cause harm.♔organization♔high♔frustrated♔New Jersey♔hospital CFO♔57♔A 2024 financial impact analysis conducted across Michigan Healthcare Freedom's 47 member hospital systems found that facilities piloting AI-assisted clinical decision support tools reduced average length-of-stay by 1.3 days and achieved a 9% reduction in preventable readmissions within the first six months of deployment. SYNTH-0091♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Joseph Hill♔University of Pittsburgh Department of Biomedical Informatics♔♔♔♔♔Logos Research Centre | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 1⏎< >⏎COMMENT OF LOGOS RESEARCH CENTRE AND THE UNIVERSITY OF PITTSBURGH DEPARTMENT OF BIOMEDICAL INFORMATICS⏎Submitted in Response to: HHS Health Sector Artificial Intelligence Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Submitted by: Joseph Hill, PhD Researcher, Department of Biomedical Informatics, University of Pittsburgh, on behalf of Logos Research Centre⏎Date: November 2024⏎⏎PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS ON FRAMING⏎⏎This submission centers on a distinct problem that Logos Research Centre finds missing from the current RFI structure: the fundamental mischaracterization of medical administrative work as a standardized processing environment ripe for algorithmic automation. The RFI inquires generally about steps HHS might take to hasten the integration of machine learning across medical environments, and within that paradigm, bureaucratic streamlining is positioned as an absolute good — a type of operational friction we should simply eliminate. Our organizational stance, rooted in an active multi-center evaluation of 37 federally sponsored clinical machine learning initiatives spanning three academic cycles, is that this perspective relies on a structural misunderstanding that will trigger severe downstream liabilities for patient safety and demographic fairness.⏎⏎One specific metric from our ongoing evaluation demands highlighting here. Less than 22% of the evaluated 37 initiatives had initiated contact with a formal regulatory approval pipeline at the moment their initial funding was granted. This is hardly a minor footnote. It indicates that the scattered nature of HHS directives across FDA, CMS, and ONC establishes compounding compliance hurdles, forcing translational informatics research into advanced validation phases long before investigators possess a coherent understanding of what real-world implementation demands. That systemic obstacle is undeniable, and the Department must rectify it. However, a parallel internal poll of 214 cross-disciplinary investigators connected to Logos Research Centre revealed that 68% viewed payment model ambiguity and liability confusion as the primary roadblocks to utilization. While undoubtedly aggravating to developers, those exact roadblocks might actually be executing a vital safeguarding role, one that an aggressively pro-acceleration policy framework would dismantle without providing a functional substitute.⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 2⏎< >⏎THE NATURE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEALTHCARE LABOR⏎⏎The core inquiry the RFI omits — though it desperately needs to ask — is what the actual substance of health system administration entails. The prevailing regulatory presumption seems to be that back-office duties like coverage authorization reviews, beneficiary navigation, eligibility verification, and care logistics are fundamentally clerical tasks: matching forms, checking rules, and verifying statuses. If that assumption held true, replacing human effort with software would be a trivial matter, and the cost-savings rationale would be unassailable. Casalino et al. (2016, Health Affairs, 35(3)) noted that American medical practices expend roughly $15.4 billion every year merely on quality metric reporting, while Himmelstein, Campbell, and Woolhandler (2020, NEJM, 382(15), 1483-1484) estimated total domestic medical bureaucratic expenditures at approximately $812 billion for 2017. Figures of that magnitude make the streamlining narrative feel exceptionally urgent. Yet the sheer volume of bureaucratic effort tells us nothing about the qualitative nature of that effort, and equating financial expenditure with systemic waste represents a profound analytical failure.⏎⏎The scholarship surrounding institutional knowledge provides a far more precise description. Polanyi (1966, The Tacit Dimension) proved that a massive fraction of specialized expertise is inherently tacit — residing in the professional's intuition, physical practice, and accumulated contextual awareness in a manner that defies strict codification. Nonaka and Takeuchi (1995, The Knowledge-Creating Company) expanded this framework into corporate environments, illustrating that organizational competence flows through interpersonal dynamics and collective memory, rather than through rigid procedural manuals. Medical administrative personnel function exactly within this tacit domain. Consider a beneficiary navigator at a Medicaid managed care entity operating in rural North Dakota. That individual intrinsically understands which informal workaround protocols exist for local psychiatric referrals, realizes which specific clinicians require a personal phone call rather than a digital message, and recognizes that a particular beneficiary's recurring authorization rejections are consistently caused by an obscure coding mismatch leftover from a 2021 database transition. Absolutely none of that critical expertise is captured in any structured digital repository. It lives entirely within the human practitioner.⏎⏎Jost and Rosenbaum (2022, Health Affairs, 41(3), 412-421) thoroughly mapped how bureaucratic convolution within Medicaid managed care directly generates beneficiary harm at the exact intersections where strict procedural adherence fails — the moments when rigid institutional rules and the reality of a patient's life diverge, requiring a human with deep institutional memory to reconcile the difference. We are not arguing that contemporary bureaucratic frameworks are perfectly engineered. They clearly are not. We are arguing that the human staff embedded within those frameworks constantly perform highly specialized reconciliation labor that the overarching institutions refuse to officially document or acknowledge. Consequently, machine learning models built using only those official procedural records will inevitably break down precisely during the high-stakes moments when human intuition is most required.⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 3⏎< >⏎SYSTEMATIC INVISIBLE ERRORS AND DISPARATE IMPACT⏎⏎The specific failure taxonomy that alarms our department most is not the spectacular, easily identifiable breakdown  — such as a blatantly absurd coverage denial that a human manager immediately spots and reverses. Rather, we are concerned with the category of mistakes Ash, Berg, and Coiera (2004, JAMIA, 11(2), 104-112) defined as "juxtaposition errors" and "entry errors" within clinical informatics networks: mistakes that are individually minute, entirely plausible in isolation, and completely hidden from view until they snowball into catastrophic patient harm. Algorithmic back-office tools relying on rigid input matching will generate this exact breed of mistake at a massive volume. A coverage authorization model fed entirely on historical billing claims possesses no capacity to realize that a beneficiary's listed residence is actually a domestic violence shelter she utilized three years prior, which she intentionally leaves unchanged to protect a delicate child custody situation. An automated care coordination agent will never understand that the individual it is attempting to route has suffered severe historical trauma involving the specific specialist it just recommended. These are not statistical anomalies. They constitute the standard reality of medical bureaucratic navigation for individuals facing severe socio-economic complexities.⏎⏎The demographic fairness implications of this failure paradigm are far from hypothetical. Obermeyer and colleagues (2019, Science, 366(6464), 447-453) revealed how an industry-standard proprietary model intended to direct population health interventions consistently minimized the true disease burden of Black individuals. It accomplished this by treating financial expenditures as a direct stand-in for clinical necessity — a metric inherently corrupted by generations of unequal healthcare access rather than reflecting actual physiological realities. Veinot, Mitchell, and Ancker (2018, JAMIA, 25(8), 1080-1088) demonstrated on a wider scale that well-intentioned health informatics implementations can actively exacerbate baseline disparities if they ignore the deeply unequal environments in which marginalized populations interact with medical institutions. Eubanks (2018, Automating Inequality) offers the definitive structural critique here: computerized bureaucratic frameworks deployed upon marginalized groups reliably internalize the prejudices of the institutions that generated their foundational datasets, which are frequently the exact same prejudices that created the inequities the software was theoretically purchased to solve.⏎⏎Bhatt and Mehta (2023, JAMA Health Forum, 4(7), e231892) analyzed the specific automation of coverage authorizations and discovered that while genuine operational improvements occurred — such as shortened turnaround times and decreased financial overhead per decision — they were accompanied by a distinct surge in rejection frequencies for specific minority subpopulations. Crucially, the implementing hospital networks had completely failed to anticipate this surge and were not actively tracking it. This is the exact catastrophe the RFI's relentless focus on operational speed ignores: superficial operational improvements at the macro level that directly manufacture individualized trauma at the patient level, distributed in a manner completely obscured when looking only at top-level performance averages.⏎⏎THE 'FREED-UP TIME' REBUTTAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE FRICTION AS PROTECTION⏎⏎The standard industry defense regarding bureaucratic automation claims that it liberates human personnel to handle highly complex scenarios. Our department treats this premise seriously but finds it empirically unsupported given contemporary workforce realities. Sinsky et al. (2017, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 92(11), 1625-1635) clearly mapped the correlation between bureaucratic overload, physician exhaustion, and clinical staff turnover. The wider academic consensus on medical administrative labor does not depict a workforce sitting on vast reserves of idle capacity waiting to be reallocated. The personnel whose schedules would supposedly be liberated by algorithmic intervention are, across virtually every hospital network our team interacts with, currently functioning at or beyond absolute maximum sustainable limits. Forcing new algorithmic tools into this environment — tools that inherently manufacture entirely novel categories of mistakes requiring human investigation and correction — does not alleviate the burden on these professionals. It merely dumps an entirely new species of anomaly-hunting labor onto their existing plates, without any assurance that such anomalies can be readily identified and resolved during standard operational procedures.⏎⏎Furthermore, there is a profound conceptual point regarding the safeguarding nature of bureaucratic friction, a concept the current RFI completely ignores. Human-operated administrative chokepoints — a coverage reviewer who pauses at a strangely contraindicated pharmaceutical combination, a beneficiary guide who realizes a client has skipped three consecutive screenings and initiates a wellness call, a financial counselor who notices a discrepancy between a patient's documented tax returns and their verbal description of their living situation and decides to ask a clarifying question — are not merely operational wastes. They are vital mistake-catching protocols functioning entirely outside the rigid parameters of the software. Friedman, Wong, and Blumenthal (2010, Science Translational Medicine, 2(57), 57cm29) correctly asserted that a functional learning health system demands unbroken feedback cycles linking physical practice with institutional knowledge. The bureaucratic tier, when properly conceptualized, operates as one of those essential feedback cycles. Eradicating it under the guise of streamlining destroys the exact information the overarching institution requires to recognize its own systemic failures.⏎⏎The specific disaster scenario our researchers are most alarmed by involves the intersection of:⏎⏎o Algorithmic networks generating systematic routing or coverage mistakes that disproportionately impact marginalized individuals⏎o Chronically overburdened human personnel lacking the necessary bandwidth or diagnostic software to spot those mistakes⏎o An absolute vacuum of formalized tracking mandates, ensuring the resulting damage remains entirely invisible to federal oversight bodies like HHS or CMS⏎⏎This is not an imagined dystopia. It is an accurate summary of what transpires when predictive software enters severely under-resourced clinics lacking rigorous demographic impact tracking. The extensive empirical literature analyzed by Logos Research Centre strongly indicates this dynamic is already unfolding across numerous early-adopter environments.⏎⏎Logos Research Centre | HHS-AI-RFI-2024 | Page 4⏎< >⏎POLICY RECOMMENDATION⏎⏎Our organization strongly advises HHS and ONC to mandate two strict, pre-implementation prerequisites as a mandatory condition for any federal payment or certification pipeline involving algorithmic tools applied to medical administration:⏎⏎1. Contextual validity assessment: The purchasing entity must definitively prove that the proposed software has been rigorously tested against patient demographics and operational environments fundamentally identical to the ones where it will actually function, not merely against its original development data. Proving a model works using billing records from a major metropolitan teaching hospital offers zero guarantee it will function safely when implemented at a remote community clinic reliant on federal funding and primarily treating Medicaid beneficiaries.⏎⏎2. Equity impact assessment with mandatory reporting: The implementing facility must carry out and provide an upfront disparate impact evaluation examining variances in mistake frequencies, rejection proportions, and outcome indicators across differing demographic groups, income brackets, physical ability levels, and coverage categories. These findings must be transmitted to HHS on a strict recurring schedule post-implementation. This mandate should draw structural inspiration from established environmental justice frameworks, which, while imperfect, offer a concrete regulatory blueprint for demanding proactive harm analysis prior to launch, rather than waiting for casualties to mount.⏎⏎These stipulations align perfectly with standard expectations in rigorous translational science. The academic collective Logos Research Centre represents would never dream of releasing a patient-facing application without first verifying its contextual accuracy and measuring its demographic effects, this being a core tenet of our methodology. Consequently, we see zero justifiable basis for allowing proprietary administrative automation to bypass these rigorous evidentiary standards. The current splintering of HHS authority across FDA, CMS, and ONC guarantees that no individual bureau possesses the leverage to enforce this standard uniformly, which is exactly why our department is elevating the issue in this broader forum rather than in a narrow rulemaking docket. The Department possesses a rare opening, via this RFI process, to forge a unified, cross-agency baseline that is currently entirely absent.⏎⏎One final addendum: the disparate impact evaluation requirement needs to explicitly incorporate an examination of the psychological and temporal toll extracted from the human personnel tasked with fixing the machine's mistakes, not merely the toll extracted from the patients. SYNTH-0092♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Daniel Ramirez♔♔♔♔♔♔Submitted via regulations.gov⏎⏎RE: HHS Health Sector AI RFI — Administrative Workforce and Tacit Knowledge⏎⏎My cardiologist at WVU Medicine flagged an atrial irregularity in February using software trained on what she described as millions of echocardiograms. I walked out of that appointment with a stent scheduled and a genuine sense of what this technology can do. I've thought about my neighbor Dolores since then, who drives forty minutes each way to Charleston to see a specialist, and how that kind of diagnostic intelligence placed in a rural clinic could change things for people like her. I'm not writing to question any of that. I work in healthcare administration, and what I want to raise is a different question entirely, one I haven't seen addressed in the materials I've reviewed: what happens when AI is applied not to reading scans but to the administrative work that actually connects patients to care?⏎⏎ON THE NATURE OF ADMINISTRATIVE EXPERTISE⏎⏎Healthcare administration is not clerical processing. I want to say that plainly because I think the efficiency research treats it that way, sometimes without meaning to. When Bates et al. published their 2021 analysis in npj Digital Medicine on AI's potential to reduce administrative burden, the underlying assumption was that administrative tasks are largely rule-bound and therefore automatable. My experience over many years in this work is that the assumption is wrong in ways that matter enormously for vulnerable patients. The knowledge embedded in good care coordination is what Michael Polanyi called tacit knowledge — knowledge that cannot be fully articulated, that lives in practice rather than in documentation. Knowing which Medicaid office in Kanawha County will accept late prior authorization paperwork if you call before noon on a Thursday, knowing that a particular patient's unstable housing situation means a phone-based follow-up will fail and you need to contact her daughter instead, knowing that the local home health agency has a three-week backlog even though their website says otherwise — none of this is in a structured data field. None of it is learnable from training sets. Dreyfus and Dreyfus made this argument in 1986 in Mind Over Machine, and it has not become less true because the computing power is now larger.⏎⏎My primary worry remains the invisibility problem. When a physician misreads a scan, there are downstream clinical signals that something went wrong. When an administrative AI misroutes a prior authorization, or miscategorizes a patient's eligibility status, or generates a care coordination note that misses a key contextual detail, the error may not surface until a patient has already lost access to a service they needed. A 2019 Science article by Ziad Obermeyer's research team showed how a broadly utilized health tracking program systematically underestimated the needs of Black patients because it used cost as a proxy for health status — an error that was invisible in the software's outputs and only detectable through careful external audit. Administrative AI will produce its own version of this problem, and the patients most exposed are those with the fewest resources to detect and correct errors on their own.⏎⏎ENGAGING THE EFFICIENCY ARGUMENT DIRECTLY⏎⏎I want to be honest that the administrative burden in American healthcare is real and serious. Himmelstein et al. estimated in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2020 that administrative costs consumed approximately 34 percent of total U.S. healthcare expenditures in 2017, roughly double the Canadian figure. I understand why that number makes automation look attractive. But the efficiency gains projected by AI proponents rest on a premise that I think is empirically shaky: that administrative roles currently have slack capacity. A 2016 paper by Sinsky's research group in the Annals of Internal Medicine revealed that physicians were already spending more than half their working hours on administrative tasks, which meant that the administrative workforce was not a buffer — it was a bottleneck. Automating into an understaffed system doesn't free capacity. It transfers work. When AI generates an error in an administrative workflow, a human being has to find it, diagnose it, and correct it, and that corrective labor is invisible in any efficiency calculation because it doesn't appear in the original task log. The GAO noted in its 2022 report on prior authorization (GAO-22-104536) that the burden on providers and beneficiaries was already severe under human-administered systems. Automating those systems without demanding proven accuracy and fairness results doesn't reduce that burden. It makes the burden harder to see.⏎⏎I want to be specific about what I mean by "invisible errors generating corrective labor," because I think the abstraction makes it easy to dismiss. Take a look at these scenarios, which are grounded in actual events I have witnessed firsthand, rather than just abstract concepts:⏎⏎1. A care coordination AI flags a patient as "low-risk for readmission" based on structured discharge data, missing the unstructured note from a social worker indicating the patient has no transportation and no refrigeration for her insulin. A human coordinator would have caught this. The AI does not. The patient is readmitted within ten days.⏎⏎2. A patient navigation tool generates a list of "in-network specialists accepting new patients" that is drawn from a provider directory updated six months prior. Four of the five listed providers are no longer accepting patients. The patient, who does not have easy phone access, spends two weeks trying to schedule before a human navigator intervenes.⏎⏎3. A benefits counseling AI correctly identifies that a patient qualifies for a state assistance program but fails to account for a recent policy change in how West Virginia's DHHR processes applications for that program, resulting in a submitted application that is technically complete but procedurally defective.⏎⏎In each case, the error is only visible after harm has occurred, and the correction requires more human time than the original task would have.⏎⏎ON WHAT HHS SHOULD REQUIRE⏎⏎I am not asking HHS to prohibit AI in healthcare administration. I am asking for two specific things, directed at the regulatory and reimbursement frameworks this RFI is designed to inform.⏎⏎First, require demonstrated equity and safety outcomes before any administrative AI deployment that affects patient access to care. Not projected outcomes. Not vendor-reported accuracy metrics on curated test sets. Demonstrated outcomes in real deployment environments, stratified by race, income, geography, and language. The Obermeyer finding should be treated as a baseline warning, not a historical anomaly.⏎⏎Second, preserve mandatory human review at every administrative decision point that determines whether a patient receives a service. This is not inefficiency. The GAO's 2022 prior authorization report detailed how human review catches errors that automated systems overlook, and that the cost of those uncaught errors falls entirely on patients. If the efficiency gains from automation are real, they will survive the addition of a human review layer. If they don't survive it, that tells us something important about where the efficiency is actually coming from.⏎⏎I recognize I'm not addressing the clinical AI questions in this RFI, and I think those questions deserve the serious treatment they're getting. But I'd ask HHS and ONC not to let the genuine excitement about diagnostic AI carry over into an assumption that administrative AI is similarly ready for deployment at scale. The diagnostic tool that caught my atrial irregularity was trained on imaging data with measurable ground truth. Administrative work doesn't have that. The ground truth is Dolores knowing that the specialist in Charleston takes her insurance but only on Tuesdays, and that if she misses the appointment there's a six-week wait, and that the social worker at the clinic can sometimes call ahead. That knowledge lives in a person. I'm genuinely uncertain what it would take to encode it otherwise, and I don't think that uncertainty has been adequately reckoned with in the materials I've reviewed so far.⏎⏎Daniel Ramirez⏎Administrative Assistant, WVU Medicine (retired, currently part-time)⏎Morgantown, WV♔♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-01-01T00:00:00Z♔2026-03-02T00:00:00Z♔4♔♔♔♔TRUE♔0♔Urge HHS and ONC to reject the accelerationist framing of this RFI and instead adopt a precautionary, human-centered policy posture that imposes strict limits on AI use in clinical care, insurance decisions, and healthcare administration — requiring demonstrated safety, equity, and accountability before any deployment, and preserving meaningful human responsibility at every point of care.♔Even administrative healthcare functions that appear routine require human contextual judgment that AI cannot replicate, and automating them will produce systematic errors that harm patients and workers.♔individual♔high♔hopeful♔West Virginia♔administrative assistant♔75♔When my cardiologist at WVU Medicine reviewed my echocardiogram findings in February, she mentioned almost in passing that the software flagging my atrial irregularity had been trained on millions of scans — something no single physician could ever study in a lifetime.
