SYNTH-0093♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔William Thomas♔Optum♔♔♔♔♔William Thomas, MD, MBA⏎Chief Medical Officer, Optum⏎[Address on file with submitting organization]⏎⏎Submitted electronically via regulations.gov⏎Re: HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information — Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎⏎EXECUTIVE SUMMARY⏎⏎Optum submits these comments in response to HHS's Request for Information on accelerating artificial intelligence adoption in clinical care settings. Our network operates across hundreds of care sites and processes clinical data at a scale that gives us direct, operational visibility into how AI tools actually perform once deployed outside controlled pilot conditions. We welcome federal engagement on this question. What we cannot support is a policy posture that treats acceleration as an unqualified good, because the evidence from our own internal assessments, and from a growing body of peer-reviewed literature on burnout, workforce surveillance, and algorithmic bias, points consistently toward a different conclusion: that the conditions under which health systems currently procure and deploy AI are structurally misaligned with clinical care improvement, and that federal policy which accelerates adoption without first correcting those structural conditions will cause foreseeable harm at scale.⏎⏎Our Q2 2024 technology assessment surveyed 312 clinicians across primary care, behavioral health, and complex care management programs within Tapestryhealth's 47 affiliated clinical sites. That survey found that 74% of respondents would expand AI-assisted workflows if clear federal coverage pathways existed. That finding is frequently cited by AI vendors and system administrators as evidence of clinician readiness. What it actually shows is that clinicians are willing to adopt tools they believe will help them care for patients. The same survey identified reimbursement ambiguity and liability uncertainty as the two most frequently cited barriers to adoption, which is a finding about regulatory architecture, not about clinician resistance to technology. The distinction matters, because the policy response to "clinicians distrust AI" looks very different from the policy response to "the regulatory environment makes responsible AI adoption economically irrational for providers who want to do it right." We are describing the second problem. HHS should not mistake it for the first.⏎⏎A separate internal utilization review, conducted across those same 47 sites, found that 68% of care teams reported spending more than two hours per provider shift on documentation tasks that AI-assisted tools demonstrated the capacity to reduce by an average of 40% in controlled pilot conditions. That 40% figure circulates widely in vendor materials and in policy discussions as proof of AI's burnout-reduction potential. What it does not capture is what happens after the pilot ends, when the productivity gains identified in controlled conditions are immediately incorporated into revised staffing models and increased caseload expectations rather than returned to clinicians as recovered time. Arndt et al., writing in the Annals of Family Medicine in 2017, documented that primary care physicians were already spending more than half their working hours on EHR and desk work rather than direct patient care (Arndt BG et al., Ann Fam Med. 2017;15(5):419-426). Downing, Bates, and Longhurst argued the following year in Annals of Internal Medicine that the field was systematically misidentifying EHR burden as a technology problem when it was fundamentally a workload design problem (Downing NL, Bates DW, Longhurst CA. Ann Intern Med. 2018;169(1):50-51). The implication is direct: deploying AI into a workload design that is already extractive does not fix the design. It makes the extraction more efficient. Shanafelt and colleagues, reporting in Mayo Clinic Proceedings in 2022 on changes in physician burnout between 2011 and 2020, documented that burnout rates worsened over a period during which health systems made substantial technology investments, which should give any policymaker serious pause before accepting the claim that more technology investment will reverse that trend (Shanafelt TD et al., Mayo Clin Proc. 2022;97(3):491-506).⏎⏎Optum Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 3⏎⏎The specific harms we are describing are not speculative. Panagioti and colleagues published a systematic review and meta-analysis in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2018 finding statistically significant associations between physician burnout and increased rates of medical errors, reduced patient satisfaction, and compromised professionalism (Panagioti M et al., JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(10):1317-1330). The causal pathway from AI-accelerated workload extraction to patient harm therefore runs through the clinical workforce, and any federal framework that treats workforce impact as a secondary consideration in AI deployment policy is analytically incomplete. The Aiken et al. study published in The Lancet in 2014, examining nurse staffing and hospital mortality across nine European countries, established with unusual rigor that each additional patient per nurse was associated with a 7% increase in the likelihood of patient death within 30 days of admission (Aiken LH et al., Lancet. 2014;383(9931):1824-1830). If AI-assisted productivity monitoring is used to justify reduced nurse staffing ratios, which our network has observed occurring in at least three distinct system-level procurement decisions reviewed in fiscal year 2024, then the downstream patient safety consequence is not theoretical. It is quantifiable, and the existing literature tells us the direction.⏎⏎The governance failure at the center of this problem is procurement exclusion. Frontline clinicians are systematically absent from the decisions that determine which AI tools enter their workflows, on what terms, and with what performance expectations attached. The American Medical Association's 2023 Digital Medicine Practice Playbook on workforce implications of AI in clinical settings documented this pattern across a broad survey of health system AI deployments, finding that vendor contracts are typically negotiated between technology companies and health system finance and operations leadership, with clinical informatics staff sometimes consulted but frontline physicians and nurses rarely given meaningful input into tool selection or deployment parameters (AMA Digital Medicine Practice Playbook, AMA Press, 2023). The Accenture Health Workforce Report published in 2023 described this as a "workforce experience gap" in which clinicians are treated as end-users to be trained rather than as domain experts whose judgment is necessary for safe deployment (Accenture Health. The Workforce Experience Gap. 2023). Kellogg, Valentine, and Christin, writing in the Academy of Management Annals in 2020 on algorithms at work, described the resulting dynamic as a new form of contested control in which algorithmic systems encode managerial preferences into the technical architecture of work, making those preferences appear objective and therefore harder to contest (Kellogg KC, Valentine MA, Christin A. Acad Mgmt Annals. 2020;14(1):366-410). When a prior authorization AI tool flags a case for denial, or a care coordination algorithm routes a patient to a lower-acuity service, the decision appears to come from the system rather than from a manager, but the values embedded in that decision were set by whoever designed and calibrated the tool, and if frontline clinicians had no role in that process, then they are being governed by a system they did not help build and cannot meaningfully contest.⏎⏎Optum Comments | HHS AI RFI | Page 4⏎⏎The equity dimension of this problem deserves more than passing acknowledgment in federal policy. Obermeyer and colleagues published in Science in 2019 a detailed analysis of a commercial algorithm widely used to manage population health programs, finding that the tool systematically underestimated illness severity in Black patients relative to white patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for health need, and cost data reflects historical access disparities rather than clinical acuity (Obermeyer Z et al., Science. 2019;366(6464):447-453). That finding has not been adequately incorporated into either procurement standards or federal coverage policy. Bates and colleagues, in a scoping review published in npj Digital Medicine in 2021, found that while AI holds genuine potential for improving patient safety, the evidence base for deployed clinical AI tools is thin, heterogeneous, and frequently limited to single-site studies that do not generalize across patient populations (Bates DW et al., npj Digit Med. 2021;4(1):54). HHS cannot responsibly accelerate adoption of tools whose performance characteristics across race, ethnicity, insurance status, and geographic context have not been systematically evaluated. The harm from doing so will not be distributed equally. It will fall disproportionately on the patients who already receive the worst care, because those are the patients whose data is least represented in training sets and whose care settings are least resourced to catch algorithmic errors before they affect clinical decisions.⏎⏎Given all of the above, Optum recommends that HHS condition any reimbursement or regulatory pathway for clinical AI deployment on the following specific requirements, which we offer not as aspirational guidance but as minimum preconditions:⏎⏎1. Mandatory frontline workforce consultation in AI procurement. HHS should require, as a condition of any federal reimbursement or certification pathway for clinical AI tools, that health systems document a structured process for frontline clinician input into tool selection, performance threshold setting, and post-deployment review. Documentation of a one-time informational meeting with a physician advisory committee does not satisfy this requirement. The standard should be iterative, documented, and subject to audit.⏎⏎2. Demonstrated safety and equity evidence before deployment authorization. No clinical AI tool should qualify for federal coverage pathways without peer-reviewed or independently validated evidence of performance across the specific patient populations it will serve, stratified by race, ethnicity, and payer status at minimum. Single-site pilot data from academic medical centers should not be treated as sufficient evidence of generalizability to safety-net or rural settings.⏎⏎3. An explicit federal prohibition on using AI-generated productivity data as the primary basis for staffing reduction decisions. This is the most specific ask we are making, and we recognize it is also the most politically contested. Health systems are financially pressured in ways that create strong incentives to use AI efficiency data to justify workforce reductions. Federal policy that accelerates AI adoption without addressing this incentive structure is not neutral with respect to that outcome. HHS should work with CMS to develop guidance, and if necessary regulatory language, establishing that AI productivity metrics may not serve as the sole or primary evidentiary basis for reducing nurse-to-patient ratios or eliminating care coordination positions.⏎⏎4. A formal requirement that AI tools used in prior authorization review disclose the clinical logic and training data underlying denial recommendations, both to the reviewing clinician and to the patient, as a condition of any CMS coverage or reimbursement pathway.⏎⏎Our network takes the potential of AI in clinical settings seriously. We are not submitting these comments because we believe AI has no role in improving care delivery. We are submitting them because the gap between controlled pilot performance and real-world deployment outcomes is large, the financial incentives that drive that gap are well-documented, and the patients who will bear the cost of getting this wrong are not the ones sitting in vendor procurement meetings. Stanton and colleagues, writing on workforce management and patient-centered care in the Journal of Health Organization and Management in 2014, found that organizational cultures which systematically devalue frontline worker judgment tend to produce worse patient outcomes independent of technology investments (Stanton P et al., J Health Organ Manag. 2014;28(1):57-74). That finding predates the current AI deployment wave, but it describes exactly the dynamic we are observing in our network and in the broader health system environment.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, Optum's policy and regulatory affairs team can be reached at the contact information provided on the cover page. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 1⏎⏎I. THE STRUCTURAL PROBLEM THE DEPARTMENT IS NOT ASKING ABOUT⏎⏎The Department's request for information proceeds from a premise that deserves direct challenge before any of its specific questions are addressed: that the primary obstacle to beneficial AI adoption in clinical settings is regulatory friction. The evidence does not support this premise.  What the evidence supports — and what any serious analysis of current deployment patterns must confront — is that the more consequential obstacle is a governance vacuum that exposes clinicians to algorithmic systems they did not select, were not trained to interrogate, and are structurally prevented from refusing. The College of American Pathologists documented this vacuum with uncomfortable precision in its 2024 Digital Pathology and AI Policy Initiative, which surveyed more than 1,200 practicing pathologists across 47 states and found that 68% were already encountering AI-assisted diagnostic tools in their laboratories, yet fewer than 22% reported that their institutions had established formal governance frameworks for validating or auditing those algorithms prior to clinical deployment (College of American Pathologists, 2024, Digital Pathology and AI Policy Initiative: 2024 Member Survey). That is not a regulatory-friction problem. That is a deployment-without-accountability problem, and the Department's framing of this RFI does not adequately reckon with it.⏎⏎The practical consequence of this governance vacuum is not hypothetical. CAP's systematic review of 34 FDA-cleared AI/ML-based in vitro diagnostic devices found that ongoing field-performance tracking protocols remain inconsistently applied across laboratory settings. Which means that algorithms cleared by the FDA on the basis of training-data performance are being used in clinical contexts where their performance has never been independently verified, where the populations they serve may differ substantially from the populations on which they were trained, and where the clinicians responsible for acting on their outputs have no institutional mechanism for flagging degradation or bias. Obermeyer and Emanuel flagged the population-mismatch problem as a first-order concern for clinical AI nearly a decade ago (Obermeyer, Z., & Emanuel, E.J., 2016, Predicting the Future — Big Data, Machine Learning, and Clinical Medicine, New England Journal of Medicine, 375(13), 1216–1219), and yet the Department is now soliciting comment on how to accelerate adoption without having resolved the monitoring architecture that would make acceleration responsible.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎II. ADMINISTRATIVE BURDEN AND THE PHYSICIAN WORKFORCE: WHAT THE DATA ACTUALLY SHOWS⏎⏎The Department asks how AI can reduce administrative burden on clinicians. This is the right question, but looking at the workforce data, the framing tends toward optimism that is not fully warranted. Shanafelt and his co-authors observed across three measurement points between 2011 and 2020 that physician burnout rates have worsened even as successive waves of health information technology were deployed with explicit promises of efficiency gains (Shanafelt, T.D., et al., 2022, Changes in Burnout and Satisfaction With Work-Life Integration in Physicians and the General US Working Population Between 2011 and 2020, Mayo Clinic Proceedings). The electronic health record is the most studied case of this phenomenon. Melnick and his research team found a direct association between perceived EHR usability and professional burnout among U.S. physicians, with low-usability EHR systems functioning as an independent predictor of burnout beyond workload volume alone (Melnick, E.R., et al., 2020, The Association Between Perceived Electronic Health Record Usability and Professional Burnout Among US Physicians, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 95(3), 476–487). Collier documented similar dynamics in the Canadian context, specifically noting that EHR systems designed around billing and compliance requirements rather than clinical workflow imposed cognitive burdens on physicians that were structurally invisible to the administrators and vendors who deployed them (Collier, R., 2017, Electronic health records contributing to physician burnout, CMAJ, 189(45), E1405–E1406). Kroth and co-investigators confirmed this in a large-sample study finding that specific EHR design and use factors — alert fatigue, documentation fragmentation, poor interface design — were independently associated with clinician stress and burnout (Kroth, P.J., et al., 2019, Association of Electronic Health Record Design and Use Factors With Clinician Stress and Burnout, JAMA Network Open, 2(8), e199609).⏎⏎The pattern across these studies is consistent and damning: technology deployed to clinical settings without meaningful clinician input into design and governance reliably generates burden rather than relieving it. The Department should treat this as a predictive model, not merely a historical record. AI systems deployed to clinical settings under the same procurement and governance conditions that produced the EHR burnout crisis will produce a second iteration of that crisis. Bates and his co-authors conducted a systematic review of AI's potential to reduce clinician burnout and found that the evidence of benefit was promising but conditional — conditional, specifically, on implementation quality, on alignment between system design and clinical workflow, and on clinician trust in the systems being deployed (Bates, D.W., et al., 2021). The Department's RFI does not adequately engage with the conditionality. It asks how to accelerate adoption; it does not ask what conditions would make acceleration beneficial rather than detrimental.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎The physician workforce consequences of getting this wrong are not abstract. A physician who retires early because the administrative infrastructure of clinical practice has become intolerable — and this is happening at scale, in Louisiana and everywhere else — is not a statistic. That is a patient who now has no primary care physician, a community that has lost institutional memory, a rural hospital that cannot recruit a replacement. The Department's enthusiasm for AI-mediated efficiency should be calibrated against the demonstrated failure of prior technology deployments to deliver that efficiency, and against the very real possibility that poorly governed AI systems will impose on clinicians precisely the kind of surveillance, documentation, and second-guessing burden that drove the EHR burnout crisis in the first place. Topol identified the genuine promise of AI in medicine — the possibility that machine learning could restore to physicians the cognitive space that administrative systems have extracted from them — but Topol was also explicit that realizing this promise requires design choices and governance structures that the current market does not spontaneously produce (Topol, E.J., 2019, High-performance medicine, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56).⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎III. AUTOMATION BIAS AND THE GOVERNANCE FAILURE THE DEPARTMENT IS INCENTIVIZING⏎⏎There is a second-order problem with accelerating AI adoption in clinical settings that the Department's RFI largely ignores: automation bias. Goddard and her co-investigators conducted a systematic review of automation bias across clinical and non-clinical settings and found that clinicians, like other professionals who work with automated decision-support systems, demonstrate measurable tendencies to accept algorithmic outputs without adequate critical scrutiny, particularly under conditions of time pressure and cognitive load (Goddard, K., et al., 2012, Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 121–127). The conditions of time pressure and cognitive load are, of course, the defining features of contemporary clinical practice. The Department is therefore proposing to accelerate the deployment of AI decision-support tools into precisely the environments where the psychological conditions for automation bias are most reliably present.⏎⏎This is not an argument against AI in clinical care. It is an argument for governance structures that treat automation bias as a predictable and manageable risk rather than an anomaly to be addressed after harm has occurred. The mitigation strategies Goddard and her co-authors identify are not technologically exotic: they include training that makes clinicians aware of automation bias as a cognitive tendency, interface design that does not present algorithmic outputs in ways that discourage scrutiny, and institutional protocols that require periodic independent review of AI-assisted clinical decisions. None of these mitigations are reimbursed under current CMS frameworks. None are required under current FDA post-approval tracking mandates as applied to AI/ML-based diagnostic devices. The Department's RFI asks about reimbursement incentives for AI adoption; it does not ask about reimbursement frameworks for the governance activities that would make AI adoption safe. That is a structural omission that will have clinical consequences.⏎⏎The nursing workforce is implicated here as well, and the Department's RFI treats nursing concerns with insufficient specificity. Arnetz and her research team recorded the relationship between nurse staffing levels, work environment quality, and burnout, finding that structural conditions of the work environment are stronger predictors of burnout than individual-level factors (Arnetz, J.E., et al., 2020, Nurse Burnout: Examining the Influence of Nurse Staffing and Nurse Work Environment, Journal of Nursing Administration, 50(10), 523–529). Dillard-Wright and Shields-Haas raised the ethical dimensions of AI and robotics deployment in nursing contexts specifically, arguing that the nursing profession has been systematically excluded from the design and governance of technologies that will fundamentally reshape nursing work, and that this exclusion is not neutral — it reflects and reinforces a devaluation of nursing expertise that has patient safety consequences (Dillard-Wright, J., & Shields-Haas, V., 2021, Nursing with Robots, Nursing Ethics). The Department should take this argument seriously. AI systems that are designed without nursing input and deployed without nursing governance participation will be optimized for metrics that nurses did not choose and may not endorse, and the resulting misalignment between system outputs and clinical judgment will be borne disproportionately by nurses and their patients.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎IV. ON RESISTANCE TO TECHNOLOGY IMPLEMENTATION: WHAT THE ORGANIZATIONAL LITERATURE SAYS⏎⏎The Department's framing of this RFI implicitly treats clinician skepticism toward AI as an obstacle to be overcome through education, incentive, and regulatory clarity. Lapointe and Rivard's multilevel model of resistance to IT implementation offers a more nuanced and empirically grounded account of why clinicians resist new technologies, and the Department would benefit from engaging with it (Lapointe, L., & Rivard, S., 2005, A Multilevel Model of Resistance to Information Technology Implementation, MIS Quarterly). Lapointe and Rivard distinguish between resistance rooted in perceived threat to existing workflows, resistance rooted in perceived threat to professional identity, and resistance rooted in perceived threat to patient outcomes. These are not the same phenomenon and they do not respond to the same interventions. Clinicians who resist AI-assisted diagnostics because they perceive a threat to their professional judgment are telling the Department something important about the governance conditions under which those systems are being deployed; they are not simply exhibiting irrational technophobia that can be corrected with a webinar.⏎⏎The implications for the Department's reimbursement and regulatory strategy are direct. If the Department creates financial incentives for AI adoption without simultaneously creating governance requirements that give clinicians meaningful authority over procurement, validation, and post-deployment audit, it will generate adoption that is coerced rather than chosen, surface-level rather than integrated, and likely to produce the kind of passive resistance and workaround behavior that Lapointe and Rivard document as the predictable response to top-down technology mandates. The EHR implementation literature is full of examples of this dynamic. The Department does not need to repeat it.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎V. SPECIFIC POLICY RECOMMENDATIONS⏎⏎The preceding analysis supports the following specific policy recommendations, addressed to the Department's questions regarding regulatory action, reimbursement design, and research-and-development priorities:⏎⏎Regarding regulatory action:⏎⏎1. The Department should condition any HHS endorsement of AI/ML-based clinical decision-support tools on demonstrated compliance with ongoing field-performance tracking protocols that are specific to the deployment population, not merely to the training population. The CAP systematic review of 34 FDA-cleared devices found that current post-approval tracking requirements are inconsistently applied; the Department should use its convening authority with FDA to establish binding standards for deployment-context performance monitoring that apply to all AI/ML devices used in CMS-reimbursed clinical settings.⏎⏎2. Any institution receiving HHS funding or CMS reimbursement for AI-assisted clinical services should be required to establish a formal AI governance committee that includes frontline clinical staff — physicians, nurses, and laboratory personnel — as voting members with authority to delay or suspend deployment pending independent validation. The CAP survey finding that fewer than 22% of laboratories had established such frameworks as of 2024 establishes the baseline against which compliance should be measured.⏎⏎3. The Department should direct ASTP/ONC to develop interoperability standards for AI audit logs that allow post-deployment performance data to be extracted, analyzed, and reported independently of the vendors whose systems generated it. Current audit log formats are proprietary and non-standardized in ways that functionally prevent independent oversight.⏎⏎Regarding reimbursement design:⏎⏎o CMS should develop reimbursement codes for AI governance activities — including algorithm validation, bias auditing, and clinician training in automation bias mitigation — that treat these activities as billable clinical quality functions rather than administrative overhead. The current reimbursement architecture rewards AI-assisted diagnostic outputs but does not reward the governance work that makes those outputs trustworthy.⏎⏎o The Department should resist the impulse to create reimbursement incentives for AI adoption that are not conditioned on governance compliance. Unconditioned adoption incentives will accelerate deployment without improving governance, which is precisely the dynamic the CAP survey data documents as the current problem.⏎⏎Regarding research-and-development priorities:⏎⏎o The Department's research agenda should prioritize implementation science studies that examine the relationship between AI governance structures and clinical outcomes, not merely studies that examine AI diagnostic accuracy in controlled settings. The gap between controlled-setting performance and deployment-context performance is the central unresolved problem in clinical AI, and the Department's R&D funding should reflect this.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 7⏎⏎VI. THE WORKFORCE DIMENSION THE DEPARTMENT KEEPS DEFERRING⏎⏎There is something that needs to be said plainly, even in a formal comment submission: the Department has been aware of the physician burnout crisis for at least a decade, has received substantial evidence linking that crisis to the administrative burden imposed by poorly governed health information technology, and has consistently treated workforce wellbeing as a secondary concern relative to technology adoption targets. Shanafelt's longitudinal data spanning 2011 to 2020 documents a workforce in sustained deterioration across a period when federal health IT policy was characterized by aggressive adoption mandates and inadequate attention to implementation quality (Shanafelt, T.D., et al., 2022). The Department did not cause physician burnout, but federal technology policy contributed to the conditions that sustain it, and the Department's current AI acceleration agenda shows insufficient evidence of having learned from that history.⏎⏎The specific mechanism by which administrative burden harms patients is worth stating because it tends to get lost in workforce-framing discussions: a physician who spends 40% of her clinical hours on documentation, prior authorization, and EHR data entry — which is a reasonable estimate based on time-motion studies conducted across multiple specialties — is a physician who has 40% fewer hours for patient contact, clinical reasoning, and the kind of sustained professional attention that produces good diagnostic outcomes. AI systems that reduce this burden, under conditions of adequate governance and genuine clinician control, could restore that professional space. AI systems that add new documentation requirements, new alert streams, new liability-driven second-guessing to the existing burden will extract what remains of it. The Department's reimbursement design will determine which of these outcomes the market produces. The current RFI does not engage with this choice with sufficient seriousness.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 8⏎⏎The pathology context is instructive here because it is concrete. A pathologist reviewing AI-assisted slide analysis in a laboratory that has no governance framework for validating the algorithm, no institutional protocol for flagging performance degradation, and no reimbursement pathway for the time spent on independent verification is not a pathologist who has been helped by AI. That pathologist has been handed liability and responsibility without authority or support. The CAP data shows this is the situation for the majority of pathologists currently encountering AI tools in their laboratories. The Department is proposing to accelerate the deployment of AI into this governance vacuum. That is not a reasonable policy position, and the academic literature on technology implementation, on automation bias, on workforce wellbeing, and on patient safety all point in the same direction: governance must precede or accompany deployment, not follow it at some unspecified future date when the political will to impose requirements on vendors becomes available.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 9⏎⏎VII. A NOTE ON PARTICIPATORY GOVERNANCE AS A PRECONDITION, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT⏎⏎The Department has a tendency, visible across multiple prior technology initiatives, to treat stakeholder engagement as a communication strategy rather than a governance mechanism. Soliciting comment on AI adoption policy is not the same as requiring that frontline clinical workers have structural authority over AI procurement and deployment decisions at the institutional level. The distinction matters enormously. Lapointe and Rivard's analysis of IT implementation resistance demonstrates that participation in design and governance reduces resistance not primarily because it makes workers feel heard but because it produces better-designed systems — systems whose outputs align with the actual clinical workflow rather than with the vendor's model of what clinical workflow looks like from the outside (Lapointe, L., & Rivard, S., 2005). Dillard-Wright and Shields-Haas make a similar argument from a nursing ethics perspective: the exclusion of nurses from AI governance is not merely a morale problem, it is an epistemological problem, because nurses possess clinical knowledge that is not captured in the data sets on which AI systems are trained and that is therefore systematically absent from the outputs those systems produce (Dillard-Wright, J., & Shields-Haas, V., 2021).⏎⏎The Department's response to this RFI should therefore include a mandatory participatory governance requirement: any institution seeking HHS endorsement or CMS reimbursement support for AI-assisted clinical services must demonstrate, through documented governance structures with named roles and voting authorities, that frontline clinical workers — physicians, nurses, laboratory personnel — are represented as substantive participants, not merely consultants, in AI procurement decisions, pre-deployment validation processes, and ongoing post-deployment audit activities. This requirement should not be optional, should not be satisfiable by the creation of advisory committees with no binding authority, and should not be waivable on the basis of institutional size or resource constraints. The governance gap documented by CAP in 2024 is not a small-institution problem; it exists across the laboratory sector regardless of institutional scale.⏎⏎The Department should further require that AI vendors seeking CMS reimbursement for their products disclose, in a standardized and publicly accessible format, the demographic and clinical characteristics of the populations on which their algorithms were trained, the performance metrics observed in deployment contexts disaggregated by patient population, and any known limitations or failure modes identified through continuous post-approval monitoring. Obermeyer and Emanuel's 2016 analysis of population-mismatch risks in clinical AI was not a theoretical concern; it described a predictable and documented failure mode that the current regulatory architecture does not adequately address (Obermeyer, Z., & Emanuel, E.J., 2016). Nine years later, the Department should not still be treating this as an emerging issue.⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science < > HHS AI RFI < > Page 10⏎⏎The practical implementation of these requirements will require coordination between CMS, FDA, and ASTP/ONC that the current departmental structure does not routinely produce. The Department should establish a cross-agency AI clinical governance working group with a specific mandate to develop the interoperability standards, audit log requirements, and reimbursement frameworks described above, with a reporting deadline of no later than eighteen months from the close of this comment period. The working group should include representation from professional societies — including CAP, whose 2024 survey data provides the most granular currently available picture of the governance gap — as well as from frontline clinical worker organizations, patient advocacy groups, and independent health informatics researchers who are not financially affiliated with AI vendors seeking regulatory approval or reimbursement access.⏎⏎The Department's request for information is a reasonable starting point. The Department's current framing of the problem it is trying to solve is not. Accelerating AI adoption in clinical care without resolving the governance deficit is not a strategy for improving patient outcomes; it is a strategy for transferring risk from vendors to clinicians to patients while generating the appearance of federal action. The academic literature on this question is not ambiguous. The workforce data is not ambiguous. The CAP survey findings are not ambiguous. What remains to be seen is whether the Department's response will be commensurate with the evidence it has received, or whether it will produce another round of adoption incentives detached from the governance infrastructure that would make those incentives beneficial rather than harmful.⏎⏎For questions regarding this submission, contact:⏎⏎jscott@cs.washington.edu⏎⏎University of Washington Paul G. SYNTH-0095♔HHS-ONC-2026-0001♔Deborah Martinez♔National Patient Advocate Foundation♔♔♔♔♔National Patient Advocate Foundation⏎Comments on HHS Health Sector AI Request for Information: Accelerating AI Adoption in Clinical Care⏎Office of the Deputy Secretary / ASTP/ONC⏎Docket: HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI⏎Submitted by: Deborah Martinez, Senior Policy Analyst⏎⏎THE THERAPEUTIC RELATIONSHIP AS CLINICAL INSTRUMENT: A CAUTION ON ACCELERATIONIST FRAMING⏎⏎Consider a patient who has been experiencing fatigue, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, and unexplained weight fluctuations for over a year. She arrives at a hepatology clinic in Phoenix in the fall of 2023, frightened and unable to fully articulate what she is feeling. She does not have the vocabulary for her symptoms. What she has is a body that is communicating something she cannot name, and a clinician sitting across from her who is, at that moment, reading not just her chart but her posture, her hesitations, the way she looks at the floor when she mentions her drinking history. That encounter — the quality of attention brought to it, the trust built within its first five minutes — is not a precondition for clinical care. It is, in a meaningful and measurable sense, clinical care itself. The National Patient Advocate Foundation submits these comments with that encounter in mind, and with concern that the framing animating HHS's Request for Information may inadvertently treat that encounter as an inefficiency to be optimized rather than a mechanism to be protected.⏎⏎The Foundation's concern is grounded in data as much as in principle. A 2024 survey conducted by the Global Liver Institute (GLI) across a network of more than 280 hepatology centers and liver disease specialists found that 73% of respondents identified diagnostic delays as the primary driver of late-stage liver disease presentations, with an average of 14 months elapsing between initial symptom onset and confirmed diagnosis. Fewer than 12% of those same facilities had access to AI-assisted diagnostic or risk-stratification tools, with reimbursement uncertainty and unclear regulatory pathways cited as the foremost barriers to adoption. These findings were corroborated at GLI's 2024 National Liver Forum, where clinical and administrative leaders across 38 states reported that the absence of standardized coverage determinations for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools has stalled procurement at the institutional level. The Foundation does not dispute that AI tools, thoughtfully deployed, may help address the diagnostic gap that these numbers document. What the Foundation disputes is the assumption, embedded in the RFI's framing, that acceleration is the appropriate organizing principle for that deployment.⏎⏎National Patient Advocate Foundation < > HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 2⏎⏎The Request for Information, published in the Federal Register at 89 FR [docket reference], HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI, asks specifically about actions HHS can take to "enhance productivity" and "accelerate adoption" of AI in clinical settings. The Foundation wants to be precise here, because this is not a general objection to efficiency. The phrase "enhance productivity," when applied to clinical care, embeds a model of medicine as a production process — inputs processed, outputs generated, throughput optimized. That model is not simply incomplete. It is categorically mismatched to what the clinical encounter actually is and what makes it work. Michael Balint's foundational work, The Doctor, His Patient and the Illness (1957), articulated what experienced clinicians have always understood: that the physician-patient relationship is itself a pharmacologically active ingredient in treatment, not merely a container for biomedical intervention. The decades of evidence that have accumulated since Balint's work make his observation not merely humanistic but empirical. Kelley et al. (2014), in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE, found that the quality of the patient-clinician relationship had a statistically significant effect on health outcomes across a wide range of conditions, with stronger relationships associated with improved adherence, reduced symptom burden, and greater patient self-efficacy (Kelley et al., 2014, 9(4), e94207). Hojat et al. (2011) demonstrated specifically in diabetic populations that physician empathy scores were significantly correlated with HbA1c control and LDL levels, meaning that a physician's capacity for relational attunement had measurable downstream effects on chronic disease management (Hojat et al., 2011, Academic Medicine, 86(3), 359–364). These are not soft findings. They are outcome data. When HHS frames AI adoption in terms of productivity enhancement, it is not simply choosing a convenient bureaucratic shorthand. It is, perhaps without intending to, signaling a model of care in which the relational substrate that generates these outcomes is treated as incidental rather than constitutive.⏎⏎National Patient Advocate Foundation < > HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 3⏎⏎Abraham Verghese, writing in Health Affairs in 2011, described the physical and relational encounter between clinician and patient as an act that has no computational substitute — not because it is sentimental, but because it is informationally dense in ways that resist digitization (Verghese, 2011, Health Affairs, 28(4), 1177–1182). The information carried in a patient's affect, the way a clinician adjusts their clinical reasoning in response to an unexpected detail offered mid-sentence — these are not merely contextual decorations around a diagnostic algorithm. They are the diagnostic algorithm, or at least an irreplaceable component of it. Eric Topol, who is not a technophobe and who has written with genuine optimism about the potential for AI to liberate clinicians from cognitive drudgery, nonetheless argued in his 2019 Nature Medicine analysis that the convergence of human and artificial intelligence should result in "more time for the human relationship," not less — that the proper goal of AI in medicine is to restore relational capacity, not to replace it (Topol, 2019, Nature Medicine, 25(1), 44–56). The Foundation reads the HHS RFI and finds that aspiration largely absent. The emphasis on acceleration, adoption metrics, and productivity gains suggests a policy framework in which AI is being evaluated primarily as a throughput tool, and in which the relational consequences of its intermediation are not yet part of the calculus. That is the gap these comments are intended to address.⏎⏎National Patient Advocate Foundation < > HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 4⏎⏎THE DESKILLING PROBLEM AND THE OVERSEER FALLACY⏎⏎There is a second concern the Foundation wishes to raise, which is related to the first but distinct from it. The RFI and the broader discourse around AI in clinical care frequently invoke what might be called the "overseer model": the clinician remains in the loop, supervising AI outputs, retaining final decision authority. This is offered as a safeguard, and in narrow technical terms it may function as one. But the cognitive science literature on human-automation interaction suggests that the overseer role is not a neutral position. Parasuraman and Manzey (2010), in a systematic analysis published in Human Factors, documented what they termed "automation complacency" — a well-characterized tendency for human operators in supervisory roles to reduce active monitoring effort, accept automated outputs without adequate scrutiny, and exhibit degraded independent judgment over time (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010, Human Factors, 52(3), 381–410). Goddard, Roudsari, and Wyatt (2012) extended this analysis specifically to clinical decision support environments, finding that automation bias — the tendency to favor algorithm-generated recommendations over independent clinical assessment — was present across a wide range of provider types and settings, and that it was not reliably mitigated by training or by explicit instructions to exercise independent judgment (Goddard et al., 2012, Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, 19(1), 121–127). The implication is not that AI-assisted clinical decision support is inherently dangerous. The implication is that deploying AI in a supervisory model, without serious attention to what that model does to clinician cognition over time, is not a conservative or cautious approach. It is an approach whose cognitive side effects are already documented in the literature and are being systematically underweighted in the current policy conversation.⏎⏎The deskilling concern is not hypothetical. Choudhry, Fletcher, and Soumerai (2005), in a systematic review published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, examined the relationship between clinical experience and quality of care, finding a complex relationship in which the atrophy of certain diagnostic and relational competencies over time was associated with measurable declines in care quality in specific domains (Choudhry et al., 2005, Annals of Internal Medicine, 142(4), 260–273). If independent clinical reasoning is a skill that requires active exercise to maintain — and the evidence suggests it is — then a policy environment that systematically repositions clinicians as algorithm supervisors, particularly in high-volume primary and specialty care settings, creates conditions for the gradual erosion of exactly the judgment that patients most need when they present with ambiguous, complex, or emotionally charged situations. The patient in Phoenix with vague hepatic symptoms and a complicated social history is precisely the kind of patient who cannot be well-served by a clinician whose diagnostic reasoning has been progressively outsourced to a risk-stratification model. Her presentation does not fit cleanly into training data distributions. Her reluctance to disclose her alcohol use is not a missing variable — it is a clinical signal that requires a human being skilled in trust-building to elicit. Tversky and Kahneman's foundational work on judgment under uncertainty is relevant here as a cautionary frame: algorithmic confidence does not track algorithmic accuracy, and the conditions under which human judgment outperforms heuristic-based systems are precisely the conditions of ambiguity and context-dependence that characterize the most consequential clinical encounters (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974, Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131).⏎⏎National Patient Advocate Foundation < > HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 5⏎⏎The Foundation also wants to note, with some care, a concern about what AI intermediation does to the experience of being cared for — independent of its effects on diagnostic accuracy. Bickmore and Picard (2005), writing in the ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, examined the conditions under which patients form trust relationships with automated systems, and their findings are instructive for what they do not show as much as for what they do: while patients can form a kind of functional reliance on automated interlocutors, the quality of that reliance is categorically different from the trust formed in longitudinal human relationships, and it does not carry the same therapeutic weight (Bickmore & Picard, 2005, ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 12(2), 293–327). This matters because medicine, as practiced in the chronic disease context that represents the Foundation's primary policy concern — liver disease, in particular — is fundamentally longitudinal. The relationship between a hepatologist and a patient with cirrhosis is built over years. It accumulates shared history, negotiated expectations, and a kind of mutual knowledge that is the actual mechanism by which behavioral change, adherence, and self-management become possible. When AI tools are inserted into that relationship as primary communicative interfaces — for symptom triage, for follow-up, for patient education — the question is not only whether they perform the discrete task adequately. The question is what their presence does to the relational accumulation that makes the entire treatment enterprise work. That question is not currently being asked in the RFI, and the Foundation believes it needs to be.⏎⏎National Patient Advocate Foundation < > HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 6⏎⏎TOWARD A REFRAMING: RELATIONAL SAFETY AS A REGULATORY STANDARD⏎⏎The Foundation is not arguing against AI adoption in clinical care. The GLI data cited above make clear that diagnostic delays are causing real harm to real patients, and that tools capable of reducing those delays deserve serious regulatory and reimbursement support. Dzau, McClellan, and McGinnis (2021), writing in JAMA on vital directions for health system transformation, identified the integration of digital tools and the strengthening of primary care relationships as complementary rather than competing priorities — a framing the Foundation endorses (Dzau et al., 2021, JAMA, 316(17), 1813–1814). The argument here is more specific: HHS should reframe its evaluative criteria for AI adoption to include explicit assessment of relational impact, not only diagnostic performance metrics or throughput measures. Concretely, this means that coverage determinations for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools should require evidence not only that a tool improves sensitivity or specificity on a target condition, but that its deployment model has been evaluated for effects on patient-clinician communication quality, patient trust, and clinician independent reasoning capacity. It means that the regulatory pathway for these tools should include post-market surveillance requirements that capture relational outcomes alongside clinical outcomes. And it means that the language HHS uses to describe its goals — language that currently centers productivity and acceleration — should be revised to center demonstrated safety for the full clinical encounter, not just for the discrete diagnostic task.⏎⏎The Foundation recognizes that relational outcomes are harder to measure than throughput metrics, and that this creates a genuine methodological challenge. But the difficulty of measurement is not an argument for ignoring what is being measured. The evidence that the patient-clinician relationship has measurable outcome effects is substantial and has been accumulating for decades. A regulatory framework that treats that evidence as too soft to operationalize is not being rigorous. It is being selectively rigorous in a way that systematically advantages quantifiable process metrics over the relational substrate that gives those processes their clinical meaning. HHS has an opportunity, in the policies it develops in response to this RFI, to set a different standard — one that takes seriously the full body of evidence about what makes clinical care work, and that holds AI adoption accountable to that evidence rather than to a narrower productivity model. The Foundation urges the Department to consider, specifically, whether the reimbursement framework being developed for AI-enabled clinical decision support tools includes any mechanism for evaluating patient-reported experience of the clinical encounter, and whether the research priorities identified in this RFI include funding for studies examining the longitudinal relational effects of AI intermediation in chronic disease management. Those are not peripheral questions. They are⏎⏎National Patient Advocate Foundation < > HHS-ONC-2024-AI-RFI < > Page 6 [cont.]⏎⏎the questions that determine whether the AI adoption HHS is working to accelerate ultimately serves patients or merely serves the systems that care for them.⏎⏎For additional information regarding these comments, please contact the National Patient Advocate Foundation's Policy Division at policy@npaf.org.⏎⏎REFERENCES⏎⏎Balint, M. The coalition does not oppose AI in healthcare. There are genuinely promising clinical applications — imaging interpretation tools, sepsis prediction models, medication reconciliation support — that deserve the kind of deliberate policy scaffolding HHS is asking about. But the RFI, in its current form, proceeds as though the most consequential deployed application of AI in American healthcare today does not exist. That application is AI-driven prior authorization denial automation, and it is already operating at scale, already harming patients, and already generating the kind of opaque, effectively unappealable coverage denials that are ending and shortening lives. The Department's silence on this question in a 50-plus-page RFI document is not an oversight. It is a policy choice, and this coalition is submitting this comment to put on the record exactly what that choice means for elderly, disabled, and low-income patients in Louisiana and across the country.⏎⏎AUA Louisiana Patient Advocacy Coalition Comments | HHS AI Clinical RFI | Page 2⏎⏎THE DOCUMENTED REALITY OF AI DENIAL AUTOMATION⏎⏎The evidentiary record on AI-driven prior authorization denials is substantial, specific, and largely uncontested. The U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations released its report "Denial, Delay, Deny: How Medicare Advantage Plans Use Algorithms to Override Physician Judgment" in November 2023, documenting that at least three major Medicare Advantage insurers — UnitedHealthcare, Humana, and CVS/Aetna — deployed algorithmic systems that generated prior authorization denials at rates dramatically exceeding the denial rates produced by human clinical review. The Subcommittee found that UnitedHealthcare's nH Predict tool, used to determine post-acute care coverage, produced denial rates of up to 22% for claims that were subsequently overturned on appeal, meaning the algorithm was denying medically necessary care at a scale that dwarfed what any reasonable clinical review process would have produced. The Subcommittee's findings are worth reading in their original form, because the scale of the problem does not fully register in summary. These are not edge cases. These are systematic patterns of denial generated by systems trained on cost-containment objectives and deployed against Medicare beneficiaries who, by definition, are among the most medically vulnerable people in the country.⏎⏎The ProPublica and Capitol Forum investigation published in March 2023 documented how Cigna's PXDX automated review system allowed physicians employed by Cigna to reject claims without reading individual patient files, with one physician reportedly rejecting over 300 claims in a single day. The investigation found that Cigna's internal communications explicitly framed the system as a cost-containment mechanism rather than a clinical appropriateness tool. This is the distinction that the RFI entirely fails to address: AI systems deployed by insurers to manage prior authorization are not designed to determine whether care is clinically appropriate. They are designed to reduce costs, and the clinical appropriateness rationale is the post-hoc justification attached to denials that are generated by algorithms optimized for a different objective entirely.⏎⏎The April 2022 OIG report — "Some Medicare Advantage Organization Denials of Prior Authorization Requests Raise Concerns About Beneficiary Access to Medically Necessary Care," OIG Report OEI-09-18-00260 — found that Medicare Advantage organizations denied prior authorization requests that met Medicare coverage rules at a rate that, if applied across all Medicare Advantage enrollees, would translate to hundreds of thousands of improper denials annually. The OIG specifically noted that the denials it examined would likely have been approved under traditional Medicare, meaning the managed care structure combined with algorithmic review is producing a systematically worse coverage outcome than the baseline program would generate. That finding is now more than two years old, and deployment of the underlying algorithmic tools has accelerated, not slowed, in the intervening period.⏎⏎The Kaiser Family Foundation issue brief published in January 2024, authored by Koma, Cubanski, and Neuman, documents that prior authorization use in Medicare Advantage plans increased by 10% between 2021 and 2022 alone, and that beneficiaries who receive denials face appeal processes so burdensome that the vast majority do not pursue them. The KFF analysis found that fewer than 10% of denied prior authorization requests are ever appealed, and of those that are, roughly 75% are ultimately approved — meaning the denial itself, not the underlying clinical question, was the barrier. When an algorithm generates a denial that is wrong three-quarters of the time when actually reviewed, but the structural burden of appeal deters 90% of beneficiaries from ever reaching that review, the algorithm is not functioning as a clinical tool. It is functioning as a deterrence mechanism.⏎⏎AUA Louisiana Patient Advocacy Coalition Comments | HHS AI Clinical RFI | Page 3⏎⏎THE POPULATION BEARING THE COST⏎⏎This coalition's membership includes patient advocates, social workers, and community health workers operating in parishes across Louisiana where Medicaid enrollment rates exceed 35% of the adult population and where Medicare Advantage penetration has reached 60% or higher in several metro and rural markets. The patients these advocates work with are not well-positioned to navigate multi-step prior authorization appeal processes. Many are elderly, many have significant cognitive or physical impairments, many lack reliable internet access or the literacy to parse denial letters written in insurance-industry prose. The Louisiana Department of Insurance's Annual Report on Health Insurance Claims Denial Rates and Consumer Appeals Outcomes for 2022-2023, published by the LDI Market Conduct Division in March 2024, documents that Louisiana residents filed appeals on fewer than 8% of denied prior authorization requests across all commercial and Medicaid managed care lines, and that the average time from initial denial to final appeal resolution exceeded 47 days — a period during which the denied care either goes unprovided or is provided out-of-pocket at costs that are, for the patient populations described above, essentially prohibitive.⏎⏎The National Health Law Program's August 2023 policy brief, "Automated Injustice: How AI Prior Authorization Tools Undermine Medicaid Beneficiary Rights," documents that Medicaid managed care organizations have adopted AI-driven prior authorization tools at a pace that has outrun existing state oversight frameworks, and that Medicaid beneficiaries — who are disproportionately low-income, disabled, and from communities of color — face the highest denial rates and the lowest appeal rates. The NHeLP brief identifies a structural problem that this coalition has observed directly in Louisiana: when a Medicaid managed care organization deploys an algorithmic denial tool, the denial letter that reaches the beneficiary contains no meaningful explanation of why the algorithm denied the claim, no identification of the algorithm as the decision-making mechanism, and no practical guidance on what evidence would be needed to reverse the denial on appeal. The beneficiary receives a form letter. The algorithm is invisible.⏎⏎This is not a hypothetical concern about future AI deployment. This is the current state of AI in healthcare, operating right now, in Louisiana, against the patients this coalition represents. The AMA's 2023 Prior Authorization Physician Survey, published in December 2023, found that 94% of physicians reported that prior authorization delays patient care, and that 33% reported a serious adverse event — including hospitalization and permanent impairment — resulting from a prior authorization denial or delay. Physicians in Louisiana who work with this coalition's member organizations describe prior authorization burdens that consume 15 to 20 hours of administrative time per physician per week, time diverted from clinical care. And increasingly, the denials generating that administrative burden are being produced by algorithmic systems rather than by human reviewers, meaning the physician's appeal is not going to a clinician who can be persuaded by clinical evidence but to a process that begins with an algorithm's output and works backward.⏎⏎AUA Louisiana Patient Advocacy Coalition Comments | HHS AI Clinical RFI | Page 4⏎⏎THE STRUCTURAL PROBLEM WITH THE RFI FRAMING⏎⏎The RFI asks, among other questions, what regulatory or reimbursement actions HHS can take to accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. The coalition is addressing that question directly, and the answer is: before HHS takes any action to accelerate AI adoption, the Department must close the accountability gap that currently allows AI systems deployed by insurers against patients to operate without the transparency, clinical validation, or oversight requirements that would apply to AI systems deployed by providers for patients.⏎⏎The legal framework analysis in Fuse Brown and McCuskey's 2024 article in the Yale Journal on Regulation, "Algorithmic Accountability in Health Insurance: Legal Frameworks for AI-Driven Coverage Denials," Vol. 41, No. 1, pp. 88-147, identifies the core regulatory gap with precision: existing federal law — including the utilization management standards codified at 42 C.F.R. Part 422 and the prior authorization requirements addressed in CMS's Contract Year 2024 rulemaking at 88 Fed. Reg. 22120 (April 12, 2023) — does not require insurers to disclose whether algorithmic tools are being used in prior authorization decisions, does not require validation of those tools against clinical appropriateness standards, and does not impose any minimum threshold for human clinical review of algorithm-generated denials. The CY2024 rule at 88 Fed. Reg. 22120 included provisions requiring Medicare Advantage plans to ensure that prior authorization criteria are based on clinical criteria, but it did not define what validation of AI tools against clinical criteria requires, did not mandate disclosure of algorithmic decision-making to beneficiaries, and did not establish any audit mechanism for denial rates generated by specific algorithmic tools. The gap between the rule's aspiration and its operational requirements is, in the coalition's assessment, the space in which harm is currently occurring.⏎⏎Schulman and Richman's February 2024 Health Affairs article, "Algorithmic Gatekeeping: AI-Driven Prior Authorization and the Erosion of Clinical Autonomy," Vol. 43, No. 2, pp. 201-209, makes the point that the clinical autonomy problem created by AI denial tools is not simply about individual physician-patient relationships. It is about the systematic displacement of evidence-based clinical judgment by cost-optimization algorithms at a population scale that no previous generation of utilization management tools could achieve. A human utilization management reviewer, however biased or inadequately trained, operates at a speed that limits the scope of harm. An algorithm can generate ten thousand denials in the time it takes a human reviewer to read a single chart. The scale differential is the policy problem, and the RFI's failure to address it while soliciting comment on how to further accelerate AI deployment suggests that HHS has not fully grappled with what acceleration means in this context.⏎⏎The Commonwealth Fund's September 2023 report by Palanker, Volk, and Lucia, "State Oversight of Health Insurer Prior Authorization Practices: Gaps and Opportunities," documents that state-level oversight of prior authorization practices — even where statutory frameworks exist — has been systematically outpaced by the speed of algorithmic deployment. Louisiana has a prior authorization reform statute, but the LDI's own 2022-2023 Annual Report acknowledges that the Department lacks the technical capacity to audit the AI tools being used by managed care organizations operating in the state. If state regulators with direct market conduct authority cannot audit these tools, the case for federal baseline requirements is, in this coalition's view, essentially self-evident.⏎⏎AUA Louisiana Patient Advocacy Coalition Comments | HHS AI Clinical RFI | Page 5⏎⏎WHAT HHS MUST REQUIRE BEFORE ANY FURTHER DEPLOYMENT IS INCENTIVIZED⏎⏎The coalition is not asking HHS to halt all AI development in healthcare. The coalition is asking HHS to answer a question the RFI does not ask: what obligations attach to the deployment of AI systems in coverage decision contexts before federal reimbursement policy or regulatory frameworks provide any form of endorsement or legitimacy to those systems? The coalition's specific recommendations on this question are as follows:⏎⏎1. Clinical Appropriateness Validation Requirements. Before any AI-assisted prior authorization or utilization management tool is used in a federally funded health program — including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, and ACA marketplace plans — the tool must be validated against independent clinical appropriateness standards by a body that is not the insurer deploying the tool. Validation must demonstrate that the tool's denial rates are not statistically distinguishable from denial rates produced by qualified human clinical reviewers applying the same clinical criteria. The validation methodology must be published and subject to public comment. The CY2024 rule at 88 Fed. Reg. 22120 gestures toward this requirement but does not operationalize it. HHS must operationalize it.⏎⏎2. Mandatory Human Review Thresholds. Any AI-generated denial of a prior authorization request must be reviewed by a licensed clinician with relevant specialty training before the denial is communicated to the beneficiary or the treating provider. This is not a novel requirement — it reflects the basic principle that coverage decisions with clinical consequences require clinical judgment. The ProPublica/Capitol Forum investigation documented Cigna physicians approving algorithmic denials in bulk without individual chart review, which is precisely the practice this requirement would prohibit. HHS should codify this requirement explicitly in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care regulations, and should define "review" to require documentation of the clinical basis for the denial in terms sufficient to allow a treating physician to understand and respond to it.⏎⏎3. Transparent Denial Rate Reporting Disaggregated by Demographics and Tool. CMS should require Medicare Advantage organizations and Medicaid managed care organizations to report, on a quarterly basis and in a publicly accessible format, the prior authorization denial rates generated by each algorithmic tool they deploy, disaggregated by beneficiary age, disability status, race, ethnicity, and diagnostic category. Without this data, neither regulators nor researchers nor patient advocates can identify patterns of disparate impact. The OIG's April 2022 report identified the denial problem at an aggregate level; disaggregated, tool-specific reporting would allow the identification of specific algorithms that are producing discriminatory outcomes.⏎⏎o Reporting should include the total number of prior authorization requests reviewed by algorithmic tools versus human reviewers.⏎⏎o Reporting should include the denial rate for each tool, the appeal rate for algorithm-generated denials, and the overturn rate on appeal.⏎⏎o Reporting should be structured to allow year-over-year comparison and should be submitted in a machine-readable format to facilitate independent analysis.⏎⏎4. Robust Appeals Rights with Algorithmic Transparency. When a prior authorization request is denied by an AI-assisted process, the denial letter must disclose that an algorithmic tool was used in the decision, identify the tool by name and version, and provide the specific criteria the algorithm applied in generating the denial. The beneficiary must receive, simultaneously with the denial notice, a plain-language explanation of the appeal process with realistic time estimates and a list of the specific evidence that would be relevant to an appeal. The KFF January 2024 brief documents that the current appeal rate for prior authorization denials is below 10%, and the coalition's assessment is that this rate reflects structural barriers to appeal, not beneficiary satisfaction with denial outcomes. Disclosure and transparency requirements will not eliminate those barriers, but they are a necessary precondition for any appeal process to function.⏎⏎5. Prohibition on Cost-Optimization Training Objectives. HHS should require, as a condition of federal program participation, that any AI tool used in prior authorization or utilization management be trained exclusively on clinical appropriateness criteria and not on cost-containment or utilization-reduction objectives. This requirement is difficult to enforce without access to training data and model documentation, which is itself an argument for requiring insurers to submit algorithmic tool documentation to CMS as part of the Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care contracting process. The Schulman and Richman Health Affairs analysis at Vol. 43, No. 2 identifies the training objective problem as the root cause of the clinical autonomy erosion they document; the regulatory response must address the root cause, not merely its symptoms.⏎⏎AUA Louisiana Patient Advocacy Coalition Comments | HHS AI Clinical RFI | Page 6⏎⏎THE ACCELERATION QUESTION, RECONSIDERED⏎⏎The RFI asks how HHS can accelerate AI adoption in clinical care. The coalition's answer is that HHS cannot responsibly accelerate AI adoption in clinical care without simultaneously establishing the accountability infrastructure that ensures AI adoption benefits patients rather than operating against them. The RBMA survey data cited in the background materials for this comment period documents that 68% of radiology practices have deployed or are piloting AI imaging tools, but that 74% of those practices identify inconsistent payer coverage policies as the primary barrier to scaling. That finding is directly relevant to the denial automation problem: the same payers whose inconsistent coverage policies are slowing beneficial clinical AI adoption are deploying their own AI tools in prior authorization processes without the transparency or accountability requirements that would apply to provider-deployed clinical AI. HHS is being asked to solve a coverage policy problem for providers while the coverage policy problem for patients — generated by the exact same payers — goes unaddressed.⏎⏎There is something genuinely frustrating about an RFI that asks detailed questions about how to support AI-assisted imaging interpretation while containing no questions whatsoever about the AI systems that are denying coverage for the imaging those tools would interpret. The coalition understands that HHS has multiple policy workstreams and that the RFI is specifically scoped to clinical AI. But the scope choice is itself a policy choice, and the coalition is asking the Department to reconsider whether "clinical care AI" and "insurance operations AI" can be meaningfully separated when the same patients are subject to both, and when the outcome of an insurance AI denial decision determines whether the clinical AI tool ever gets used at all.⏎⏎The legal accountability framework analysis in Fuse Brown and McCuskey's Yale Journal on Regulation article at Vol. 41, No. 1, pp. 88-147, identifies the existing legal hooks for federal action on AI denial automation — including the utilization management standards at 42 C.F.R. Part 422, the Medicaid managed care regulations at 42 C.F.R. Part 438, and the ACA's prohibition on arbitrary coverage denials — and concludes that HHS has substantial existing statutory authority to impose the accountability requirements described above without waiting for Congressional action. The coalition agrees with that assessment. The question is not whether HHS has the authority. The question is whether HHS will use it.⏎⏎AUA Louisiana Patient Advocacy Coalition Comments | HHS AI Clinical RFI | Page 7⏎⏎The coalition acknowledges that the regulatory asks above are significant and that implementation would require substantial CMS rulemaking work. The coalition also acknowledges that reasonable people can disagree about the precise design of validation requirements, reporting frameworks, and human review thresholds. These are genuinely complex technical and policy questions, and this coalition does not claim to have resolved all of them in this comment. What this coalition is not willing to accept is the argument that the complexity of the regulatory design justifies continued inaction while AI denial systems operate without accountability at a scale that the November 2023 Senate Subcommittee report documented and that the OIG documented before it.⏎⏎The patients this coalition represents in Baton Rouge, in Shreveport, in rural parishes along the Mississippi Delta — these are not abstractions in a policy debate. They are people receiving denial letters generated by algorithms they have never heard of, for care their physicians prescribed, with no meaningful information about why the denial was issued or how to challenge it. The 47-day average appeal resolution time documented in the Louisiana Department of Insurance's 2022-2023 Annual Report is not a regulatory statistic. It is 47 days during which someone is not receiving care their doctor ordered.⏎⏎HHS is asking what it can do to accelerate AI in clinical care. Before this coalition can support any acceleration agenda, it needs the Department to answer a prior question: what accountability requirements will attach to AI systems that are already deployed, at scale, against patients, in coverage decision contexts? The answer to that question should appear in any rulemaking or guidance that follows from this RFI. If it does not, the Department will have used a clinical care RFI to build a policy framework that benefits providers and payers while leaving the patients most harmed by existing AI deployments exactly where they are now — holding a denial letter with no practical recourse and no clear path to the care they need.⏎⏎The coalition requests that HHS specifically address, in any subsequent rulemaking or guidance, the five accountability requirements described above, and that the Department commit to a rulemaking timeline for AI-assisted prior authorization oversight that is no longer than 18 months from the close of this comment period. The RBMA data on imaging AI adoption suggests that clinical AI deployment is moving faster than regulatory frameworks can track. The Senate Subcommittee data on algorithmic denial automation suggests the same is true on the insurer side. The difference is that the clinical AI gap produces delayed benefits. The denial automation gap produces active harm, right now, at scale, in every state including Louisiana.⏎⏎The coalition also requests that HHS's follow-on activities from this RFI include a specific public comment opportunity on AI in insurance coverage decision processes, separate from the clinical care framing of this RFI, so that the patient advocacy community, consumer organizations, and state insurance regulators have a formal venue to address the accountability questions that this RFI's scope has foreclosed. The Commonwealth Fund's September 2023 Palanker, Volk, and Lucia report documents that state-level oversight frameworks are inadequate to the current deployment environment; federal baseline standards require a federal public comment process in which the right questions are asked.⏎⏎The coalition is available to provide additional information, testimony, or technical assistance to HHS staff working on the policy questions raised in this comment.
